RETAIL SHOP TALK CLASSICS FROM RHINO-With the heavy resurgence of interest in mu- sic from rock's early days, especially from the 1960s, California based RHI- NO RECORDS, have not only provid- ed rare and previously out -of -print faves such as the Nuggets Series and most of the Monkees catalog, they place a special emphasis on sound quality which is sometimes lacking with some re -issues. "We go through extreme steps to make sure we get the best qual- ity tapes to use for our re -issues," ex- plains Bill Inglot, technical director for Rhino. "We go back to the earliest generation tape available." Their latest collection, the GOLDEN ARCHIVE SERIES, features eight compilation LPs which have been totally remas- tered. The series includes The Beau Brummels, The Spencer Davis Group (featuring Stevie Winwood), The Everly Brothers, The Bobby Fuller Four, Love, The Standells, The Turtles and Ritchie Valens. "Portions of these records had been is- sued before on Rhino. In the interim, Rhino has taken steps to improve the quality of its product line," says Inglot. He emphasized that while it has been a standard practice for all labels who re- leased re -issues to cut new discs from tapes made from a master or "mother" disc, Rhino has been actively seeking out original tapes to master their discs with. "They're all mastered from first generation tape sources, not from copies. When you do that, there is a substantial improvement in sound quali- ty because every time you have to go a tape generation, you have generation loss and degradation." When mixing from the tapes, Inglot says that while several adjustments are made, the origi- nal aesthetics and feel are not only left intact, but they are enhanced. Among the improvements are "level compensa- tion, if one track isn't as loud as anoth- er, or it they're lacking in bass or top end frequency or if the vocals are bur- ied. The only thing that's changed is that there is substantially more informa- tion on the disc simply because there were certain sub -frequencies and levels that you could not cut to a disc in the `50s. Frequency response is now im- proved. There's more sound there." VIDEO NEWS - Paramount Home Video announced record -breaking combined sales of 3.2 million units for its "Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom"(over 1.3 million) and "20 Great Video Gifts Under $20" holi- day promotion. According to Timm Clott, senior vice president and gener- al manager of Paramount Home Video, "We're delighted that our distributors and retailers have responded so over- whelmingly to this campaign. But even more significant is consumers unprece- dented enthusiasm for purchasing these titles. We've never before seem such tremendous consumer demand, nor have retailers ever taken so many pro - orders from their customers as they have for these movies." This is not sur- prising considering that some of the ti- tles in that under $20 promotion are Beverly Hills Cop, Raiders of the Lost Ark, Witness, Death Wish, all three Star Trek feature films, Trad- ing Places and Chinatown among others. Paramount released details of the promotion to its distributor network last August 14. The order cut-off date was October 8, with shipments sched- uled to commence October 29. All spe- cial pricing on the "20 for $20" titles remains if effect through January 31. On that date, "Temple of Doom" will be pulled from the market and they will cease accpeting distributor orders. Many retailers had already predicted in- creased sell -through on videocassettes when prices started dropping. VIDEO NEWS AUDIO/VIDEO PRINT MEETS VIDEO-Lion- heart Television is syndicating some- thing unusual to the television market, .something we all need a whole lot more of - more talking heads! But seriously folks, the new offering is called Video Ink, and it features some of the nation's top columnists, holding forth on their latest topic (from politics to sports) for 60 to 90 seconds. Twelve such "col- umns" are included in each Video Ink package, which are produced by public affairs and communications company Media Group, and satellite -fed for availability to TV stations. The idea is to insert the columnist's segments into locally originated programming, such as talk shows or public affairs pro- grams, and believe me, the line-up of writers is impressive: Tom Wicker of The New York Times; Mark Shields of The Washington Post, Pete Hamill of the Village Voice; Mike Barnacle of The Boston Globe; Robert Novak of News America Service & McLaugh- lin Group; Jack Germond of The Bal- timore Sun and "McLaughlin Report"; Charlie Peters of Washington Month- ly; Washington Post sports columnist Tome Boswell and independents Judy Bachrach and Diana McLellan. MTV COMES TO TOWN-When MTV comes to town to screen their newest videos, L.A. video writers get clued -in as to the latest happenings on the channel (which many of them have precious little time to watch). Good food, drink and enlightening schmooze are also had. MTV's most recent L.A. screening, held at one of S.I.R.'s Holly- wood locations, featured new clips from the Pretenders, Eurythmics, Po- lice, Wang Chung, Rod Stewart, Howard Jones, "Weird Al"Yanko- vic, Communards, Rob Jungklas and Robbie Nevil. Most notable of these was probably the Jones clip, You Know I Love You, Don't You?, directed by Wayne Isham, in which Isham makes exciting use of color xerography and animation. Newcomer Robbie Nevil is well -directed by Peter Care in his Manhattan Records debut video, C'est La Vie, a clip which features some of the most intelligently photographed women of any video in recent memory. The Pretenders' new one, Don't Get Me Wrong, is kinda' cute. Seems Chrissie Hynde is heavy into the old Avengers series, so she tagged Stuart Orme to build a video around it. Also seen at the MTV screening were selections from the 800 -odd clips the channel has re- ceived in its "MTV/Madonna: Make My Video" contest for Madonna's "True Blue" single (she's not doing a video of her own), which were surpris- ingly high in quality, for the most MTV NIGHTMARE-Oa Halloween night, MTV features Alice Cooper in a live performance from Detroit. part, if a wee bit comical. The winner, as voted by viewers, has not yet been picked as we go to press, but he or she stands to win $25,000 and the chance to have his or her video go into rotation on MTV (each of the ten finalists was shown on the channel just pryor to the voting last Thursday). HOME VIDEO REVIEW OMD- Crush: The Movie - Sony Video Software - $29.95 This 70 -min. docu- mentary on the recording and video - making enterprises of one of Britain's top recording acts gives viewers some first-hand insights into just how boring those enterprises can be for those be- hind -the -scenes. Die-hard OMD fans may thrill to sequences where the band sits around on video sets discussing nothing in particular, but others may not. Still, Crush: The Movie does boast an interesting segment or two, such as news footage from a bloody Greens- boro, NC Ku Klux Klan riot which served as Andy McCluskey's inspiration for the tune "88 Minutes In Greens- boro." The tape also includes four OMD videos in their entirety: So In Love, Hold Ibu, Secret and La Femme Accident, as well as bits from their pro- duction in progress. Gregory Dobrin NEW FACES TO WATCH When the smash dance and pop sin- gle “Rumors,” by the Timex Social Club topped the charts and sold over one million copies, making it one of the most successful independently released records in recent years, Jay King, who produced the cut, was probably not sur- prised. King knew the song had potential and after shopping the song around to several radio stations, he stood by it re- leasing it on his own label, Jay Records, waiting for something to happen. “I sold all my furniture. I was eating pea- nut butter sandwiches waiting for this to break,” says King. “My mother brought me groceries, it got so bad, but we always said this record would be number one.” King parted ways with Timex Social Club when the band signed a contract with someone else. “We shook hands and they said ‘Jay you got a deal’ and the next day they went and signed another contract for $7,500. not a piece, but as a group. They signed over 100% of publishing and copyrights.” King says he didn’t have the money to give them a contract early on, but assured them that they owned the record, not he, until he could offer them a contract. “When they look at their contract and where they’re at, it should be obvious who the crook is.” In the final analysis, King chalks the split up to their “distrust.” “We were work- ing on a handshake,” he says regretful- ly. “I’m sad about it. They end up losing and they’re good guys.” He, along with Denzil Foster and Thomas McElroy, had heard a demo tape and knew there was something there. “They (Timex Social Club) had wrote the song,” King explains during an interview with Cash Box,“we re- wrote the songs and we re-recorded the song. We added to the song and we played the song.” In essence, the mem- bers of King’s new band, Club Nou- veau, had actually been responsible for the Timex Social Club’s musical and production direction. “They had one vocalist, one guy who wrote the lyrics and one guy who tried to play the key- boards and he was no better than I am and I’m not a keyboardist by any stan- dards,” King says. “These guys are the music," he says pointing to Denzil Fos- ter and Thomas McElroy who handle vocals, keyboards and drum program- ming along with King in Club Nouveau. “We sit down together and we write, but they actually produce together. When I do write and I play, they come back and replay it. They play better than I do. Musically... this is Timex So- cial Club.” Jay King is both soft spoken and in- tense about music. He is a multi-faceted individual: concert promoter, dancer, singer, musician and businessman. Al- though he is very much the guiding force behind Club Nouveau, the band, which includes vocalists Valerie Watson and Sameulle Prater, is very much a cooperative enterprise. “We don’t al- ways agree. We argue just like every- body else, but we’re all entwined, ” says King. “I’m not as good a producer with Club Nouveau out Denny and Thomas. My songs a not as good if they’re not involved a the vocals are not there without Val a|w Samuel. When I give them my son..: it’s not mine. They add so much. I’m fans of them. Val is a greater voca than she even knows and it well be e dent to people when they hear album.” Denzil Foster and Thomas McEl are what King calls studio “rats.” K doesn’t like being in the studio as mi as they do. Foster and McElroy learr how to “produce” with a four-track r chine. “We didn’t know we were p ducing,” says McElroy. “Ther!' different definitions.” McElroy, a cla caily trained pianist was playing in li jazz bands when Foster, a synthesis dance music fan recruited h and “You have to simplify somewhat,” s; McElroy, “It’s a totally different fee Foster gleaned a lot of his product) skills watching and learning in sch:l and at recording studios. “I’ve alw, wanted to make music you could dai and listen to,” says Foster. ===== PAGE 14 ===== [stanley\s+jordan|bobby\s+mcferrin|magic\s+touch|spontaneous\s+inventions]
Terrence Blanchard (r) and Donald Harrison (c) share a laugh with Dizzy Gillespie. BLANCHARD AND HARRI- SON— “The more you learn, the bet- ter you become as a musician,” says Donald Harrison “To play the mu- sic, you need so much knowledge that you have to get it from everywhere you can get it. And that’s what I think we’re trying to do. Terence has a lot of knowl- edge, so 1 feel I can draw from that. We start on the same wavelength — emo- tionally, mentally. A lot of the things he plays I understand, and a lot of the things I play he understands. On ‘Na- scence’ we’re just playing together.” For a pair of young guys — Donald’s 26, Terence is 24 — Donald Harrison and Terence Blanchard have been playing together for quite awhile: they first met some ten years ago in their native New Orleans. “Donald doesn’t remember this,” says Terence, “and I don’t know how he got there, but I was working some- where with this band that will remain unnamed, in a part of New Orleans that’s not known, in a bar that wasn’t known for jazz. And we were working in the back — they had a little room in the back — and in comes Donald. I was in ninth or tenth grade and he was going to Southern University at the time. And Donald kept saying, ‘Yeah, man, we’re going to play together, man.’” Flash ahead a few years. Donald and his alto saxophone are ensconced at the Berklee School of Music, in Boston. Ter- ence and his trumpet are holed up at Rutgers, in New Jersey. Saxophonist Paul Jeffrey, at that time a Rutgers professor, hears Donald in Boston and invites him to participate in a “talent deserving wider recognition” concert at Rutgers. Voila! “And Terence and 1, at the end of the concert, played together with the rhythm section,” says Donald, “and Paul Jeffrey said, ‘Man, you have to stay together.’ And from that point, in- stead of going back to Berklee, I spent more time at Rutgers and we spent more time hanging out and playing. That was the winter of ’81. And when Wynton and Branford left Art Bla- key, in ’82, we just got into Art Bla- key’s band.” Teams — genuine teams — are rare in jazz. Terence Blanchard and Donald Harrison — after four years with Bla- : key’s Messengers (they left the band i this summer), and three co-led LPs (two Concord, “Nascence,” the new one, for Columbia) — are a genuine team. Terence is the romantic of the pair, Donald is the firebrand, and what one hears in their music is the sound of two men growing. Using the hard bop idiom as a springboard, Terence and Donald are not content to just rattle the rafters — they are intent on expanding their music. One who has followed their careers can hear the palpable growth in each man’s playing; and going to hear them live is to hear two young men grappling and experimenting — two young men staring jazz in the face. One frequent criticism of the new young players — particularly the Blakey alumni — is that they are too conserva- tive, that they are not pushing the mu- sic forward. In fact, say some, jazz hasn’t moved one step forward since John Coltrane was laid to rest some 20 years ago. “They want us to be instant masters of the jazz vocabulary,” says Donald Harrison. “But the thing people have to under- stand,” says Terence Blanchard, “ is that John Coltrane, in his early days, had to develop. When Coltrane first started playing people didn’t pay atten- tion to him, because Sonny Rollins was on the scene. When Miles was with Bird, people thought he couldn’t even blow his nose. I think a lot of that has to do with the fact that we’re living in an instant society — we have instant foods, instant everything. They want us to just turn out everything in an instant, in one second. But it’s a life experience. We might be playing some different shit by the time we’re 30 or 40; we might be way out — wearing rubber suits with roses in our hair.” “I mean, we’re still trying to be our- selves,” says Donald, “we’re still trying to learn the art form as well as be our- selves. I don’t think in terms of innova- tion. I think in terms of playing the music and taking things from your life- time and making them pertinent to your music. ’Cause I think that’s what all the great musicians did — they took every- thing in music, they learned as much music as possible, and then took their life experience and just played it. And that’s innovation — if you’re playing youself, then you’ll be an innovator. So that’s what I try to do. If we can do that enough and get to the point where we’re masters of the art form, and can really get that together, then I think we’ll be innovators.” Their path there — or their path to an ultimate cul-de-sac — is going to be well worth watching. “Nascence” means a birth, and it seems that Terence Blan- chard and Donald Harrison (as they were billed on their first two albums) or Donald Harrison and Terence Blan- chard (as they’re billed on “Nascence”) are two men — or one team — on their way somewhere. “You have to keep searching,” says Terence. “You just can’t sit still and ex- pect some shit to drop out of the sky.” Lee Jeske CASH BOX JAZZ ALBUMS Title, Artist, Label, Number, Distributor = Available on Compact Disc = Platinum (R1AA Certified) = Gold (RIAA Certified) TUTU MILES DAVIS (Warner Bros. 9 25490-1) J MOOD WYNTON MARSALIS (Columbia FC 40308) DOWN TO THE MOON Andreas Vollenweider (CBS Masterworks FM42255) DOUBLE VISION BOB JAMES/DAVID SANBORN (Warner Bros. 25393) LIFE STORIES EARL KLUGH (Warner Bros. 25478) WHILE THE CITY SLEEPS GEORGE BENSON (Warner Bros. 25475-1) BREAKOUT SPYRO GYRA(MCA 5753) DUTONES KENNY G.(Arista AL8 8427) 9 JOYRIDE PIECES OF A DREAM (Manhattan ST53023) IBI EARTHRUN LEE R1TENOUR (GRP-A-1021) 11 LOVE WILL FOLLOW GEORGE HOWARD (TBA-TB 210) IT! RETAIL HOP TALK\ <IEW LABEL, NEW APPROACH - 4usic West Records, a San Francis- :o based-label, has developed a innova- ive marketing tool for their catalog — in informative, colorful bin divider which could be an industry standard, 'he card, a heavy-duty plastic construc- ion, was developed by Music West resident, Alan Kaplan and promo- ional manager, Geoff Workman. Ka- lian cites figures of one study which odicates that as much as 38% of retail ecords are impulse buys. This is espe- ially true for stores located in malls, 'he divider features the artists name at he top with an invitation to browsers to Lift Here.” The face of the divider of- ers a brief biography, excerpts from wo record reviews, three “Fan Mail” Jtters which could include (as it did on he sample Shop Talk inspected) one rom a retailer, a radio station and a onsumer, as well as part numbers and he Music West logo and phone num- 15 .her. Gary Chappell, who handles lanufacturing and promotions for Mu- H ! ic West, says the retail response to bin ard has been phenomenal. “Music 16 Vest is really the first company to come ut with such an item and it’s being well sceived. Using the bin card to tell a y little bit about the artist gives people a fiance to see what the music is all !1 bout before they buy it. The stores ie’ve talked to are all using them be- ® ause they stand out, compared to what’s out in the bin. It’s a great use of oace,” Chappell says. The cards were a zcently introduced in Tower Re- ords, Sound Warehouse, Music Plus and Peaches. The cards are available for cassette, LP and CD prod- uct on Music West. Music West has re- leased several artists including Ray Lynch, a guitarist/synthesist whose second release, “Deep Breakfast,” has already sold 100,000 units, Gary’s brother Jim Chappell, who has two solo piano LPs on the label among oth- ers. Chappell emphasized the differ- ence between Music West and other so called “New Age,” type labels. “Com- pared to a lot of the new age labels, our music is more melodically structered, more song oriented as opposed to mood oriented.” Chappell also works for an all-acoustic independent produc- tion company, Unspeakable Free- dom. The artists on Music West, he pointed out, all come from self-con tained sources, like his own production company, without any tampering of the artists’ original intentions. “The idea is to bring together independent entities that already know what their direction and vision is,” he says. “It all has a statement that comes directly from the artist with no interference.” ATTENTION VSDA MEMBERS! - The Video Software Dealers Asso- ciation (VSDA), is sponsoring a Christmas Promotion Contest which in- cludes three grand prizes — three free trips for two to the 1987 VSDA Con- vention in Las Vegas, four trips for one as second place prizes, and free convention registration for four third place winners. The top three prize pack- ages include air fare, hotel and registra- tion for two. “Promotions accomplish all sorts of things — whether it’s opening a new sotre or showcasing a new or unique product,” says VSDA execu- tive director Pam Cohen. VSDA is sponsoring the ‘Great Christmas Pro- motion Contest’ to generate energy among the membership. Our goal is to see promotions from all stores which encourage consumers to consider video tapes as the ideal Christmas gift.” Par- ticipants can enter one of three cate- goris — retail, distributor or rack jobber. Three special divisions were created within the retail category because of the diversity of store or chain type: 1-5 stores, 6-20 stores, 21 or more stores. Participants will be judged by a panel comprised of representatives from the trade press, advertising bureaus and agencies. The criteria involves use of “Watch What You Want When You Want” logo in promotion campaigns, inclusion of product and promo pieces from more than just one manufacturer, creativity and originality, and effective- ness, increased store traffic, additional sales and rentals. Participants also must send photographs or videotapes and a summary of promotion(s) — including the goal of the promotion. The deadline is January 31. All participants must be VSDA members. To enter, send name, title, company name, address, phone number, category to VSDA, 1008-F As- toria Blvd., Cherry Hill, NJ 08003. Call (609)424-7117 for information. WELCOME BACK NIPPER, ONE—RCA, the one major label that has ignored jazz consistently through- out this decade, is back in the saddle. Under the guidance of Steve Backer, the label has revved up a sextet of reis- sues, a duo of newly-recorded jazz re- leases (by James Moody and Adam Makowicz, due November 24), and a trio of new age albums. The center- pieces of the reissues — boxed sets of material from Duke Ellington and Benny Goodman — will be dealt with here later. The other four double-album jazz reissues, available under the Blue- bird logo, are an interesting, if schizo- phrenic, lot. They are Sonny Rollins: The Quartets Featuring Jim Hall,” “Charles Mingus: New Tijua na Moods,” “Coleman Hawkins: Body and Soul,” and “The Complete Bunny Berrigan Volume II.” What are represented on these four LPs are four different approaches to reissues. Sonny Rollins recorded six LPs for RCA between January ’62 and July 64. What producer Ed Michel has done here is cull all of the material based around a tenor/bass/drums/guitar quartet — representing an entire album, “The Bridge,” and several selections from each of two albums — four tunes from “What’s New” (including one, “Don’t Stop the Carnival,” previously issued only in France) and three songs from “The Standard Sonny Rollins." Michel’s contention is that since the lat- ter two albums are made up of different sessions, it makes sense to group every- thing around a specific instrumenta- tion — in this case, the Quartet with Jim Hall. This, to my mind, makes for a ter- rific double album, musically, but tends to confuse matters. French RCA has is- sued all six of the albums in three dou- ble albums and one-half of a single album (they too screwed around with “What’s New,” spreading it over two albums). Except for “What’s New,” the French albums present each of the al- bums as albums — they are reissued as they were originally issued. By cutting up two albums, American RCA has made it difficult for people to gather the six Rollins’ — you have to seek out two expensive French double albums if you want the three albums complete — and has laid unusual groundwork for future Rollins reissues. Presumably, unless RCA issues alternate tracks or takes, something Rollins is vehemently op- posed to, the future RCA Sonny Rollins reissues will be hodge-podges. Good music, unusual programming. The Mingus album is one of the cle- verest assemblages I’ve ever encoun- tered. Here Michel has taken a single classic album — “Tijuana Moods” — and paired it with a complete second ver- sion of the album, gathered from alter- j nate takes. Mingus, who believed in the j cut-and-paste approach to recording, ! left enough alternate takes and solos • ound for Michel to re produce the al- The original album holds up as t Mingus’ best, and the second al- bum offers some marvelous alternative approaches to the ensembles and solos (great work from Jimmy Knepper, Shafi Hadi, Clarence Shaw, and Dannie Richmond). A fascinating reissue. The Hawkins set, produced by Bob Porter, is another hodge-podge: sever- al sessions from the ’30s and 40s, in- cluding the one containing the galvanizing recording of “Body and Soul,” along with a complete album, “Hawk in Hi-Fi,” from the ’50s. The great tenor saxophonist is majestic throughout these sides and they give a good indication of his range, but I would have preferred a complete set of earlier recordings, to be followed by reissues of the ’50s material. The Berrigan set, also produced by Porter, continues an earli- er Bluebird reissue program: the great Swing Era trumpeter’s complete ses- sions presented chronologically. If the series continues — if it gets to the end of Berrigan’s RCA stint — then, for my money, this is the way to reissue jazz: neat, orderly, complete. And both the Hawkins and Berrigan albums contain exhaustive liner notes, something the others do not. While all of the music on these al- bums can be very highly recommended, collectors will have to pick and choose Dave Grusin (r), GRP's co-owners, recently tossed a N Y party in honor of singer Diane Schuur (c), who seems tickled by the attention. HIS WAY—Columbia has just issued an attractive six-record boxed set called “Frank Sinatra, The Voice: The Co- lumbia Years 1943-1952." The pack- age represents a transitional stage of Sinatra’s career — the bridge from big band crooner to ring-a-ding-ding hip- ster— and can be recommended mainly to those who already have the classic Capitol LPs that followed the years at Columbia. This is not all of the material Sinatra waxed for Columbia: they’ve weeded out the drivel and arranged the albums into homogenous groupings: an album each of film songs, an album of saloon songs, etc.. There are numerous masterpieces here — like the haunting “I’m A Fool To Want You” — but ar- ranger Axel Stordahl was no Nelson Riddle, and Frank Sinatra was not quite yet Frank Sinatra. A nice Christ- mas item, but the 20-record set from English Capitol (American Capitol is asleep here), available around as an im- port, is the ultimate Sinatra stocking stuffer. NEW BEGINNING-Club Nou- veau originated after the break up of Timex Social Club in late June. The producer. Jay King, de- sired very much to create a follow- up group to the Social Club, in order to complete his musical ideas for the "Rumors and Jealousy” audi- ence. His final judgement created a group with five performers: Valer- ie Watson, Denzil Foster, Thomas McElroy, Samuelle Prater and of course Jay King. This group was dubbed "Club Nou- veau." Jay King, the key motivational force of the group, says that Club Nou- veau is a vehicle to adequately ex- press his inward feelings through what he writes. It is a single dimen- sion of Jay King: the songwriter. During his formative years, King at- tended Vallejo High School. Upon graduation, he joined the Air Force for a one year term, after which he was enthralled in the art of break- dancing during a stay in Alaska. When King finally tapped the source of his true passion, music, he extend- ed himself fully to become a Bay- area best, which he has accomplished in a short span with the rapid success of the single "Ru- mors." Jay, being an excitable, yet very serious-minded human being, is driven by extensive pressure. He ex- pects nothing short of excellence from himself and his crew, which performs up to standards to main- tain Jay's utmost respect. Jay feels that this group is a never- ending, close-knit, family entity. "The worst thing they ever did was allow me into the record industry be- cause now I am here to stay," closes Jay. The next member, Denzil Foster, has accompanied Jay even previous to the Timex Social Club. Denzil was studying music in college, when he and Jay began a collaboration pro- ducing the song "The Battle Beat." His talent and creativity dominate throughout the groups songwriting, although he is of a very laid-back temperment. Denzil loves movies and candy, and feels that the group's relationship is that of a fam- ily's. "I would be doing this even if I was not receiving any monitary rewards. ..just don't ever lose sight of your dreams." Thomas McElroy, who was also with Jay and Denzil originally, is the quiet relaxed member of the group. Thomas and Denzil first met Jay's ac- quaintance while at ex-Confunkshun member's house, Felton Pilot. It was there where they began their discus- sions of music in the making. Thom- as, Jay and Denzil are the backbone to all music made within the group. Thomas studied music in college, where he acquired the talent to effi- ciently manipulate a keyboard. Thomas McElroy enjoys relaxing, and conversing with his close friends. He feels the relationship the group has is special. Thomas McElroy's phi- losophy on life states, "Life is noth- ing without friends,- the ones who are good to you that you can really trust and love." The youngest member of the group, at 19, is Samuelle Prater. Samuelle and Denzil Foster became a musical detante in high school, in Pinole Val- ley. Samuelle was later introduced to Jay, and on the same day they recorded "Jealousy." Samuelle, a very excitable but con- trolled young man, feels mutually about the group's family-like rela- tionship. Samuelle says that the group is "In no hurry to hit the top because they know they will arrive soon enough." Valerie Watson, the only female member, came to know Jay when they were neighbors. "Jay and I were childhood companions who played war games together." Jay and Valerie lost contact for ap- propximately nine years. Ironically, their paths crossed again when Jay was to sing with Timex Social Club. You can imagine how astounded she was to find that the Jay King of TSC was the same Jay King who resided only a few houses away as a child. Valerie is a fun to talk with, yet mys- terious woman. B/C PROFILES Earnest L Janies President/General Manager J.A.C.I. Inc., Ohio Pam Robinson Program/Music Director KACE-FM, Los Angeles, Ca. Earnest L. James is president and general manager of J.A.C.I. Inc., a broadcast communications company which owns and operates WCIN-AM in Cincinnati, Ohio. Previous to his founding of J.A.C.I., Inc., in 1985, James held the position of vice presi- dent of Viacom's black radio division, of which he was responsible for the management of KDIA in Oakland, CA., WDIA in Memphis and WWRL in New York City. James' career spans over a three decade period, which initiated in Oklahoma, in 1966, on KIOO where he was a volunteer announcer. He lat- er moved onto work with KYAC of Se- attle, and KPRS of Kansas City, Missouri. The management phase of his ca- reer began with WABQ, Cleveland, where he was the program director. He later held similar posts with WJMO, Cleveland and WDAO, Day- ton. In 1979, he relocated to Chicago to secure a position as program direc- tor of WBMX. Under his direction, the station soared to the number one posi- tion in the 18-34 year old market. James then graduated to vice presi- dent and general manager of WVON/WGCI. He quickly earned a promotion to president a year later through his outstanding efforts. While in Chicago, James was quite active in civic and community activities. His efforts and contributions were of- ten rewarded. He won the "NAACP Merit" award in 1977, was the recipi- ent of the "Outstanding Business and Professional Person" award in 1979, and received the Paul J. Hall Boys Club "Distinguished Humanitarian" award in 1980. He was also an active member of Big Brothers, and currently holds a lifetime membership with Op- eration Push. Upon returning to Ohio in 1985, James has continued to demonstrate an enormous commitment to communi- ty service. He currently maintains a membership in Rotary Club #17, Re- gion 667, the Chamber of Commerce, the Cincinnati Minority Development Council and serves on the board of directors for numerous organizations including Parents Anonymous, the lo- cal chapter of TransAfrica, the adviso- ry committee of the School for Creative and Performing Arts and is a division leader of the 1 986 United Ap- peal Drive. Earnest is presently the host of AWARE, a public service program which features some of Cincinnati's most exemplary citizens discussing controversial issues. Born in Admore, Oaklahoma, he is a graduate of Governors State Univer- sity, in Park Forest Illinois, with a Bach- elors Degree in Business and Communications. He later went on to earn a Presidential Key Executive MBA from Pepperdine University in Malibu, California. Robb Longg Go lady go! RETAIL WOP TALKM IN MEMORIAM — Rob Myers, a 12- year employee for Camelot Enter- prises, passed away August 24 after a lengthy and brave struggle with leuke- mia. He leaves his wife Cindy, also a Camelot employee for the past 12 years, and their two children, Lindy, 7, and Adam, 2. A piece that appears in the November/December issue of Just For the Record, the Camelot Enter- prises newsletter, contains the following portrait of this extraordinary individual. “The overwhelming sadness that all of us felt here at 8000 Freedom (Came- lot’s Ohio Headquarters) was only over- come by the inspiration Rob gave all of us as he refused to give in to his illness and managed to maintain as normal a life as possible under circumstances more trying than most of us can even imagine. Rob came to work each and every day right up until he went to the hospital for the last time in August. His job was a physical one, moving skids of merchandise through our warehouse. He was often very ill from the disease or in great pain from his chemotherapy treatments, yet he literally limped through his duties each day and seldom missed any work. Rob always had a smile for you, a good word-and never a complaint. He’s gone but he won’t be forgotten by his extended family here at 18000 Freedom. ” A college fund has i been set up for his children. Anyone who wishes to participate can send a ((donation to: The Lindy and Adam *1 Myers Education Fund c/o Cindy IMyers, Camelot Enterprises, Inc. P.O. Box 2169 North Canton, Ohio 44720 -0169 . RETAILERS HESITANT ON NON MUSIC AUDIO CASSETTES -A recent Audio Publishing Report sur- vey of 40 of the largest record store chains found that while approximately 43% of the stores carry non-music au- diocassettes, an “overwhelming num- ber of stores that carry audio only handle a small amount of product and enthusiasm for the product was mild at best, with few stores saying they planned to add additional tapes in their outlets.” Tapes of old radio shows were found to be the best sellers “as long as they’re priced under $4.” The other popular categories were self-help tapes and children’s cassettes. Many of the chains in the study are still testing the market, trying small quantities while others have given up, such as Camelot Music, who say tried carrying them last holiday season and had “no luck.” CYPRESS RECORDS SHIPS FIRST TWO ALBUM RE- LEASES — Cypress Records, a new- ly-formed label focusing on new product by artists from the “baby boomer” gen- eration, has released its first two al- bums— “Famous Blue Raincoat”, by Jennifer Warnes, and “High Risk” by Tim Weisberg. Warnes’ new LP is her first since recording the Grammy-winning duet “Up Where We Belong” with Joe Cocker. The album contains material written by Ca- nadian composer/poet Leonard Co- hen, including three new compositions written specifically for this album. Weis- bergs’ LP had been previously released late last year through an independent distributor and mail order set up by Weisberg and is now being re-released by Cypress. The LP was inspired by Weisberg’s penchant for airplanes, the theme of “High Risk” is flying with spe- cial thanks to his friends in the Blue Angels flight squadron. The releases are being distributed in the U.S. by PolyGram. Gregory Dobrin NEWFACES TO WATCH Manahattan recording artist Robbie Nevil is exuberant about the way his career is shaping up. Seated on a couch in his manager’s office, the face of the 24-year-old singer/songwriter registers a cross-section of emotions as he ex- plains his reaction to the success of his debut self-titled LP. The emotions range from excitement, to pensiveness, to unbridled gratitude. These days, the once struggling young artist has plenty to get excited, pensive and grateful about. “C’est La Vie,” the first single from his self-titled debut LP is bulleting up the Cash Box Singles chart, and its accompanying vid- eo, artfully directed by Peter Care, has gone into active rotation on MTV. “I’m being played in other cities that I’ve never even heard of. I feel like 1 better get in the car and go travel just so I can find out about these places!” he enthusiastically joked. For the L.A. born-and-bred musician, positive feed- back to the album is a dream come true, the ultimate payoff. He savors every moment. “People ask me what it’s like to hear myself on the radio. I say, ‘It’s the best.’” Not that Robbie Nevil has never had a song recorded before. His tunes have been covered by the Pointer Sisters, Sheena Easton, A1 Jarreau, El DeBarge, Vanity - he even had a cut on the “We Are The World”LP. But it was an artist deal that Nevil had originally intended for himself, and through his songwrit- ing, an artist deal was what he finally got. “Many things can be a means to an end,”he commented. “That’s the nice thing about this industry. It’s kind of like going fishing. You throw out the lines you can, and they all kind of connect.” The signing happened by chance, and it happened at a time when Nevil had more or less put his own recording ambitions on hold. After submitting some new material for artists on the Capitol roster, he got a call from one of the label’s a&r people who had heard his tape. A meeting was scheduled. Ne- vil was asked if he’d be interested in an artist deal. “Of course!,” he replied. “That’s what I was interested in initial- ly!” Then he was introduced to Manhat- tan Records founder Bruce Lundvall, who said he wanted to sign him as the first artist on the new label. Nevil is the first to admit the fairy- tale qualities of this story. “The Robbie Nevil whole thing was so extraordinary, after all those years of wanting it so bad, and doing anything I could. And at that par- ticular time it was no longer the main goal. It was so easy. I couldn’t help but smile. It was like a dream.” Nevil grew up listening to the radio. When he sang too loudly in his gram- mer school singing class, the school principal took notice, and asked him to sing at graduation. He picked up a real guitar after years of playing “air guitar” to his favorite records, which included everything from Led Zeppelin to Mo- town. Songwriting came naturally. Now, with a label deal under his belt, " all of the elements of his craft, including live performing (though there are no tour plans at present), have finally gelled. The album was recorded in Lon- don, and produced by Alex Sadkin, with ex-Cure member Phil Thornally. Nevil waited a year and a half to work with the much-in-demand Sadkin, whose credits include the Thompson Twins, Duran Duran and Grace Jones, but the more he listened to Sadkin’s work, the more he wanted to work with him. The wait was worth it. “Alex sees what you see, and embellishes it,” he remarked. The result is an R&B inflect- ed pop album, featuring a direct, gutsy approach, led by Nevil’s soulful, ener- gized vocals. Clearly, after years of hav- ing to farm it out to foster parents, Nevil’s music is very much his own. ONJAZZ PASSING ON—Eddie “Leckj®*-” Davis, the rough and tumble tenor sax- ophonist, died November 3 of cancer. Davis was an exciting soloist who could shake the walls — something he did quite handily with Count Basie, as part of a jousting two-tenor team with Johnny Griffin, with various organ trios, particularly one led by Shirley Scott, and in various tenor-for-hire situ- ations. “Jaws” had a love-hate relation- ship with playing; he frequently packed up his horn and worked as a booking agent. His last appearance was at Dick Gibson’s Colorado Jazz Party over La- bor Day weekend, where he surprised the assemblage with a single number. Eddie “Lockjaw” Davis was 65. Sippie Wallace, who died Novem- ber 1 at the age of 88, was, perhaps, the last of the great female blues singers who came to prominence in the 1920’s. She recorded with Louis Armstrong and Sidney Bechet back then and ex- perienced something of a revival when Bonnie Raitt not only recorded her songs — most notably “Woman Be Wise” — but had Sippie open many of her concerts. Sexy, saucy, and sassy till the end — I last heard her only a couple of years ago at the Nice Jazz Festival, where she tore it up — the likes of Sip- pie Wallace will never pass this way again. I’d like to note three other recent deaths. Theorgeir Stubo, a promi- nent Norwegian jazz guitarist, died of cancer October 22 at the age of 42. Richard Calandra, co-producer of Spyro Gyra and co-owner of Bear Tracks recording studio in Suffern, N.Y., died October 20 of cancer at the age of 45. And Louis Lorillard, the tobacco heir who co-founded the Newport Jazz Fes- tival with his then-wife Elaine in 1954, died of pneumonia November 5 at the age of 67. BENEFIT TIME—A benefit will be held at the New School of Social Re- search in New York, December 11, to raise money for the establishment of a Zoot Sims Scholarship at the school. The saxophone great’s friends, sparked by Arnie Lawrence, are the one’s who are behind this, and many of Zoot’s musical compadres — including A1 Cohn, Dizzy Gillespie, Gerry Mul- ligan, Jon Faddis, and Scott Hamil- ton— are expected to take part. It’s a benefit for the homeless of New York and al- ready signed up to appear are Lionel Hampton, Tommy Flanagan, Woody Shaw, Lester Bowie’s ‘'M'tasy, Amina Claudine Cherry, Hilton Ruiz, ibbey Lincoln, Gil Evans, and many others. It'll take place from 2 to 10 pm and a call to (212) 280-5223 will get you ticket details. EKAPA—Abdullah Ibrahim is, to my mind, one of the very best pianists, composers, and bandleaders currently working. A complete original, he is re- ponsible for two of the best jazz albums of this year — “Water From an Ancient Well” (Blackhawk) and “South Africa” (Enja). Now Blackhawk has picked up distribution of Ekapa — a label that Ibra- him began a couple of years ago with his wife, vocalist Sathima Bea Benja- min— releasing Sathima’s “Memories and Dreams” (as well as the new “Wind- song”), and Ibrahim’s “Ekaya” and “Live At Sweet Basil, Volume 1.” They are all worth having, and Ibrahim is par- ticularly worth hearing live: he’ll be set- tling into N.Y.’s Sweet Basil the first two weeks in December and a stop there is highly recommended. RETAIL HOP TALKM j HE MOSS “CD WALLET”: AN , >EA WHOSE TIME HAS COME - "I s no surprise that compact disc sales ive exceeded everyone’s expecta- >ns. As more CD plants go on-line, 'ailability, which has been a major >ntributing factor in keeping CD ices high, is starting to loosen and a >od quality compact disc player can >w be had for around $100, yet the >st of the average CD (around $13) is ill prohibitively high for the average merican music consumer. Ira Moss, •esident of the Moss Music Group, 1 independent distributor, has devel- Ded a new package for the compact sc, the “CD Wallet, ”a self-contained orage protector and marketing tool H hich is cheaper to produce than all of le components which comprise the rrrent CD packaging — the jewel box id its plastic insert, which is now being ' ackaged into a cumbersome clam shell y r long box which the consumer romptly disposes of “Comparing it to lWi jewel box, the insert and the long box, le difference is a minimum of a half- dollar savings to the manufacturer,” U ays Moss. This, he says, translates to at fast a $2 savings at list price. “A jewel lIi;ox is a very handsome, rigid and dura- le package, but this (the wallet) does ^ le same trick and allows the consumer 22 ) get into the price area of CD’s.” The 3!D Wallet, constructed of durable jxoard, similar to traditional LP packag- jig, stores the CD in the a special pro- 's! 2ctive plastic cloth, the same which ictories use to ship them in, which fits m 1 ito the wallet. The package measures » If 5”x 1 1 V4 ” x 1/8” when displayed with a stiffener, which can be used to adver- tise catalog which is discarded after the package is opened. The wallet is one- third the thickness of the standard CD long box, making them lighter, and therefore cheaper to ship, display and warehouse. “Three of them will fit in the counter in the place of one long box,” Moss explains, “so if you can only stock one 3’x5’ table with CD’s in the store, you can fit 1000 CD wallets, but you can only fit 350 in the jewel box in either of the long box configurations. You can ship five CD wallets for the price of shipping one CD jewel box.” When the consumer opens the wallet, there is ample room for liner notes, credits and an extra pocket for another CD. The wallet is then folded to 4V2”x 5”, the same size as the jewel box, for easy storage. “From the consumer’s point of view, this packaging is intended to offer a safe and adequate storage fa- cility. It has considerably more liner notes than do most records, the pack- age is not breakable, the CD can’t fall out. It’s like a double record jacket.” While Moss acknowledges that a cos- metic comparison of the CD wallet with the jewel box is akin to “comparing a Cadillac with a Chevrolet,” he empha- sized that since the CD itself is a much more durable format than vinyl, the jew- el box is not a necessity. Indeed, the wallet is actually more functional to the consumer and more cost effective for the manufacturer and the dealer. Moss, who won a NARM award for Marketing Achievement in 1983, for expanding the base of the classical market relative to popularly priced cassettes, devel- oped the wallet to differentiate Moss Music’s new Vox Prima classical line since classical CD’s are sorted out by composer making them “unbrowsa- ble.” “Since promotion is very expen- sive now, the most important thing for us is to get our merchandise segregated from the rest of the product by having unique packaging,” says Moss. Since Moss has made the wallet available for licensing, sample wallets have been sent to all the major labels, manufacturers, and independents. Dealer reaction has been enthusiastic including retailing heavies Russ Solomon, (Tower Re- cords), Barry Bergman (Record Bar) and Joe Bressi (Camelot). “We’ve had definite and specific inter- est from some of the independent la- bels, but the majors, with all of their various inabilities to make decisions are waiting to see what happens,” says Moss P-O-P displays are now in the stores with 25 CD titles which list for $12.98, yet most retailers are selling them at $9 .98 ' He is concerned that his classical CD line may not be a true indi- cator since the classical target market is more affluent and don’t mind paying for the“Cadillac.” “They’re (manufactur- ers) missing the boat by not going into pop right away. From a pop point of view, the wallet makes more sense.” Moss says the wallet has only been ship- ping for two weeks and not all of the responses have been positive. “Some are very negative, to be honest, but out of 105 responses, 91 said they would look for more product and see a cata- log,” he says, but more interestingly, “a number of them said, if this packaging is what brings the price down, we’re all for it. We recognize that if we went out at the same price as a jewel box, we wouldn’t stand a chance.” In an infor- mal Shop Talk poll, I found that CD aficionados who purchased their play- ers early on, many to satisfy their audio- phile needs, tended to be stuck on the “high-tech” aesthetics of the jewel box. Since the prices of the units have dropped, however, the complexion of the CD buyer is rapidly changing. Newer player owners, I found, are all for the package if it reduces prices. Be- ing a member of the CD elite corps my- self, I was skeptical about the CD wallet, yet when all the benefits are weighed, it won me over. For me, the extensive liner note area and the ease of removing the disc from the plastic pouch instead of wrestling it off of the plastic insert inside the jewel box are important benefits, but the prospect of paying $10 instead of $13-$16 for a CD is particularly convincing, especially when statistics say I’ll purchase about 50 of these addictive polycarbonate discs per year. In sum, the CD wallet is a not only a viable alternative to current CD packaging, it could be a catalyst for CD sales for the industry and make the CD more accessible to the average con- sumer. “After all,” says Moss, “they’re not buying a package. They’re buying the music.” Brian Kassan l! A CASH BOX TOP 40 COMPACT DISCS FORE! It’s something that’s not go- ing to be able to be stopped.” Despite his positive feelings about fusion, Stanley Clarke says that he is none-too-im- pressed with the current crop of fusion bands. He goes to clubs in L.A., where he resides, and he finds himself yawning. Flash, he thinks, is replacing substance. “1 have a feeling it has something to do with the fact, to be point blank about it, that the guys don’t practice like we practiced. 1 just know that they don’t, I can tell. I’ve taught a lot of bass players and I can look at a musician and tell when they’ve spent more time on their equipment. It sounds to me, when I got to these clubs, that I’m hearing four individuals that kind of just walked off the street from different locations and start- ed playing. There’s some semblance of something happening, but they just didn’t play enough together. ‘‘It’s funny, I can't even blame the musi- cians, totally. There just ain’t enough time to figure out how to put a whole Midi sys- tem together, and get that going, and then practice, really practice, in one day. We had shitty equipment back then, but we used to practice 10 hours a day. Religiously, every day.” The “back then” Stanley refers to is the early ’70s, the glory days of fusion; the “we” is Return To Forever — Chick Corea, A1 DiMeola, Lenny White, and Stanley Clarke. If Clarke and DiMeola and White have their druthers, Return To Forever will return to performing — and show these young fusion whippersnappers a thing or two. “Lenny and A1 and I are ready to go,” says Stanley. “We are definitely going to tour. We’re just waiting on a few little things in Chick’s head, which I think will be real easy to solve, and we’re going to go. “When we got together for the last re- union, I had to stop everything that I was doing: I couldn’t produce anybody, 1 couldn’t see my family, I was constantly do- ing interviews, touring and rehearsing. It re- minded me of when I was 19 or 20 and basically all I used to think about was music. So it’s nice. That would actually, for me, be kind of an icing on the cake that would help propel this instrumental thing seriously into the ’90s. RTF could do it real easy.” In the meantime, Stanley will hit the road with his own ensemble, finish producing flutist James Walker’s classical fusion LP, and begin preparing the follow-up to “Hide- away,” which he says will “probably be more along the lines of some of the more creative songs on that album.” However, don’t look for it to contain Stanley’s best bass playing. “I’m not as serious about albums as some people are,” he says. “I think a lot of jazz musicians are like that, because you usually play your better stuff live anyway. I’ve nev- er been, and probably never will be, cap- tured on a record.” Kwiker (continued from page 25) market, which at the time had yet to take off. Ten Superstars *Rock For Amnesty’ Sugar Hill Names MCA In $240 Million Suit NEW YORK — New Jersey-based Sugar Hill Records filed a $240 million lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Newark last Tues. (18) charging that it was defrauded and forced into near-bankruptcy in a racketeering scheme engineered by executives of MCA Records and reputed organized crime figure Salvatore J. Pisello. Sugar Hill claims in the civil suit that ex- ecutives of MCA and its distribution arm, MCA Distribution Corp., conspired with Pi- sello to take control of Sugar Hill and force the company to sell, at a deflated price, it’s interest in the Checker/Chess/Cadet cata- logue of, primarily, rock and roll and blues recordings. According to the suit, this was done through “concerted participation in fraudulent, illegal and corrupt activities” in violation of the Racketeer-Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act. MCA Records, in response to the suit, vigorously denied these charges. MCA re- leased the following statement: “MCA Re- cords is outraged by the news that Sugarhill is accusing it of violating the RICOH Act. Considering that over the past several weeks MCA Records has confronted Sugar- hill with extensive evidence indicating Su- garhill’s apparent massive fraud and material breaches in its dealings with MCA Records, it is obvious that this lawsuit is a bad faith effort to try to avoid facing MCA Records’ claims and obscure the real issues. MCA Records intends to vigorously defend against this frivolous lawsuit and aggressive- ly pursue its legitimate claims against Sugarhill.” According to the suit, after taking over the manufacturing and distribution of Sugar Hill in November, 1983, MCA executives and Pisello conspired “to create fraudulent transactions which could then be charged against income otherwise due and payable to Sugar Hill,” including allegedly false re- turns of recordings sent back by indepen- dent distributors that MCA then charged against MCA, the preparation and mailing of “fraudulent accounting reports” to Sugar Hill, and the unauthorized “secret sale” of Sugar Hill’s inventory as cut-outs. As a re- sult of these transactions, the suit claims, Sugar Hill was compelled to sell the Chess/ Checker/Cadet catalogue to MCA for “less than its fair market value,” ultimately forc- ing Sugar Hill to seek relief under Chapter 11 of the bankruptcy code. Sugar Hill’s suit asks for triple damages, totalling $240 million. Named in the suit in addition to Pisello, MCA Records and MCA (continued on page 7) Bruce Box Debuts At #1—Out Of The Box! who got to know Sting. Three weeks after the tour was concluded, her 19-year old son was picked up in Chile, beaten, and had kerosene poured over him and was burned by the military. Three days later he died in the hospital. Sting was so affected by it that he decided to do a new track for the album.” “Sting actually did it as a lament to the 19 year old boy,” Duffy told Cash Box. ‘“Strange Fruit’ is about blacks in the (U.S.) deep south in the thirties, and the strange fruit is, of course, dead bodies hanging from trees. ..Sting recorded the song all himself with nobody else. He put down the bass line and accompanied himself with a vibraphone and just sang.” One reporter asked why only one of the songs on the album (John Mellencamp’s “Pink Houses”) was by a U.S. artist. “The reason the artist line-up is as it is, for the most part these were the people I knew and could contact at short notice. Because, see- ing how we started the project in July, we had to be wrapped up by early September. But as to why (U.S. artists) are not thinking up these projects, that is something that is a very heavy comment on American society.” Still, the album has a decidedly interna- tional bent, with songs about South Africa (Gabriel’s “Biko” and Elton John’s “Passen- gers”) and world peace in general (“Broth- ers In Arms,” “Pipes Of Peace”). “Touring musicians are by their very nature working internationally,” said Gambaccini. “Just traveling from country to country you see the different traditions that prevail and it can’t help but make you think in an interna- tionalist way.” A telegram from Jim Kerr of Simple Minds, read at the press conference, seemed to bolster that contention. “During our travels this year,” the telegram said, “we have discovered that more people have become aware and, more importantly, ac- tively involved in the work of Amnesty International.” Howard Jones, speaking by phone from Dublin, said that the December issue of his fan club magazine would contain an appeal by Amnesty International on behalf of politi- cal prisoners. Jones said that he re-recorded “No One Is To Blame” for the album. “I got together with Phil Collins and Hugh Padgham and we recorded a much bigger, larger than life version of the song.” Internationally, the album is called “A Conspiracy Of Hope,” but the U.S. title was changed to “Rock For Amnesty” so as not to be confused with the recent tour of the same name. All royalties will be donated to Amnesty International. By Brian Kassan “Bruce Springsteen & The E Street Band Live/1975-85” debuts this week at #1 with a bullet on the Cash Box Top 200 albums chart, only the fifth album in the history of the recording industry, as well as the first ever multi-record set to hit the top out of the box. The first four LPs to achieve this feat were Led Zeppelin’s final studio LP “In Through The Out Door” (September 8, 1979), The Eagles’ “The Long Run” (Octo- ber 20,1979), Elton John’s “Captain Fantas- tic” (June 7, 1975), and Stevie Wonder’s “Songs In The Key Of Life” (October 16, 1976). Springsteen’s last studio LP, “Born In the U.S. A.,” debuted at #10 with a bullet on June 23, 1984 and shot up to the #1 spot the following week. That LP, still on the Cash Box Top 200 Albums at #190 after 127 weeks, has sold over 10 million copies nationally, with just over 18 million copies worldwide. Springsteen’s highest debut had been #8 with 1980’s “The River.” Very often a hit album will stimulate sales for an artist’s older catalog — this week Bos- ton’s debut album, “Boston,” is back on the chart at #116 on the heels of Boston’s new long-awaited “Third Stage” album which has been # 1 on the Cash Box charts for a month. Charting is based on sales reports from retail outlets around the country. For the first week after the release of the 40-song live retrospective, every single retailer re- ported the set as the number one seller, but even more impressive, the typical retail re- port would be 2,000 sets sold, with the sec- ond highest selling album at 200 units. Sources at CBS said the five album, cas- sette or 3 CD set shipped approximately 1.7 million sets — 700,000 LPs, 700,000 cas- settes and 300,000 CDs. At press time, most retailers have sold out the CD, and although a spokesman for CBS said more would be available before Christmas, some retailers had been warned by the label not to expect more CDs until early 1987. MORE NUGGETS FROM RHI- NO— Rhino continues with their best selling “Nuggets” titles, outstanding compilations of hits and undiscovered classics of the psychedelic/garage era, with five (count ’em) new volumes of ’60s pop gems each of which concen- trates on a specific style or region con- taining some popular selections and several long-sought-after obscurities, some of which are available on album for the first time anywhere. With the resurgence of the Monkees and the growing proliferation of neo-paisley pop bands like Three O’CIock, Rain Parade and the Bangles, a whole new generation of fans have discovered the joys of ’60s pop music. Volume 8, “The Pacific Northwest,” features sounds from the Seattle/Portland area including classics “Louie Louie” by The Kingsmen, “Just Like Me” by Paul Revere And The Raiders as well as regional faves The Weeds, The Initial Shock and The Surprise Package among others. Volume 9, “Acid Rock” is a collection of mind- expanding monsters by The Straw- berry Alarm Clock (“Incense And Peppermints”), Iron Butterfly (“In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida”), Vanilla Fudge (“You Keep Me Hangin’ On”), The Byrds (“Eight Miles High”) along with other psychedelic classics. Volume 10, “Folk Rock,” ex- plores the Dylan-influenced folk move- ment of the early ’60s with performances from Barry McGuire (“Eve Of Destruction), The Byrds (“Mr. Tambourine Man”), Scott McKenzie (“San Francisco”), The Turtles, The Sunshine Company, and The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band along with obscure classics from P.F.SIoan, MFQ, Peanut Butter Conspiracy, The Grass Roots and Jake Holmes (who performs the origi- nal version of “Dazed And Con- fused” that Led Zeppelin later recorded) among others. Volume 11, “Pop, Part 4” continues the wealth of Beatle-inspired garage pop, serving up such gems by The Left Banke (“Pretty Ballerina”), The Grass Roots (“Let’s Live For Today”), The Sunshine Company (“Happy”) along with many obscurities by Keith, The Blues Project, and The Crit- ters among others. Volume 12, “Punk, Part 3,” represents the third in a series concentrating on the grungy Rolling Stones/ Yardbirds style rock which spawned a whole genera- tion of garage bands. This volume com- bines hits by Paul Revere And The Raiders (“Steppin’ Out”), The Syndicate Of Sound (“Little Girl), and The Hombres (“Let It Out ) with obscure punk rock classics by The Lollipop Shoppe, Kenny And The Kasuals, Mouse And The Traps, The Uniques, and others. ONJAZZl WELCOME BACK NIPPER. TWO—The newly-reactivated RCA Bluebird line has just come out with a pair of boxed sets that, in many ways, represent the apex of the Swing Era. “Benny Goodman: The RCA Years,” a 16-LP set, includes some of the best and most popular music of the period: the Benny Goodman Orchestra’s Blue- bird sides. “Duke Ellington: The Blanton-Webster Band,” a four-LP package, includes some of the finest jazz big band music ever recorded, in- deed some of the finest jazz of any sort- ever waxed: the Victor recordings of Ellington’s stunning band of 1940-42. Many of these are essential, absolutely essential, jazz recordings — items that no jazz record collection should be without. The Benny Goodman material has been available stateside for several years: the last RCA incarnation of Blue- bird actually managed to complete an eight double-LP issue of the Goodman records, records that Benny Goodman considered his finest achievement. The boxed set collects the eight doubles and even reprints Mort Goode’s excellent, anecdotal liner notes. The set has been digitally remastered and there is an im- provement soundwise in the new set — not enough of an improvement to justi- fy replacing the doubles with the box, however, but an improvement nonethe- less. There are over 250 recordings here, all made between April, 1935 and May, 1939, and many of them are spec- tacular: Fletcher Henderson's charts on “King Porter Stomp,” “Down South Camp Meeting,” “Christopher Colum- bus” and so many others; the magnifi- cent Quartet (Lionel Hampton, Teddy Wilson, Gene Krupa), re- cordings; the work of such beautiful sidemen as Jess Stacy, Vido Musso, Harry James, and Davey Tough; the brilliant Goodman clarinet. There was no greater white band recording during the Swing Era, and this set wraps it up into a terrific package. There was no greater band recording during the Swing Era — during any Era — than the Duke Ellington Orches- tra and, finally, RCA/U.S. has acknowl- edged its existence. This four-record set (it’ll be available on three CDs) contains a generous 66 songs, excellently anno- tated by Mark Tucker, and to list its masterpieces is to finish out this page — forget it! This is the peak of Ellington’s career — a career that contains more im- pressive peaks than the Himalayas — and it is truly mind-boggling: how can so much brilliance be created in just over two years? With an awe-inspiring band — Wallace Jones, Cootie Wil- liams (later, Ray Nance), Rex Stew- art, Tricky Sam Nanton, Lawrence Brown, Juan Tizol, Barney Bigard (later Chauncey Haughton), Johnny Hodges, Harry Carney, Otto Hard- wick, Ben Webster, Jimmy Blan- ton (later Junior Raglin), and Sonny Greer — and with the assistance of his celebrated alter-ego, Billy Strayhorn, Duke Ellington spun gold with astonish- ing consistency. The perfect blend of writing and playing. What is not includ- ed here are alternate takes (“This set is not meant to cater to people who are interested in alternate takes,” says pro- ducer Bob Porter) and Ellington’s small-group recordings of the period. For complete RCA Ellington, French RCA is still the place to go. But for a jazz fan who doesn’t have this stuff, this is the stocking-stuffer of the year: sim- ply no greater music has been issued, or reissued, in 1986. Papa is a Rolling Stone GATHERING NO MOSS— Last year Charlie Watts — you know, the grey-haired timekeeper for the Rolling Stones — decided to live out a fantasy and put together a jazz big band. So he made a few phone calls and, begorrah, the London jazz community went bon- kers: players of every age and size were clamoring to get in. This week Colum- bia is issuing “Live at Fulham Town Hall,” which features Watts and a 33- piece band (including such well-known British players as Evan Parker, Stan Tracy, Paul Rutherford. Courtney Pine, Peter King, John Stevens, Harry Beckett, Alad Skidmore, and Annie Whitehead) rumbling through six appropos jazz standards. Well, look out. the Watts bohemoth is floating stateside: they’ll be in Hartford (11/29), Philadelphia (12/1), N.Y.C. (12/2-4), Boston (12/5), and Toronto (12/6&7). On the merits of the players alone, this is a not-to-be-missed jazz gig. ONJAZZ^^^ ATLANTIC JAZZ—Last year Atlan- tic released a stunning collection, “At- lantic Rhythm and Blues: 1947-74,” an 18-record set (also available in nine dou- ble albums) that handily summed up an entire musical era. When it comes to vintage r&b, Atlantic is the label of re- cord (oh sure, there are exceptions, James Brown and the Motown crowd being the most obvious). Now Atlantic has tried a similar approach with its jazz catalogue. “Atlantic Jazz” is a 15-re- cord set (available boxed or as three double and nine single albums) and, for obvious reasons, it isn’t a patch on the r&b set. Atlantic Records simply was not nearly as meticulous about covering the jazz field as it was about covering the r&b field and when Atlantic was found- ed the great eras of New Orleans-style jazz, swing, and bebop were more or less over. Atlantic came along too late to document jazz’s golden ages. So while this set — taken as a set — is just what it’s advertised to be — a survey of jazz recording on Atlantic Records — it is by no means a comprehensive survey of the history of jazz (only Columbia Re- cords could approach that, and, indeed, they have had a similar 15-record series on the shelf now for about four years). The album breakdowns, then, are somewhat misleading. They are “New Orleans,” “Kansas City,” “Bebop,” “West Coast,” “Mainstream,” “Post Bop,” “Singers,” “Piano,” “Soul” (the last three are the doubles), “The Avant- Garde,” “Introspection,” and “Fu- sion.” The point is, Atlantic did the lion’s share of its recordings from about 1955 to about 1963 and, not surprisingly, the albums here that are the strongest are the ones that capture the essence of those very important years: the vol- umes dedicated to the avant-garde, west coast jazz, soul jazz, post-bop, sing- ers, and “mainstream” jazz. Each of these volumes paints a successful por- trait of a time and place. Atlantic was savvy enough to record the jazz avant- garde at its birth, and that album in- cludes works by Ornette Coleman, John Coltrane. Eric Dolphy (with Charles Mingus), Rahsaan Roland Kirk (never strictly an avant-gardist), and The Art Ensemble of Chicago. The west coast set includes Shelly Manne, Shorty Rogers, Jimmy Giuffre, etc.. The soul album crackles with the likes of Shirley Scott, Jack McDuff, and King Curtis. The post- bop album contains pieces by Teddy Charles, Sonny Rollins (with the Modern Jazz Quartet), The Jazz Modes, and others. The singers album, though not nearly comprehensive, of- fers a good sampling of such warblers as Helen Merrill, Betty Carter, and Chris Connor. And the “mainstream” set — a fairly all-encompassing term, that — includes Ira Sullivan, Tony Fruscella, Coleman Hawkins, and guys like that. The piano, “introspec- tion” (Atlantic’s term, and a good one. for pretty acoustic music from musi- cians better associated with fusion), and fusion sets are okay spot surveys (the piano set is a particularly wide survey), but the New Orleans, Kansas City, and bebop sets are less-useful. The New Or- leans set features New Orleans revival bands of the ’50s and ’60s but none of that city’s great jazz innovators. The Kansas City album doesn’t scratch that surface of Kansas City swing, though it does include some fine later Joe Turner and Jay McShann. And the bebop set is stretching things: some of it would have fit more comfortably under a “post bop” heading. Part of the problem here — and this is really no problem at all — is that Atlan- tic has been unusually conscientious about keeping albums in print. Many of the LPs of Ornette Coleman, John Col- trane, the MJQ and others have re- mained in print since they were recorded. And Atlantic has done a pret- ty good job in restoring out-of-print items to their catalogue via their Jazz- lore series. 15 well-chosen full albums from the Atlantic catalogue could make a nicely representative series of jazz cir- ca 1955-63. This set doesn’t quite do it, though, like 1 said, a number of the al bums are worthy in their own right. What is tantalizing here are the numer- ous tracks from collectors-item Atlantic records still long out-of-print: albums by Teddy Charles, The Jazz Modes, Max Roach and Hasaan Ibn All, and Buster Smith. Hopefully, the Jazzlore series will restore these, and several other out-of-print items represented here, to print in the near future. For the most part, the albums in “Atlantic Jazz” can be most useful as samplers. WEST COAST JAZZ?— There is room here for only a brief mention of a fascinating- sounding concert series slat- ed for December 1-5 and 8-12 at Bill Graham’s Wiltern Theatre in L.A.. “JAZZVIS10NS...Made in America,” is the bizarre title, since the line-up is won- derfully international and includes musi- cians who don’t necessarily play jazz at all. TAIL SHOPTALKM THE BOOK OF DISCS—Since the 1984 premiere issue of Digital Audio, a magazine wholly dedicated to review- ing and rating those keen little polycar- bonate discs, many early CD consumers who read the publication began to rely on the 50-100 CD reviews which ap- peared in each issue before plunking down $20 (prices have been dropping, although import CDs will still cost an arm and a leg) for a new disc to feed the hungry machine. Indeed, publisher Wayne Green, in the first issue pro- claimed, “If I can save you from buying one bummer of a Compact Disc at around $20 a whack, you’re a winner.” As the number of titles has increased (from a mere 16 CDs in April 1983 to more than 6000 midway through 1986), the need for a CD reference guide has become apparent. Presto! Bantam Books has published Digital Audio’s Guide to Compact Discs, a 320-page compilation which presents over 1500 reviews and ratings from the first two years of the publication in con- cise, quick reference form. The guide is alphabetically arranged by musical cate- gories which include pop/rock, coun- try, soundtrack, original cast, Christmas, jazz, classical and classical collections. It also includes informative articles titled “The Compact Disc Phe- nomenon: How It All Began,” “How To Buy A CD Player: A Basic Shopping Guide,” and “The CD Player Checklist: Some Expert Advice” and a short edito- rial, “When Will CD Prices Come Down?,” all of which Shop Talk found informative, and easy to understand. Each rating consists of two graphic 1 to 10 scales or “digital thermometers” which rate the artist’s performance (def- initely a more subjective category and not the prime consideration here) and the more important of the two — the disc’s sound quality. Each review con- tains the CD’s playing time, the year of release, and the year of recording for each classical disc. The SPARS (Society of Professional Audio Recording Stu- dios) code (AAD, ADD, DAD, or DDD), which is a summary of the disc’s record- ing source, the recording mix-down and the mastering, is also included. While the SPARS code appears on a minority ofdiscs, some aficionados contend that a DDD would be vastly superior to an AAD or an ADD. Just how important the code is in relation to sound quality still seems a matter of personal taste and more importantly, the quality of the original recording which cannot be mea- sured until it is heard. The mostly brief reviews which follow focus, for the most part, on the sound quality of the disc in a well written, interesting man- ner. Disc retailers would be well-advised to sell the book over the counter, or at least own a copy to increase product knowledge among store employees. GUEST EDITORIAL Music Is Changing The Way We Watch T.V. By Phillip Carter President of Phillip Carter Music, a music consultant group that creates and produces music scores for commercials, industrials and other film projects. There’s a new challenge facing pro- ducers and composers today: commer- cials. Instead of television viewers rustling around in the kitchen during commercials (some people can make it to the kitchen and back in 30 seconds), we find them becoming involved in watching commercials again. One of the primary reasons is music. The demand for popular music in commercials is becoming more impor- tant, and no longer are we consistently bombarded with the “bouncing ball” mentality in ads. In some cases we may even find ourselves thinking and possi- bly waiting that extra 30 seconds before hitting the bathroom. Music in a commercial, if it’s strong or unusual, may attract a viewer back to the tube, grab them before they leave or better yet, get them to buy the product being advertised. Which would you rather be? A vic- tim of a jingle or the person who feels that they’ve made an intelligent deci- sion staying in front of the TV or not punching their radio to another station while driving home from work. Producing music that will hold an au- dience the way Rod Stewart, Elton John, Michael Jackson or Phil Collins can hold an audience is no easy task. Yet, major corporations have seen the merits of how these artists can sell their products. Today’s young audience expects their audio and visual mediums to be equally hot. They are aware of the tech- nology in music and they want the ads to sound the same way. Why shouldn’t they? That Phil Collins and Genesis may work with one beer company on and off screen to support an extensive tour has become the norm. The challenge be- comes one of writing music that turns heads for the product the same way hit records do. Of course, they are done on a schedule that can be grueling. The music must sound like a record; it must have a hook; it must employ state of the art technology and if all goes well, it will magically end at 30 seconds. Plus, it must compliment the film. These de mands can only make good composers better (or lose them completely) Artists are reaping the benefits of participating in these multi-million dol- lar campaigr.s. In some instances, re- cord companies are enjoying revenues from licensing hit tracks. +r.acks have to be carefully mate the products, and out of respe-' : leii craft, a concept may be dror.e pletely. For certain groups, the expo- sure of performing in commercials can really give a boost to their careers. We’ve all seen ads featuring The Long Riders or the Bus Boys. Regionally, viewers even got to see Aretha driving her pink Cadillac into a certain type of gas station askin’ to fill ’er up. These spots were done to entertain, not bore. Working with the professionals in ad- vertising, we find that they are open to the possibilities that are available to them in music. There is a change from “safe” to bold in the choice of music. Of course, the quality of the film helps. More and more advertisers feel com- pelled to link the power of the “hit” record with the product. Hearing hit music in the ad gives on the feeling that, as a consumer, you are not really being sold something. Of course, not all products can be supplied with a proven “hit.” Budget considerations, you know ... So then the task of the composer becomes one of creating a hit feeling within the ad. At Phillip Carter Music, we have met the challenge of composing music for Jordache Basics, Gillette and Vidal Sas- soon. In each of these campaigns, this year, we have had to satisfy the appe- tites of the youth audience or be zapped! The way young people watch TV and commercials has changed. We know the video clip business has sifted down into advertising. Sadly, not all commercials which borrow from music video make it as entertaining. Smoke screens and drum machines do not al- ways add up to success in spots. The standards are high for what works, and with this new level of achievement, we are seeing more performers leaving the arenas and collaborating on music for commercials. It’s challenging, fun, fresh and very lucrative for them. Agencies and their clients place mu- sic high on the list of production chores. Account execs are becoming film and A&R specialists. They read the trades, have relationships with managers and other music types because the need is there. What we all hope for is that these innovators don’t get stuck in the same groove that many of the music video directors have gotten caught in. We have to continue to attract more talent to this part of the media industry, rather than isolate them from it.
