Oi^JAZZi CD RIDER—Okay, okay, !’m con- vinced: CDs are it. The best way to hear music, without a doubt, be it digitally- recorded music or music recorded unto a wax cylinder is, for the moment, on compact disc. I am late in coming around to technological advancements, but I have no doubt about it: every time I compare an album on vinyl to the same album on CD, the CD wins. But CDs have certainly made things confusing, haven’t they? Let’s take, as a quick example, RCA/Novus, the re- cently-inaugurated jazz line of Bertels- mann, A.G.. The new albums on Novus have, at least in some cases, extra tracks. If you’re a James Moody fan, you’ll have to get the CD to get all of Moody’s new “Something Special.” Fair enough. CDs have the capability of holding more music than LPs, so why not toss on an added track or two — after all, it costs 15 bucks or so to ac- quire one of those digital platters. Now you’d figure this would also hold for reissues. Despite the propondarancc of 30-minute CDs of jazz reissues (I won’t name the guilty parties), a number of labels, spurred by PoIyGram, are going out of their way to add extra tracks to the CDs — alternate takes, previously- unissued takes, anything to beef up the CD. Now let’s go back to RCA. The RCA/Blucbird CDs — at least the Charles Mingus and Sonny Rol- lins — have less music on the compact disc. This is because the vinyl versions come on two records, whereas the CDs are singles. This is good in a way — it reduces the difference in price between the long-playing records and the com- pact discs, and it allows for compact discs of generous lengths — but it will be a thorn in the side of collectors; indeed, anybody who wants things complete. And, to confuse matters further, the lin- er notes in the CD are in no way adjust- ed — they mention the missing tracks as if they were present and accounted for. Weird. The point is that the Mingus and Rollins CDs contain exceptional sound — the Mingus CD (“Tijuana Moods”) ranks with PolyGram’s “Clif- ford Brown With Strings” in its almost miraculous upgrading in sound from the original LP. The castanets on “Ysabel’s Table Dance” explode on the CD — the sound takes the breath away. The thing is, the double album contains two takes of the 10-minute piece while the CD only contains one. For two takes of “Ys- abel’s Table Dance” — something any Mingus fan is going to want — one must buy the double vinyl set. Very confusing. And, oh yes, while I’m in a digital mood, what do you call something that is available on LP, CD, and cassette? Answer — my answer — you call it an al- bum. Nobody ever said that “album” had to refer to vinyl only; in fact. I’m not sure anybody ever said that “record” had to refer to vinyl only. So, on this page anyway, “album” can mean any format. MORE!— I’d like to briefly mention a few reissues that have slipped through here recently. “The Legacy of Bobby Jones” features the late, underrated saxophonist in a fine ’72 session (origi- nally out on Cobblestone, now on Muse). Also on Muse, the previously- unreleased “Sung Heroes,” clarinetist Tony Scott in ’59 sessions with Bill Evans, Scott LaFaro, and Paul Mo- tian. From PoIyGram comes “Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Irving Berlin Songbook,” “Fred Astaire Sings the Irving Berlin Songbook,” “Glenn Mil- ler in Hollywood,” and “Dinah Washington Sings the Bessie Smith Songbook.” 1 know 1 don’t have to tell you about three of those, but if you think Fred Astaire is only a great danc- er, get that Fred Astaire album! Sunny- side has reissued a previously impossible-to-find album from one of my favorite contemporary singers, Meredith D’Ambrosio, “Another Time,” (she made it for her own label a few years back). And Mobile Fidelity Sound Labs — you know, the people who license albums and then half-speed master them into aural heaven — have just spiffed up (along with classic Bea- tles and Bob Dylan albums) Albert King’s “Live Wire/Blues Power,” Sa- rah Vaughan’s “A Time In My Life,” and Maynard Ferguson’s “The Blues Roar” (those three on CD), and (on LP and cassette) Gerry Mulligan’s “Live at the Village Vanguard.” THE TRIO — Oscar Peterson (I) was visited backstage at N. Y. 's Blue Note recently by another pair of ivorymen: Roger Kellaway (c) and Billy Taylor. BOPPING AROUND—Somebody would like me to point out that two fine albums by Rob McConnell & The Boss Brass, that roaring Canadian big band, are out, though nobody knows about it. They are “Atras Da Porta” and “Boss Brass & Woods” (that’s Phil Woods) and they are the product of Calabasos, California’s Art Sound Re- cords. YET ANOTHER NEW CD & CAS- SETTE PACKAGE -Shorewood Packaging, a leading packaging man- ufacturer in the industry, has developed a new construction for both the current 6x12 CD carton and the 4x12 cassette carton which was created in response to a need for better in-store packaging se- curity. The new construction, which is patent-pending, internally locks either a CD jewel box or a Norelco cassette box approximately 1 Va inches from the base of the carton which a small card- board tab which is connected to the base of the container. “This packaging innovation,” says executive VP of mar- keting, Floyd Glinert, “achieves two primary packaging objectives: It greatly reduces potential pilferage, and it can be easily adapted to the automatic packaging equipment that most CD and cassette manufacturers currently use.” Several companies including Arista, CBS, MCA, RCA/Ariola, and WEA have begun evaluating and testing the new package. NARAS Panel according to arbitron ratings, began by de- scribing the differences between a music di- rector and a program director. He says PDs have much less time to listen to music be- cause they are in charge of numerous func- tions including music, promotion, air talent, the sales department and advertising. “You’re in the hot seat. All decisions come through that (program directors) department.” When Schlesinger asked if radio has been playing it too safe, not breaking enough new acts or if radio has “gotten a bum rap,” it became apparent that PDs representing the “oldies” and “classic rock” formats such as the new KLSX or KLOS, were notably ab- sent from the forum. “The great disappointment I have,” said Palmese, “is with the AOR (Album Orient- ed Rock) formats.” He was careful to ex- clude KROQ, a station listed with Arbitron as AOR. “AOR stations used to play many tracks from new albums. They are sheepish now and won’t play a track unless it’s a single. I’d like them to regain their heri- tage.” He called the “classic rock” format “terrible.” “The future of our business is in new music.” Palmese qualified this adding that the the PDs on the panel weren’t afraid to play new music. Wyatt quipped, “You couldn’t get those programmers here to- night because you would have killed them.” Carroll said these “classics” stations seem to be able to hit the 25-54 year old market. “That’s why radio is the way it is. That’s where the money is, but a current AOR sta- tion is the missing format.” Wyatt coun- tered, “If the 25 to 54 year old audience is your market, why not give him ‘White Room’ by Cream if he only listens 10 min- utes per day, not the new David and David cut which he won’t be familiar with.” Car- roll responded, “Just because your over 25, it doesn’t mean you don’t like new music.” Carroll, whose “rock of the 80s” format has become very popular and has generally brought KROQ a consistently high rating for • the 12-17 year-old demographic, ex- plained some misconceptions about the sta- tion. “There is a great illusion from listeners that we are a wild, free form radio station. Virgin Sets Distribution Deal With Atlantic/WEA By Paul Iorio NEW YORK — As expected, Virgin Re- cords has signed a manufacturing and distri- bution deal with Atlantic Records/WEA Corporation. As part of the three-year agreement, Virgin will be responsible for all marketing and promotional functions. It will also maintain its own promotion field staff, headed by Phil Quartararo, vice president of promotion. In a prepared statement, Virgin Records managing directors Jeff Ayeroff and Jordan Harris said: “Each of us has a longstanding history with the WEA family, and consider it the best distribution system in the United States. We look forward to releasing Virgin worldwide acts as well as developing an American rostter which we feel comple- ments and enhances the strengths of the WEA system.” Atlantic Records vice chairman Sheldon Vogel commented: “We are very pleased to welcome Virgin Records back into the At- lantic family. We have the greatest admira- tion for the entire Virgin organization, a label marked from its inception by innova- tion and creativity. Atlantic is proud to be part of Virgin’s new American venture, and we look forward to a fruitful relationship.” Virgin Records’s first release via this new agreement will be the Ennio Morricone origi- nal soundtrack for the Warner Bros, film The Mission. Songwriters Strut Their Stuff At 2nd Annual NAS Salute By Brian Kassan LOS ANGELES — Some two-dozen song- writers performed some of their most mem- orable compositions to a packed house for the National Academy of Songwriters sec- ond annual “Salute to the American song- writer” at the Beverly Theater last week. CD RIDER, TWO— Last week I bab- bled on about CDs: specifically about how good many of the jazz reissues on CD sound. You know it’s funny, but jazz listeners seem to be less willing to bow to sound innovations than listeners of, say, popular music or classical music. I think this has to do with the fact that so much great jazz was recorded in such primitive conditions that jazz listeners have never considered sound that im- portant — “give me some scratchy Lou- is Armstrong over some digital Wynton Marsalis any day,” that kind of attitude. So many of the jazz hounds 1 know have resisted the compact disc era. Well, the time to end that resistance is now. Not because of sound, not be- cause of the fact that the thing plays and plays without having to flip the disc, not because of anything like that at all. Look, it’s one thing to get an alter- nate take or two on a CD, but now things have gotten serious. The new al- bums by jazz veterans Carmen McRae, McCoy Tyner, Phil Woods, and Art Blakey have just come out and, egads, they’re available as CDs. That’s right, no vinyl to be seen. Denon is, not surprisingly, leading the way. Japan's oldest record compa- ny is also its first in innovation, and Denon, who have been recording digi- tally for almost 15 years now, started what they call the Denon Jazz Project earlier this year. Up to now that meant “Long Live the Chief,” the excellent CD by the Count Basie Orchestra, but now that means new product — ex- ceptional new product — from McRae, Tyner, and Woods. “Any Old Time,” Carmen McRae (CY 1216), produced (as was the Tyner) by Tom Ueno, is a marvelously re- laxed session from that recently under- recorded jazz diva. La Carmen has never sounded better — and I do mean that two ways — and somebody had the inspiration to add Clifford Jordan’s tenor and John Collins’ guitar to the date. “Double Trios,” McCoy Tyner (CY- 1128) captures McCoy’s bombastic pi- ano in all its glory: one hears the overtones a-ringing. This is an oddly- titled album, since it leads one to expect a single sextet. Not so, in fact in pre- sents McCoy helming two different quartets — one with his regular rhythm men, bassist Avery Sharpe and drum- mer Louis Hayes, and percussionist Steve Thornton, the other with elec- tric bassist Marcus Miller, drummer Jeff Watts, and Thornton. McCoy sounds unconvincing trying to get funky, but he doesn’t really try that hard. Good Tyner. “Gratitude,” Phil Woods (CY-1316), produced by Bill Goodwin (at 70 min- utes the three CDs), fea- inetist), k in- it the helm of his e‘ Ouin- ieatures red-hoi 1 . Tier ’. Solid • bebop. “Feeling Good,” Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers, is on Delos (C/ CD 4007), and was produced by Orrin Keepnews and Lupe De Leon. What can 1 say? 70 minutes of blistering hard bop from the master and his newest set of progeny (Kenny Garrett, Wallace Roney, Tim Williams, Jean Tous- saint, Donald Brown, and Peter Washington). So there it is, proof positive that if you want to keep up with jazz (and who doesn’t want to keep up with the likes of Messers. Tyner, Woods, and Blakey, and Ms. McRae?) you’ve got to go laser. Got to. SHOP TALK NARM CONVENTION NEWS- Imagine Florida’s winter sun, a garden, and an ocean view as a backdrop to NARM’s 1987 Convention Exhibit Area which will be located on the grounds of the Fountainebleau Ho- tel, Miami Beach. It provides the sin- gle best opportunity for suppliers to reach music merchandisers at one time and location. The latest in products and services will be on display during a three day period of for the 29th annu- al NARM 1987 Convention (Febru ary 14-16). Everything imaginable can be found at NARM ’87 exhibits includ- ing pre-recorded products, blank tape, video accessories, computer hardware and software, etc. Suppliers to NARM’s regular and associate members have the opportunity to meet with their cus- tomers and potential customers during specified hours on Saturday, Sunday and Monday afternoon. Permanent ca- banas and a tent (specially designed and built by IBM) create a perfect exhibi- tion environment in the garden. The 82’x 100’ tent contains 57 exhibit spaces, complete with carpeted floor, ceiling fans, screens and lighting. Each booth measures 8’x 10’ and includes the pipe and drape for the booth, a 7” z 44” company identification sign, a 6’ conference table draped and skirted, two chairs and 24-hour security. Reser- vations for booths must be made simul- taneously with general convention registration. Because of the Presidents’ weekend and the tendency for NARM Conventions to sell out quickly, reserva- tions should be made now. Only Narm Members may attend. The Year In Review ’86: Oi Legal Problems And Boxe< Sets And Benefits Galore By Lee Jeske NEW YORK — For the music industry, 1986 may be remembered as the year of the courts and Congress; as lawsuits and allega- tions of various wrongdoings were released almost as quickly as compact discs. It will certainly be remembered as the year the CD took hold — really took hold — and the year of the Bruce box. Executives were on the move at a brisk pace in ’86, and companies came and went with unsual alacrity — there were a whole lot of shake-ups going on. And the music industry continued its giving ways; with new benefits raising money and consciousness’ and old benefits reaping in some additional green. On the legal side of things, NBC Televi- sion opened a seamy can of worms early in the year with a report linking various inde- pendent promoters to organized crime. La- bels panicked, dropping their indies; indies panicked, scuffling to pay their bills. Mafia connections were also mentioned as Rou- lette Records president Morris Levy was ar- rested, along with Roulette controller Howard Fisher, and charged with extortion and racketeering. Probes of possible payola and strong-arm tactics in the music business were said to be well under way in New York, Los Angeles, Newark, Cleveland, Mi- ami, and Philadelphia. “Sue You, Sue Me,” may resound as an ’86 theme. Solar brought a breach of con- tract suit against Elektra/ Asylum and Warner Comm.; Sugar Hill named MCA in a $240 million suit claiming “concerted par- ticipation in fraudulent, illegal, and corrupt activities” regarding the sale of the Check- er/Chess/Cadet catalogue; MCA filed a $10 million suit against Scorpio Records; the RIAA filed a suit to try to get Tower Records to refrain from bringing in parallel imports (that was later settled) and then saw to it that bigwig record pirate Anthony Dharmawan was duly convicted and sen- tenced (two year suspended sentence and a $100,000 fine). And the Dead Kennedys were charged in L.A. with distributing harmful matter to minors, thanks to a ques- tionable poster contained with their “Fran- kenchrist” LP. Congress had music in its ears this year — in fact, the RIAA announced it was moving to D.C. next year to get closi action. Home taping — and, i the dreaded approach of Digital Tape recorders — had the record la in arms. To that end, a Senate Ji Subcommittee approved home tapir lation in the spring and held a hearin summer on recording equipment. In a bill was introduced in the Senate to that DAT recorders include “copj encoders. Earlier this month, the companies and the RIAA headed to ( to meet with representatives of Ja manufacturers, who, in effect, told tl to jump in the lake. But the RIAA v the only music industry watchdog in ington this year, as BMI and ASCAP ued their uphill battle to protec blanket licensing deals with broadcai the fight was joined in front of the Judiciary Committee in the spring, eryone’s surprise, the PMRC wai through most of ’86, but, just before mas, they reared their heads once naming 15 ’85 albums that they served warning stickers. On the companies-on-the-go side, mann bought up all of RCA Record G.E., a move that was finally signed, and delivered just last week. Not coil tally, RCA offered its employees “vol lay-offs” in the fall as part of an effort its staff; an effort that, apparently, mi some success. Also rolling along wer (continued on '. Cash Box December 27, Japaii M«j©cts Mecard Industry l^i«a For Momm Taping Curbs By Stephen Padgett LOS ANGELES — Record company execu- tives from America and Europe meeting with representatives of the Japanese con- sumer electronics industry could not come to an agreement on the controversial issue of an anti-home taping “chip” last week in Vancouver, British Columbia. The Electronic Industry Association of Japan rejected pleas from representatives of the recording industry to install a lockout device in new digital audio tape (DAT) ma- chines that would prevent consumers from taping commercially recorded music. The DAT machines, which will hit the consumer market place as early as the first quarter of 1987, pose a serious threat to the viability of pre-recorded music, according to mem- bers of the recording industry. DAT can re- produce master-quality sound matching that ofthe compact disc. DAT cassettes are about half the size of conventional audio cassettes. “The meeting failed to reconcile sharp differences on whether to shield copy- righted sound recordings from master-quali- ty home taping facilitated by DAT,” according to a statement issued by the Re- cording Industry Association of America (RIAA). The record industry hoped that the Japa- nese would cooperate in supporting legisla- tion to be brought before Congress that would require manufacturers of DAT to in- stall the copyright protection chip to pre- vent home recording. In a statement released Thursday, De- cember 11, Shoichi Saba, chairman of To- shiba and chairman of the EIAJ said, “The electronics industry is moving toward an era of all-digital products. To cripple or delay one of the key elements of this era simply would mean less growth, less progress and a poorer environment for con- sumers and the industries that serve them.” The RIAA already insists that home taping siphons $1.5 billion in revenues from the record in- dustry annually. The advent of the sonically perfect digital taping process makes home taping now a real threat to record manufacturers. Shoichi rejected this reasoning by record company representatives, stating, “We be- lieve the digital audio recorder, like every other consumer electronics product, will be used wisely and responsibly by consumers to the benefit of the hardware and recording industries alike.” It is the electronics indus- try opinion that the most aggressive home tapers are also the largest consumers of pre- recorded music. ON JAZZ CASH BOX JAZZ ALBUMS IT’S A WRAP—Usually 1 use this space at this time to recap the general year in jazz. However, such a recap ap- peared in out jazz issue in September, so there’s no need to go into all of that again. I would, however, like to go over what has been an extraordinary year in the jazz record business. Extraordi- nary in terms of volume: I reckon that over 450 albums of new or previously- unissued jazz (or stuff claiming to be jazz) have been released along with over 240 reissues. Extraordinary, too, in terms of quality — in both categories. Elsewhere in this issue, you’ll find my list of the ten best jazz albums of the year. Now, normally, I can easily come up with a half-dozen entrants; then I choose a few other worthy contenders to fill out the list. Not this year: a list of my 30 top jazz albums of ’86 wouldn’t have covered all the exceptional prod- uct that has been made available. I mean exceptional. First, a few remarks about the list. In order to be fair, I arrange everything alphabetically by title (fair to myself — I’d spend a week debating over whether something should go seventh or eighth). However there was one album in ’86 that stands out above the rest, and that is “Song X.” The other nine are tied for second, but “Song X” is, for my money, the best jazz album of the year. Another thing is the subject of reis- sues and previously-unissued material. I never consider these albums for my Top 10, since I feel that they were, per- haps, the best albums of some other year. It’s not really fair to compare the best work of contemporary artists to ac- knowledged — or even previously-un- heard — masterpieces of the jazz elders. For what it’s worth, the tag of Reissue of the Year must go to the extraordi- nary 21-record boxed set “The Com- plete Keynote Collection” (PolyGram), because it brings back into print scores of classic jazz performances and adds dozens of worthy previously-unissued items. PolyGram also reissued stunning boxed sets of material from Sarah Vaughan and Helen Merrill. Other magnificent and weighty boxed sets in- clude the Benny Goodman and Duke Ellington sets from RCA and the just-issued-within-the-past-few-days “Complete Riverside Recordings of Thelonious Monk” (more on that next year). 1 would be remiss if I didn’t also point out fine single and double al- bum reissues from the Fantasy group (the OJCs just kept on coming). Blue Note, Sonet, and the rejuvenated Im- pulse! and RCA Bluebird lines. Bravo! As to previously-unissued material. Sonny Rollins’ “Alternate Takes” (Contemporary), “The Terry Gibbs Dream Band” (Contemporary), and the second volume of Charles Mingus’ “Tijuana Moods” should be mentioned. As to the new stuff, the most impres- sive thing to note is that, for the first time since I’ve been doing this, all ten of Top 10 are American albums. Incredi- ble, positively incredible. This has been CRUSADING — Violinist L. Subramaniam (c) stopped by N. Y. ’s Blue Note recently to catch a set by Joe Sample (!) and Wilton Felder, aka The Crusaders. such a good year for jazz albums that several artists have released two fine albums, including Ornette Coleman (Geffen and Caravan of Dreams), the World Saxophone Quartet (None such and Black Saint), Abdullah Ibra- him (B1ack Hawk and Enja), the George Adams/Don Pullen Quar- tet (Blue Note and Soul Note), the Phil Woods Quintet (Black Hawk and Denon), and Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers (Concord and Delos). There’s no space to go into specifics, but others who have put out fine al- bums this year include Stan Getz, Ray Anderson, Donald Harrison /Ter- ence Blanchard, Steve Lacy, the Paris Reunion Band, Walt Dicker- son/Richard Davis, Khan Jamal, Mark Johnson, Joe Henderson, Carmen Lundy, Muhal Richard Abrams, Leni Stern, Butch Morris, Third Kind of Blue, The Paris Re- union Band, Branford Marsalis, Gene Harris, Miles Davis, The Leaders, Mel Lewis, Dino Betti Van Der Noot, and Nabil Totah. I’m sure there are numerous others I’m leaving out. I don’t really want to name labels — it would take me all day — but I’d like to point out that Black Hawk, in its first year, has managed to get out an unusually large number of quality re- leases, and that Columbia — which has always been a leader in jazz — has been asleep at the switch. A promised pro- gram of reissues never materialized, and its new jazz recordings were few and far between. With such labels as Atlantic, MCA, and RCA hustling and bustling to get the jazz out, it’s odd to find Columbia snoozing away. So there you have it: a lot of good sounds have passed my way. I finally became a CD convert (kudos to Denon, PolyGram, Impulse, RCA, and several others who have kept the jazz CDs brimming in the stores — reissues, main- ly, but Denon is big on CD-onlys) and I now just have to find a way to make room on my built-for-LPs shelves for the little digital platters. So, if you ask me (and somebody re- cently did ask me), I think the state of jazz is pretty healthy. But no jazz writer is a real optimist, and 1 am no excep- tion. The bubble could burst any sec- ond, but I think the bottom line of all this is that more people are beginning to appreciate jazz and I think this is going to last for awhile. Or I hope it is. rOGELMAN TO RECEIVE AWAMD -The American Jewish Committee, a national pioneer hu- man-relations agency dedicated to the protection of civil and religious rights of Jews here and abroad, and advancing the cause of improved human relations for all people, founded in 1906, will hon- or Lou Fogelnaan, president of Show Industries, at a dinner-dance to held at the New York Hilton Hotel on Satur- day evening, February 7, 1987. The an- nouncement that Fogelman would receive AJC’s annual Music Industry Human Relations Award was made by Joe Cohen, of Leslie Group, the general chairman of the dinner. Cohen listed the following industry leaders in- volved in various aspects of the plan- ning: Paul Smith, of CBS’ Henry Droz, of WEA; Sal Licata of RCA’; and Nicholas Santrizos, of Vista Home Video, co-chairpersons. Harry Anger, of PolyGram, program chair- man. Others were Marcia Kessel- man, of Coliseum Video, East Coast chairperson; Paul David, of Came- lot Enterprises; Joe and Rachelle Friedman, of J&R Music World’ Jim Schwartz, of Schwartz Broth- ers, Inc.; Barrie Bergman, of Re- cord Bar; and Roy Imber, of Elroy Enterprises, honorary chairpersons. “This year’s recipient of the Human re- lations award is a very special man,” says David M. Gordis, executive vice president of the AJC. “A man of pur- pose and of destiny, a man with a dream who has won the respect and admiration of all who know him by the extraordinary example he has set.” Fo- gelman left Holland from the ashes of World War II. “At the young age of seen, he came alone from Holland as a stranger in a strange land, unfamiliar with its customs or its language, forti- fied only by a deep sense that all would be possible in the United States.” In- deed, that dream became reality 12 years ago when Fogelman and three close friends opened the first four Mu- sic Plus record stores. Today he is president of Show Industries which encompasses 46 Music Plus stores, and the largest One Stop Operation on the West Coast — City 1 Stop. In 1979, the National Association of Record Merchandisers (NARM) presented the Retailers of the Year Award to Music Plus, and in 1980, Fogelman was honored as Music Re- tailer Personality of the Year. A long-time member of NARM, he has served on its Board of Directors and as its president. He was also instrumental in the chartering of the Video Soft- ware Dealer’s Association (VSDA) and currently serves on its Board of Di- rectors as vice president. Cohen says Fogelman deserved the committee’s tribute as “an individual who had had a profound impact on both home video and the music industry as a whole, while adhering to the highest standards of personal integrity and dedication to the betterment of the community as a whole. He is being honored not merely because he has the skills of a successful leader in exceptional measure, but more, because of the underlying princi- ples which have governed his choices and the direction of his efforts.” RHINO BRINGS BACK THE 78 RPM — The Santa Monica, CA based Rhino Records, purveyors of unusual recordings, oldies and a recent surprise CHR hit, Billy Vera’s “At This Mo- ment,” have done it again. They’re bringing back the 78rpm record as part of “Jukebox Classics,” a 25-disc box set which features 50 (count ‘em) 1950’s hits such as Jerry Lee Lewis’ “Whole Lotta shakin’ Going’ On” and the Chordettes’ “Mr. Sand- man,” which were released in the for- mat at one time. The set is primarily of interest to collectors whose classically designed jukeboxes only play 78s. r pearing for the first time since 1959, e 78 format, contrary to popular misc i- ception, disappeared because of s bulk, not audio technology. The new. 5 and 33 1/3 pressings were more n - ketable. According to musicologist < d radio show host Dr. Demento, “a v II pressed 78 sounded better than m;; of the 45s. For instance, Elvis’ Sun : - gles sound much better in their I pressing than at 45.” With the appc - ance of the 12-inch single in the last f ; years, bulkiness no longer seems to > an issue with customers. POINTS WEST SCHMOOZATORIUM—Get ready for Music Business Symposium 3. This year’s keynote speaker is Bruce Lundvall. president of Manhattan Records, who appears at the opening night presentation and cocktail recep- tion at the Beverly Theatre April 2. The symposiunn will once again be held at the Ambassador Hotel, April 2-5, where you’ll find 25 panels with a slant, this year, toward the international market. RAISING THE SOUTH—Southern rockers the Georgia Satellites opened here for Bob Seger last week at the Forum, delivering a fiery set of heavyweight rock'n’roll. It was refresh- ing to see an act that dares to dress down, or at least not dress up, for a show. They were a tough act to follow (sorry. Bob) the night Points West at- tended, at any rate. It was one of those rare instances when an opener takes the audience with 'em when they leave, if ya’ knowhutimean, Vern. IN FROM GOTHAM— Reliable sources tell us that EPA v.p. of market- ing Ron McCarrell will leave to take the same job at Capitol in L A. by the end of January. Neither record com- pany, beinmg record companies, will confirm this. BEL-FIRES KEEP BURNING— The Beh Fires have a date coming up at Club Lingerie January 15. THE LOCAL BUZZ—What better way to ring in the new year than with an earful of one of the more promising West Coast guitar bands around these days, soon to deposit an LP on the Birdcage label for your listening plea- sure. The band we speak of is the Bcl- Fires, who earned a feature pick in these pages last spring with a cut from their debut EP single “Pall For The Sky.” Vocalist Cynthia Isabella’s got a voice that gets to the heart of each thoughtful lyric, sounding something like a Deborah lyall/Siouxie/ Martha Davis hybrid - plaintive, but not adolescently so. Shades of U2 come to mind musically, with guitarist George Steeley in the lead. The new LP, untitled as we go to press, is being produced by Jim Hill, known for his work with such acts as the Dream Syndicate and Wall of Voodoo. The band spent last summer touring the southwest. They make it back to L.A. clubland January 15, with a show at Club Lingerie. Also worth a listen in 87 is an EP called “Uptown Thinking” frorr! Attack, with members most re- cently ir. -arnated as L.A.’s The Dogs. Attack has Detroiter’s rock sensibility (bassist Mary Kay and guitarist/lead vocalist Louren Molinare hail from there), and from the band’s ferocious name, some people think they’re a heavy metal outfit. Not so. Well, not entirely. Attack encorporates anthe- mic, heavy metal-ish choruses into oth- erwise roots-rocking tunes, creating a unique texture, spearheaded by Molin- are’s rough & ready rock'n’roll vocals. The album was produced by Paul Sabu. WHEN LAST SEEN TOGETHER— Charlie Sexton (!) and Tonio K were last seen performing together at a benefit at the Whisky, before Sexton hurt his hand and couldn ’t join K onstage at the Palace a week later. POLYGRAM’S CD PRICING COUP—A report which appeared in Daily Variety last week concerning Po- lyGram’s plans to break the $10 CD price barrier was rather premature, ac- cording to Harry Palmer, PolyGram’s vice president of special markets (ap- parently, the information was given as a sideline to another issue, but our hats go off to reporter Ken Terry for gain- ing the news from Palmer). At present, the company has no firm details of the move, though the price slash will indeed take place. No titles have been decided upon. Palmer told Cash Box, nor has the company arrived at any prices. An announcement outlining the final out- come of such decisions will be made soon, he said, perhaps as early as next week. IN PARTING—Congrats, conragts, to Claudia and Larry Vallon (Larry is executive vice president of the Univer- sal Amphitheatre), on the release of their first single, Kelly, who debuted at 71/2 lbs and 21” . . . Warner Bros. Records has a proud announcement of their own. Seems “Skeletons From The Closet,” the 1974 collection of Great- ful Dead tunes, has been certified Pla- tinum by the R.l.A.A. . . . Composer/ producer Morgan Ames has been busy of late. Ames (who co-wrote “Bar- etta’s Theme” with Dave Grusin) is co-producing, with Jeff Weber, a live album for Diane Shuur and the Count Basie Band this month in To- kyo. Upon her return from Japan, Ames will then set about scoring a new syndicated TV series, Karen 's Song, for Fox Television . . . Stop the presses! This just in: Elton John’s byopsy re- sults find the singer’s been suffering from a non-malignant throat lesion. OVER STORY ^ad Or Alive: Recluses Ready For A Breakthrough By Paul lorio YORK — Dead Or Alive are an ano- in pop music in that they have had ijuccess without doing many concerts rviews. The British quartet currently blanket ‘no interview’ policy which aim is partly the result of having been [, ated too many times. Not only that, ey didn’t even tour behind their pre- album and don’t have any firm plans / live any time soon. Even their publi- lotos (see above) conceal more than veal. Whether or not all this reclusion Iped them commercially, it is noneth- fair bet that their new album, “Mad, taind Dangerous To Know” (Epic), may I breakthrough they’ve been looking w |is album will do it for them in Amer- bys Jerry Jaffe, the North American Dement consultant for the band, ip hoping that in the same way Ma- 1 broke through the clubs to pop radio feos, that we’re going to try and take ck also .1 think for the first time in t time we’re using the clubs as a real I jse.” ce club play has been largely respon- ir the band’s success so far, particu- |i England where they have had a ! )f hits. “Youthquake,” their previous sold respectably in America as well, vjng a top ten single in “You Spin Me i (Like A Record).” Their first single i‘Mad, Bad . . .” is “Brand New ^ ’ and that promises to do at least as ‘Brand New Lover’ will go top ten . d then I think it will be re-released in t ” says Jaffe. “I think we’re going to t ligger success with ‘Brand New jihere than in Britain where it kind of If at #31 for technical reasons.” *:he band’s unwillingness to actively ^j||ie their records has kept them hover- 1'ie gold level when many believe they ie much bigger. “I’m hoping they’ll s ver and tour a bit more on this album ' ! they didn’t do any touring at all on I' one, which I think certainly held i| ick to an extent,” says Annie Rose- , the CBS UK A&R director who i: lead Or Alive in 1983. “They’re not overly keen to perform live, or they haven’t been until now, but I think this album will see them touring a lot more than before.” Says Jaffe: “While they have a huge follow- ing in Britain and a big dance club base there, they haven’t gone to the Duran Duran area yet.” Dead Or Alive came out of the early eighties independent record scene in Britain that produced such artists as Julian Cope, Pete Wiley of Wah, and Echo and the Bun- nymen. Dead Or Alive — comprised of Pete Burns, Mike Percy, Steve Coy, and Tim Lever — initially recorded for Inevitable Re- cords, a Liverpool-based independent com- pany, releasing singles that placed high on the indie charts. “They had two very suc- cessful independent singles, and prior to that they had been a band called Night- mares In Wax which had a relatively high profile as an independent band,” says Rose- berry. “They had had a fair amount of press, they hadn’t done much live work, and I suppose the press was making us more and more aware of them, and it was around that time when there were a lot of interesting things going on in the independent scene in the U.K. And we went up to see them (in late ‘82) at one of their few gigs and we just saw a great show, a great live act, great material, and we signed them shortly after that.” Roseberry says the band’s predilection for privacy was evident even when they were an indie band. “You had to actually go out and seek them,” she says. “I think we were one of the first record companies to get in there. We had a fair amount of com- petition to sign them but at that stage they kind of kept themselves away from major record companies.” Is all this just a calculated effort to give the band an aura of mystery? “There could be an element of that,” she says. “But I don’t think that’s necessarily a bad thing. Maybe (vocalist Pete) Burns had reached a stage in the UK where he’d been overex- posed, therefore he would draw back and not tell anybody anything. He has very strong control over his career . . . He’s very much of an enigma.” M Sox January 17, 1987 EAST COASTINGS SHAVE OFF THAT VACATION beard and thoughtfully dispose of those Christmas cards because it’s time to get back to the rude business of coping with yet another new year. To soften the blow, I headed to MTV’s New Year’s Eve Ball, which was immeasurably bet- ter than last year’s Starship/Hooters extravaganza, and paid tribute to a year that had everyone asking what the hell happened to the Del Fuegos anyway. TWANGIN’ — Dave Edmunds (I) was joined 6y Brian Setzer (r). Marshall Crenshaw, and Carl Perkins during his set at MTV’s New Year's Eve ball. Like I said, this year’s ball was much better — mainly because of Dave Ed- munds’s set. Not only did Edmunds play a half-hour of his greatest hits, but he also brought on Marshall Cren- shaw, Brian Setzer, and Carl Per- kins to play. The Perkins/Edmunds match-up was particularly inspired, and their version of “Honey Don’t” was as relaxed and intimate as a front-porch jam. Granted, it’s still a thrill to hear Ed- munds do “Crawling From The Wreck- age,” “Girls Talk,” “Queen Of Hearts,” and “I Knew The Bride” in quick succession, but after recently seeing him do the same tunes at the Felt Forum the kick wasn’t as great. Unfor- tunately, this revivalist is currently in the business of reviving songs he re- corded seven or more years ago, most of them from the classic “Repeat When Necessary” album. Why doesn’t he play songs from later albums like “D - E - 7” or “Twangin’’? Or, better yet, de- velop new material, covering songs by writers like Steve Earle (“Gettin’ Tough”), The BoDeans (“Angels” — imagine what he could do with that one in a “Girls Talk” arrangement), and re- cent Elvis Costello (“Big Light”)? I mean. I’m looking forward to Ed- munds’s new live album, “I Hear You Rockin’’ (Columbia), as much as the next person, but I’m looking forward even more to Edmunds one day blowing “Repeat When Necessary” out of the water with a new, equally brilliant stu- dio album. (Edmunds plays the Ritz Jan. 30 and 31.) BY NOW everybody’s probably tired of hearing how Alice Cooper prefi- gured the punks, how “1 Wanna Be Se- dated” sounds just like “Elected,” and how Husker Du and Gone sound just like side two of “Killer.” But the fact is, it’s true. Seeing Alice Cooper’s recent show at the Sun Dome in Tampa, Flor- ida reaffirmed my belief in Cooper as a seminal force in ‘70’s rock. But in ‘80’s rock? Probably that too; after all, arena bombast and club thrash are still rock staples, even in the ‘80’s. Perversely, this makes his old songs sound fresher than his new ones, the same way, for example, Iggy Pop’s “Lust For Life” sounds newer than “Cry For Love.” Though “Constrictor” (MCA) has its moments, and though songs like “Teen- age Frankenstein” worked up the crowd as much as the big hits, it was “Under My Wheels” that had fans sing- ing all the way down the stairs and into the parking lot. MOJO NIXON AND SKID Roper have one less thing to write about now that MTV VJ Martha Quinn has left the station for points unknown. Though Quinn is gone, the guest VJs are defini- tely not; MTV has made the guest seg- ments a fortnightly feature, and the first VJ of the year was no less than Ray Davies. The head Kink recently talked with Cash Box {see interview in this issue) and had high praise for some New York musicians, particularly Suzanne Vega. “Suzanne Vega writes neat little tunes, with good little chords — and a nice voice. I mean you can’t knock her really,” he says. “1 think when folk loses that grey beard, bald head, and fat gut image it will be a source of new writers coming through. Because if we can get that stigma away from folk — something like Suzanne Vega and The Pogues do — it would be a very good time in popular music.” TRUE BLUE DUO — Madonna is being nabbed by a megaphone wielding Coati- mundi on the set of the upcoming Warner Bros, film Slammer. II!/ , t Box January 17, 1987 ON JAZZ MONKERY— Last year was a banner year for jazz boxed sets, but it took until the very last days of the year before the biggest of the sets was issued. “The Complete Riverside Recordings of Thelonious Monk” is a 22-record mountain of a set — it’s the biggest box of records I’ve ever encountered — which, quite simply, includes the very best recordings of one of the greatest jazz figures we’ve ever had. There is no way to adequately de- scribe the talents of Thelonious Sphere Monk — you just have to hear him. His witty, offbeat compositions, his jagged, dissonant piano playing, his square- shouldered rhythm — nobody has ever sounded like Monk, written like Monk, or, for that matter, looked, walked or dressed like Monk. The Riverside years, from the mid-’50s to the early-’bOs, saw Monk’s transition from obscure cult-fi- gure to widely-acclaimed cult-figure — when he left Riverside he went on to a lucrative contract at Columbia Records and even landed on the cover of Time Magazine. Monk had many sides and this set captures them all: from solo piano to big band, from his breathtaking origin- als to his sparkling interpretations of standards, from the classic quartet for- mation with Charlie Rouse to various- sized ensembles featuring, amongst many others. Sonny Rollins, John Coltrane, Coleman Hawkins, Clark Terry, Art Blakey, Max Roach, Johnny Griffin, Roy Haynes, Oscar Pettiford, Kenny Clarke, and Gerry Mulligan. For my money, this is some of the best music made by anyone this century and this weighty set is well worth its weighty price-tag and the chore of lugging it home from the store. It should be noted that most of this ma- terial — there are a couple of new alter- nate takes scattered here and there — has been readily available from the good people of Fantasy, but there is nothing quite like having it all in one handy package. Appropriately, Orrin Keepnews, who produced all of the original sessions, put the set together. For somebody who has not quite exper- ienced the world of Thelonious Monk- ...well, just watch their faces as the music unfurls. A landmark jazz collection! COMING ATTRACTIONS—There will be more about all of this in the com- ing months, but I’d like to point out a couple of things that the jazz record bu- siness has in store for ’87. Last month 1 criticized Columbia Records for its jazz- light ’86. So, nu, now Columbia up and finally unveils an enormous project called “Columbia Jazz Masterpieces,” a series that takes classic Columbia jazz albums — and I don’t think any label has a larger holding of classic jazz albums — and digitally remasters the pants off them. Now they tell me there will be between 60 and 120 of these things re- leased this year — in all three formats, by the way — many of them items that have been in the Columbia catalogue for ages. Can “Kind of Blue” sound any better? We shall see. Columbia is also promising a slate of new jazz record- ings Tim Berne, Eddie Gomez, and Grover Washington Jr. are among the new signings. Blue Note, which slowly began drip- ping out CDs last year, promises a flood of the discs this year, including lots of stuff from the catalogue, most of it beefed up with alternate takes and pre- viously-unissued tracks (Columbia in- sists on keeping the LP lengths intact on their CDs). PolyCram will, any minute now, re- vive the Verve imprint for new record- ings, and Island’s new Antilles New Directions label will give us jazz and al- most-jazz recordings from, among others, Courtney Pine, Nana Vas- concelos, Helcio Milito, and Jim Pepper. BRANFORD AND SON - Branford Mar- salis introduces the next Marsalis generation, son Renee, to Sting backstage at L.A. 's Be- verly Theatre, where the saxophonist was performing with his quartet. SAUTER-FINEGAN BEGIN AGAIN—One of the most delightful jazz big bands, to my ears, was the one that arrangers Eddie Sauter and Bill Finegan led from 1952-1957. Witty and swinging and adventurous, any good opportunity to hear that band’s music is a welcome one. At New York’s Town Hall on January 25, a reunion of the 15 of the 19 members of the original band, under the baton of Bill Finegan, will take place, with guest soloists Jim Hall, Lew Soloff, Eddie Daniels, Marvin Stamm, and The New York Saxophone Quartet. Saxophonist Wally Kane is producing the thing, and a good time is guaranteed for all. The box office number is (212) 840- 2824. CROSSROADS— “Music at the Crossroads: An American Sampler” is the name of a nice series that features free early-evening concerts at the 42nd Street branch of the Whitney Museum (that’s in the Philip Morris Building — they sponsor the series — across from Grand Central Station). Muhal Ri- chard Abrams and Marian McPart- land kick things off on January 20 and Jimmy Heath and Tito Puente end things on March 17, with such interest- ing acts as the Kronos Quartet (March 10) and a double-bill of Vassar Clements and the Andy Statman Klezmer Orchestra (February 3) in between. NARM AWARDS BANQUET NEWS — Elektra Records’ emerging performer Anita Baker will perform at the National Association of Re- cording Merchandisers (NARM) Awards Banquet on February 16, to cli- max the 29th annual NARM conven- tion. This year’s convention, scheduled for February 13-17 at the Fontaineb- leau Hotel in Miami Beach, Flor- ida, is themed, “Music... The Beat Goes On.” Baker’s warm, versatile soul/jazz stylings have made her one of the country’s most sought-after R&B/ Pop performers. She is currently in the middle of an extremely successful American tour, which has been high- lighted by a Radio City Music Hall sell-out performance. Her debut album, “Rapture,” has sold nearly two-mil- lion copies and features two charting singles including “Sweet Love” and the title track. The 1987 Banquet will also feature the return of Joe Smith, the newly appointed vice president and chief executive for Capitol Indus- tries-EMI, Inc, as Master of Ceremon- ies. The Awards Banquet has traditionally closed every NARM Convention since 1958 and features the presentation of the NARM Best Seller Awards, which represent the only industry recognition of artists and product that is based on actual sales in stores. Other awards to be presented at February’s gala include both the Retailer and Wholesaler of the Year. Attendance at the NARM Ban- quet is open to registrants for the 1987 NARM convention Call (609) 596-2221 for more information. VSDA APOLOGIZES TO PARA- MOUNT HOME VIDEO -The Vi- deo Software Dealers Association printed a letter in the “We Write Let- ters,” column in their December issue of the VSDA Reports newsletter writ- ten by VSDA president Arthur Morowitz which chastised Para- mount Home Video for allegedly providing “certain distributors (The term ‘distributors’, of course, includes rack jobbers)” with copies of “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom,” and allowing them to put it “into the hands of their retail customers” before the street date “to the competitive in jury of the other non-favored retailers and distributors.” The VSDA has sent out a letter of apology to Paramount and to their members as well as the let- ter from the senior vice president and general manager of Paramount Home Video, Timothy Clott, which prompted the apology. It seems that the VSDA did not receive a press re- lease that Paramount sent out No- vember 4, which “outlined our actions against street date violators.” VSDA president Mickey Granberg apolo- gized for not pursuing a “response to the letter, to have been printed simul- taneously with it” and for a “lack of professionalism” on the part of their journalism. POINTS WEST AWARD OF MERIT— Elvis Pres- ley would have been 52 this month, but the really unbelievable thing is that it’s been ten years since he died, Presley will be honored this year by the Ameri- can Music Awards, which plans to bestow its annual “Award of Merit” to the King of Rock ‘N’Roll during the big show at L.A.’s Shrine Auditorium Janu- ary 26. It will be the first posthumous Award of Merit presented by the Ameri- can Music Awards in its 14-year history. The American Music Awards have also announced this year’s list of presenters, which includes such notables as (pre- pare your eyes, the list is long] Anita Baker, Stephen Bishop, Belinda Carlisle, Peter Cetera, Chubby Checker, Earl Thomas Conley, Bil- ly Davis, Jr., El Debarge, Sheena Easton, Exile, the Forester Sis- ters, Bob Geldof, Mickey Gilley, Herbie Hancock, Apollonia Ko- tero, Lisa Lisa, Kenny Loggins, Gloria Loring, Marilyn McCoo, Reba McEntire, Meatloaf, Roger Miller, Ronnie Milsap, Eddie Mon- ey, New Edition, Billy Ocean, Ray Parker, Jr., Anita Pointer, Lou Rawls, Ronnie Spector, Stephen Stills, Randy Travis, Tanya Tuck- er, Luther Vandross, Billy Vera, Steve Wariner, Dwight Yoakam, plus members of Cameo, Miami Sound Machine and Mr. Mister. Inci- dentally, the American Music Awards nominees are compiled from the year- end charts of . . . guess who? The show is produced by Dick Clark Televi- sion Productions. It will be hosted by Diana Ross and televised on ABC. And please folks. Cash Box doesn’t give the awards, we just supply the chart information. (You’d be surprised at how many calls we get from people with questions about plaques and statues and inscriptions and stuff). LATE AND GREAT— The American Mu- sic Awards honors Elvis Presley this year with its first posthumous Award of Merit. Gregory Dobrin NEWFACES TO WATCH “It sounded like a really good name for a band,” explains Rob Vandeven, one half of the Lucy Show. “It was origi- nally a bit of a laugh and it stuck.” Fellow Canadians Vandeven, who plays bass, and Mark Bandola, who plays guitar and Keyboards, are the nu- cleus of the band whose first album, “Undone,” received rave critical re- views, largely appealing to the alterna- tive/college crowd in America. On their new LP, “Mania,” the Lucy Show continue and improve their guitar textured sound. “It’s quite a bright sound, and tuneful as well,” says Van- deven. “We go very much for melody and harmony in our music, but the songs are first and foremost before the sound. I suppose we are singer/song- writers dare I say.” Vandeven and Bandola, friends since high school, grew up in Calgary, Alber- ta where they acquired a penchant for melody listening to the Beatles, the Monkees and the Beach Boys. “My parents gave me piano lessons at the age of five for about four years,” says Bandola. “All that time I really hat- ed playing the piano and the thought of being forced to play music, but as soon as the lessons stopped, I started compos- ing my little tunes on the piano and when pop music became more important to me I became interested in learning guitar like most little boys would and from what I learned on piano, 1 sort of taught myself to play guitar. I’m still grateful to my parents for making me go through that hellish experience of piano lessons.” Vandeven, who had no formal musi- cal training, learned how to play the bass with help from Mark and just “learning onstage.” Vandeven recalls his child- hood. “I used to have these wooden cut- outs of guitars. My brother did the sawing and they looked really good with little strings painted on with felt pen. We pretended we were the Beatles.” When Bandola went to art school in London for a couple years, Vandeven followed for an “extended holiday” and stayed as well. Eventually, the two formed the Lucy Show, generating quite a stir with their first single “Leo- nardo Da Vinci,” which landed them a record contract. Although both have similar vocal styles resulting in the smooth harmo- nies which characterize their sound, they prefer to write their songs sepa- rately, yet arrangements are often done THE LUCY SHOW in the studio. Lyrically, Bandola plores personal themes whereas, \i deven is more narrative and visual. “Just in the initial stages of writirl song,” Bandola says, “I’m not very] terested in having people around w I’m struggling with it or toying with tend to feel more comfortable if room is empty.” They released their first LP as a fcj piece band and after they used same musicians on the new album, tij realized that they wanted to have m control over their compositions. “When we had the four piece,” s Vandeven, “we kind of let things spread out and the band lost it’s sej of direction.” This case of too m;; chefs spoiling the broth led the paii| begin working with a revolving cas players including Dave Ruffy worked with Aztec Camera and the \ terboys as well as the former Lotus E, i ers guitarist. “It exposes them,” s. f Bandola, “and we’re not confined one sound. We can use their talent c use the Lucy Show as an umbn which is more fun for us. We can p: and choose ideas they present, but good to have the control.” The new LP was produced by Jc Leckie of Simple Minds fame. ONJAZZ\ THAT TIME AGAIN— Last year at this time I went into a whole harangue about the Grammy Awards. This year I’ve decided not to go into a whole ha- rangue about the Grammy Awards. I’ve decided, for the most part, to ignore them. Although this year’s jazz nomina- tions are a scintilla better than last year’s (thanks only to the fact that Sting didn’t make another “jazz” al- bum this year), the Grammy nomina- tions still display a general lack of knowledge about current jazz record re- leases— the nominations only rarely represent the best records in each cate- gory. One quick example: Bobby McFerrin’s “Spontaneous Inventions” (Blue Note) is, in one man’s opinion, the finest jazz vocal album of the past two years. The Grammys do not include a nomination for “Spontaneous Inven- tions,” but they don’t ignore the bril- liant McFerrin. They nominate a single track by him: the title tune from the “Round Midnight” soundtrack (Colum- bia) in the Best Jazz Vocal Performance, Male category. This is, in a word, hog- wash. Enough said. PAGING COLONEL NORTH—The Swiss Bank Corporation — that’s right, the Swiss Bank Corporation — has jour- neyed where few American banks have ventured: into the waters of jazz. Now, look. I’d expect the Swiss Bank Corpo- ration to put its money up for yodelers and alphorns players — I’d expect Citi- bank and Chase Manhattan to fund jazz — but I’m certainly not complain- ing. The extraordinary Hat Hut record label was one beneficiary of the SBC’s funds, and the extraordinary George Gruntz Concert Jazz Band was an- other. The Gruntz unit will receive the support for three international (that is, away from Switzerland) tours over the next three years: the U.S. this October (October 6-20), Asia in ’88, and some lands as yet undisclosed in ’89. Larry Stanley (212-580-4654) is handling the bookings for this year’s tour. SERIES’ BUSINESS— The New York concert scene will, as usual, be enlivened by aral concert series’ this winter and spring. First up is Sweet Ba- sil’s “Music is an Open Sky” festival which twice-a-year highlights some of the leading ensembles in what producer Horst Liepolt refers to as “today mu- sic.” The festival starts this week and the line-up is: the String Trio of New York (1/20-21), Gerry Hemingway/ Mark Helias/Ray Anderson (1 /22), The Group— Ahmed Abdullah, Marion Brown, Billy Bang, Sirone, Andrew Cyrille (1/23 24), Roger Kellaway (1/25), the Gil Evans Orch. (1/26), the Frank Gordon Quintet (1/27), the Rova Sax Quar- tet (1/28), the Ray Anderson Quar- tet (1/29), Sam Rivers’ “Rivbea” Orchestra (1/30-31), and “Wind and Thunder Presents Yoruba Proverbs” (2/ 1 ). Jack Kleinsinger’s “Highlights in Jazz” series, which presents what could best be called “yesterday music” at NYU, offers a 12th Anniversary Gala with A1 Cohn, Joe Newman, Carrie Smith, and others (2/12), a Salute to Maxine Sullivan with, among others. Milt Hinton, Doc Cheatham, and the lady of honor (3/12), “Dynamic Duos” showcasing Dave McKenna/ Daryl Sherman, Gene Bertoncini/ Michael Moore, and tapdancers Chuck Green and Ralph Brown (4/ 16), and “Bebop Spoken Here,” includ- ing James Moody, Red Rodney, Jimmy Knepper, and Sheila Jor- dan (5/21). And the newly spiffed-up and re- named Weill Recital Hall at Carnegie Hall offers a contemporary jazz se- ries— “today music” again — spotlight- ing Cecil Taylor (2/20), Julius Hemphill (3/27), and Don Cherry (5/1), as well as the Composer’s Fo- rum in a two-day “Ornette Coleman Celebration” (3/14-15). PROFILES I n what sounds like a modern-day fairy tale the story of a determined, talented young man's rise to success in the competitive :rld of CHR radio. Lori Campbell of WBZZ/ FM overcame a lot of obstacles before Riding in her current position as music direc- ,'lof the station. A modern day Cinderella "i'y?. . . sort of. Lori started out on the I' )und floor of WBZZ and in less than five ]' irs time has chalked up numerous accom- j-ihments and won the respect of her peers. 1 Early on in life, Lori realized her goals and set out to make them a reality -"I've been interested in music since I was born. . . practi- cally. So I thought radio would be a good place to get into music. I started out at B94 as an intern when I was 17. They didn't have an internship program then, they just knew that they needed someone to help them out around the station. So I come up here and asked 'Can I do anything free for you? I'll answer phones, whatever you want me to do - I'll do it for free.' So they liked that, obviously." Opportunities began to come quickly; when the station initiated an internship pro- gram, Lori's experience made her the most likely candidate to be in charge of it - thus, she undertook the task of hiring and supervising all interns that passed through the station. Soon thereafter the station found itself with an opening for a research director - Lori assumed the responsibility (a position she still holds in addition to her other duties), and began working full time and earned a slot on the company's payroll. When the station found itself in need of a Music Director in September of 1985, Lori "pushed and pushed" to be given the oppor- tunity. Her determination proved to be suc- cessful, and she soon found herself wearing the title of MD. "It was hard to prove to the people that had been in the business for years that Lori Campbell deserved to be a music director." She recalls "... I think that I really came a long way and I am satisfied that I have earned the respect that I have from them now. They are finally looking at me like a MD and recognizing that I have the ability to do it." Faced with this new challenge, Lori was not about to sit around idle. She assumed the responsibilities of Music Director with a vigor "I work directly with the record people, I have a lot of say in what we ploy, a lot of say in our rotation. I appreciate being given the chance to show what I can do." She participates in many of the stations concert promotions and she is constantly going to see live shows, leav- ing her very little free time. . . "I have one day off a week," she sighs, "... and I'm thinking about radio." Campbell is very outspoken when the sub- ject is radio and/or programming: She feels the classic rock invasion ". . . is great, but stations should be careful just how much of it they program" in order to avoid overkill. She foresees a strong resurgence of straight ahead rock and roll in the year to come, pre- dicting that "1987, from what we've seen from late '86 . . . will see bands like Cinderel- la and Bon Jovi topping the charts." She also acknowledges the strong response to dance music to Pittsburgh's growing club scene, cit- ing records by Stacey Q., Miami Sound Ma- chine, and Janet Jackson as examples. She feels that "... a lot of urban records have been breaking that maybe in the past wouldn't have - the club scene is definitely an important factor here." Lori will clock in five years at WBZZ this coming June, and it is certainly visible just how far she has come since her early days as an intern. Lori envisions a future In the music in- dustry ". . . one day down the line I would like to get Into the 'record' end of it; actually working with bands, doing A&R, manage- ment. . . " but for the time being, Lori is quite comfortable at WBZZ "I have no Immediate plans to leave here, I love B94 and I love radio - so I'm real happy here, it's a good place to work . . .I'm really reluctant to even think about going someplace else, I often wonder if another situation could be like this one - the people here are great, they've given me a lot of support. People like Nick (Ferrara, B94's Program Director), gave me a lot of freedom to learn, thought I could do the job and really gave me a chance to do it. I was given the opportunity to do what I want to do. " Tom De Savia FLASHBOX 'T MUSIC USA'' ZONES KENNY LOGGINS "Air. AKA PABLO—Pablo Records, the mainstream jazz label begun some 15 years ago by Norman Granz, has been sold to Fantasy Records (you know, that’s Fantasy /Milestone/River- side /Prestige /Contemporary /Etc./ Etc. Records), further enhancing that la- bel’s enormous wealth of jazz holdings. Granz began the label in the early- ’70s to fill a void: jazz was at one of its nadirs and Granz realized that the art- ists he loved — like Count Basie, Ella Fitzgerald, Duke Ellington, Dizzy Gillespie, Oscar Peterson — were being somewhat neglected by the re- cording industry. Granz had made his fame and fortune with these artists and many of their contemporaries some years earlier with Verve Records and the Jazz at the Philharmonic tours, and he determined to do for the ’70s what Verve did for the ’50s — record these players in numerous formats, most no- tably organized jam sessions. To fi- nance the venture, Granz sold off some of his large collection of contemporary art, naming the label after his favorite artist, Pablo Picasso. Over the years Granz built an impres- sive catalog of some 300 records — nu- merous albums by Ella, Basie, Gillespie, Peterson, Sarah Vaughan, Joe Pass, Zoot Sims, Milt Jackson, and many others. He mixed and matched artists (Sims with Basie, Basie with Gillespie, Gillespie with Peterson, Peterson with everybody), continued the series of Ella Fitzgerald Songbooks, recorded Basie and Ellington in various small-group for- mats, and waxed LPs by dozens of jazz greats in the swing and bebop styles. The sale of Pablo is likely to mean the end of the recording career of Norman Granz — one of the first men who insist- ed on the best treatment for his artists (he took them out of clubs and put them in concert halls, took them out of steer- age and put them in first-class, took them out of dives and put them in five- star hotels). One has only to look at Po- lyGram’s success with reissues of the Verve material to realize Granz’s influence. I must say, the label couldn’t have ended up in better hands. Fantasy, which has been aggressive in all types of jazz reissuing (midlines, CDs, boxed sets, etc.) will make the best use out of the Pablo catalogue. It should be noted, there are still a number of Pablo record- ings of recent vintage that have not yet seen the light of day and, presumably, numerous unreleased items in the vaults. Fantasy will begin issuing these items, as well as the material that has been out and about, in the near future. AKA STORYVILLE— Truism: Eu rope has often done a better job of issu- ing jazz records than America. Falsism: Every major European jazz label is widely-distributed stateside. Storyville Records, the Danish/Swedish label founded by Karl Emil Knudsen (sort of a Danish Norman Granz), has been sadly absent from these shores for a number of years. Gazell Productions was formed last year to rectify this situ- ation somewhat — they put out some of Storyville’s more recent recordings. Now Gazell is going the whole hog (is that a mixed metaphor?) and launching a comprehensive program of advertis- ing and public relations for its new recordings as well as the 200-title catalogue. “I think many people will be suprised at the wonderful things there are in the Storyville catalogue,” says Bill Bar- clay, Gazell vice-president. “Every- body is here, from Charlie Parker to Louis Armstrong. A new series, “Masters of Jazz,” has albums by Billie Holiday, Duke Ellington, Art Ta- tum, and Coleman Hawkins, among others, and younger artists included in other new releases are exciting talents like John Stubblefield, John Tchi- cai, Charles Tyler, Ernie Wilkins, and the David Liebman-Richard Beirach duo.” The label has also just released its first CDs. U.S. distribution for Storyville is be- ing handled by Bayside (west). Master Takes (midwest), and Rounder (east), but the label is looking to expand its distribution network. Storyville/Ga- zell’s New York office is at 204 W. 20th St., New York, NY 10011. THE JOY OF DEX - A bevvy of talent was out in Washington, D C. recently for a concert tribute to Dexter Gordon. JOOD FOR THOUGHT -In the lat 1 1 issue of the VSDA’s First tmendment Update newsletter, Jong with several reported crackdowns f d raids of video stores who carry X- ' ted or adult video product, mostly in j3 East, according to an ABC/Wash- ington Post Poll conducted earlier this year, the number of American adults who are watching X-rated mov- ies has increased 50 percent in the last five years. Thirty percent of all adult Americans watched an X-rated movie last year. The rise in viewership of X- rated movies is attributed to the sales of VCRs which allow people to watch such films in the privacy of their homes. But despite that trend, the same poll shows that a majority of the public (three-in- five) favor stricter laws including ban- ning newsstand sales of pornographic magazines. Although a slim majority (55percent) of all adults think pornogra- phy is not harmful to adults, an over- whelming nine-in-ten think it is harmful to children who read or see it. THE LIPMAN REPORT CONTIN- UED— In the coming weeks, Shop Talk will print the answers to nine basic questions that were posed to retailers in the fourth annual “State Of The Busi- ness” year-end survey that was touched on in the last issue of Cash Box (1 /24/ 87) which was compiled by Macey Lip- man Marketing, an independent pro- motion firm. The information sent to industry executives free of charge is an informal summarization of the dealer re- sponses compiled Monday, December 29th from approximately 170 retail re- cord and video stores of all types. The information obtained notes general trends which should be of use to retail- ers. Here are the first three questions and their answers: “Was your holi- day business up or down over last year? 121 dealers (81%) said that their xmas business was up, 10% of our pan- el said that their business was the same, and 9% said it was down. We noted that the corn belt section and oil pro- ducing region fell into the latter catego- ry. Overall, holiday business for the year was up by 17% with some stores reporting an increase of as high as 35%. Were you satisfied with Christmas business? Of the retailers contacted, 78% said yes, while 14% said no and 8% were somewhat satisfied with holi- day business. Any surprises this Christmas (i.e. certain LP, or mul- tiple purchases)? Compact Discs were generally bigger than expected or anticipated. The Springsteen pack- age sold less than expected (during the xmas rush). Bon Jovi was by far the sales leader during the height of the sell- ing period. Other very big sellers were the Bangles, Beastie Boys, Billy Vera, Cinderella, Anita Backer, and both Lionel Ritchie and Madon- na had a very strong resurgence in sales. Other top sellers were Janet Jackson, Bruce Hornsby, Paul Si- mon, Luther Vandross, and Geor- gia Satellites. Christmas product included Manheim Steamroller and George Strait. There were some re- gional surprises like Book Of Love from the Houston area. Specialty cate- gories did well, like the complete Rob- ert Cray catalog and Youssou D’Nour and other native African mu- sic. Overall, stores seemed better pre- pared than ever with plenty of inventory and selection. Gift certificates were as big as last year. Some stores told us that they nearly ran out of gift certificates (Odyssey Records in Birmingham).” Brian Kassan NEW YORK LOVES GENE LOVES JEZEBEL—As part of a continuing promotional and concert tour on behalf of their debut Ceffen LP, “Discover, ’’Gene Loves Jezebel stopped by Tower Records in New York for an in-store autographing session attended by a multitude of fans. SWING HEIL—A number of books about jazz have come out recently: most of them collections of magazine and/or newspaper -R-fricIes by leading jazz critics. (The two most notable of that lot are Whitney Balliett’s Ameri- can Musicians , which collects all of the biographical pieces that Balliett has written for the New Yorker over the years; and Francis Davis’s In The Mo- ment: Jazz In The 1 980s , the first book by one of America’s more astute youn- ger critics. Oxford University Press pub- lishes them both — $22.95 for the Balliett; $18.95 for the Davis.) One jazz book, however, goes after something different, though not quite as different as its title might imply. The book is La Tristesse de Saint Louis: Jazz Under The Nazis by Mike Zwerin ($16.95, Beech Tree/Morrow), which carries the cover-line, “When jazzmen under Hitler achieved a music that defied the sav- agery of war.” A spectacular idea. Despite an offi- cial ban, jazz survived, in some respects thrived, in Europe under the Nazis. Django Reinhardt was entertaining in occupied France, Svend Asmus- sen was entertaining in occupied Den- mark, things like that. What was the deal? Anybody who is acquainted with Mike Zwerin’s writing knows that they are not going to get the answer to that question in this book. You see, Mike Zwerin, a Paris-based music correspon dent for the International Herald Tri- bune, writes, mainly, about Mike Zwerin — his world view, riddled with Jewish angst, is completely his own, ev- ery sentence he writes is autobiographi- cal. This is not bad; in fact, it’s terrifically entertaining: Zwerin has been a noted musician and the presi- dent of a steel company and he’s an exceptional writer. But he won’t, he can’t, stick to the subject. “Sticking to ‘the subject’ is bad form,” he writes. “Only the widest de- fensible definition is adequate. Every- thing is linked, including the life that surrounds the writing of these words. The bio of the author on the jacket is part of the book.” So what we have here is Mike Zwerin roaming the world musing on the link between jazz and freedom: How does a music that needs to be free survive when its repressed? Zwerin takes us to Germany where he meets with a former SS officer who, it seems, is, aside from being a jazz fan, a good guy. He takes us to Poland, where jazz is currently hav ing its problems; and to South Africa, which he calls Sad Afrika and which, with typical guilt, he toured as a musi- cian for the US1A. He justifies his tour there, just as he, in a way, justifies the willingness of Django Reinhardt, Svend Asmussen, and others to pursue their musical course in the face of occupa- tion. He is told, by an elderly German, that nobody who liked jazz could be a Nazi. He tells us how much weight he has lost recently, how he fears he’s wasting away. He paints a beautifully- wrought picture of Django Reinhardt, encountering dozens of Django’s “cous- ins” along the way, and quotes numer- ous sources — on jazz, on Nazism, on repression. Hasn’t jazz always suffered repression? “Lack of purpose, indecision, a search for some kind of meaning,” he writes. The world of jazz is clogged with negative emotion. One level removed from direct emotion, we are looking over our shoulders, a negative emotion. We think about what we are playing and why rather than just playing. We are obsessed by the size of the audience rather than the quality of the music. What is catching up with us? The syn- thesizer? Funk? Is ‘inefficient’ public acoustic interior exploration still func- tional? Does it reach anybody? Who has time for it? Money to spend on it? Shouldn't we be making more noise? Has ‘the classical music of the twentieth century’ lost its relevance before the century even ends?” Zwerin never answers any of the questions he raises. But the way the questions are raised makes for excellent reading. The Nazis, the book seems to say, have come and gone, jazz has sur- vived. This is the way things were meant to be. Jazz, and the human spirit, will survive, too, in Poland and Sad Afrika. La Tristesse de Saint Louis is an insightful, fascinating book. TWO CATS AND A DAWG - Danish violin great Svend Asmussen (r) recently made a rare stateside appearance, guesting with David Grisman (!) at New York’s Fat Tuesday’s . Here the dawg and great Dane relax with visitor Toots Thielmans. A GRAND EVENT—No matter how you slice it, Benny Carter is one of the true giants of jazz. One of the finest alto saxophonists of all time, he is also a gifted composer, arranger, bandleader, and trumpeter. His nickname is “The King” and, though he plays it down, it’s rather appropriate. Benny Carter works, for the most part, as an altoist these days, but on February 26, at New York City’s Cooper Union, the full range of his talent will be on display, as the American Jazz Orchestra sa- lutes Benny Carter, ostensibly in honor of his approaching 80th birthday. Car- ter will be on hand to play, and to con- duct some of his big band gems (as well as a new extended piece written for the concert). AJO music director John Lewis, who is also expected to mount the podium for some of the concert, will be at the piano. It is, by any definition amajor jazz event, the one that should really put the AJO on the map. Lee Jeske Box February 7, 1987 13

DETAIL HOP TALK 11 23 ;arm convention agenda SET — For the second year, the Store Managers Program, which is geared toward retail record store managers, small independent retailers who are cus- tomers of one-stops, and branch person- nel of NARM wholesalers, will take •jjdace February 15 and 16, during the 29th annual National Association of Recording Merchandisers Conven- tion which you probably know is sched- uled for February 13-17 at the Fontainebleau Hotel in Miami Beach. A $50 registration fee entitles antendees to sample two full days of convention Activities. The program kicks off sun- day with the seminar, “In Store Dis- plays: How To Be Creative With Limited Time and Space.” Consultant Peter Glen, who advises many manu- facturer and retailer clients including Nike, Sears Roebuck, and Chess 12 King, will conduct a hands-on demon- stration of display building, featuring presentations by field merchandisers 12 from WEA, CBS, and The Handle- man Co. Winners of the NARM/CMA display contest — both rack jobber and retail — will also be on hand giving dem- onstrations. Product presentations from Columbia-Epic-Portrait and Associated Labels — Chrysalis- Masterworks; RCA-A&M-Arista distribution; and MCA and Motown round out the afternoon’s schedule. The A&R Lifeline: It Drives the Beat,” will be Sunday’s featured evening semi- nar, set to begin at 4 p.m. Panelists from 'several A&R departments, including chairman Bob Sherwood of Colum- 16f 19 bia Records, will discuss the process involved in discovering the music, the artists , and getting a viable product to the streets. Sunday night’s highlight will be a “Miami Splash” party, sponsored by Spec’s Music Company, which will be held at their flagship Coral Ga- bles store, the event will feature food, entertainment, a raffle drawing, and surprise appearances by major record- ing artists. Buses will be available to transport attendees from the Fontaine- bleau Convention base to the Spec’s store. MTV VJ Alan Hunter will be on hand as M.C. for the raffle drawing giving away numerous prizes including the grand prize — an all expense paid trip to London, England to complete a record run at Tower Records’ Lon- don store. Second grand prize is also a record run at their Miami store. Other prizes include VCRs and CD players. The Monday program begins at 7:30 with the seminar, “Security: The Cus- tomer and the Employee.” Mike McCaffrey, who heads his own securi- ty consulting firm, will lead the discus- sion of the latest developments in preventing retail theft, which was prompted by the increased number of CD thefts in the past year. Product pre- sentations from WEA, PolyGram, and CEMA round out the afternoon’s schedule. “The Computerized Record Store,” seminar is set for 4 p.m. and will feature a panel discussion by Bob Schneider of Western Merchan- disers. He will guide the examination of computer hardware and software de- signed to help small to medium retailers prepare their companies for the age of telecommunications. The Store Manag- ers Special will conclude Monday eve- ning as participants are invited for the first time to attend the NARM Awards Banquet, which has traditionally closed every NARM Convention since 1958, and features the presentation of the NARM Best Seller Awards. Registra- tion for the program can be completed on-site, however, NARM members are encouraged to register early. For more info call (609) 596-2221. The program’s theme, featuring the Movie Mogul character, will be incorpo- rated into a million dollar advertising and promotional campaign that in- cludes national television spots, trade and consumer print ads. Special point- of-purchase materials will be shipped to retailers during the limited-time offer. The p.o.p. kits include announcement sheets, posters, four page color catalog sheets, counter cards with take-ones and a unique pop-up display piece.
