Edge has five acts under contract — J. Blackfoot, Marshall & Babb, the Main Ingredient, David Dee, and Bobby McClure. Says Rick Frio, Edge vice presi- dent, “Our main thrust initially has been black music with crossover potential. A more artist-oriented approach, rather than trying to find a sound. We do have a couple of pop things that we’re just waiting for the right time to release.” “We started off with some basic bread and butter acts,” says Bell, “with a view towards building towards youth-oriented product, as well as some gospel, jazz, pop, and country in the future. Once we got in- volved, the idea was to go on and build a major independent record company. And that’s the plan at the moment, to do just that. One that deals with all kinds of music save classical.” The attention is on quality and unique- ness, and the idea is to find, and develop, new acts. “The talent is out there,” says Bell, “we just haven’t had the outlet for them in the industry. At Stax we always developed un- known artists. The difference between my Stax days and my present days is, at Stax we had our own studios and we had an open-door policy where an artist could come in off the streets and we’d take a lis- ten. And we were beating the bushes, so to speak, by virtue of our open-door policy. And so, if you play something — even if it’s played well — if peo- ple don’t feel that it’s significant for the mu- sic, then it’s not going to work. On Manhattan it’s a different kind of focus. You can do stuff that’s kind of, ‘1 don’t know how long this is going to last, but this is where I’m at right now.’” One jokingly suggests that, if Stanley pur- sues his sometimes-mentioned notion of dip- ping his toe into the waters of classical music, he’ll need yet another label — he may have to be lent out to Angel. “Well I’ve been talking to Angel about doing some things,” he says quite seriously, “but my feeling is that 1 don’t want to do that right now. Actually, I’d be more inter- ested in getting acceptance as a composer than as a guitar player in that world.” Some things on Stanley Jordan’s agenda for the not-too-distant future: the formation of a band (Stanley’s tired of the solo thing, he says he prefers to play in a band), the completion of a book detailing his tap-the- strings technique, further exploration of the stick (Emmett Chapman’s fret-only instru- ment), the possible design of a guitar with two extra bass strings, the eventual comple- tion of the Manhattan album, and a “Stan- dards Volume 2” for Blue Note. Stanley becomes slightly defensive when it’s pointed out to him that some people might not agree with his categorizing, oh, “One Less Bell to Answer” or “The Sounds of Silence” as a “standard,” in the tradition- al sense. “Look,” he says, “when Art Tatum played ‘You Took Advantage of Me,’ or something, he knew that song when he was younger. So, in a way. I’m just doing the same thing that he did then. To a lot of people of my generation, these songs are standards. “I hope people get the point of what the album is about, beyond just the songs. It’s not a real flashy technique album, I wasn’t trying to show off everything I could do, but 1 was trying to make the most out of what 1 have to bring out the most in the songs. And, in a way, 1 guess 1 was trying to make the guitar sing, to make it dance. “It’s real easy to take a song and cover it up with a lot of complex changes and every- thing you learned in theory class. Every- thing you learned in theory class you can apply to every song. But 1 found that when 1 was playing the standards that I grew up with, I knew when I was getting away from the song. Whereas the older standards, 1 might play the song without having ever heard the original version, and so 1 don’t really appreciate what it is I’m doing to the song. The songs that I put on the album, because I’d heard other versions before, I have a much better sense of when I’m losing a song — and I feel the responsibility to re- spect a song — no one has to explain that to me. And then the next time I hear some- body say, ‘You’re losing a song,’ I’m not going to say, ‘Oh, they don’t know anything about jazz.’ I’m going to say, ‘Oh, let me check it out, maybe it’s true.’” Don’t expect Stanley Jordan to be a flash in the jazz pan — he’s far too talented, far too committed, for that. Plus, for somebody who won’t be seeing his 30th birthday this decade, he has an unusually long view. When Stanley Jordan was at Princeton — he studied music, specifically computer music, at Princeton for four years — he had the op- portunity to meet one of jazz’s eminences grise, the great Benny Carter, who was teaching there at the time. “I’d signed up for his course,” says Stan- ley, “and I kind of timidly went up and said, ‘I’d like to play with you in your concert.’ And 1 brought my guitar over, and we jammed on ‘My Old Flame,’ and he said, ‘Sure, you can be in the show.’ “He was tremendously supportive and it was really good to know him and be in- spired by somebody who’s been in the mu- sic so long, who is such a survivor. 1 saw myself some day as a grand old man who people could look up to, and I’d know it all and they’d want to learn it from me.” Beatles CD Sales (continued from page 5) preorders for all four titles at $49.99. Gregory Dobrin When one hears Henry Johnson’s guitar playing, one hears a jazz style that’s washed in the blues. So it’s not surprising that Henry Johnson, whose debut album, “You’re The One,” was released late last year on Impulse!, grew up in two of the bluesiest cities on Earth: Chicago and Memphis. “I got the blues from Memphis, of course,” he says, “and when 1 came back to Chicago I worked on the South Side a lot. I always liked the blues, I always liked B.B. King and those guys. And, you know, being young in the ’60s, I’d end up listening to Isaac Hayes or Sly & the Family Stone. But every once in a while, you hear something that just turns your head around, and at that particular time I heard Wes Mont- gomery. This was right before he died, and it just freaked me totally out. So, after that, I just wanted to find out what this music was all about. I didn’t under- stand it, but the only thing I knew was there was just something about it that 1 just really liked. And the more I listened to it, the more I got addicted to it.” Henry’s addiction to Wes Montgom- ery is evident in his playing. He never did get to see the guitar great live, but he did get to work, at the age of 14, with an earlier influence: the aforemen- tioned Isaac Hayes. “That was my first professional gig, around the time of the ‘Hot Buttered Soul’ album. Before that I played churches, playing gospel stuff.” After resettling in Chicago, Henry Johnson began the various slate of ac- tivities: playing in top 40 bands, leading his own trio, working in society orchestras. “Then after that, about 1976, I went on the road with Jack McDuff for about a year, which really got the blues stuff happening. Then I stuck around Chica- go for about a year, before getting called by Donny Hathaway.” After Hathaway’s death, Henry be- gan working with Ramsey Lewis, the first of two stints in Lewis’ outfit, but his real formative years were from 1982- HENRY JOHNSON 85, when he worked around Chiq with hiw own quartet. By Brian Kassan LOS ANGELES -Love Tractor? Even the name of the band elicits chuck- les from the uninitiated, but those fans who are familiar with the positively bright, hap- py-go-lucky instrumental strains of this Georgian band probably chuckle frequently anyway. Love Tractor emerged out of Athens, Ga. in 1980, where a unique college party scene spawned from the lack of dance clubs in the area. The B-52’s, Pylon, R.E.M. and Love Tractor were among a handful of “dance” oriented bands who played at these “front- porch” parties, drawing a steady crowd of college students. “Athens had no clubs per se to really go to,” says Love Tractor guitarist Mark Cline in an interview with Cash Box, “and within the art school crowd there was a massive party scene. It was really a group of about 100 people in the core of it. When we start- ed, we were considered a dance band. You were a good band if people could dance to you. We were doing these bands for fun. No one was serious. I mean it was a joke, some- thing to do to while away the hours.jj Cline and fellow Tractormen, Anp Wellford (bass, vocals), Michael RicnC: (guitar, vocals) and Andrew Carter have recently signed with Big Time F (distributed by RCA) after two duced LPs and one EP for the indcf label db Records. Shown (l-r): Glenn Frey, Don Henley, Irving Azoff. SPECIAL REV!EW\ We Love Them, Yeah, Yeah, Yeah!!!— It is a little like discovering a magician’s methods. The pristine digital capacity of compact discs has given us a view of The Beatles that heretofore existed only in the memories of the four from Liverpool and their producer, George Martin. With the unprecedented Number One, Two, Three and Four debut on last week’s Cash Box CD chart of the initial Beatles CD releases, the Fab Four once again show their remarkable resilience and the power they have continually exerted on the music world. The event of the release of these first four CDs was a media spectacle approaching the magnitude of John, Paul, George and Ringo’s touchdown at JFK in 1964. “Please Please Me” (CDP 7 46435), “With The Beatles” (CDP 7 46436), “A Hard Day’s Night” {CDP 7 46437) and “Beatles For Sale” (CDP 7 46438) contain, in their original British formats, digitally re-mastered and CD-captured versions of the classic songs that are so permanently etched in the world’s collective consciousness. Here you have all of the innocence of George Harrison’s halting, frustrated first attempts at Chuck Berry guitar licks. Lennon and McCartney can be seen moving from the throw-away pop fizz of 1963’s “Please Please Me” toward the greater introspection of the later “No Reply” and “I’m A Loser.” The schmaltz of record company-induced covers like “A Taste Of Honey” and “Till There Was You” gives way in “A Hard Day’s Night” and “Beatles For Sale” to albums completely written by The Beatles or their rock and roll heroes like Chuck Berry, Carl Perkins and Buddy Holly. But always, there are those voices, those songs, that indescribable “way” with an arrangement. The riveting performances captured on these CDs maintain all of their original charm. Only the veil of period technology that prevented most of us from hearing them clearly has been lifted. The magicians’ tricks are exposed. The only difference is, the magic is still there, and all of 1987’s new listeners can still marvel and wonder, “How did they do that?” Stephen Padgett IheBestSeofoodta^ MARYLAND VIOUSE “The taste ofthe Chesapeake” Lunch & Dinner Tues. thru Sun. ONJAZZ Terry Gibbs GIBBS—The best jazz big band album released in 1986 did not win a Grammy; in fact, it wasn’t even nominated for a Grammy. That may be because the best big band album released in 1986 — year in which the Grammy nominees in the category were the formidable bands of Lionel Hampton, Mel Lewis, Benny Goodman, Woody Herman, and Doc Severinsen — was recorded in March of 1959. “Terry Gibbs Dream Band” (Contemporary) is a smoking, wallop-packing album that features great charts (by Bill Holman, Bob Brookmeyer, Al Cohn, Marty Paich, and Manny Albam), great players (like Conte Candoli, Med Flory, Joe Maini, Mel Lewis), and great big band tunes (like “Don’t Be That Way,” “Cottontail,” “Jumpin’ at the Woodside”). “I’ll tell you the whole story,” says Terry Gibbs, in New York for a week- long engagement with Buddy De- Franco, his frequent partner. “When I moved to California, there were a few rehearsal bands — Bill Holman had one, Med Flory had one — and they were nice. 1 had a good contract with Mercu- ry where I could record what I wanted to record, so I decided 1 wanted to do a big band album. But I heard that this one guy got fined $1,000 by the union for rehearsing a band for an album. And I didn’t just want to record a band — because I did that in New York one time, just went in the studio and didn’t really know what the hell we were do- ing. I wanted a tight band. “At the same time, there was a club called the Seville, in Hollywood, that had some Latin music and they were bombing. So they called me up to come in with a quintet. I went in on a Tuesday night, and it went good. Then I heard that you could rehearse a big band for a nightclub engagement, which is ridicu- lous, but not for a record date. So I got an idea: why don’t 1 put a big band in ^ the club? That way I could rehearse my band. And they were paying me enough money — the scale was only $15 a night in those days — so I went to the club owner and said, ‘How would you like to have a 16-piece band for what you’re giving me for five?”’ So in came the Terry Gibbs Big Band, and, about five weeks later, in came Wally Heider to do some re- mote recording. And, voila, out came the best big band album of 1986. And, perhaps, the best big band album of 1987 — there is another live volume due from Contemporary in May. And — who knows? — maybe the best big band al- bums of 1988 and 1989. All told, Gibbs has been sitting on enough tapes for four albums. They didn’t come out when they were recorded, because the band recorded many of these same songs on their studio albums (Emarcy, out-of-print). They didn’t come out earli- er, because Gibbs says he didn’t want them on a fly-by-night label that would “have ripped it off and put it in their closet.” The reason the first album is so pow- erful — it explodes off the turntable — is that, according to Terry Gibbs, “for the first album, I took all my closing tunes and flagwavers, because 1 wanted to shock everybody. I knew how good the band was, but I wasn’t sure it would be accepted by anybody else.” It has been accepted. So accepted, in fact, that Gibbs — who has for years been concentrating on playing his vibes in small groups, these days with De- Franco at his side if it can be ar- ranged — has been fielding offers to reform the band, something he is reluc- tant to do “because it’s a headache.” Terry Gibbs has been playing the vibes professionally for some 50 years, ever since, as 12-year-old Julius Gu- benko — the son of “one of the biggest Jewish bandleaders” — he won a Ma- jor Bowes amateur contest in 1936. The next day, young Julius made his professional debut at the Stanley The- atre in Pittsburgh where. Variety re- ported, he “just about steals the show.” Somewhere along the line, Julius Gu- benko became Terry Gibbs, and the wunderkind of the bar mitzvah circuit became a fleet-handed bebop vibes man. He was a big attraction in the ’50s — his small band, with Terry Pol- lard on piano and, at times, second vibes — was a huge success. Perhaps Terry Gibbs’ name value, in the grand scheme of things, would be higher if he hadn’t moved to Southern California in the ’50s. But, then, the rootin’-tootin’ big band might have really been just a dream band. “The next album coming out, the tempos are more groove tempos, more toe-tapping tempos. Because the first album was like — how can I explain it? — it’s like watching Don Rickies: zing-bang-bang-zing. Could you imagine what it sounded like in person? You know what it was, it was a bunch of maniacs having fun.” It is possible, just possible, that if the next album receives a warm response, the Terry Gibbs Big Band — or some version of it — will be back in business. Under Terry Gibbs’ terms. “You can’t just have guys, they have to be of the calibre of Conte Candoli playing a solo. After hearing my library played that good, that’s how 1 want it played.” Lee Jeske '1‘ihBox March 21, 1987 15

A spokesman for Harmony House says, “This was not only one of the most successful cross-promotions we have ever run, it was, by community social conscience standards, the most rewarding.” LIEBERMAN ENTERPRISES RE- PORTS RECORD SIX MONTH RE- SULTS — In the February/March issue of their bi-monthly newsletter, Lieber- man Enterprises reports record sales and income for the second quarter and first half of fiscal 1987. Sales for the second quarter which ended November of 1986 were up 20.7 percent and net income was up 13.8 percent compared with the same period last year. Net in- come per share (primary) was $.51 com- pared with $.45 in the second quarter last year. For the first half which also ended in November, 1986, sales were up 21.9 percent, net income up 5.1 per- cent and per share income (primary) was $.69 vs. $.66 in the same period last year. David Lieberman, chair- man and CEO, said, “The company’s pre-recorded music has continued to grow, with compact disc sales more than doubling during the quarter. Our video movie and music business contin- ues to increase substantially, with sales to our mass merchant accounts almost doubling and sales to rental stores also increasing nicely.” LARGE IN-STORE PROMO FOR SYNERGY — Passport’s Audion Recording Company has planned the largest in-store marketing campaign ever mounted around a New Age/in- strumental album to launch Synergy’s LP “Metropolitan Suite,” an album of original symphonic music composed and performed entirely on electronic equipment by Larry Fast — a long-time collaborator with Peter Gabriel. Au- dion Records will supply over 50 retail stores with “nuon” fluorescent signs and “Lyte” audio visualizers — devices which employ LED’s to generate visual images based on the pulse of music. The audio visualizers will be used in conjunction with in-store play of the Synergy compact disc, which will be sent to over 300 retail record stores. Audion will also sponsor a nationwide retail display contest with prizes that include 20 CD players, complete cata- logues of Audion releases, and all five previous Synergy albums personally signed by Larry Fast. Additional back- ing for Audion’s campaign will come from the Sony Corporation. NEWS RIAA Applauds Congress’s Consideration Of Intellectual Copyright Protection 11 ; 'JEW YORK — The House Ways and Means !ommittee began its consideration of com- >rehensiue trade legislation, March 10. The 'ommittee has a draft prepared by Dan fostenkowski. Committee chairman, and >am Gibbons, chairman of the trade ubcommittee. Jason Berman, the new president of the JIAA, was enthusiastic about the possibi- tes for copyright protection in the bill. In a 'repared statement, Berman stated: “I am larticularly pleased to see the draft include new section on intellectual property pro- action. This continues a united effort by J.S. copyright industries — including re- ords, movies, books and computer soft- ware— to ensure that protection of our works against piracy is made a part of U.S. .'ade law. “American music is a valuable trade as- et. It needs to be protected against piracy and counterfeiting abroad — a problem that costs our industry alone over $500 million annually. “The Committee’s bill calls for indentify- ing ‘priority’ countries where piracy and counterfeiting are a way of life and where the economic harm to U.S. industries is clear. A ‘priority’ country is then subject to a self-initiated Section 301 trade complaint by the United States Trade Representative. In effect, the U.S. government becomes our petititioner. “Another important feature of the bill is that it shortens the traditional time frame for Section 301 intellectual property protec- tion cases. This is particularly significant be- cause of the nature of our business and the fact that piracy, like the record industry, is a ‘hits’ business. Current, popular recordings are the focus of most piracy and counterfeiting” THE WINNERS IN MCA—MCA Records promotion stsff recently held their annusl conven- tion in Los Angeles and presented awards in select categories. Records Vice President/ Publicity David Bowie Pacts With EMI For New Album and Tour By Paul lorio NEW YORK — David Bowie announced plans for a major international tour in sup- port of his upcoming “Never Let Me Down” album, at a press conference here (3/18). The album, his first since re-signing to EMI, will be released April 20, and the tour, per- haps his last ever, will begin in Rotterdam a week later. Joe Smith, Capitol/EMI CEO and vice chairman, called the tour “one of the most ambitious programs Bowie or any other art- ist has ever undertaken.” It will last six months and cover more than sixty cities and fifteen countries, according to Smith. Pepsi Cola will sponsor the North American leg, which includes at least thirty stadium and arena shows, and Bowie will appear in one Pepsi television advertisement. Bowie and his six-piece band gave a live preview of the ‘Glass Insect’ tour at the news conference, performing the LP’s first single, “Day-In Day-Out,” and the album’s closing track, “Bang Bang.” Clad in a black leather jacket, Bowie totally captivated the small Cat Club audience, while lead guitarist Peter Frampton came alive with a flashy solo on “Day-In Day-Out.” The perfor- mance was broadcast nationally on radio immediately following the press conference. “It’s a lot more theatrical,” said Bowie of the tour. “If you can get anywhere near a rock ‘n’ roll revue, it’s somewhere in there.” Though he said it’s more like his live shows of the early seventies, he added that “it’s noth- ing like Ziggy,” referring to his extravagant shows in support of “The Rise and Fall Of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders From Mars.” Apparently, this will be Bowie’s last tour. “David is taking it to the road one last time,” announced Pepsi senior vice presi- dent Mike Lorelli at the conference. Bowie suggested this, as well. “Is it my last tour? My activities in the future are diversifying fast,” he said. “And 1 am an old man.” (He hinted that a film project with Mick dagger was in the works, saying “It is in the air.”) His band includes Frampton, guitarist Carlos Alomar, drummer Allen Childs, bass- ist Carmine Rojas, keyboardist Richard Cot- tle, and synthesizer player Erdal Kizilcay. “I think this tour will punch it on the nose that (continued on page 23) Coury Prevails In Cara Suit .35 ANGELES — Liz Beth Rosenberg has >;en named vice president/publicity at 'iarner Bros. LOS ANGELES — A two-year-old court case brought against Al Coury, Al Coury Inc. and Network Records by recording art- ist Irene Cara was decided in Coury and Network’s favor March 5 by the California State Labor Commissioner. In her petition, Cara claimed that her re- cording contract with Network was used as a facade by former Network president Coury (now head of Geffen Records’ pro- motion department), who, she alleged, pro- cured employment for her without license to do so, acting as an agent. However, as the decision states, “all acts alleged to have constituted ‘procurement’ were exempt under the recording contract exemption.” The case was further derailed under the labor code statute of limitations adopted January 1, 1983 (Cara had a year to file her claim before the statute became law, but her action wasn’t filed until two years later). Furthermore, the decision states, “Even if the . . . statutory provisions did not dispose of this case, no violation of the Talent Agencies Act was shown to have occurred here.” The commissioner ruled Network to be a “bona fide record company which em- ployed the services of petitioner Irene Cara for the purpose of producing master record- ings.” “If she (Cara) had prevailed,” Coury told Cash Box, “it would have meant that any record company that doesn’t have its own manufacturing or its own distribution - which is most all record companies except for the six or seven majors - would be in effect vulnerable to the same kind of an at- tack by any artist who is under contract to them,” Cara brought two actions against Coury and Network, one before the Labor Com- mission, and a still pending Superior Court suit (Labor disputes take precedence under California state law). “This was merely the first phase of what promises to be a long fight,” said Cara’s attorney, David Braun. 5

GUESTEDITORIAL Guest Lists: A Necessary But Heavily Abused Facet Of The Music Industry. By Matt Kramer Talent Coordinator, At My Place In many careers, the employee is paid for on the job training. Quite the opposite in the music industry. 1 don’t believe there is another industry where the creator of the product has to give away so much for free as part of the rocky road to a questionable career possibility. In Japan, when someone opens a new business, friends and family show up and pay cash to help the entrepre- neur get off the ground. Many of an artist’s friends will help out in a similar fashion, at least at the first couple of gigs. Whether or not they keep coming back is a reflection of how well the mu- sic works for them. That’s how good business works; you promote your product and if people like it, they buy it. However, there exists a breed of animal that strives to live without ever paying for the music it professes to love. To be asked to purchase a ticket is an insult to its status either as a member of the mu- sic industry or as a friend of the act. This animal claims that it is supporting its artist by just showing up. Maybe, just maybe, it will make a connection to move the artist’s career. For the most part, what really happens is detrimental to the artist. For example, when an art- ist is drawing well enough to fill up a room, that free guest is denying a pay- ing customer the opportunity to come in. Therefore, besides not contributing financially to the artist’s compensation, the ‘friend’ is taking money out of the artist’s pocket. Worse yet is the emo- tional pressure put upon the artist. I feel that one of the best things you can give an artist is space and solitude to pre- pare for the {performance. Recently, two musicians {Vonda Shepard and Russ Freeman) who perform At My Place on a monthly basis, told me how distracted and stressed they get before a show by the calls from friends de- manding to be put on a list. Many of these people are merely acting out of habit and have no desire to understand the effect of their demands either upon the artist or the venue. A publicist for a record label called me to apologetically ask for guest passes for someone else. He said, “1 feel like a pimp when I do this, but I have to ask.” This is part of the scene with people who actually know the act. Then there are the game players who just try to get in for free using their wits. Grandstanding and ha- rassing of the door staff sabotages the staff’s ability to give good service to the paying customers. During a sold-out show, there are many distractors and these people take advantage. The staff cannot pretend to know who is and is not telling the truth, and they cannot leave the front door unattended to find an artist and put him on the spot. (There’s a person named Joe at the front door, he says he’s a friend of your manager and he’s really upset cause you didn’t put him on the list). A lot of squeaky wheels acting real greasy often manage to bull their way in. Other ruses include phony press passes and manu- factured emergencies. I have no argu- ment with legitimate press representatives who make arrange- ments in advance. The reality is that honest profession- als will support their industry and not make an issue of getting in for free. We take a position that we as a club and the musicians as artists are offering services and crafts and deserve to be compensat- ed for those services. If you’re one of those who feels you shouldn’t have to pay for a ticket, please think again. A lot of people work real hard to bring you their music. If you can’t support them in live {performance, stay home and play the radio. Spring Draft Over: Warner Nashville Announces Line*Up LOS ANGELES — Jim Ed Norman, execu- tive vice president, Warner Bros. Records, Nashville division, has announced the spring draft choices for the Nashville staff. In the promotion department, Doug Grau is promoted to national promotion coordi- nator and will be responsible for the market- ing of the label’s singles and albums. Grau replaces Chris Palmer who has been pro- moted to national promotion manager and, along with Bob Saporiti, will work with pro- motions head, Nick Hunter. Nancy Solinski, former national promotion director, takes over in the newly created position of nation- al in-house marketing director. She will work as a liaison between all Warner field personnel and retail outlets. The press and artist development depart- ment, under the leadership of Janice Azrak, has promoted Ronna Rubin and Susan Niles. Rubin is upped to national director, press and artist development, while Niles becomes national publicity coordinator. In commenting on the staff promotions, Norman remarked, “it is my pleasure to re- port that no one has been sent back to the minor leagues. The Warner Nashville team has proved a winning combination, recently celebrating the best season in our history. The Mets may have claimed the pennant, but Warner Bros. ONJAZZ\ ORNETTE COLEMAN ORNETTE— After a couple of years of more-or-less public inactivity, Or- nette Coleman is currently on some kind of a roll. Most years don’t see a single Ornette Coleman album issued, last year saw two: “Song X’’ (Geffen), the brilliant collaboration with Pat Metheny, and “Opening the Caravan of Dreams” (Caravan of Dreams), with Ornette’s electric band, Prime Time. This year should also see the release of two Ornette Coleman albums on Cara- van of Dreams: the complete recording of his symphony “Skies of America,” performed by Prime Time with the Fort Worth Symphony, and an ex- traordinary-sounding project, currently in the mixing stage, which reteams Or- nette with the members of his original 1958 Quartet — Don Cherry, Charlie Haden and Ed Blackwell. The re- cord features the Quartet playing new Ornette Coleman music and Prime Time playing the same music. Called “Ornette,” it’s due in May or June., “1 did it because so many people think I’m playing different music with Prime Time,” says Ornette Coleman. The two bands are going to do a con- cert at New York’s Town Hall in June that promises to be one of the year’s most noteworthy jazz events. “1 haven’t played any of the old mu- sic with the Quartet,” says Ornette. “Don Cherry is always asking me, ‘Let’s play this, let’s play that,’ but I haven’t played any this year with them. I’m try- ing to get them to come up to ’87.” Although the album doesn’t have a full-scale harmolodic blow-out, with the two groups combined, it is a possibility for the concert. “That’s what we were thinking about doing in June. I had a piece that 1 was going to record with all of them, but the Quartet guys were in California when I had Prime Time here, so it didn’t work out. But we’re going to try something like that when we perform live.” Last weekend (March 14 & 15), Or- nette Coleman was present at Carnegie Recital Hall for a fascinating two-night retrospective of his chamber music (a taste of which can be heard on the re- cently-released Caravan of Dreams al- bum “Prime Design/Time Design”). This summer. Prime Time will tour Eu- rope, stopping in Verona for a full per- formance of “Skies of America.” Ornette credits a lot of his recent ac- tivity on the fact that he finally has a manager that he feels he can trust: his son. Prime Time drummer Denardo Coleman. “Since Denardo has been handling me — it seems that everyone likes him and he communicates to me very well — things are becoming more natu- ral. I’ve given up the idea that. ..the op- portunism of the day. In 1965, 1 played Berlin, at the Sports Plaza, with David Izenzon and Charles Moffett, and there were about 20,000 people there, it was sold out. And we were playing something — some song, 1 don’t know what — and right in the middle of it, while we were improvising, every per- son stood up at that very moment and started screaming and cheering because of how good it sounded to them. And, you know, when I got back to America, they said, ‘Well, you don’t have an audi- ence, nobody wants to hear you.’ So I say: well, I had my Madison Square Gar- den experience 20 years ago. What it made me realize about America was that the particular producers and en- trenpeneurs actually make whoever they want successful, because of the re- lationship they want to have with that person. And I just haven’t found that person who feels that way about sup- porting me. But at least the Caravan of Dreams has given me some light in the tunnel.” Indeed. The Fort Worth-based arts complex and, now, record label, is, it seems, dedicated to Ornette Coleman and his harmolodic progeny (Ronald Shannon Jackson, James Blood Ulmer). “In America, it’s true, you have to have someone to be able to relate to people that doesn’t necessarily want you to make them feel bad because they don’t know what you’re doing. Those are called managers and entre- peneurs, and lots of those people may not even be interested in what I’m do- ing. But now it’s gotten better.” Ornette talks of future projects with enthusiasm — his long-standing dream to have a harmolodic orchestra made up of some 140 musicians (two from each state and 40 from around the world). He’s been composing a piece, “The Old- est Language” for the orchestra, but he acknowledges it’s not likely to happen “unless money falls from the sky.” He also talks about writing a piece for his former uncle, 8Tyear-old trumpeter Doc Cheatham (who bought the teen- aged Ornette Coleman his first saxo- phone), to play with Prime Time. And what of last year’s acclaimed “Song X” album and tour. “I tell you, it was really good,” says Ornette Coleman. “I mean, I have the best admiration for Pat, he’s a really fine person. He really played beautiful- ly. From the experience we had togeth- er, from when he first started playing, it was like hearing a caterpillar turn into a butterfly.” Is the collaboration done? “I don’t know. We’ll probably play together again some time. There’s no reason to stop that right now for good.” Lee Jeske 8, 1981j Hash Box March 28, 1987 13

PROFILES ^Phil Quartararo I V.P./National Promotion Virgin Records It was a warm, sunny Southern California Friday afternoon, and Virgin was rockin' . . . Music was blaring throughout their chic Bev- erly Hills offices and staffers, perhaps buoyed by the phenomenal out-of-the-box success of Cutting Crew (Virgin's initial foray into the unpredictable world of Top 40 radio), were talking and laughing like a midnight beach party at Laguna. Since the weather was so beautiful, the in- terview was transferred to the roof, and the first two employees of Virgin's promotion de- partment prepared to chat about their bands, dheir staff, and their strategies for conquering dhe alternative and Top 40 markets. Working a roster peopled with such under- frecognized acts as Microdisney, Killing Joke, iiand Heaven 1 7, Phil Quartararo finds himself •lin a unique position. Virgin's Vice President/ 'JNational Promotion is piloting a major label 'promotion staff of industry veterans - but the majority of Virgin's artists are familiar only to a college radio crowd. Is this a problem? No way. Quartararo, who began his career as 'A&M's college rep at Syracuse University In 1975 and since has enjoyed stints at RCA, 'Island, and Arista, feels that the cyclical and expanding nature of public sentiment and ra- dio acceptance is in Virgin's favor. "The only .constant in our business is change, and acts that are considered alternative today will be tomorrow's mainstream," he asserts. "Acts yike The Police, Joe Jackson, Squeeze, and (Split Enz were definitely considered alterna- tive when they started, but in their heyday fhey became mainstream. There are so many variables - the market changes, the radio lis- tener changes, the consumer changes." It is these variables that make Iris Dillon's lob so exciting. She is Virgin's National Direc- tor/Alternative Promotion, and it is a tribute lij both to her exceptional abilities and to the 1 importance of her position that she was the I'first person Quartararo hired upon taking over his post. At Virgin, Alternative Promotion 1 means much more than simply progressive ra- dio. "The title is somewhat misleading," states |.3uartoraro."lf you were to call her every- thing that she is, it would be National College, Club, Dance, etc., etc . . . The title would be onger than the Santa Monica Freeway, and it ; ivould defeat the purpose." The difficulty of 'jOillon's position is not lost on her boss either. jrThere's a lot more to it than doing Top 40, SAOR, Country or Black. It's somewhat less defined and it requires much more creativity and imagination. It's a tough job to be able to start that many plates spinning at one time and keep them all spinning." Dillon's background falls primarily within the dub scene. She spent six years as a disc jockey and started her own record pool (now known as Impact Record Pool), and she also worked local promotion for A&M in San Fran- cisco. This experience prepared her well for the many vagaries inherent within the realm of alternative promotion, and she agrees with Quartararo's assessment of the probability for success of Virgin's younger acts. "Many of the acts that you see gaining widespread ac- ceptance now started the same way that we are starting Microdisney or Spear Of Destiny. These are the early Simple Minds, the early Human Leagues. We lay the groundwork at the college and club levels. We realize that we have some acts that are baby developing acts, and the first or second albums we put out on them are going to reach their widest accep- tance in the alternative vein. But that's what alternative is all about - building a base so that these acts can go from there to wider acceptance." Past experience at a street level is a large weapon in Dillon's arsenal, and she plans to use this practical training to help her work with college and club programmers every- day. "The street is where you are always go- ing to be able to pick up on something new, and if someone calls me needing information or a copy of a record, even if I've never heard of it before, my reaction time is going to be quicker. I came from being a DJ and running a pool so I can understand what these people are going through. I'll do everything that I can to help that person, whether it's videos, post- ers, cassettes, albums, CD's, or whatever it is that they need to be successful." This attitude bodes well for progressive programmers and dance jocks, who are often frustrated in their attempts to deal with majors. Virgin obviously will not be satisfied with merely playlisting at dance clubs and 5000- watt college stations. They plan on creating mass appeal artists by releasing consistently top-notch product and backing it up with thor- ough support from an experienced staff. Suc- cess means national Top 40 airplay and exposure, without compromising the initial ideals of the fledgling label. Promotion chief Quartararo believes that the time is right for his roster of "young vir- gins." The ever-tightening playlist seems (with fingers crossed) to be a creature of the recent past, and more previously unknown artists are popping up around the country than in the last few years. Virgin's Cutting Crew is a per- fect example of Top 40 radio's willingness to embrace a quality song without a track re- cord of chart successes to back it up. The em- phasis is on song loyalty, not artist loyalty. iris Dillon National Director/Alternative Promotion Virgin Records and Quartararo hopes that this tendency will continue. "The amount of variety and new music is encouraging. Acts like The Psychedel- ic Furs, INXS, and The Cure, which were once considered fairly avant-garde, can now have really big Top 40 records, and that would not have happened four or five years ago." Another recent development has the Virgin ears buzzing, and that is the emergence of the hybrid Dance/Top 40 stations, whose adven- turous playlists are providing exposure to a wide number of acts previously relegated to dance club duty. Dillon is excited about the initial successes of this format and sees two major advantages: "One of the best things they have done is to give outlets to the records that are hitting in the clubs fairly early. I think they've kind of lit some fires in those markets and they've encouraged the other stations to at least test those songs that they otherwise might not have played. Also, it definitely hits in a market that is severely overlooked and that is the Spanish/Latin marker They buy records, they make records, they do as much as anybody else, and I'm glad to see them get a chance. It's not a trend, it's here to stay." Quartararo agrees that this hybrid format will be around for some time to come. "Look at it this way - four of the six largest metro areas in this country (New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, and Miami) have an enormous Latin population. The demographics are different, but that's why these stations are so successful. That's not a trend, these people are part of the population. The big news is that they are active listeners, they are spending money, and now the advertisers are trying to reach that audience. That's going to change our indus- try." Only time, and Arbitron, will verify the ultimate result of this unique programming direction, but early returns certainly indicate a profitable future. Obviously, Quartararo and Dillon are not the sole members of Virgin's outstanding pro- motion staff. Backed up in L.A. by Vice Presi- dent/Field Promotion Michael Plen and National Director/Album Promotion Jeff Naumonn, the field staff is composed of nine Regional Promotion Managers who have been plucked from different segments of the industry. Quartararo is genuinely enthusiastic when discussing the merits of his team, and feels that Virgin has assembled a crack squad of well-rounded industry professionals who have the ability to do anything that is asked of them. "We needed people who understood how clubs, promoters, retailers, and promo- tion people interacted and how they all af- fected each other. We didn't have time to train nine people from scratch, so we needed people who could hit the ground running, who could be hired in January and be work- ing a Cutting Crew record by February." The early success of the first Cutting Crew single, "(I Just) Died In Your Arms" has made believ- ers out of anyone doubting the young label's ability to produce hits. Not content with merely storming the gates of Top 40 and AOR radio, the Virgin Promo- tion army will also be tackling the Black/Ur- ban frontier in the near future. Plans to expand in that direction have been put on hold until the spring, but by April or May Virgin will be releasing product aimed direct- ly at the Black market. "We're looking to build a roster and we're looking to have a larger visibility in that format," confides Quartararo. "We have attacked fairly suc- cessfully in our first few months the pop, AOR, and dance side of things, but there is obvious- ly a lot more. We're staggering our expansion so that we don't overload ourselves. We know that it's going to take a couple of years to get this up to a full-service record label. We want to do one thing at a time and do it right." Plans are also in the works for Classical and New Age labels to fly under the Virgin banner. The label has made a strong initial effort to present o unique and stimulating graphic treatment in everything from logos to adver- tising to artist videos, and Dillon plans to use this to her advantage when attempting to break new acts. "I think one of the big advan- tages of video for me is that I can get a video played in a club and at the end they will tag who the artist is. That helps me to create visi- bility. If you hove an act that is doing well at college rodio, then you need something else out there to be seen, and you also need the MTV's to give the unknown acts some visibility. Videos are great - but not in lieu of touring. Acts still need to get on the road because people need to have contact with them. But to create that buzz in the beginning it's almost essential to have videos." Upcoming releases from Virgin include a solo comeback album from Boy George (June), an album of new material from the legendary Roy Orbison, the next release from Grammy winner Steve Winwood (slated for 1 988), and many surprises to be sure. For the moment, however, the majority of their re- leases are young up-and-coming acts who have placed their careers in some very capa- ble hands. It is left to Alternative Promotion Director Iris Dillon to sum up the Virgin strate- gy toward their artists: "We are really into the music, and we will find a way to get them the exposure that they need. It doesn't make sense to sign a group if you're not going to do that for them." With leaders like Dillon and Promotion V.P. Phil Quartararo behind them, the Virgin team is in strong shape for 1987, and is looking toward the future with bright hopes. Rob Yardumian

Brian Kassan OINGO BOINGO’S INTO LA— Two thousand “Boingo-Maniacs" recently showed up at Tower Sunset for an intimate in-store with the band which was actually held in the store’s parking lot. The event, hosted by KROQ jock Jed the Fish, coincided with that day’s release of the band’s latest MCA LP. Language implementing the proposal was presented as a recommendation to the Copyright Royalty Tribunal for adoption as forma! regulations. Counterfeit Label Indictment In MS, Tapes Seized In CA, KY NEW YORK — James Lee Long of Tupelo, MS was indicted by a federal grand jury on February 17 on five counts of trafficking in counterfeit cassette tape labels. Each count carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The indictment alleges that Long, doing business as Roadrunner Enterprises, traf- ficked in counterfeit labels from March, 1984-August, 1985. A three year investiga- tion by the RIAA’s anti-piracy unit, the FBI, and various state and local police depart- ments showed the alleged distribution of counterfeit cassettes by Long in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida. Long, who was taken into custody by the FBI and later released on a $10,000 bond, pleaded not guilty to all five counts. In an unrelated incident, nearly 5,000 al- leged counterfeit cassette tapes were siezed from three vendors at the Salinas, CA Sky- view Drive-In Theatre Swap Meet on Febru- ary 28. The vendors — Mustafa Yasin, Mahmous Yasin, and Lacila Masical — were cited and released for violations of Califor- nia's True Name and Address, Counterfeit Trademark, and Counterfeit Merchandise Statutes. In another unrelated incident, 427 alleged counterfeit tapes were seized at Louisville, KY’s State Fair Grounds Flea Market on February 28, and Shirley S. Gambrel and Coris S. Howe were arrested and charged with violating Kentucky’s True Name and Address Statue. They were cited and re- leased on their own recognizance. ON JAZZ PASSING ON— I’d like to note the recent deaths of two important figures in jazz: Eddie Durham, who died March 6 at the age of 80, and Allan Jaffe, who died March 9 at the age of 51. Durham, an original member of the Count Basie Orchestra, was a noted trombonist, a pioneer on the electric guitar, and a widely-respected compos- er and arranger. Jaffe was the founder of Preservation Hall and a guiding force in keeping the traditional jazz flame alive — by organizing, and touring as a tubaist with, the Preservation Hall Jazz Band. REISSUING ON— Hoo-hah, have the reissues been coming hot and heavy lately. For those who doubted the gen- uiness of RCA’s efforts in that depart- ment, the label has just issued a bundle of gems under the Bluebird banner. On double albums (single cassettes and, where available, CDs) are Dizzy Gil- lespie’s “Dizziest,” some of the bebop pioneer’s finest recordings, notably the essential late-’40s big band work; Louis Armstrong’s “Pops,” the greatest jazz musician of them all in some prime ma- teria! from ’4647; “The Complete Fats Waller Vol. IV,” continuing the long- delayed series of several years ago that intends to reissue all of that piano gi- ant’s massive RCA output; and “Short Stops,” the first in a proposed series that will issue all of the ’50s RCA work of “cool jazz” pioneer Shorty Rogers. On delectable single albums are won- derful works by two of the tastiest solo- ists in jazz history: Paul Desmond’s lovely “Late Lament,” ’61-62 sessions teaming the alto great with strings and Jim Hall’s guitar; and “Triple Play,” an album featuring three all-star 1967 sessions by alto colossus Johnny Hodges. From Blue Note comes three prime examples of the Blue Note sound from the ’60s: Academy Award nominee Dexter Gordon’s “Gettin’ Around,” McCoy Tyner’s “The Real McCoy,” and Lee Morgan’s “Search for the New Land.” From Delmark, which has been quiet in the jazz department of late, we get “The Albert Nicholas Quartet,” fea- turing the excellent traditional clarinet- ist in the company of Art Hodes, “All The Gin is Gone,” a properly low-down session led by tenor saxophonist Jim- my Forrest (and including, among oth- ers, Elvin Jones and Grant Green), and “Bouncing with Bud,” Bud Pow- ell in Copenhagen, vintage 1962. And from PolyGram’s Verve and MGM vaults comes CD versions (most with extra tracks) of Ella Fitzgerald’s “Ella at the Opera House,” “Stan Getz and J.J. Johnson at the Opera House” (73 minutes of music on that one), Charlie Parker/ Dizzy Gilles- pie’s “Bird and Diz,” Kenny Burrell’s “For Charlie & Benny,” Lee Konitz’s “Motion,” and three Clifford Brown albums: “Jams 2,” “Best Coast Jazz,” and “Clifford Brown All-Stars.” And, while we’re on the subject, Co- lumbia is beaming over its Jazz Master- pieces roll-out, claiming over a quarter- million units shipped on the first 12 releases, with another seven items due momentarily. SWING MOODS - NARAS/N. Y. recent- ly sponsored a seminar called “Big Bands Revisited" at N. Y.U. Here, remembering the good old days, are (I - r) trumpeter Roy El dridge, jazz historian George T. Simon, vo- calist Fran Warren, and arranger Sy Oliver. FESTIVITIES— It’s that time again, time to start thinking about jazz festi- vals. The first out of the box, the New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival, is also the most fun, though it’s the one that has the least to do with jazz. Set for April 24-May 3, the music and food ex- travanganza — and I do mean extrava- ganza— will present thousands of musicians, among them Fats Domino, Branford Marsalis, the Neville Brothers, the Fabulous Thunder- birds, Robert Cray, Wynton Mar- salis, Carl Perkins, Leon Redbone, Rockin’ Sidney, Ellis Marsalis, the Timeless All-Stars, Toots & the Maytals, the Dixie Humming- birds, Delfeayo Marsalis, Clifton Chenier, Jose Feliciano, the Four Tops, Gatemouth Brown, the Timeless All-Stars, Johnny Riv- ers, Jr. Walker & The All-Stars, Jay McShann, Wilson Pickett, Rockin’ Dopsie and the Cajun Twisters, the Dirty Dozen Brass Band, King Sunny Ade, Allen Toussaint, Pete Seeger, and the Sa- maroo Jets. Did somebody say Jazz Festival? P.O. Box 2530, New Orleans 70176 is the place to write for the whole list. For those thinking summertime, the fantastic JVC Grande Parade du Jazz at Nice will run from July 9-19 on the French Riviera with, to name just a few, George Benson, Miles Davis, Chuck Berry, Dexter Gordon, Her- bie Hancock, the MJQ, Benny Car- ter, Stephane Grappelli, Wynton Marsalis, Stanley Jordan, and Stan Getz in tow. Write to 8ter, rue Traver- siere, 92100, Boulogne, France. And, around the same time (July 2- 18), the Swiss banks of Lake Geneva will resound to the sounds of the 21st Montreux Jazz Festival, featuring many of the same artists who will be at Nice, and many who won’t (like Brazil’s Joao Bosco, Nany Caymi, and Simone). Write to the CH-1820, Montreux, Switzerland. TAKE FIVE, NYET?—The Dave Brubeck Quartet is presently glas- nosting it through the Soviet Union. 1ETAIL SHOP TALK I S VSDA NEWS -Lou Berg, of Au- dio/ Video Plus in Houston, has been appointed to serve the incomplete term of office of Art Ross, who has ten- dered his resignation from the board of directors of the VSDA. Ross, who has retired from the video business, was a charter member of the organization, and served on the board of directors since 1984. Mickey Granberg, execu- tive vice president of VSDA, says, “Art was known in the industry for his very articulate support of the position of the small video dealer. He was a true con- tributor both to the board and this orga- nization. His chairmanship of the membership committee was extremely valuable during the period of tremen- dous growth in numbers of our constitu- ency." Berg, who will serve the last few months of Ross’ term, which expires in August of this year, is the 1987 VSDA Convention Chairman, and is closely in- volved with the association’s activities- .Rudy Neely has also resigned from the board of directors. He had served on the board since August 1985 and as sec- retary in the 1986-87. His resignation followed the closing of the Video Show Store in Fullerson, California. The VSDA board of directors has unani- mously elected Joan Weisenberger, a member of the board of directors, to serve as secretary until the end of the association year. She has been active in VSDA activities at the local level, both with the Southern California chapter and as organizer of the Riverside chap- ter before joining the national board- ... presidents of the 33 regional chapters of the VSDA were on hand at the third annual Regional Leadership Confer- ence to visit the newly constructed na- tional headquarters, attend intensive meetings and seminars highlighting the responsibilities of the regional chapter, and for the first time, participate in per- sonal meetings with VSDA’s national leadership. The conference was held early last month at the national VSDA offices and the Viscount Hotel, both lo- cated in Marlton, N.J. NAME CHANGE -The American Can Company, parent company of their specialty retailing outfit, The Mu- sicland Group which operates 525 stores in 46 states under the names "Musicland," "Sam Goody," "Dis- count Records," and "Licorice Piz- za," has announced plans to change it’s name to Primerica Corporation, subject to approval by shareholders at the company’s annual meeting on April 28, 1987. The named Primerica, which was unanimously approved by the com- pany’s Board of Directors, is derived from the words prime — meaning first and foremost, and America, which ties to the company’s 86-year history. The company decided a name change was needed to reflect the sweeping changes that have occurred at the company in the past five years. Since 1982, Ameri- can Can has transformed itself from a predominantly manufacturing firm, to a services company with major interests in financial services and specialty retailing. MGM/UA HOME VIDEO ADOPTS UPC CODES — MGM/UA Home Video has joined a growing number of manufacturers who have gone along with the recommendation made by the VSDA Packaging Committee in adopting the UPC product coding sys- tem on its VHS and Beta video cas- settes and its Laserdiscs. “The first five numbers in the UPC Code,” explains MGM/UA Home Video director of cre- ative services, Ardis Rubenstein, “represent MGM/UA Home Video as the supplier and will remain constant. The next four numbers are the catalog number for the title and the final digit designates VHS (3), Beta (5) or Laser disc (6). In addition to its obvious utility as we move into the area of mass mar- keting, we believe the UPC Code will be of enormous value to us as a source of information retrieval. And it will be- come increasingly important to the more sophisticated retailers, suppling them with demographic information and a more efficient method to process orders. In the long run, these retailers will be able to check inventory and to take advantage of market trends as they develop.” Brian Kassan GLASS ACT—Manhattan recording artists Glass Tiger recently visited Record World in Hackensack, N.J. That position enunciated by Jason S. Kastenmeier A/I) is chairman of the House Copyright >-Committee. The bills (S-506 and HR-1384) pending committee consideration in h houses. Additionally, a House Com rce Committee trade legislation includes provision: that bill is awaiting clearance he House Rules Committee before it can taken up by the full House, lerman told the dozen legislators that r “poses the most significant technologi- threat to the American music industry r faces.” The reason, he said, is that DAT eliminates the distinction between originals and copies. With DAT he says, “every copy becomes a new original, the equivalent of a master recording ...” DAT he says, “is only a copying machine, serving no purpose other than home taping ...” Berman urged the enactment of the DAT legislation as a temporary measure until Congress can take up the basic issue: home taping. Charles D. Ferris, Washington attorney and spokesman for the Home Recording Rights Coalition (recording machine and tape manufacturers), argued that there is no justification for imposing a copy coding de- vice machines. DAT cannot allow perfect digital to digital recordings, based on an agreement among manufacturers, he noted. The fact the DAT machines can make ana- log copies is not germane, he contended, since home taping is not illegal if it is not for commercial gain. Ferris was backed by Leonard Feldman, owner of an electronics laboratory as well as a writer on audio technology. Feldman maintained that, “digital audio tape record ers . . . are a step forward in technology. The copy coding scanner is a step backward.” During a morning hearing, both sides demonstrated their respective systems with David W. Stebbings, CBS Technology Cen- ter, which developed the copy coding scan- ner system, rebutting Japanese demonstrations of the CBS device that os- tensibly degraded the music. Feldman also demonstrated the “flag” system used by the makers of DAT recorders that prevents digi- tal to digital copying. JVC Jazz Festival/New York Sets Ambitious Schedule By Lee Jeske NEW YORK -The JVC Jazz Festival/New York, which used to be the Kool Jazz Festi- val/New York, the Newport Jazz Festival/ New York, and, years and years ago, the Newport Jazz Festival, announced an ex- panded line-up of concerts for this year’s event, to be held June 19-28 in various ven- ues in and around the New York area. The expansion is seen as a deepening of JVC’s commitment to the Festival, which it took over at the eleventh-hour last year. Although the Festival is heavily-weighted towards traditional Festival favorites, there are several new twists. Perennial headliners Sarah Vaughan and Mel Torme will share concerts with recent Grammy winners Bob- by McFerrin and Diane Schuur, respective- ly. Dizzy Gillespie, who will be celebrating his 70th birthday later this year, will be at the helm of a stellar big band featuring Sam Rivers, Jon Faddis, Frank Wess, Steve Turre, James Williams and many others, in a concert that co-bills the bopmeister with Wynton Marsalis. The Modern Jazz Quartet will premiere a new work with the New York Chamber Symphony. Most of the concerts, as usual, will take place in Carnegie Hall and its Weill Recital Hall (unavailable to the Festival last year due to renovations), Avery Fisher Hall and Town Hall, with the Festival roaming as far afield as Waterloo Village, in Stanhope, New Jersey, and Stamford, Connecticut. The Festival is also affiliated with two other George Wein productions to be held concur- rently with the Festival’s final weekend: Newport Jazz at Saratoga, in Saratoga Springs, and Newport Jazz in Rochester, New York. Some of the other expected highlights of the Festival include a reunion of the original Ornette Coleman Quartet sharing a pro- gram with Coleman’s electric band, Prime Time; an evening with Ella Fitzgerald, who has spent a year inactive due to heart trou- bles; the Festival debut of Ruben Blades; and an all-star salute to Hank Jones. Returning are the series of one-hour pi- ano recitals at Weill Recital Hall, music cruises on the Hudson, the Waterloo tradi- tional jazz picnic, and an evening of David Chertok’s jazz films. As usual, several out- side producers will be used, including three record companies — CBS, Blue Note and Grama vision. ON JAZZ MORE MASTERPIECES—Colum bia Records has just released its second batch of “Jazz Masterpieces” — seven digitally remastered goodies from its large catalogue (these are not stricty re- issues since most of them have been in print continuously), each available in all three formats. They are the Dave Bru- beck Quartet’s “Gone With the Wind,” Miles Davis’ “’Round About Midnight” and “Porgy and Bess,” Duke Ellington’s “At Newport” (which features Paul Gonsalves’ gal- vanizing workout on “Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue”), Errol Garner’s “Concert by the Sea,” Charles Min- gus’s “Mingus Ah Urn,” and “The Quintessential Billie Holiday, Vol- ume I.” The Holiday is the only thing in here that is new — that is, that is new in this form. Over the years Columbia has issued Billie Holiday’s large output for the label in many different ways. What we have here, quite encouragingly, is simply the first 14 sides the great Lady Day made for Columbia, fully annotat- ed by the savvy Michael Brooks. If Columbia keeps this going apace, “The Quintessential Billie Holiday” will fill, perhaps, 14 albums, and that’s not in- cluding alternate takes and whatnot. It’s all worthy of rerelease. The Japanese, in fact, have reissued all of this al- ready— on an eight-disc CD set (with some 21 songs per disc) with somewhat questionable sound. I’d also like to men- tion something about the Mingus al- bum, which 1 think is one of Mingus’ true masterpieces. A few years ago, Co- lumbia put out a double-album, under its old Contemporary Masters Series, called “Nostalgia In Times Square,” containing restored versions of five of the nine songs on “Mingus Ah Um,” which apparently was subjected to seri- ous editing at the time of its release. The restored versions are now, sadly, out of print. It would have been nice if Columbia somehow included both ver- sions, a la the RCA Mingus reissue (“Ti- juana Moods”), either on a double album or on the single CD, but Colum- bia’s policy is strict on this — the LPs and the CDs will be identical. list. DISQUES CONTENT—DRG, which has been doing a fine service in issuing French sessions by American jazz greats that have never been available stateside, has just popped out four wor- thy new items (under their Disques Swing imprint). They are “Lionel Hampton in Paris,” a gently-swinging sextet date; “Benny Golson in Paris,” (actually mostly recorded in New York) featuring, among others, Lee Morgan, Bobby Timmons, and Philly Joe Jones; “Zoot Sims in Paris,” a bop- pish session with trumpeter Jon Eard- ley; and “The International Jazz Group Volume II,” an all-star set under French pianist Andre Persiany that includes Budd Johnson, Lawrence Brown, Eddie Barefield and Taft Jordan. Everything was recorded between ’56 and ’58 and everything sounds terrific. SCOTT’S DEAL — Saxophonist Tom Scott recently signed to GRP Records. Here, at the pacting pow wow, are (I - r) Larry Ro- sen, GRP co-president; Scott; and Scott's at- torneys Malcolm Wiseman and David Braun. I SEE A RHAPSODY—You say you want jazz films on videotape? Well, New York’s Rhapsody Films has quietly been releasing some fine jazz tapes over the last couple of years — there are now two dozen items in their catalogue — and, begorrah, they have just reduced their prices, to $29.95 for tapes under 30 minutes, $39.95 for the rest. Some of the better tapes available from Rhap- sody: The Last of the Blue Devils, Bruce Ricker’s Kansas City jazz epic; Talmage Farlow, Lorenzo De Ste- fano’s insightful portrait of the great guitarist; Sonny Rollins Live at Laren ; Jazz, a delightful session with Earl Hines and Coleman Hawkins; Different Drummer: Elvin Jones ; Jackie McLean on Mars; and Robert Mugge’s properly bizarre Sun Ra: A Joyful Noise. RETAIL SHOP TALK\ IT’S THAT TIME OF YEAR—RE- LEASE-MANIA -It took the new U2 album, “The Joshua Tree,” to de- pose those Beastie Boys as the num- ber one seller for most retail outlets across the country. However, the boys from Ireland will have some stiff compe- tition from the likes of the Purple Paisley one’s new double-record “Sign O’ The Times” which hit the street last week as well as new releases from David Bowie, Bryan Adams (the cassette single “Heat Of The Night” is selling nicely for retailers at press time) and the imminent resur- gence of Fleetwood Mac, not to men- tion the second batch of Beatles CD’s — “Rubber Soul,” “Revolver” and “Help” — which are scheduled for release later this month. Although the first four by the fab four sold well initial- ly with same type of graphic sales spike that characterized the Springsteen Box set (Capitol Records declined to give sales figures), most retailers agree that these three latest titles are a stronger set, capable of perhaps setting a CD sales record. Definitely no dearth of strong product in the stores now or in coming weeks. HAVE A PROBLEM WITH SHOP- LIFTING? READ THIS -It appears that a technological solution to combat shoplifting, which costs U.S. retailers $30 billion each year, is at hand. The Knogo Corporation based in Hicks- ville, New York has developed the Chameleon electronic article surveil- lance (EAS) system which uses a virtual- ly invisible, inexpensive target called Electro Thred (sic), a small thin light- weight wire encased in an adhesive strip. A recent study conducted by CBS Technology and sponsored by a joint sub-committee of the National Asso- ciation of Recording Merchandis- ers (NARM) and the Video Software Dealers Association (VSDA) tested the use of these threads in both audio and video tapes. The Knogo Electro Thred targets can re- peatedly be turned “on” and “off” — a basic requirement in a record/video re- tail environment. The system, tested both in the lab and in-store, did not alter the playback quality of an audio tape after one deactivation or videotapes af- ter they were deactivated and reactivat- ed 300 times. The targets are deactivated when the item is sold or rented, and can easily be reactivated if it is returned. The target can be inte- grated into the carton as it is folded and glued allowing potential shoplifters no clue either to its existence or location. The targets will work with magnetic sys- tems which some reatilers may already have. Manager of Micromagnetic sys- tems for Knogo, Bill Ogg, told Shop Talk that a two panel system for a typi- cal mall store would run about $5,000. Benefits to retailers: The Electro Thred can be incorporated into the manufac- turer’s packaging of all configurations. The “built-in” protection eliminates the labor cost of tagging each item in-store. Since the manufacturer adds the EAS protection as “a value-added service” the retailer doesn’t pay for the cost. Ma- jor music industry packaging vendors INDUSTRY STANDARD?— This bouquet of targets used in Knogo’s new Chamelei ; Micro Magnetic EAS system is a quick illustration of the system's versatility with patenU Knogo Electro Thred. Especially useful for protecting hard goods. Chameleon ’s MM Elect " ' Thred can masquerade as a bar code, (left); be self-adhering in a 2 1/2" Double Thread; hide a pfinted label; be built into a lockable, reusable lollipop tag for soft goods, or be virtual' invisible as a 4" strip of hair-thin Electro Thred. are now working with the NARM/ VSDA security device subcom- mittee to help define the manufactur- ing parameters which they hope will lead to a unified decision on utilization and placement of EAS targets. Harms Music Wins Copyright Infringement Suit Against Jem NEW YORK — The U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey has decided in favor of T.B. Harms Music Company in its copyright infringement action against Jem Records. Harms had sued Jem for infringing its copyright of “OR Man River” by import- ing records containing performances of the songs by Frank Sinatra without obtaining the consent or authority of Harms. Even though the records were lawfully made in New Zealand by WEA, and Jem had WEA’s permission to import them, the court held in ruling on Jem’s motion for summary judg- ment that such importation by Jem violated Section 602 of the U.S. Copyright Act and Jem is liable to Harms as an infringer. Judge John W. Bissel, in a 19-page opin- ion, determined that the copyright owner of a song has the exclusive right to authorize importation of recordings containing perfor- mances of the song. Beck, who comes out of the Austin jazz/blues scene, was responsible for bringing in Stevie Ray Vaughn, who plays guitar on the album’s first single, “First We Take Manhattan,” giving it a blues rock edge. Improving the aural quality of records was another ambition Sussman and Warnes shared from the outset, and many “tricks” were used to improve the album’s sound (most of which Warnes understandably pre- fers not to give away in print). The album was cut digitally at L A ’s Complex. “One of the unique things about this record is that it’s folk songs within a digital context,” she remarks. The album, which she says was much supported by the passion and enthusiasm of all the musicians and technicians who worked on it, gave her that long awaited chance to blossom, a thing too often ham- pered by corporate over-involvement. “Art- ists who are living experimental lives - like Leonard Cohen - have social information that’s very useful for the people who want to buy the records,” she says, “and if the corporation puts five a&r people between that process, it dilutes the information, and the telegram gets garbled. “What I’m in this for is the exchange of new information. It’s a communications thing, that’s what we’re all doing. I would (now) plead and beg with the corporations, that when an artist is ready - and maybe 1 wasn’t ready until now - to stay out the way. Stay out of the way and just let it go! Let it roll . . . Some artists you need to just leave alone.” A video to “First We l ake Manhattan” is in the works, and a tour i; .heduled for this summer. Warnes also plans to complete an album of her own songs, which she was in the midst of when she jumped at the chance to record the Cohen material. Cohen, Warnes maintains, has been strangely battered by critics in this country, and indeed, comparisons between his deliv- ery and wet cement have not been uncom- mon. Certainly, our national obsession for surfaces has much to do with such artist- bashing (Cohen may have been relegated to cult status here, but he’s widely acclaimed in Europe, as well as his native Canada, where his writings are even taught in schools). If there is a last laugh to be had in this story, it’s Warnes’ and Cohen’s, but bit- terness plays no part here. Human ness does, and music. Warnes, armed with the songs of one of the world’s great songwrit- ers, has set about restoring a sense of inti- macy that’s been sorely missed. IN CASHBOX* April 13, 1957—JOHANNESBURG, SOUTH AFRICA — For the first time, the music of the modern urban African has been introduced to the public on high-fidelity long-playing records with the release of Trutone Africa Limited’s “Music was Born in Africa.” This re- cord was conceived as an ideal souvenir for tourists visiting the Union who want- ed to take away some memento of their stay. The music of the urban African is a blend of ancient tribal chants and modern jazz idioms that results in a dif- ferent type of listening. “Music was Born in Africa” was compiled from re- cordings made in all the major centres of South Africa during 1956... Pictured (l-r) are: John G Healey, executive director ofAmerican Operations, Amnesty International: GilFriesen, president ofA&M Records; Charlie Burchill, Simple Minds; Jim Kerr, Simple Minds. Simple Minds’ Gains Prisoner Release Via Amnesty Push LOS ANGELES — Last year’s postcard campaign on behalf of Amnesty Internation- al, organized by Scottish group Simple Minds, has yielded the release of at least one Sri Lankan man, according to the group’s U.S. label, A&M. Simple Minds distributed Amnesty International postcards at its con- certs to spur letter writing campaigns on behalf of “adopted” prisoners of conscience. P. Udayarahan had been incarcerated for up to three years according to Amnesty In ternational. He was a member of a religious minority at odds with the Sri Lankan gov- ernment and had been held without trial or charges. Amnesty International’s San Diego office was contacted by the government of Sri Lanka to inform them of Udayarahan’s re- lease. The prisoner was released on June 16, 1986. Simple Minds performed in San Diego in April. The San Diego office then informed Simple Minds’ Jim Kerr by letter that Udayarahan’s release was as a likely re- sult of the postcard distribution at the group's San Diego concert. “Our chapter here in San Diego passed out postcards on (Udayarahan’s) behalf to every member of While some writers are somewhat artists in a sense because they write material meant for themselves, Levy says there are “only a handful of writers” who work that way and can use the material in a another situation. “We do have some writers who give us ma- terial and say, ‘What do you think?’ but more often than not, we are working with writer just like an editor would sit down with a book writer and say ‘the market tells us we can sell romance novels to the following de- mographic with these types of characters and x amount of pages.’ The writer says ‘gotcha’ and goes off and knocks it out.” Often, says Levy, the artist may be a great lyricist but need melodic input or vice versa. “We try to put those marriages together as well.” Several of MCA Music’s writers who the audience at your concert,” the letter said. “All of us are absolutely delighted,” said Kerr. “This is a credit to the people who attended our show and made the effort to fill out a postcard and mail it in,” he added. During its 1985-86 world tour, Simple Minds endorsed the postcard campaign at each of its concerts. In addition, the band donated the entire proceeds of one Ameri- can and one British concert to Amnesty International. John G. Healey, Amnesty International’s executive director of American Operations thanked Kerr and Simple Minds for keeping “alive the spirit of our ‘Conspiracy Of Hope’ ” and added, “That a prisoner can be freed as a result of a postcard campaign shows that the effort to make peaceful change doesn’t end with the last benefit con- cert. In fact, we are just beginning.” President of A&M Records, Gil Friesen commented, “The release of P. Lang THE ROXY, L.A. — The kid’s got talent. Does she ever! Sire’s K.D. Lang has a voice that can prod cattle to polka or make other- wise composed folk get all dreamy-eyed. Is she country, is she pop ... is she kidding? These and other questions permeated the pre-show buzz here recently. The answer, delivered with raucous energy by Lang and her frolicking band The Reclines, was all-of- the-above and none-of-the-above: Yes, the sound is country, but not purely; and yes the sound has a rock/pop edge, but not much; and yes, Lang does have fun with the corni- er aspects of country, but her heart seems to be in the right place while she’s doing so. What Lang and her band proved here was that there is indeed an intersection where Patsy Cline’s country blues, Frank Yankovic’s polka, Rose Maddox’ western swing and Gene Vincent’s rockabilly can meet and intertwine in a barn-shaking square dance of styles. COLLINS & “BRUNO " ROCK OUT—A! bert Collins, recent Grammy winner for his Alli- gator LP, ‘‘Showdown!" (also featuring Robert Cray and Johnny Copeland), performed his hot ‘‘cool’’ sound of blues before two sold-out crowds at Los Angeles’ Music Machine. Join- ing Albert on stage for a few numbers was TV's “Moonlighting ” co-star Bruce ‘‘Bruno’’ Willis. Pictured (l-r) are: Collins, Willis, (c) and saxman Sam Franklin. Lang’s rich, voluminous voice is a plea- sure. With apparent ease and considerable stage poise, the former performance artist from the Canadian sticks nearly blew this venerable Sunset Strip venue off the boule- vard with her deliciously resonant pipes. It’s true, Lang does sound a bit like coun- try legend Patsy Cline (to whom she’s been continually compared by the press), espe- cially when covering the late singer’s materi- al. Lang opened the show with her own bluesy, downtempo rendition of Cline’s torchy, barroom-busting “Don’t Ever Leave Me Again,” which she milked for every note while casually leaning on the keyboard stand singing to keyboardist Michael Creeber. Much of the humor in her act - criticized for its apparent irreverence toward country music - was so subtle that it took sharp ears to catch it, while some was so broad that it was impossible to miss (such as the three cigarettes Lang manipulated while singing Cline’s “Three Cigarettes In An Ashtray” - a romantic ballad whose ashtray imagery is so bizarre that it’s funny). The evening’s line-up of tunes included the Joanie Sommers ‘60’s pop hit “Johnny Get Angry,” which was given particularly campy treatment. Working the tune into a violent climax (in which an imaginary “Johnny” finally hauls off and whallops her), Lang lay prone in silence for a good two minutes, only to bounce back and finish the song. Lang and The Recline’s country single, a EMIA. rockabilly cover of Joe South’s “Rose Gar- den” was delivered with infectious impact, featuring guitarist Gordie Mathews’ strong instrumental lead. “To dance is human,” the singer ex- claimed before charging into one of several polka numbers, “but to polka is devine!” And indeed, Lang and The Reclines, aided by Ben Mink’s fiddle, brought enough vitali- ty to this rather quaint (albeit rip-roaring) country dance tradition as to make it seem new. Lang and her band’s L.A. debut was re- freshingly original. Much more than the mere novelty act much of this material might well have constituted in the hands of a less talented, endearingly witty singer and less superbly proficient musicians, this show had that ineffable magical edge that spells quality and longevity. Gregory Dobrin on Pullen THE PUBLIC THEATRE, N.Y.C.-Don Pullen, the volcanic modern jazz pianist and co-leader, with George Adams, of one of the finest bands in jazz, turned to his roots last Monday night for a terrifically entertaining evening at the Public Theatre. Nancy Weiss Hanrahan, who initiated a series of New Jazz at the Public Theatre commissions last year, had the ingenius idea of having Pullen organize a band around his organ playing — an instrument he used quite a bit in the or- gan-heavy ’60s but had ignored in recent years. From the first notes of the first tune, “Zet,” Pullen made it clear where he was coming from — he was coming from the jukeboxes of the 1960s. For the most part, Pullen and his bandmates could have been recording for the Blue Note of 20 years ago. It was a refreshing, exceptionally enjoyable night of music. Opening with a septet — drummer Bobby Battle, guitarist Melvin Sparks, trumpeter Joe Gardner, pianist Jeremy Bacon, alto saxophonist Charles Williams, and trom- bonist Frank Lacy — that was vintage Blue Note, Pullen churned out swirling, thick or- gan chords, stomped-off fine sturdy organ bass, and generally unleashed the down-ho- meist organ sound this side of Brother Jack McDuff. Right in there with him were Sparks, who cooked like crazy on “Blues at Hanna’s House;” Williams, who cooked like crazy on a deep-fried “Send Me Someone To Love;” and Battle, who cooked like crazy every second of the way.
