" COVER STORY EAST COASTINGS Surface Surfaces With A Crossover Hit Paullorio NEW YORK - “It’s scary how you write a song and accidently touch on a subject that’s real sensitive to a lot of : people,’’ says Dave Conley of Surface. ' “Last night it hit me when everyone (at a party) kept saying, ‘do you know what your record is doing to us?’ It was almost scary the way they were putting it.’’ Certainly this is the kind of scary few artists fear. Scary or not. Surface is getting across in a big way with “Happy,’’ the first single from their self-titled Columbia debut album, which is turning into one of the big crossover stories of the year. I But, like most breakthroughs, this ! one was partly accidental; “Happy” j would never have happened if it I weren’t for Conley’s twelve year old 1 nephew Steven. “My nephew ran downstairs and f said you gotta come upstairs and see I what (bandmember) Dave (Townsend) i is doing,” says Conley. “So he j grabbed me and Bernard (Jackson) and i we were listening to Townsend sing this line ‘only you can make me happy.’ Immediately Bernard picked up his pen and I jumped on the syn- thesizer and we started working on the song. Inside of an hour the song was complete.” “Every time I hear that record I think of my little nephew and how it hit him. And he’s not even into this style of music, he’s into rap,” says Conley. Apparently, Surface is appealing to I a lot of people who don’t normally lis- I ten to the type of quiet-storm balladry I the trio plays. Not only is “Happy” ! still top five on the B/C and twelve- 1 inch charts after more than three I months, but last week it made the kind I of crossover most artists just dream about, debuting at number 86 bullet on the pop singles chart. “It’s really strange that this record’s crossing over into pop now,” says Conley. “This is totally unex- pected because we’re r&b guys strictly and we don’t stray away from what we do.. ..It’s very soft on the ear, it’s not abrasive, it’s not fast, it’s not slow, it’s right in the middle of the road. Indeed Surface is about as far from rap or hard funk as imaginable. Still, its range and appeal have always been wide, even when they formed in 1983 as a non-performing songwriting trio, writing for such acts as Sister Sledge, Gwen Guthrie, and New Edition. “We’d like to believe that it doesn’t matter what style of music you do,” he says. “If you have something that’s good people will get into it. If it’s good and it just happens to hit home with the lyrics we think that people will just like it. And that’s probably what’s happening with it crossing over like that, just because of what we’re saying and how we’re put- ting it.” Conley believes Surface has just scratched the surface of what they’re capable of doing. “The name ‘Sur- face’ came up because all of our music was sort of below the surface and as soon as we got a break we decided to name the group Surface because this was the first time that our music actual- ly came out of the basement. “It took a long time before any- thing started surfacing,” he says. “We were just hitting it so hard trying to get anything to happen. When we decided to put the group together there was real- ly no other name we could even think of using. And we believe we still have things to be surfaced. AT HIS RECENT BOTTOM Line show, Chris Isaak came off like a digital Presley or a Sun Sessions Springsteen or Johnny Carroll in a turquoise suit, though his stage patter was Richard Price on a binge for sure, and his band, Silvertone, clob- bered the beat like few since CCR, and the lead guitarist, ex-Avenger Jimmy Wilsey, a real comer, played with violin brilliance on “Waiting For The Rain To Fall” and swamp know-how on “You Owe Me Some Kind Of Love,” overheating just about every song on Isaak’s self- titled second album for Warner Bros. Isaak’s new album might do for roots-rock what Robert Cray’s “Strong Persuader” did for the blues, though comparisons to “The Wild, The Innocent, and the E Street Shuffle” also obtain if only because Isaak is an artist with enough runaway charisma to break through with a “Bom To Run” next time around. In concert he generated the kind of heat that turns gold into platinum, and while his new album is not even near gold, remember that 50,000 units is all “The Wild...” moved in ‘74. Still, this shouldn’t be a waiting game, the guy’s ready now; he’s got the chops, the tunes, tlie duds, and a fervid cult following that could easily spill into the mainstream if AOR would give “Heart Full Of Soul” or “You Owe Me Some Kind Of Love’ ’ half a chance. SHELL SHOCKED LOLK - Michelle Shocked has been causing a buzz in folk circles lately with her “Texas Campfire Tapes’’ (Cooking Vinyl) album. She opens for Loudon Wainwright III at Town Hall June 13. JOHN ELANSBURGH of They Might Be Giants organized an AIDS benefit concert at CBGBs featuring performances by six of New York’s finest indie bands - Glenn Mor- row’s Rage To Live, They Might Be Giants, The Ordinaires, Peter Stampfel and The Bottlecaps, The Cucumbers, and The Last Round- Up. Morrow played “Amore Taken” and other new songs, the Giants used a large vaudeville stage hook as a musical instrument, Stampfel revved up “96 Tears,” and The Ordinaires did their contrapuntal thing. But more importantly, the con- cert raised more than $1,200 to battle an epidemic that Washington refuses to fight in anything resembling a responsible manner. The music in- dustry has already taken the lead with “That’s What Friends Are For,” which has reportedly raised more than a million dollars so far for the American Foundation For AIDS Research. Now is the time for some- one like Bob Geldof to organize a massive AIDS-Aid benefit concert, enlisting the support of superstars from Bruce Springsteen on down. And if Geldof isn’t available, well, maybe Flansburgh has some ideas of his own. BRIEFINGS - Tom Kimmel’s “Five To One” (PolyGram) is a debut album of major significance, with ten songs that will probably change a lot of lives. Most per- suasive are the last three tracks - “Violet Eyes,” the Mellencampish “No Tech” and the powerhouse title track. GLORY DAYS — Steve Earle’ s ‘ ‘Exit Zero’’ (MCA) isn’t an album - it’s an event. For anyone who thought nobody could top “Guitar Town,’’ start with “Nowhere Road’’ and don't stop. The song “Five To One” is like a fully-detailed “My Hometown” in which Kimmel vows to “go down swinging” to save a deteriorating neighborhood where there are “bars on the windows when the day is done” and “bars over churches, maybe five to one.” It’s a knock-out song, well developed by Bill Szy- mczyk and Bob Clearmountain’s production, and it may send the album to the top of the charts. This is Dick Wingate’s first signing as PolyGram ’s senior vp of A&R, and what a way to start. More on Kimmel in a future issue.. ..Arthur Russell, the avant-funkist responsible for Dinosaur L’s “Go Bang,” and Loose Joints’ “Is It All Over My Face,” has an album out on Upside called “World Of Echo.” With only cello and vocals, Russell creates a sound unlike anybody else’s, most ef- fectively on “Let’s Go Swimming” and “Wax The Van,” which was a dance club hit for Lola... .Columbia’s Gary Lucas recently brought to my at- tention the striking similiarity be- tween the cover art of U2’s “The Joshua Tree” and that of Captain Beefheart and The Magic Band’s “Ice Cream For Crow.” Both covers were shot by photographer Anton Corbijn....U2’s The Edge wrote, co- produced, and performed the Cap- tive film soundtrack, which has just been released by Virgin Records. The ten tracks were written prior to the recording of “The Joshua Tree”. ...Marshall Crenshaw’s new album, “Mary Jean & Nine Others,” will be released June 2d by Warner Bros. It was produced by Don Dixon and features backing vocals by Marti Jones... .The Midnite Gypsies, who have an album out on Natural Enemies Records, recently played the Central Park Bandshell, and, as on vinyl, their strongest song was the soulful and hooky “Heartache,” which alone makes the band worth j tracking. ON JAZZ PASSING ON-Bassist Wilbur Lit- tle and pianist Victor Feldman both succumbed to heart attacks in the past couple of weeks. Little was a big-toned, flexible bassist who was widely admired; he worked with Kenny Dorham, Elvin Jones, J.J. Johnson and many others before moving to Europe, where he became one of the most in-demand bassists on the continent-backing visiting Americans and enlivening local groups with his sohd work. He was 59. Feldman was a British-bom pianist and vibes-player who lived and worked in California. He was a popular studio musician, a pioneer in the fusing of jazz and classical music, and a sideman who worked with Miles Davis, amongst many others. He was 53. A memorial service was held last week at New York’s St. Peter’s Lutheran Church for Buddy Rich, who died last month. Except for an outrageously vulgar and incoherent outburst from Steve Gadd, the two- and-a-half-hour afternoon was filled with gentle reminiscences and swing- ing music. Max Roach, Roy Eldridge, Sonny Igoe, Burt Korall, and Chico Hamilton were among the speakers; Stan Getz, Ruby Braff, Joe Bushkin, Jane Harvey, and a Rich alumni band under the baton of Rich stalwart Steve Marcus were among the performers; and David Chertok supphed appropriate film chps. Hook-Music Director WICO AM/FM-Salisbury, MD C.R. Hook recently celebrated his 19th Anniversary at WICO, which Is a long time to be at one station. During those 19 years at the station, he has witnessed the change in country music - from traditional to the new con- temporary country-pop sound. And although he isn’t fond of that change at all, he has stuck with both the music and the sta- tion through the years. Hook’s radio career started back in the GO’S. In 1964 he was in- jured in a car accident and spent a year in the hospital. When he left the hospital in 1965, he landed a part-time position at WBOC, abig band/middle-of-the- road station in Salisbury. He worked part-time with the station for three or four months, and then went to a full-time position. WBOC was both an AM/FM and televisionstation. "They liked my voice and they put me on TV doing sports," he says. "And I did that for a few months along with doing a radio show." When he left WBOC some people found it hard to un- derstand why he would leave a radio and television position, when most radio announcers would have jumped at the chance to be a television an- nouncer as well. But Hook just wanted to play music. "I’m a radio person," he says. "I love music, and 1 love country music." So in April, 1968, he joined country music station WICO. In 1969 he became the station’s Music Director, the same posi- tion he still holds. At WICO these days he also works in sales and has a morning on-air shift as well. When he gets off the air on Mondays and Tues- days he takes all the music calls that come in. He also writes and records commercials and spends the afternoon calling on clients for sales. He tries to lis- ten to a few records each day. Of all his duties, he especially enjoys those involving the music. "I love music, but in a small market you can’t make a living just being a Music Direc- tor," he says. What Hook doesn’t enjoy is the change in country music that’s been going on during recent years. "I enjoy playing the songs as long as they’re country, not the rock that they call country now." WICO plays a well-balanced mix- ture of both oldies and currents. Independents and locals are also given a good deal of airplay. "We’re really making an effort with independents," Hook says. "We’re giving them slots now in our morning drive time to try to help the new artists, at least to get people familiar with them." After 19 years in country music radio, it is evident that C.R. Hook loves the music, and he plans on staying with it, as long as it’s countiy. "I’ve been very, very distressed at what is called country now," he comments. "To me, it’s not country music. Right now, with our oldies and people like Randy Travis and Reba McEntire, there’s still some good country music that’s coming out. if it continues that swing, then I’d be perfectly satis- fied to retire in it. If it increases any more to contemporary or rock, then 1 really don’t know." Sandy Daens HIGH PRIORITY John Wesley Ryles is our priority. So is K.D. Lang and so are all our new artists. But please don't forget the other ones, because they are great also. BOB SAPORITI Warner Bros. Priorities for RCA are K.T. ONJAZZ FANTASY-IZES^G4f Fantasy Re- cords is still issuing OJCs then vinyl can’t really be dead, can it? The latest batch of the midlme goodies have just arrived and, in a pair of new twists, the albums are all culled from the same label-Fantasy-and the first 2,000 copies of each are pressed on red vinyl. Fantasy, founded by Max and Sol Weiss, was the label of San Francisco jazz and, in the mid-’50s, was quite an influential operation, thanks in great part to Dave Brubeck, their biggest-selling artist. But Fan- tasy had a number of other influential performers on their roster-including Lenny Bruce-and they recorded some of the then-popular fusions of jazz and latin music spearheaded by the likes of Cal Tjader and Mongo Santamaria They also had the inter- esting habit of issuing their albums on colored vinyl, years before this be- came an au courant practice in the rock game (among my souvenirs are several red vinyl Lenny Bruce LPs). Well, these 20 new OJCs include no Brubeck or Bruce, but they are rich in a sweet, innocent, percolating sound- a soimd that very much reflects the ’50s and early-’60s, but a sound that holds up very nicely today. So, forget the compact discs for now. It’s time to head for the turntable, with, per- haps, a Kerouac novel by your side, a jug of cheap Italian wine, and the sounds (and red vinyl sight) of Cal Tjader’s “Mambo with Tjader,” “Tjader Plays Mambo” (snappy tit- les, those), “San Francisco Moods,” “A Night at the Blackhawk,” “Con- cert on the Campus,” “Cal Tjader Plays, Mary Stallings Sings,” and “Plays Harold Arlen,” Bola Sete’s (he was the early bossa nova guitarist who died this year) “Bossa Nova,” “The Incomparable,” “Autentico!,” and “Vince Guaraldi & Bola Sete Live at El Matador,” Guaraldi’s “Jazz Impressions,” “The Mont- gomery Brothers In Canada,” “A Date with the Mastersounds” (Buddy and Monk Montgomery minus brother Wes), “Swinging with the Mastersounds,” Mongo San- tamaria’s “Sabroso,” and “Yambu,” “Stan Getz” (featuring, who else?. Cal Tjader), “Gerry Mul- ligan/Paul Desmond, and “Modem Music From San Francisco,” a com- pilation featuring Guaraldi, the Ron Crotty Trio, and the Jerry Dodgion Quartet. During this 50th anniver- sary of the Golden Gate Bridge, it’s nice to remember that San Francisco was a hot-bed of musical activity long before the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane and Huey Lewis & The News. TWO JOE HENDERSON (Blue Note BT 85126) L O W C 1 27 2 19 3 41 4 41 9 5 6 24 5 34 7 27 JAZZFEATURE PICKS JAZZ CLASSICS IN DIGITAL STEREO: NEW ORLEANS (VOL. 1), CHICAGO (VOL. 2), NEW YORK (VOL. 3)-BBC CD 588, 589, 590 (dist. by Mobile Fidelity Sound Labs)-Producer: Robert Parker “How the great jazzmen really sounded!” is the tagline of this series and you’ve got to believe them. Australian Robert Parker started fid- dling around with acoustic-era jazz a number of years ago and now, final- ly, the fruits of his incredible labor are getting stateside distribution. These three CDs feature the hkes of Louis Armstrong, Earl Hines, JeUy Roll Morton, King Oliver, and the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, all recorded in the early days of record- ing (the ODJB track is from 1918) and all gloriously clear and rich. Parker calls his “digital stereo” “a subjective balancing act for the trans- fer engineer, juggling opposing fac- tors such as high-frequency response and surface noise on one hand, and deep bass response and rumbles on the other.” No matter, you’ve got to hear it to believe it. Feld believes that the DJ’s were treated unfairly, and that informa- tion was withheld from them during their contract negotiations. “At the same time that they were promising these guys the commitment to KMET, to the call letters and to the rock and roll format, there was a billboard being planned for The Wave, or a jingle being recorded, or research on audience reaction was being con- ducted. These things were being done at the same time.” Hammer denied these allegations, saying, “the informa- tion was not withheld from them at the I time of their negotiations . ’ ’ Ladd, Perry and Snyder had all been independently offered full-time f: employment last year at KLSX, a Los ! Angeles “Classic Rock” station, but turned the offer down in order to at- tempt to return KMET to its former position at the top of the album rock ratings. In numerous meetings with sta- tion manager Bloom, the three disc jockeys were assured of management’s commitment to the Album Rock for- mat, and all rumors of a possible for- mat change were quickly squelched. One of the album’s more ingenious- ly chosen cuts is its title track, tlie Gladys Knight and The Pips chestnut, “If I Were Your Woman,” produced by Ken Kersey. Mills, a confirmed Knight fan, has a vocal field day with the song. ‘ T like singing music that has a lot of feeling and a lot of soul to it,” she says of the album as a whole, which is more ballad-oriented than previous ef- forts. “I like dance music to go out and dance to, but I don’t think I’m a dance artist. I don’t think that’s what my forte is. I think ballads and maybe uptempo songs are, but moderately uptempo - not dance dance music. ’ ’ A native of Brooklyn, N.Y., Mills first appeared on Broadway at age 9 in “Maggie Flynn,” with Shirley Jones and the late Jack Cassidy. A single recorded for Burlington Music helped land her the lead role in the “The Wiz,” the triumphant all-black, rock music stage adaptation of The Wizard of Oz. Her success during that show’s five-year run set the stage for con- tinued success as a recording artist. Her debut album, a 1979 teaming with James Mtume and Reggie Lucas, “Whatcha’ Gonna Do With My Lovin,”’ sold more than a million copies. The successes kept on coming. In 1980 she won a Grammy for Best Female R&B Vocalist with her gold “Sweet Sensation” LP, and in 1981 of the three men suspected that despite the public and private assurances to the contrary, a secret plan was being devised to ultimately do away with their jobs and the station itself, neither Ladd, Perry, nor Snyder would have committed themselves to KMET over the other opportunities presented to them.” ‘ T think our possibilities of winning are very good,” continued Feld. “There is a concept known in the law as fraudulent inducement to contract, which means that two sides dealing at arms length for a contract must have equal bargaining power. The employer- employee relationship is a fiduciary relationship based on trust, and ob- viously the management had informa- tion that the DJ’s had no access to so they were not dealing fairly. ’ ’ The three disc jockeys admit con- fusion when contemplating the reasons for the station’s abrupt dismissal of the air staff after such a short attempt at rectifying the poor ratings. “The ques- tion of why this was done is something that we’ve been asking ourselves since it happened,” stated Perry. “It’s some- thing that I hope a judge will ask, be- cause I have a feeling that when they find out the answer, someone’s going to have to write us a check. garnered an American Music Award in the same category with her album “Stephanie.” A year later, her “Merci- less” album was nominated for a Grammy. Returning to theatre in 1984, Mills set a record as the youngest actress to do a revival of a role she created with her return to the revival production of “The Wiz,” which toured widely. Even so, success in her other occupa- tion - that of a recording artist - was never far away. Her “I’ve Got The Cure” album, recorded during that time, spawned the hit dance tune “The Medicine Song.” Her unusual ability to maintain careers in theatre and recording con- tinues. Following a 25 -city summer tour as part of the Michelob Class Act Concert Series (along with The Whispers and Robert Brookins), Mills will return to the Great White Way late this year in another original role. The show is an updated, ’80’s musical adap- tation of the 1960’s coming-of-age film classic. To Sir With Love, in which she’ll co-star with Dorian Harewood (Roots). In it. Mills plays the part created 20 years ago by British record- ing star Lulu, as well as singing the title song (the rest of the score will be new). Meanwhile, “If I Were Your Woman,” with its first single already taking the charts by storm, promises to mark a further milestone in the career of this charttopping, audience wowing “Wiz” kid. SPECIAL REVIEW Capitol Records this week commemorates the 20th Anniversary of the release of the Beatles’ “Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Heart’s Club Band” with the first-time release of the CD version of this monumental treasure of rock and roll. Twenty years after its onginal release, the new technology gives the LP’s original details striking new life. Most “ambitious” albums in rock and roll history have ended up just that, ambitious. It took the singular brilliance of The Beatles to combine ambition, vision and execution. The result was the cultural landmark that is today still haded as the finest rock and roll album in history. The glory of CD brings to the listener’s attention every sparkling sotmd from rock’s first (arguably) “concept” album. The tape loop experimentation, al- most buried on traditional vinyl, leaps out at you from the CD. The layers of sounds, orchestrations, voices, effects, etc.—what producer George Martin calls ‘ ‘sound collages ’’-are all more intelligible on CD. This CD is the only one that Capitol has released seperately. The previous tv/o batches included four and three CDs, respectively. The decision to release “Sgt. Pepper’s” (CDP 7 46442) by itself demonstrates the power of this title. When it was first released in 1967, it spent 15 weeks at Number One and sold 2.5 million copies in just three months. For more on the release of “Sgt. Pep- per’s” see Paul lorio’s comments in this week’s East Coastings, page 13. Stephen Padgett

ONJAZZ^^m SOVIET GARAGE?-Pat Meth- eny’s latest tour will be opening tonight at the Jubilee Hall in Leningrad. Leningrad? Yep, Meth-, eny and his band left last week for an unusual tour of the Soviet Union. Un- usual in that this is working hke a real tour-the Metheny Group is play- ing 13 concerts in three cities, each in a 7,000 seat haU; is bringing their own sound and lighting; and is actual- ly getting paid by the Soviets (that’s Goskontsert, the official goverment concert agency). For those who want to know such things, the tour is at Jubilee Hall, June 8-11; Moscow’s Dynamo HaU, June 13-17; and Kiev’s Sports Concert Hall, June 20- 23. The concerts, Metheny proudly notes, were sold out in no time-and to regular paying customers at that. After the Soviet Union, the Metheny Group (Lyle Mays, Steve Rodby, Paul Wertico, David Blamires, Mark Ledford, Armando Marcal) plays Europe before beginning a U.S. tour (including Radio City) in August. This wiU all coincide with the release of “Still Life (Talking),’’ the first Geffen album by the Metheny Group. Metheny, you’U recall, began his Geffen deal last year with the fantastic “Song X,’’ the col- laboration with Ornette Coleman. The plan was for this album to be a collaboration with Milton Nascimen- to, but, says Pat, that has been put off for the next album (he and Geffen figured it’d be better to slip a group album out in-between). Metheny, by the way, says he will not be flying into Moscow in a Cessna. A call to Ticketmaster 1-800-682-8080 gets the poop. PASSING ON-Turk Murphy, one of the most steadfast keepers of the traditional jazz flame, died May 30 of cancer in San Francisco. Murphy came to prominence in 1940, during the heart of the traditional jazz revival, playing trombone in Lu Wat- ters’ Yerba Buena Jazz Band. Mur- phy formed his own band in the ’40s and has performed constantly since then, sticking to his traditional jazz guns. He never left San Francisco- playing long engagements in residence at various San Francisco boites and hotels. Last year, the Mur- phy band participated in a sold-out Carnegie Hall concert in tribute to the trombonist. His burly, tailgating sound was spry and uplifting, and the music was pure and lovely. Turk Murphy was 71. JAZZ TIMES-The Jazz Times Con- vention is scheduled for October 14- 17 at New York’s Roosevelt Hotel and I’ll be going into more detail about it later on. PROFILES KLSX - “Classic Rock” Here To Stay On September 27, 1986, Los Angeles radio listeners were in- troduced to an inventive, new radio concept, "Classic Rock.” The inception of KLSX 97.1 FM in the L.A. marketplace quickly proved successful, and soon many stations across the country followed suit. The demise of one-time L.A. market kingpin KMET only aided the cause - freeing up many of that stations popular on-air talent to fill positions at the infant KLSX. "I think what we have done with KLSX is we’ve been able to fill a void that existed in this marketplace,” stated the sta- tion’s General Manager Bob Moore during a recent interview with Cash Box. He continued, “ ... a void that we talked about for two and a half years and didn’t know what it was, fortunately the audience has labeled it 'classic rock.’ ” A programmer’s definition of classic rock, according to Moore, " ... is music that has outlasted a fad or a popularity of a particular time.” Yet he credits one of the stations listeners with the ideal analogy, "He told me, ‘An oldie is ‘Sugar Sugar,’ a clas- sic is ‘Layla.’ ” I think that is the perfect definition of a classic.” He emphasized, "We are expos- ing product to people that they haven’t been able to hear in years.” One myth Moore would like to shatter is that of the narrow reach of the classic format. “Too many people try to categorize classic rock as a handful of ar- tists, it isn’t a handful of artists - it’s over 35,000 songs, that’s our library.” He continued, “What we have done is solidified that once and for all to the world that there is a format called classic rock, and it is a real format. It isn’t 25 records, it isn’t a morning show, it’s a very, very intricate, com- plex format that reaches a mass of people - and if you do it cor- rectly it is something that can continue to grow and continue to expand. Our goal is to have over a million listeners, have them all happy and interactive with the radio station. And I think that that’s a very realistic goal for us to achieve. The bottom line is that the audience feels very favorable to what we’re doing and showing tremendous sup- port of the station. The station is being programmed on a daily basis utilizing our audience and their reaction to everything, and that’s the single most important thing. Radio is a part of the entertainment industry, but it’s really a part of the communica- tion industry. We encourage not only praise, but criticism.” “ an oldie is ‘Sugar Sugar, ’ a classic is ‘Layla’ . ” Although on the air only a few short months, KLSX has refused to remain dormant and familiar. One major shift has been that of programming a heal- thy dose of current rock within the playlist. "We play a lot of currents, I personally think that there are a lot of classic acts today that make classic rock - the Talking Heads is one of them, U2 is on the border of that right now. The Police are definitely classic artists ... At this time we are playing five cur- rents an hour out of fifteen records an hour. We play Paul Simon, we play a lot of Eddie Money, we’re playing a lot of the new Greg Allman. The currents have to be by an established art- ist or an artist that has outlasted a fad. We have tried to carve out the music that has lasted throughout whatever that initial fad was.” He assured, “We are constantly testing the water, what we will do is see what lasts KLSX prides itself on its “no repeat days,” never playing the same song in one 24 hour period. Moore recalls “ ... when we started in the market, one of our friendly competitors had a no repeat Thursday. I was talk- ing to their General Manager and he was telling me how dif- ficult it was to have a "no repeat day” - because you have to be really careful, you can burn out your library real quickly. I kind of snickered in the back of my mind and thought, ‘our approach is going to be no repeat weeks!” On the subject of KMET (now KTWV - new age format, no disc jockeys), Moore ex- plained that “The greatest benefit we received from KMET’s demise, was the freeing up of some incredible talent: Jim Ladd, David Perry, Jack Snyder, Paraquat Kelly, Cynthia Fox, etc.” He continued, "KMET, un- fortunately, died a long time ago, they just buried the body recent- ly. It did have another effect, be- cause it gave us the opportunity to reach another level of people that I think had hung on to KMET much longer than the norm. KMET, I think, was one of those caring, concerned, in- volved radio stations - and when they went away, there was a part of certain people’s hearts that went with it. ” KLSX has made a point of devoting itself to community ser- vice and public awareness. The station has been active in aid for Vietnam veterans, L.A.’s home- less, and many other aspects of involvement. KLSX recently sponsored The Doobie Brothers reunion concert benefiting the Vietnam vets, and donated much on air time devoted to the cause via auctions and public service announcements. Moore commented, "We’re not taking out our costs. We don’t have ad- ministrative costs or overhead, we’re happy to turn over the proceeds because it’s a cause we believe in very much. We are very, very involved with the L.A. homeless, it has become a major problem. We are what 1960’s FM radio was all about - being concerned, getting in- volved. We are not a music machine. The worst thing that could happen to us is a billboard saying ‘New format, no disc jock- eys’ - that is not us. The enter- tainers that we have on the air are definitely aware of what’s going on in the world and they definitely speak their piece about it.” Moore insists “My radio sta- tion is not ‘60 minutes,’ it’s not in- vestigative reporting, it’s not changing the face of America. But I think it’s making people aware that besides this music there were some very powerful statements made with this music, and still being made with this music.” He concluded, “and not only is it an entertainment medium, but it’s also an informa- tion medium, and that’s what radio is supposed to be.” Tom De Savia KLSX 97.1 FM 7^/4 " S •40^ IllOam

While sitting in my office, Pamela Lewis asked me how I would like to meet Townes Van Zandt. I tried to conceal my excitement with a professional attitude, but I was feeling like a kid on Christmas Eve! You see, Townes Van Zandt has always been one of my heroes. I couldn’t wait to meet the talented man with the brilliant songwridng mind! Last Thursday, Townes Van Zandt walked into our Cash Box offices. This time, I was like a kid on Christmas morning. I could see that one of my long- awaited moments m life was at hand. It was even more pleasant than I had im- agined. Townes Van Zandt is one of the most personal and humble people I have ever met. In front of me was a man who has had his songs recorded by Emmyloe Harris, Don Williams, Doc Wateon, WiUie Nelson, Guy Clark, and Merle Haggard, just to mention a few. He brought special attention to The Carlisle Family because diey were the first to cut one of Hs songs. And, yet, here in front of me was a man who made me feel important for my paltry contributions to the music business. Townes Van Zandt was bom in Fort Worth, Texas. His father was in the oil business, and the family must have moved around quite a bit. Townes said, ‘ ‘We moved from Fort Worth, when I was eight years old. I won’t go through all the moves, but I’ve lived in Houston; Midland, Texas; Montana, Colorado, Chicago; and I went to school in Minnesota,” Townes’ lovely wife, Jeanene, nodded and smiled. She is another native Texan, but her smile told me she has seen a lot of country witii Townes. “Dad always had the radio on,” Townes continued, “Hank Snow, Hank Williams, and Lefty Frizzell were among my first memories of recorded music. But, there was a lady, named Francis Edwards, who helped us at home. She wasn’t a maid, or anything like that. She was just a pst of the fami- ly. She took me to a Pentecostal church, and I remember the spiritual music, too. But, when I made tiie choice to be a musician was when I saw Elvis Pres- ley on the Ed Sullivan Show. I realized how successful he had become by play- ing a guitar and singing, and that’s what I wanted to do! I was yoimg enough to still believe in Santa Claus. I told my dad I wanted a guitar for Christmas. He said that it might happen, if I would write Santa a letter and promise him that the first song I would learn would be “Fraulein.” I wrote Santa. He brought the guitar, and I lemied Fraulein first. I stiU play it in my show. ’ ’ ‘ ‘I started writing pretty late in life. I remember, when I was in high school, I caught dad going down the hallway and invited him into my room to hear my version of Bob Dylan’s “Blowing In The Wind”. He told me it wasn’t bad, but he tiiought I should write my own songs. At first, I wrote a lot of talkin' blues songs. I played some rought spots m Houston, and I had to choose my own style. I guess tiie first six months of my career could be called comic relief. But, I had spunk!” Townes said he released his new album, “At My Window”, on Sugar Hill Records, simply because, “it was time”. He had tiie new songs, and com- mented how blessed he was to have his old friends working with him m the studio again. He named many of those old friends, but I won’t list tliem be- cause I may leave someone out. Townes would feel badly if I did. Townes Van Zandt is a wealthy man, when it comes to counting friends. After die inter- view, he can certainly count one more! In fact, after I promised him I wouldn’t eat the bait, Townes said he would take me fishing. Joe Henderson GLENTS’’ SNODDY RETIRES. 40REUNITED 36 10 ELVIN JONES McCOY TYNER QUINTET (Blackhawk 52101) JAZZFEATURE PICKS DEXTER GORDON T ONG TALL REDUX-Dexter -^^Gordon is back. Again. After a four year lay-off due to ill health (“My health was very rundown after all these years of my life,” says Dex- ter), Dexter Gordon, saxophone in hand, faced a hve audience the week before last, as a guest soloist with, of all things, the N.Y. Philharmonic. He played on a new David Baker piece called “Ellingtones,” and, after a second or two, it was clear that Dexter Gordon’s sound was still in- tact. The real sharp chops, perhaps, will follow; the chops at Avery Fisher Hall were, in fact, not bad at all. Dexter, of course, comes and goes. In 1960 he came back, after years of obscurity and a prison term. In 1976 he came back, after 14 years of living and working in Europe. Last year, of course, he came back on film, cop- ping a Best Actor nomination for his troubles. This year, the six-foot-five- inch bebop giant is back in the flesh. The weekend before the Philhar- monic gig, Dexter guested on the up- coming Tony Bennett album. At the end of the month, he embarks on a tour of Europe with Bobby Hutcher- son, Cedar Walton, Billy Higgins and Pierre Michelot, four players who participated in Round Midnight. At the end of the tour, the band wiU wax a live album for Blue Note (the first Dexter Gordon album, not count- ing the two Round Midnight soundtracks, in five years). And after that? “I haven’t really thought too much about that,” says Dexter slowly, very slowly. “I’ve been thinking about getting myself back together, which I seem to have done. I’m in better shape than I was in four years ago. “I’m not really planning on getting back on the circuit and playing aU the joints. Mostly I’ll do concerts. But, you know, we just talked to Max Gordon [the owner of the Village Vanguard, where Dexter made his much-acclaimed 1976 “Homecom- ing”] and he wants us to come into the club. Basically, there will be very few clubs that we’ll be doing. But maybe we can do a special weekend later in the year at the Vanguard just to pay our respects. Because he did a lot for me, you know. When I came back from Europe in ’76, not too many people remembered me, and he gave me a shot. And it turned out fan- tastic.” And what about taking another ac- ting assignment? Certainly, the Academy Award nomination must have caused a couple of scripts to waft Dexter’s way. “Oh yes, no hesitation, as long as it’s in my bailiwick. It wouldn’t have to necessarily be a jazz musician. I don’t want to be typecast all my life. ’ ’ '^UBE-BOP-The amount of jazz ^ on TV is a joke, right? Right. This is a shame, right? Right. T/\LENT T he Kinks/Joan Jett THE GREEK THEATRE, L.A.- Joan Jett’s appearance here sharing the bill with legendary British rockers the Kinks was like drinking a Coke before tasting an excellent champagne: Both are enjoyable in their own way, but you wish you’d tasted them on separate occasions. As with Coke and that other fizzy beverage, Jett’s style, with its heavy metal chum, is geared toward a younger, seemingly adolescent crowd, while the Kinks, a thinking man’s rock band whose songs are often laced with social and political statements, are a baby boomer’s band with age-defying appeal. The trouble at this Friday evening show was that Jett’s audience seemed far out numbered by older, yuppie- looking Kinks fans, who appeared to be about as excited about shouting “Yeah, Oh Yeah’’ at Joan’s bidding during “Do You Want to Touch” as cats are about swimming. Jett’s rabble- rousing efforts didn’t have the affect they could have - or should have. Musically, Epic’s Jett and her band flew in tight formation. Ricky Bird’s lead guitar churned with heavy metal intensity, as did Jett’s. Paul Harkins’ drums and Bret Cartwright’s bass were also in fine form. StUl, there was a cer- tain energy missing from the set, due partly to the band’s droning, electric guitar sound, and partly to Jett’s lack- luster performance style, which was mirth-free even during such uptempo, energetic shakers as the Stone’s “Star Star.” Tommy James and the Shondel- les’ “Crimson and Clover” was the Jett set’s high point, delivered with haunting poise. The evening took a sharp turn when MCA’s Kinks took over. Frontman Ray Davies proved himself a seasoned pro from the outset, when he, brother Dave Davies on lead guitar, Ian Gib- bons on keyboards, Jim Rodford on bass and Bob Henrit on drums, kicked into a highly-charged set that drew from material both ancient (1964’s “You Really Got Me”) and recent (tunes from their latest album, “Think Visual”), but never seemed to ride on laurels from the distant past. In fact, the refreshing thing about watching these British invasion originals per- form is that while one is conscious of their ’60’s Golden Oldies aspect, one never doubts for an instant that the creative energy that set them in motion more than 20 years ago has never ceased to fuel them. As lead singer and focal point for the band, Davies is a captivating, world-class rocker. His sly, gender- bending sexuality, a device used by many an English popster, seemed fresh. And the band’s rebellious. East End sensibility was as alive and genuine as could be, especially on this night, which happened to be the eve of Britain’s national election (which Davies admitted the band takes very seriously). Dave Davies’ guitar provided rol- licking, electrifying interludes to the entire show. Both Davies have con- siderable stage presence, and both brothers sing, but Dave’s primary con- tribution is that he, and a handful of other brash Englishman, play as if they invented the art of scintillating guitar riffs. They certainly redefined them, and Dave Davies played like an original during Friday’s show here. Traditional Kinks themes of pover- ty and national decay, of loneliness and political deceit - conveyed with equal parts ethos pathos - plus pensive, romantic ballads (such as the mes- merizing “Lost and Found”) aU mingled to form that rarity of rarities: a thoroughly captivating, thought provoking and high energized show. W olf Trap Celebrates Dizzy Gil- lespie WOLF TRAP, VA-It was the headiest, most dazzling tribute to a single living jazz musician one could imagine. Dizzy Gillespie, who will turn 70 years old in October, was the centerpiece of a star-studded, jam-pack- ed Wolf Trap program that, despite its five-hour length, only scratched the sur- face of his incredible jazz career. PBS’ Great Performances, to its credit, was on hand to record the whole event-the concert, the rehearsals, the special American Zephyr train carrying Dizzy and company from New York to Washington, the works-but, no doubt, the program, which will air in the fall, won’t scratch the surface of the weekend. This review won’t scratch the surface of the concert. Chronologically, this is what hap- pened: Lalo Schifrin led a sensational big band (we’re talking sensational-the trumpet section was Wynton Marsalis, Freddie Hubbard, Jon Faddis, Jimmy Owens and Vaughn Nark!) in the “Fan- fare” and “Toccata” from his “GU- lespiana Suite.” Wynton, Benny Carter, J.J. Johnson, Hank Jones, Rufus Reid and Mickey Roker (with Dizzy on the sidelines) es- sayed “Groovin’ High” and “Birks Works.” Dizzy and Sonny Rollins (I!!!!!!), with the same rhythm section, un- corked smoking versions of “Wheat- leigh Hall” and “Stella By Starlight.” Dizzy and Sonny Rollins! Imagine! Dizzy and Carmen McRae teamed up for lovely and delicate versions of “Round Midnight” and, with Carmen at the piano, “A Beautiful Friendship.” Dizzy, James Moody, Jimmy Owens, Slide Hampton, Mike Longo, Chris White, and Charli Persip played “Con Alma” con alma. Mongo San- tamaria was added for a lush “Kush,” and Jon Hendricks joined Dizzy and Moody for a madcap scat “Oop-Pop-A- Da.” And then Marsalis, Hubbard, Faddis, Owens, Nark and Gillespie strutted their high-flyingest stuff for “Tour de Force.” Faddis, with a heavy dose of Louis Armstrong, took the honors. And that was the first half. The first half! And even the intermission had music-films of Dizzy and his ’40s big band, Di 2:zy and Charlie Parker, Dizzy and Louis Armstrong, and just plain Dizzy. The second half began with the Blues Alley Youth Orchestra, con- ducted by the honoree, scraping through ‘ ‘A Night in Tunisia. ’ ’ Dizzy and Oscar Peterson then in- spired each other to rare heights on a couple of duets: “All the Things You Are” and “Autumn Leaves.” Dizzy, Ignacio Berroa, Candido, Mongo, Nicky Marrerro, John Lee, Ed Cherry, Dave Valentin, Sam Rivers, Amie Lawrence, Jimmy Owens, and David Amram then bubbled-we’re talk- ing percolated-through a Cu-bop drenched “Tin Tin Deo. ’ ’ Then a funny thing happened: Flora Purim and Airto Moreira led a three- song set of their own. Dizzy didn’t par- ticipate, and his connection to it was, at best, a little hazy. And, to close, that beautiful big band, with all those percussionists, played “Things to Come,” “A Night in Tunisia,” “Olinga,” and, of course, ‘ ‘H appy B irthday . ’ ’ In case you’re wondering. Dizzy Gil- lespie, at the age of 69, played superbly throughout. The long concert, moreover, firmly established the wide- range of his talents and the long shadow of his influence-he is so much more, so very much more, than Charlie Parker’s straight man in the creation of bebop. Dizzy Gillespie is one of the dozen most important jazz musicians of all time. It was one hell of a night. Lee Jeske V ernon Reid’s Living Color CBGB, NY - Vernon Reid’s Living Color goes for a Zeppelinish brand of imperial bombast, the kind that works best when it’s bouncing off stadium walls. Though they mix it up with reg- gae, calypso, and funk, they still sound like an updated version of a kickin’ early- ‘70 ’s hard rock band. In concert (June 2d), they overpowered this small club, sounding not loud but big, far too big to remain unsigned for long. The clincher was “Desperate People,” which foreplayed like a Jour- ney song, got into some AC/DC chord- ing and Ozzy “Wicked World” Os- bourne vocals, and climaxed with Reid’s baroque guitar wizardry. For a generation informed by punk but raised on Zep, this was Johnny Lydon making peace with Jimmy Page at the wedding of Prince and Journey. The marriage works because Reid hears the link between generations; his guitar work is pure Hendrix without being retro, if one accepts the fact that Hendrix pretty much created metal and its latter-day mutations. After all, it’s not a long jump from “Purple Haze” to the guitar solo in “Beat It” or from “Crosstown Traffic” to Prince’s “Lady Cab Driver” and even AC/DC’s “You Shook Me All Night Long.” For a generation informed by punk but raised on Zep, this show was John Lydon making peace with Jimmy Page at the wedding ofPrince and Journey, Indeed, Living Color’s “Glamour Boys” may start off sounding like a great lost track from “1999,” but it’s powered by a progression straight from Clapton’s “After Midnight.” Though Reid uses reggae to get the song’s funk across, it rocks along basically genre- less, with loyalty only to the groove. The groove often became unstop- pable as when drummer Will Calhoun soloed with staggered rhythms and Muzz Skillings plucked along on bass. Vocalist Corey Glover meanwhile pounded the stage, jumped into the audience, screamed, and crooned for aU he was worth, proving himself a bet- ter showman than musician, with an onstage razzle dazzle that recalled both James Brown and Mick Jagger. Living Color’s got the chops and moves for a bigger stage, and in fact it might be more appropriate if the band’s next showcase were at Giants Stadium. Paul lorio Cash Box June 20, 1987 15

Capitol and Cinema Launch New Venture Paullorio Mazza Out, Licata In EMI America and Manhattan Merge By Stephen Padgett LOS ANGELES-The long-rumored dissolution of EMI America finally took place last week. Joe Smith, vice chairman of Capitol Industries-EMI, Inc., announced on Thursday (June 18), that EMI America Records would merge with Manhattan Records. The new label, now called EMI America/Manhattan Records, will be based in New York. Sal Licata, current- ly president of RCA-Ac&M-Arista Dis- tribution, has been named chief execu- tive officer and will report directly to Joe Smith. Bruce Lundvall, who headed Manhattan, will now become president of the new label, reporting to Licata. Licata told Cash Box that he expects to begin his new position sometime toward the middle of July. Jim Mazza, formerly president of EMI America, resigned his post and does not figure in the realignment. He is said to be pursuing “other interests’’ Plan Begins In ‘88 according to a statement. Lundvall was out of the office and could not be contacted. According to a company statement, his duties will be supervising the A&R and creative aspects of the new merged label, in- cluding the Blue Note jazz division. Sue Satriano, director, public rela- tions/communications for EMI Music, North America & Japan, told Cash Box that the futures of other EMI America executives and employees was still un- determined. “What has happened is that some people are being asked to move to New York,’’ she said, “some people will be needed here in L.A. in the newly combined label. And some will, hopefully, be assimilated into Capitol.’’ The fate of EMI America’s Sunset Blvd. headquarters is also not known. Abrams WASHINGTON - A system for peg- ging mechanical royalty fees for the next decade to the Consumer Price Index becomes official July 15th and will apply to records made on or around January 1, 1988. The system, accepted by The Copyright Royalty Tribunal and published in the June 15th Federal Register, is a result of negotiations that began more than six months ago among the Recording Industry Associa- tion of America, TJie National Music Publishers Association, and The Songwriters Guild of America. The plan gained the support of SESAC and Music Royalties, Inc. In essence, the measure calls on the C.R.T. to figure the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index every two years and to adjust the mechanical royalty rate accordingly. It also specifies that the adjusted rate shall be no greater than 25 per cent of the then- current fee, and no lower than the exist- ing fee. It also calls for the adjusted rate to be rounded to the nearest l/20th of a cent. The first change is to be based on the percentage difference between the Con- sumer Price Index published for December, 1985, and that published for September, 1987. Thereafter, the C.R.T. is required to use the Index published for September, 1987, and bi-annually to 1995 to deter- mine the percentage change, and to an- (continued on page 18) Atlantic To Begin Issuing Classic Jazz CDs NEW YORK-This week, Atlantic Records wiU release the first titles in an extensive reissue program of compact discs culled from its enormous and in- fluential jazz catalogue. 23 titles are due in June and July, with a projected 100 titles due by year’s end. Nesuhi Er- tegun, who produced many of the original sessions, is supervising the transfer to digital, with Ilhan Mimaroglu and Bob Porter active in the program. “We’re ver>' excited at the prospect of having these great recordings now available in the brilliant sound quality offered by the compact disc,’’ said Dave Glew, Atlantic’s executive vice president/general manager. The discs will include the original artwork and liner notes and, where possible, addi- tional tracks. Poker in Las Vegas. 40 YEARS AGO IN CASH BOX June 23, 1947-The recent proposal by James C. Petrillo, President of the American Federation of Musicians, to ban recordings as of December 31, was met by recording officials and executives throughout the nation with mixed feelings this past week. Several independent record executives queried were of the opinion that the edict would never come to pass; and also pointed out that should the ban be effected, it would almost immediately put the greater majority of independent record manufacturers in the country out of business. When questioned as to their beliefs regarding Petrillo ’s threat to put the union into the record business, figtires in the industty scoffed at the idea and il- lustrated that such an enterprise would be a violation of federal anti-trust laws. It is well known that Petrillo’ s threatened ban on recordings came along with present labor legislation in Congress which would harm working agreements the union now has. ..Columbia Records, Inc. announced to the trade this past week the forthcoming release of many old jazz recordings, in line with their program to make the old jazz waxings available to the public once again. In- cluded in the expected releases, are masters previously cut by several labels which were absorbed by the plattety through the course of years. “Featured ar- tists such as Duke Ellington, Billie Holiday, Bessie Smith, Louis Armstrong, Jack Teagarden, Benny Goodman, Bunny Berigan, Chu Berry and many others will now be available for public consumption,’’ said George Avakian, head of Columbia’s jazz department. ..The Nation’s Top Ten Juke Box Tunes: 1. “Mam’seUe,” Frank Sinatra, Dick Haymes, others. 2. “Linda,” Paul Weston, Gordon Jenkins, others. 3. “My Adobe Hacienda,” Art Kassell, Kenny Baker, others. 4. “Across the Valley From the Alamo,” Stan Kenton, Woody Herman, others. 5. “Peg O’ My Heart,” Ted Weems, the Har- monicats, others. ..Hot in Harlem: 1. “Them There Eyes,” Roy Milton. 2. “When I Write My Song,” Herb Jefries. 3. “Walkin’,” Joe Liggins. 4. “Jack You’re Dead,” Louis Jordan. 5. “Peg O’ My Heart,” the Har- monicats. CASH BOX JAZZ ALBUMS B opping AROUNi>=odds and ends, flotsam and jet- sam, kibbles and bits. ..Since we are right now smack dab in the middle of the WC/New York Jazz Festival (first reports due next week), it seems a good idea to mention that tickets are now on sale for the Newport Jazz Fes- tival. Now you need a genealogist to figure all of this out, of course, since the Newport Jazz Festival moved to New York in 1972 and has been there ever since: called, in order, the New- port Jazz Festival/New York, the Kool-Newport Jazz Festival/New York, the Kool Jazz Festival/New York and, as of last year, the JVC Jazz Festival/New York. (Why nobody ever thought to just call this the New York Jazz Festival I’ll never understand.) In any case, JVC, a few years back, began sponsoring jazz festivals, including one in, of course, Newport, Rhode Island. That, of course, is called the JVC Jazz Fes- tival-Newport though, as all jazz buffs know, the Newport Jazz Fes- tival is the JVC Jazz Festival/New York. Got it? Forget it. In any case, the weekend event in Newport is set for August 15 and 16 this year and will feature Nancy Wilson, Stanley Jordan, Kenny G, the Crusaders and Wynton Marsalis on day one, and George Benson, Branford Mar- I salis, Dianne Reeves, Michael Brecker and the Dizzy Gillespie Big Band on day two. NEWS EMI/Manhattan (continued from page 5) mastering lab. “I don’t know if they’ve figured that out yet,” Satriano said. The artist rosters of both labels will be merged. Manhattan’s roster in- cludes recent successful artists like Robbie Nevil and the Partland Brothers. EMI America is enjoying the success of David Bowie and Peter Wolf. Also on the label are Kate Bush, Corey Hart and Kim Carnes. ‘‘This is an extremely positive move,” said Smith in a statement. ‘‘Together, Licata and Lundvall form a strong team in both the creative and marketing fields. Bhaskar Menon, chairman and chief executive officer of EMI Music Worldwide, commenting on the latest development said, ‘‘The merger of EMI America and Manhattan will con- siderably strengthen both labels and make it possible to support our artists with far greater focus. ’ ’ Sal Licata Mechanical Royalties (continued from page 5) nounce revisions in mechanical royalty fees beginning November 1, 1989, and eveiy two years thereafter. In the 1909 Copyright Law, the mechanical royalty rate was set at 2 cents a song. This was increased to 2.75 cents a song in the 1976 Copyright Law revision. In 1980, the C.R.T. held weeks of hearings to determine whether the rate should be increased as sought by copyright owners and opposed by record manufacturers. In December that year, the Tribtmal fixed the new fee at 4 cents a song (or 0.75 cents per minute of playing time for extended compositions). The record industry ap- pealed, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia upheld the C.R.T. ruling except for a plan that would have empowered the Tribunal to order yearly proceedings to take into account the effect of inflation. The court said this was beyond the Tribunal’s authority. However, the industry submitted a step increase plan to take into account inflation. This was subsequently ap- proved by the C.R.T., which saw the rate move every two years to its present 5 cents a song (or 0.95 cents per minute for extended play). MELBOURNE - Disctronics, Australia’s first compact disc plant, of- ficially began production with its ini- tial CD on May 21. The ceremony was presided over by Australian Record In- dustry Association (ARIA) Chairman and WEA Records Managing Director Paul Turner, who commented, ‘‘Australia now has its own CD plant which is important to both consumers and artists alike so that we can have simultaneous release on all formats.” The first disc, ‘‘Whispering Jack” by John Famham, was a special gold CD, made with pure ore extracted from the Kalgoorlie goldfields. Disctronics, located in the Mel- bourne suburb of Braeside, was set up through the initial investment of over 40 million dollars by the company and its owners, Pro-Image Studios Limited and Quatro Limited. The result is a state-of-the-art facility, with digital mastering being added to the process to guarantee complete production from master tape to finished disc in a few weeks. Full production runs at the plant have been online since March, and ac- ceptance rates on many of the early CD runs have been high, reflecting the plant’s commitment to stringent quality standards. The clean air standards j throughout Disctronics are Class 100, and the Australian-designed air system j will enhance the efficiency of the 1 plant’s operation. 1 Production capacity for the first year I of operation is projected at 25 million units, and major export markets are al- ; ready in place for European and f American distribution with major and , independent record labels. Offices I have been established in Sydney, Lon- ji don, and Los Angeles to facilitate the j export traffic. j Disctronics Managing Director ' Roger Richmond-Smith, commenting ' on the commencement of official production, added ‘‘though our plant is now in production, we haven’t finished yet with the improvements. With the in- stallation of Sony laser glass cutters and total mastering facilities, as well as the clean air standards we will main- tain at Class 100 throughout the plant, ^ Disctronics intends to remain a world j leader in Compact Disc manufactur- ing,. Box July 4. 1987 EMI Execs Axed Sweeping Layoffs In Wake Of Merger By Stephen Padgett LOS ANGELES-Executive level layoffs and general uncertainty fol- lowed last week’s armouncement by Capitol Indus Cries-EMI vice chairman Joe Smith that EMI America would be merged into Manhattan Records and moved from the west coast to New York. In addition to president Jim Mazza’s armounced resignation. Cash Box has learned that Colin Stewart, vice presi- dent of marketing and sales, Tony Smith, director national album promo- tion, Neil Portnow vice president A&R and David Budge, director national press/artist relations, among many others, received their pink shps two weeks ago. Smith conducted one-on-one meet- ings with EMI America staffers after Thursday, June 18’s general meeting in which the plarmed merger was un- veiled. In these individual meetings Smith discussed each person’s future with the company. Most of the west coast office was dissolved. Severance packages were delivered at this time. Some, including vice president crea- tive services/merchandising Frcnchy Gauthier and vice president business af- fairs Mark Berger, were offered six- month interim positions, their ultimate fate to be determined later. Ken Benson and John High, both album promotion men, were offered and accepted positions in the new com- pany’s New York headquarters. Caroline Prutzman, manager nation- al press/artist relations, and John Guar- nieri, director A&R have interim posi- tions as well. Just what is in store for EMI America’s nearly 50 west coast employees is still to be determined. The sixth floor of Capitol’s famed Hollywood tower was cleared out the same week the merger was announced. Speculation about that space’s new use includes the relocation of the Screen Gems publishing unit from its present office in the EMI America building to the tower. ONJAZZ^^m The JVC/New York Jazz Festival Day-by-Day, Part One: F riday-The JVC/New York Jazz Festival started off this year like it starts off every year-with hot dogs at Gracie Mansion (that’s the official home of our scandal-ridden mayor). Nathan’s did not supply the wieners this year, a big mistake. Officially, things got under way (as they always do) with the first of the one-hour piano recitals at Weill (formerly Carnegie) Recital Hall. Marian McPartland had the lead- off spot and she played a pretty, florid hour that mixed a couple of rhythmic swingers into the balladic brew. Carnegie Hall, two hours later, was the site for some vocal muscle-flex- ing from Sarah Vaughan and Bobby McFerrin (separately, of course). La Vaughan sang a no-nonsense set of ballads-the voice magnifique, naturalmente, the phrasing perfec- tion. McFerrin did his delightful solo thing—a couple of haunting jazz stand- ards, a couple of wordless improvised explorations, and such items as “The Beverly Hillbillies Theme’’ and his capsulized version of The Wizard of Oz. The audience, mostly Vaughan’s crowd, was on its feet screaming. Next year, they’ll buy tickets to see McFerrin alone (which, in jazz terms, is known as building an audience). Then Miles Davis, the grand old man of fusion, shared an Avery Fisher Hall bill with Kenny G, the new superstar of fusion, and there were some surprises. First of all, Miles’ band was surprisingly tight and funky-saxophonist Kenny Gar- rett, guitarist Joe McCreary, and drummer Ricky Weldman are wel- come new members, and the band was more cohesive than any Davis unit since his comeback. However, old Miles hardly played at all, and when he did it was the tired “Human Nature’’ and “Time After Time” (after time, after time, after time...). The other surprise was Kenny G, who’s got some serious soprano sax chops, though his music ain’t meaty enough (maybe he should have played with Miles’s band). Saturday-Town Hall hosted a double bill of the World Saxophone Quartet, which played, without ques- tion, the best set I’ve ever heard them play (and that’s saying a lot); and Branford Marsalis, who, with a quartet including ex-Wyntonians Kenny Kirkland and Jeff Watts, played watered-down John Coitraneisms that were boring at best. Sunday-A Carnegie Hall evening with the Modern Jazz Quartet is al- ways an enticement, and, during the second half of the show, it was clear why: the MJQ is still one of the most musical small bands in jazz, and they played a model set of blues and stand- ards and John Lewis tunes. During the first half of the show, the MJQ was joined by the New York Cham- ber Symphony for the Lewis pieces that sound so good on “Three Win- dows” (Atlantic), but sounded so dull -I in the flesh. 2 Monday-A solo piano concert, at the Recital Hall, with old Sun Ra, who dug into his roots for some mossy blues, heady stride piano, fril- ly romanticism, thunderous avant crashes and all sorts of other things. It was an expansive, let’s say Arkestral, performance. George Shearing then presided over a Town Hall concert called “Musical ‘Amusements’ of Chef George,” that was broken into three sets: dixieland, piano duo and bebop. The dixieland set was spirited and in- fectious, thanks to the fine players on hand (Kenny Davern, Warren Vache, George Masso, Slam Stewart and Oliver Jackson) and the leader’s cheerful good humor. The set of piano duets with Hank Jones was musical, but not that successful (their styles didn’t really come together). The bebop set-with Dizzy Gillespie, Jimmy Heath, Eddie Gomez and Jimmy Cobb-was some- thing of a mess. GOlespie’s chops were off, and Shearing ain’t a bebop pianist. Heath, Gomez and Cobb, however, got some good hcks in. Tuesday-Dick Hyman-that walk- ing repository of jazz piano styles- played an inspired hour of Irving Berlin tunes (inspired, somewhat, by the death the previous day of Fred Astaire). The tunes were mostly from the ’10s, ’20s and ’30s-eras that are right in Hyman’s rag- time/stride/swing wheelhouse, and the hour purred. And then the eagerly-awaited “Or- nette In All Languages” program at Town Hall that was, almost, worth the wait. The problem was that the concert was too short. The set with the “original Quartet” (which saw Ed Blackwell, the real original drum- mer, replacing Billy Higgins, who replaced Blackwell shortly before the band came to New York in ’59) was only 45 minutes long. It was brilliant and, surprise of surprises, they not only played Ornette’s lovely new music, but they whipped “Lonely ’Woman” and “The Sphinx” out of their memory banks. Ornette has moved on to other things, of course, but his collaboration with Don Cher- ry, Charlie Haden and either Hig- gins or Blackwell is too good not to continue, even sporadically. Prime Time, the other things, played the first set of the concert and Ornette seems to be coohng them down-the set was filled with high- flying funk rhythms and zipping electric basses and guitars, but the music was subtler, less frenetic than in recent years. Again, the set was too short-there’s nothing like listen- ing to Prime Time smacking you in the ears for a couple of hours. The closer was a combined Prime Time/Quartet blow-out on “Theme From a Symphony” that was just as you’d imagine it-spewing rhythms like some kind of harmolodic vol- cano. Afterwards, at a post-concert party, I complimented Ornette on the con- cert and new album. ‘ ‘It was a good idea, wasn’t it?” he asked. CB—When had you finalized your decision to to ahead with the merger? Smith-It had been discussed over a period of time, I guess over a period of two years they had been thinking of doing something like that. When we got here in February we let everything remain in place but it soon became clear, to me anyhow, and anybody in management, that it didn’t work well. We had this promotion force out there, both pop and black music, being directed from two sides. The priorities got mixed up. We ran into some tremendous collisions where David Bowie vis a vis Robbie Nevil, Richard Marx and John Waite, things that were happening out there and we had no con- trol. The geography didn’t work well. Here we had enough artists, a really solid artist roster to make one great company, and here was Manhattan who was doing very well breaking new acts—Richard Marx, Nevil, Glass Tiger, a few others-but a long haul to really get in there with no catalog to back them up. When we merge them we have the enormous United Artists agreement with EMI America. The deal includes such artists as George Thorogood and the Destroyers (three times gold for EMI America), the Neville Brothers ( whose recently released LP is in a critical stage of its promotion according to Rounder) and the True Believers (whose record is ready to be released pending comple- tion of artwork, a problem exacerbated by the dissolution of the west coast of- fice). “Bruce Lundvall called this morn- ing,’’ said Marian Leighton, president and co-owner/founder of Rounder, last Wednesday (June 24). “Everyone has been very cordial, very supportive, wanting to get things moving along. But right now, it’s so transitional, I don’t think anybody on either end has any answers to just exactly how it is going to function day to day,’’ she added. According to Leighton, Rounder ex- pects to continue its relationship with the new company. “We like the brief contact we’ve had with the new people at the company,’’ she said, and is glad that the overall bureaucracy of the new label is basically small, similar to EMI America. catalog, the Liberty, the Imperial catalogs, and along with that you add the Blue Note, and now you’ve got a catalog company. Plus, you’re adding George Thorogood and Pet Shop Boys, and David Bowie and a whole bunch of other artists to the mix. Now you’ve got a real up and going record com- pany that can afford the services that each one of them alone could not af- ford. Now you can really give yourself some meat, where each company split. It’s just a business judgment that it doesn’t work well with two. When Warners put together Warner, Elektra and Atlantic, they bought three com- panies. They had bought Warner Bros., it was already running. They bought At- lantic which was already miming. And then they bought Elektra which was al- ready miming. Here, we started two of these labels from nothing. EMI America and Manhattan. And so they have never really matured as yet into two full blown labels. And the wait was going to be a long one. And so this just made sense, it’s not hurting anybody. All of the artists have the same promotional representation out there that they always did. It’s not a case of us throwing all this product out. They were working on all these artists anyhow. CS-When you made Thursday’s an- nouncement, how soon before that had you decided to do the merger? Smith-We had finally closed the situa- tion with Sal Licata just a couple of days before that and were not able to announce it, for RCA’s own reasons, they asked us not to announce it, imtil that Thursday. The speculation was on. Anytime you start the planning of something like this, a lot of people know about it, and then all the rumors started for six or seven weeks. But, there was no way for us to shortcut that process. We had identified the man we wanted, Licata, and we had to now wait until he could get clear. Cfi-Was there any pressure on you to hurry up your decision as a result of the rumors that had escalated in the last few weeks? Smith-I would have loved to have done this the moment the first rumor hit. It was impossible to do, so we had to live with it. The pressure, of course. It was self-imposed pressure. You can’t let people hang like that. It was affecting everything. Artists were call- ing, and nervous about whether their records were going to come out. To everybody’s credit, they kept it going. The John Waite and Nona Hendryx records look terrific. Bowie had a hit single all during this period and another big AOR record. Everybody hung in there. And they’re still hanging in there, only Jack Sattcr has moved into national promotion, Gerry Griffith has moved into A&R, and Sari Becker has taken over press, and all these department heads, they’re all out here this week, meeting everybody and look- ing into these projects and reviewing what we’ve got on the boards here. CJ5-Whcn you came to Car’’* January, it was one of your expressed purposes to improve Capitol’s north American market share. Are you meet- ing your objectives? Smiths think so. We’ve had a rcmtrk- able jump. But I’m not kidding myself Some of that’s attributable to the Beatles. But everybody takes credit for whatever they sell, so I shouldn’t be ashamed of it. Whatever you sell, you seU. But, no, we’ve had a remarkable jump. You can’t do that quickly. What you can do is make a better record company. And the rest fol- lows. I think anybody whose been ob- serving this business feels that Capitol is a much stronger label than it was four months ago. It’s a player out there now. In the talent market it’s very ag- gressive in promotion and marketing. And that’s with the infusion of a few new people. And there’s a great new feeling about Capitol Records. I think the same feeling is starting to hit Man- hattan and EMI, certainly—I’ve been working out of EMI for the last couple of days—those pieople are really pumped about the new feeling. We’ve now removed the clouds, and here’s a very positive motivating guy, Licata, coming in. And Lundvall remains and he’s a beloved and a very effective talent guy. I think its a terrific team and I hope it works out well. And then the talent flows and then the records go. But the first thing is to build a structure. CB—Was former EMI America presi- dent Jim Mazza ever given anything like an ultimatum to perform? Smith-No, no. I had a meeting with EMI people, not with Mazza there, but with everybody there, and explained to them that the clock was ticking here, and that there had been a sentiment to move ahead with this and it had been going on for some time. But I would have preferred not to do it if things went well and it looked like it could work. It just became clear to me after that that it was never going work really well. And we just had to bite the bullet and do this. Cfi-Would a better performance out of Bowie, Wolf and Hendyrx have cauterized the hemorrhage and saved EMI America? Smith-Nah, I don’t think so. NEWS The Doors Light A Certification Fire In June NEW YORK-The Doors earned the most certifications in the RIAA’s June list of gold, platinum and multi- platinum albums, with eight different titles by the popular ’60s and ’70s band gaining plaques-back catalogue items that had never been submitted for cer- tification before. Going multi-platinum, with sales of two million each, were “The Doors,” “The Doors’ Greatest Hits,” and “L.A. Woman.” On the platinum list are “The Best of the Doors,” “The Doors,” “The Soft Parade,” “The Doors 13,” “L.A. Woman,” and “Waiting for the Sun.” Hitting the gold jackpot were “The Best of the Doors” and “Alive She Cried." Joining Jim Morrison and company on the platinum list for June arc Spyro Gyra’s “Morning Dance,” Bryan Adams’ “Into the Fire" (simultaneous- ly certified gold), and Kenny G’s “Duotones.” Joining the Doors and Bryan Adams on the gold list are Spyro Gyra’s “Car- naval,” Atlantic Starr’s “All in the Name of Love,” “Whitesnake,” The Cutting Crew’s “Broadcast,” Ex- pose’s “Exposure,” Herb Alpert’s “Keep Your Eye on Me,” and Evie’s “Come On Ring Those Bells.” OOTBALLFANS-Reunited at Denver's Mile High Stadium for a first-ever “old Tiers' 'football game, former Bronco halfback Floyd Little (l)faces offagainst ex- akland Raider foe Lyle Alzado (r) under the watchful eyes of the “Pony Ex- ess’’ alumni. Michael Jackson To Launch First Solo World Tour LOS ANGELES-With a late sum- ier release date rumored for his first bum since the 40-million selling Thriller” LP, Epic recording artist Iichael Jackson is set to launch a mas- ve, 12-country solo tour in Septem- sr, beginning with nine shows in ipan, announced Frank Dileo, Jack- in’s manager, during a Tokyo press inference last week. The tour is Jackson’s first since the 984-85 Jackson brothers’ “Victory our,” and his first solo world outing, he tour also marks Jackson’s first ap- earance in Japan since the early 970’s, when he performed there with he Jackson Five. The tour kicks off in Japan’s largest cities, beginning with Tokyo’s Korakuen Stadium, September 12, 13 and 14, moving on to Osaka’s Nishinomiya Stadium September 18, 19 and 20, and Yokohama Stadium September 25, 26 and 27. These con- certs will be presented by Nippon Television Network Corp. and Nippon Telephone and Telegraph Co. Further dates are yet to be announced. Said to be “unprecedented” in its technical scale, and including 240-inch video screens, the show will be taped and broadcast in Japan as part of a television special by the Nippon Television Network. Tickets for the Japanese leg go on sale July 12.
