===== PAGE 16 ===== [stanley\s+jordan|stanley\s+turrentine|tony\s+williams|bobby\s+mcferrin|it.s\s+about\s+time|BT[-. ]?851\d\d]
onjAzzmmm The JVC/New York Jazz Festival Day-by-Day, Part Two: EDNESDAY-Kenny Barron had the solo slot at Weill Recital Hall, va- cated at the last minute by an ailing Dave McKenna. Barron played rollicking versions of standards, everything un- derpinned by a nicely percussive left hand and a scintillatingly effective right Good stuff. Ella Fitzgerald, who hadn’t per- formed in a year (she’s had heart trouble), had the main slot at Avery Fisher Hall and she turned up in good voice and, obviously, quite strong. She did two sets and they were swing- ing, no two ways about it. Ella’s voice isn’t what it once was—she’s 69, folks-but she is in tune and, when she scats the bejeezers out of “Flying Home,” there’s no question that the woman belongs on a concert stage. After several erratic performances a few years ago, Ella turned in her third fine JVC/New York performance in a row. THURSDAY-Cedar Walton had the Weill slot and he played a pretty hour, but it was too pretty. Even a medley of Monk tunes was too pret- ty, too impressionistic. I waited for Cedar to bop out, but he never did. Joe Williams, Nancy Wilson and the Count Basie Orchestra were the headliners at Carnegie later that night, but, oy, where there problems. First of all, the amplified sound at Carnegie Hall, which stunk all week, was at its stinkiest-at times it was al- most like a mime show. That aside, I thought Nancy Wilson was going to avow herself of the opportunity to sing some jazz with the Basie Band. She didn’t-she avowed herself of the opportunity to sing some pop schmaltz with her own band (and string section) and then to bring out Carl Anderson for some pop schmaltz duets. Then, with time a-wasting, Frank Foster led the Basie Band through a full six numbers, including two by the band’s vocalist, Carmen Brad- ford. Were there not enough vocalists on this bill? By the time Joe Williams hit the stage, there was about a half-hour of concert left. What he sang sounded okay (what you could hear of it)-he and that band are still a supreme combination- but it was over too fast. He didn’t do “Every Day” and he didn’t do “Cherry Red,” which he had even promised some loudmouth in the audience. I then slid over to Avery Fisher for Ray Charles. Ray turned in a good set-Ray usually (but certainly not al- ways) turns in a good set. How he can still sing “I Can’t Stop Loving You” and “Georgia On My Mind” with such feeling, such, well, soul, I’ll never understand. But who wants to unders tand—owwwwww! FRIDAY-Mel Torme is always on the New York Jazz Festival. Always. Usually he’s paired with some com- bination of George Shearing and/or Gerry Mulligan. On this night, at Carnegie and called “A Grand Night for Singing,” he was joined by Diane Schuur, Lonette McKee, the Mel Lewis Orchestra and Stan Getz. It was a jam-packed, but quite good, concert. Mel was in good voice. Diane was not only in good voice, but she seems to be shaving some of her tendency to oversing from her perfor- mances (and, backed by the Lewis Band and Getz, she had some first- class accompaniment). McKee was in good voice, but she’s a Broadway belter, not a jazz singer. (She was good as Lena Horne in “The Cotton Club” because, as a singer, she resembles Home.) The Lewis Or- chestra, by itself and behind all of the singers, was in good instrument. A good concert. SATURDAY-Roger Kellaway made like Keith Jarrett and played a numbingly boring, pretentious hour of neo-classical noodling at the Reci- tal Hall. Yawn. Ruben Blades turned in a solid two-plus-hour concert at Carnegie that featured excellent singing, excel- lent streamlined salsa playing from Seis del Solar (actually Siete del Solar), and genuine emotion, anger and concern. Not only did Blades sing about injustice, racism and the serious problems of Latin America, but he made sure everybody had English translations so that us gringos in the crowd would not just sit there and groove to the music—and it was music to groove to-but would under- stand as well. I hope Ruben doesn’t decide to become president of Panama, he’s too good a musician. And good musicians always make more of a mark on the world than leaders of countries. I closed the night at Merkin Con- cert Hall, where an ambitious series called “Improvisations” (co-spon- sored by the World Music Institute) was coming to a close. Craig Harris and Tailgater’s Tales was who I heard, and I liked what I heard quite a bit. Harris is a splendid trombone player with a burly sound (he plays the trombone like it’s a trombone, not as obvious an observation as you’d think) and this updated dixieland in- strumentation (Don Byron on clarinet, E.J. Allen on trumpet, An- thony Cox on bass and Pheeroan Ak Laff on drums) is an excellent vehicle for his wide-ranging writing, which, like most good jazz writing, looks forwards and backwards at once. SUNDAY-Hank Jones was the sub- ject of a Town Hall concert called “The World of Hank Jones” and it’s about time. Ask any jazz fan for a short list of favorite pianists and Hank Jones’s name is on it nine times out of ten. Yet Hank has spent his career quite quietly-he’s never really made a name for himself as a leader, but his playing is always superb and always improves any band he’s in. Here he was featured in numerous set- tings: from solo (fantastic) to duo (with George Mraz and Kenny Bar- ron) to trio (with Eddie Gomez and Keith Copeland) to quartet (the trio plus Frank Wess) to various sextets, septets and octets (with a revolving cast of hom players-Al Cohn, Urbie Green, Joe Wilder and Wess-and Marvin “Smitty” Smith, Ray Drummond and Rodney Jones), to backing two singers, Jackie Paris and Bob Stewart. It was a low- keyed, elegant and exceptionally musical concert. NEWS UNIVERSALELTON-MCA recording artist Elton John celebrated his return to the label and new release, ‘ ‘Elton John Live In Australia with the Melbourne Sym- phony Orchestra ” by holding a press conference on the Universal Studios lot recently. Shown afterwards (l-r): James Newton Howard (arranger and conductor for Australian concerts), Bemie Taupin (songwriting partner), John Reid (John s manager), Elton John, MCA' s Irving Azoff (president, MCA Music Entertainment Group), Richard Palmese (executive vice president, marketing and promotion), Jheryl Busby (executive vice president artist acquisition and development), and Larry Solters (senior vice president, artist development). Former Elektra Mrktng & Promo Head Bone To Replace Craigo As Chrysalis President NEW YORK - Mike Bone has been named president of Chrysalis Records, replacing Jack Craigo, it was learned this week. Bone most recently served Elektra Records as senior vice presi- dent of marketing and promotion. It is not known whether Craigo left volun- tarily or was relieved of his duties. Reasons for the change were unan- nounced, and representatives at Chrysalis had no comment at press time. R.I.A.A. Backs DAT Scanner LOS ANGELES-The Recording In- dustry Association of America (R.I.A.A.) announced plans to better ac- quaint recording industry executives with the copy-code scanner technol- ogy. Scanner requirements in Digital Audio Tape (DAT) machines are part of proposed in legislation now in com- mittee on Capitol hill. Demonstrations of the copy-code system developed by CBS Records Technology Labs will take place for in- dustry executives in Nashville on July 21, in Los Angeles on July 23 and in New York on July 28. The system is scheduled for an im- partial testing by the National Bureau of Standards. Members of Congress have asked that equipment manufac- turers refrain from importing DAT machines and that recording companies refrain from encoding product until a legislative decision has been reached. Marantz, a maker of DAT machines, has already pledged to begin introduc- ing DAT into the U.S. in October. Critics have said there is audible sound degradation in the copy-code scanner system. The demonstrations in the R.I.A.A. offices are meant, in part, to show this criticism to be groundless. BMI SALUTES HANCOCK — Herbie Hancock, the award-winning composer/in- strumentalist, was recently saluted by the international music press at a party hosted by BMI. Pictured here with BMI pres and CEO Frances Preston and Han- cock are (l - r): Branford Marsalis; Tony Reedus; Darius Brubeck, (obscured), James Williams, Dave Brubeck, Bob Cranshaw, George Coleman, Jimmy Owens, George Shearing, Herbie Hancock, Frances W. Preston, Harold Mabern, Lionel Hampton, Donald Byrd, Buster Williams, Bob Brookmeyer, and Tony Williams. Seeks Injunction, $50 Million Songwriter Sues Lionel Richie LOS ANGELES-Michael Frenchik, a Los Angeles-based songwriter, has filed a $50 million lawsuit against Lionel Richie claiming that Richie’s song “Dancing On The Ceiling’’ was an infringement of his copyright. According to Frenchik, Carlos Rios, an employee of Richie and the law firm of Manatt, Phelps, Rothenberg, Tunney & Phillips, also named in the suit, un- duly influenced him to relinquish authorship rights in his original musi- cal work to Richie for inadequate com- pensation. The law firm, according to Frenchik, represented both himself and Rios, knowing their interests were ad- verse to each other. Frenchik claims that a demo tape of his song was given to Rios in Decem- ber, 1984 and that Rios “appropriated said musical composition without Plaintiff’s lawful authority, right, title or license and converted” his song over to Rios, Richie and Richie’s publishing company, Brockman Music. Richie released “Dancing On The Ceiling” in July 1986, and, according to the suit, did not credit Frenchik for writing the song. Frenchik seeks an injunction enjoin- ing the defendants from further dis- tribution of “Dancing On The Ceil- ing,” $50 million for copyright infr- ingement, unfair competition and con- version and a full accounting of all defendants’ profits. Named as co-defendants in the law- suit are Richie, Brockman Music, Motown Records (Richie’s label), Rios, Jody E. Graham (an attorney with Manatt, et al) and Manatt, Phelps, Rothenberg, Tunney & Phillips. A Guide To The New Music Seminar Shows By PauIIorio NEW YORK - When Mark Joseph- son called this year’s New Music Semi- nar “a music festival,” he wasn’t kid- ding. Josephson, an NMS director, helped shape this year’s Seminar around performances by over 250 acts. In many ways, these shows mean more than the panel discussions taking place this week at the Marriott Marquis Hotel (13 - 15). A wide variety of music is scheduled, and nearly every genre is represented, from rap and ska to country and rock. As might be ex- pected with an event of this size, there are a few glaring omissions. For ex- ample, Tim Beme, wrongly excluded from Columbia’s recent JVC show- case, should have been given a hearing at NMS. And bands such as Sonic Youth, The Young Fresh Fellows, The Feelies, and others should also have been featured. But, overall, the choice of bands is superb and the amount of talent is stag- gering; you won’t be able to attend a single show without missing another one that’s just as good. This guide is a semi-hopeless attempt at simplifying matters. MONDAY, JULY 13. TOP SHOWS: Two shows stand out: Homestead’s showcase at CBGBs and Relativity’s at Nirvana. The former includes performances by Phan- tom Tollbooth, Live Skull, Salem 66, Big Dipper, and others. Live Skull, a particularly hot live act, and the other I bands can be sampled on a new Homes- tead compilation called “The Wailing Ultimate.” Relativity’s show features Scruffy The Cat, Thelonious Monster, Bleached Black, and The Brandos. Best bet is Scruffy, whose second album, “Tiny Days,” translates well on stage. ON JAZZ VC REFLECTTONS-I would say that, on the whole, the 1987 JVC/New York Jazz Festival was a success. I know it was a commercial success, but, on le whole, I believe it was an artistic uccess as well. The “on the whole” usiness refers to two things: the atro- ious amplified sound in Carnegie lall, and the problems for a jazz fes- val that insists on using such halls in le first place. That aside, the rogramming was somewhat more im- ginative than in years past (yes larah Vaughan and Mel Torme osted Carnegie Hall shows again, but ith Bobby McFerrin and Diane Ichuur on their respective bills; thus iuilding an audience for the younger ingers from the audience for the ilder singers). The idea of musical etrospectives (Ornette Coleman euniting his original Quartet, Dizzy jSillespie heading up a big band, George Shearing and Hank Jones Presiding over musical auto- biographies) worked well-audiences :ame and the concerts were well- lone. And the use of the World vJusic Institute’s “Improvisations” series to bring some more adven- uresome jazz to the Festival was :ound (as was the sound, and the am- bience, in Merkin Concert Hall, vhere the “Improvisations” series ook place and where more JVC con- certs should be planned in the future). Hiat’s all. Not a perfect jazz festival- md still not a “festival” in the festive ways of such festivals as those held tnnually in New Orleans, Nice, and nany other locales- but a solid one lonetheless. PARTY ALL THE TIME-One hing that did return at this year’s Fes- ival was the party-record companies, rnd others, throwing little celebra- ions for their artists. Most elaborate was BMI’s Tavern on the Green unch for Herbie Hancock, which 'eatured-along with the food, drink rnd speeches-some jamming from he likes of Hancock, Lionel Hampton, Donald Byrd and Jimmy Owens. Second most elaborate was Atlantic’s Russian Tea Room bash complete with blini table) for the Modern Jazz Quartet-a classy party (or a classy ensemble. Least ela- borate was Caravan of Dreams’ Cen- :ury Cafe party for Ornette Coleman-sort of a harmolodic party. And I can’t speak for the Columbia party at the NYU club, having not been there (scheduling conflicts, you know), but I’m sure it was a killer. Welcome back to jazz, largesse. OJCDs-Lots of jazz reissue com- pact discs coming out-lots and lots- and I’m trying to keep up with them all (but I’m not complaining). MCA pushed up their CD-only-twofers June release to August, and RCA pushed up its CD-only Bluebird release to the same month, but Atlan- tic’s finally come around on the CD stick, and Columbia has just rolled out some more Jazz Masterpieces. But let us not forget the indies, espe- cially the biggest, baddest jazz indie of them all-Fantasy. They’re becom- ing increasingly more bullish on CD; case in point-Original Jazz Classics CDs. Now these are like the Original Jazz Classic LPs, in that they list for a couple of bucks less than the regular Fantasy CDs and they are drawn from the vaults of Prestige, Riverside, Milestone, Contemporary and Fan- tasy and feature original artwork, liner notes, etc. (unlike the LPs, though, they do include an extra track here and there). Hot off the presses (do CDs come hot off the presses?) are “Milt Jackson Quartet,” Miles Davis’s “Dig” and “Collector’s Items,” “Clifford Brown Me- morial,” Eric Dolphy’s “Outward Bound,” “Thelonious Monk Plays Duke Ellington,” “Thelonious Monk & Sonny Rollins,” Rollins’s “Moving Out” and “The Sound of Sonny,” Bill Evans’s “New Jazz Conceptions,” Coleman Hawkins’s “The Hawk Flies High,” Art Blakey’s “Caravan,” Dave Bru- beck’s “Jazz at Oberlin” and “Jazz at the College of the Pacific,” Tadd Dameron’s “Fontainebleau,” Abbey Lincoln’s “Abbey is Blue,” “Red Garland’s Piano,” John Coltrane’s “Settin’ the Pace” and “Traneing In,” Wes Montgomery’s “Wes Montgomery Trio” and “So Much Guitar!,” “King Pleasure Sings/Annie Ross Sings,” Paul Gon- salves’s “Genin’ Together,” Lucky Thompson’s “Lucky Strikes,” Gene Ammons’s “Blue Gene,” Benny Carter’s “Jazz Giant,” “Vince Guaraldi Trio,” “The Cannonball Adderley Sextet In New York,” Chet Baker’s “Chet” and “Barney Kessel Plays Standards.” Great sound on them all, too. In other Fan- tasy news, Richie Cole has just signed with Milestone, Barney Kessel has resigned with Contemporary, Frank Morgan is in the midst of his first European tour and Sonny Rollins is, finally, set to release a new album: “G-Man,” due later this summer. r Tl—1 wm n MEDITATION - Antonio Carlos Jobim (seated , l) was recently at NY's Record Plant mixing his forthcoming Verve album, “Passarim,” in the company of (l - r) Richard Seidel, vp, PolyGram jazz; Jacques Morelen- baum, co-producer ; and studio owner Roy Cicala. LIKE A VIRGIN-Yep, another jazz festival to report on. The Virgin Islands Jazz Festival will swing the Is- lands of St. Thomas, St. Croix and St. John, August 10-16. Dizzy Gillespie, Freddie Hubbard, Gary Bartz, Richie Cole, Bobby Hutcherson and Paul Horn will be on hand and a note to P.O. Box 6201, St. Thomas, V. It Cash Box July 25. 1 987 misrepresents us.” Indeed, battles with the notorious Fleet Street news hoimds have already begun, attested to by Vol- peliere-Pierrot’ s given nickname of “Dirty Ben.” When asked about the freedom of the press, Volpeliere-Pier- rot replied “they feel they should sort of own you. But then, when the story gets out of control and widespread, they feel the need to write something else to shock the people into reading their paper. It just bugs me, really. It wastes a lot of my time.” Curiosity Killed The Cat want more than anything else to be accepted as a strong band playing intelligent pop music to an appreciative audience, and one listen to “Keep Your Distance” should be enough to convince any skep- tic of their qualifications. “We want to avoid being pigeonholed as a teenybop band,” Drummond reiterates. “That’s the most important thing. It’s nice when it starts as a word of mouth thing, that’s how it started in England. But then it gets spoiled by the big machine like the record company.” Polygram reports that the band’s first dates in the U.S. will be at a series of showcases in August. Rob Yard umian EAST COASTINGS ROFILE RECORDS presi- dent Cory Robbins and vice president Steve Plotnicki are on their way to the U.K. this week to begin staffing the label’s London office, which is scheduled to open early next year. In terms of the U.K. roster, Plotnicki says they’re “looking for dance records and mainstream rock ‘n’ roll bands as well as things that arc a little more offbeat.” Why did they wait until now to expand overseas? “We were waiting to have something that’s an international hit so we can establish world-wide scale,” he says. Another factor in the timing is that London Records has only one more option on Run-D.M.C,, at which point U.K. rights revert back to Profile; with a U.K. presence. Profile can more effectively work Run and its other acts internationally. The label is also planning to hook-up with a major label distributor in the U.K., though they still refuse to do the same in the U.S. Meanwhile, Rock Hotel, the hard core label funded by Profile, has a welcome new addition to its roster: The Nils. This Montreal foursome are in the studio readying their first LP for the label, and the rough mixes show a lot of promise. The Nils sound like a cross between Soul Asylum and “Ware- house” Husker Du, with well-articu- lated well-shaped thrash and plenty of hooks. Top tracks are the single “River Of Sadness,” the semi-acous- tic “Daylight,” and the melodic “But For Now.” The LP is being produced by ChrisSpedding. BRIEFINGS - Does life imitate video? Last week, Pfeifer, the ex-Human Switchboard leader, did just that, taking a job at Epic Records as west coast A&R manager. Expect high quality sign- ings. ON JAZZ VSOParty - Herbie Hancock was the guest of honor at a recent BMI party at New York's Tavern-On-The-Green. Here, hanging out on the patio with BMI pres and ceo Frances Preston, are some of the musicians who turned out: (I - r) Branford Marsalis, Tony Reedus, James Williams, Dave Brubeck, Bob Cran- shaw, George Coleman, Jimmy Owens, George Shearing, Hancock, Preston, Harold Mabern, Lionel Hampton, Donald Byrd, Buster Williams, Bob Brook- meyer, and Tony Williams. C lassic, live - “Classi- cal Jazz” is the name of Lin- coln Center’s first concert series devoted exclusively to jazz and, needless to say, it’s high time. August 3-5 are the dates and Wynton Marsalis is the artistic adviser. The breakdown is like this: “Ladies First-A Tribute to the Great Ladies of Jazz,” with Betty Carter, Janis Siegel, Sasha Daltonn, Carrie Smith and Marian McPartland and others (8/3); “A Tribute to The- lonious Monk,” with Carmen McRae, Barry Harris, Walter Davis, Sphere and others (8/4); and“Bird Night-A Tribute to Char- lie Parker,” with Tommy Flan- agan, Jay McShann, Hank Jones, Charles McPherson, Frank Mor- gan, Vi Redd, Percy Heath, Red Rodney, Billy Higgins and Roy Haynes (8/5). The series is presented in association with WBGO-FM and (212) 362-1911 is the number of call for the lowdown. Speaking of ’BGO, they have a new general manager: AnnaKosof. CLASSIC, ON DISC - “Colum- bia Jazz Masterpieces” continues apace with 12 interesting new items— some reissued, one previously-unis- sued, others reissued in new con- figurations. In the latter category comes “The Essential Count Basie Volume 1” (’36-39 performances, but by no means complete—they don’t even include the complete Jones- Smith, Inc. session, one of the great recording sessions in jazz history); Benny Goodman, “Roll ’Em Volume 1” (airchecks, mainly); “The Quintessential Billlie Holiday Volume 2” (complete so far); and four compilations-“The 1930s-The Big Bands,” “The 1940s-The Singers,” “The 1950s-The Singers” and a sampler. In the first category comes Thelonious Monk’s “Monk’s Mood” and “Underground,” Duke Ellington’s “Jazz Party,” and Miles Davis’ “Miles Ahead.” In the first category comes “Live Miles” (see review this page). EMARCY REDUX - PolyGram Jazz, which reactivated the Verve label not long ago, is about to start up another jazz label from the past, Emarcy Records (which was a division of MerCurF). Up first on the new Emarcy are “Ray Bryant Plays Basie and Ellington” and “Billy Ecstine Sings with Benny Carter,” both due next month. Coming soon from Verve, by the way, are new al- bums by Antonio Carlos Jobim, Shirley Horn, Joe Williams and Paco de Lucia. BOPPING AROUND - Kid Thomas Valentine, one of the last New Orleans trumpeters from the ear- liest days of jazz, died June 16 in New Orleans at the age of 91...By the way, in all the tributes to Fred As- taire’s dancing, not enough people paid tribute to Fred Astaire’s singing. He was a swinging, elegant singer- one of my favorites.. .Felix Grant, the veteran Washington, D.C. jazz disc jockey, will have a new home come August 1. He’s moving from WRC, which is going to all talk, to WDCO..Bting has not turned tail on jazz. In fact, he’s been collaborating with the great arranger, Gil Evans, on some Jimi Hendrix tunes, which are due on Sting’s next album and should get a live airing this month at Italy’s Umbria Jazz Festival...New Blue Note signings: Charnett Mof- fett (whose name combines the first names of his father, Charles Moffett, and his father’s mentor, Ornette Coleman), Jack Walrath and Dianne Reeves.. .Westport, Connec- ticut’s Levitt Pavillion will host the annual Don Elliot Memorial Concert, July 19, with Mike Abene, Jay Leon- hart, Phil Bodner, Teddy Charles and many, many others taking part. ===== PAGE 10 ===== [bruce\s+lundvall|manhattan\s+records]
POINTS WESTM ACE-LIFT-Okay, so we’ve devoted an inordinate amount of ink to a building lately in this space, but it ain’t just any ol’ edifice, it’s the Capitol Records Tower, the first major-label headquarters on the West Coast. Recently we mentioned the circular building’s peculiar architecture (resembling a stack of records with a needle on top), and the way its awnings went crashing to the ground in that rully, rully fab sequence in the movie Earthquake (while also men- tioning the fact that label artist Steve Miller recently got a star on the Hol- lywood Walk of Fame, which runs past the Capitol doorstep). Did we know, at the time, that Capitol was planning a party to celebrate the 31- year-old building’s renovation? The Capitol Tower Indeed, we did not. Fact is, the com pany staged a bash at its freshly res- tored digs last week, where such celebs as Peggy Lee, Martha Davis, Ima Sumac, Duran Duran and Ella Mae Morse (who had the label’s first hit single in 1942, a ditty called “Cow Cow Boogie’’) were expected, as of press time, to be in attendance. Aside from a lot of new paint, both in- side and out, the face-lift extends to the editing suites, which, among other things, have new consoles; the windows, which were tinted gray; the Capitol signs - re-lit at the party - for which new molds were made; and the Tower’s beacon (meant to resemble a stylus), which has beeped out the word “Hollywood” in morse code to passing air traffic since 1956, has been fuUy restored (since going on the blink in recent months). As far as the cost, the restoration is on-going, and no current estimates were avail- able from the label. Incidentally, the Capitol Tower, which cost $2 million to budd in 1955-56, was the first air- conditioned high-rise office building in Hollywood. It’s also said to be the first circular high-rise office building ever built. Class dismissed. TARANTULA-Bob Dylan’s 1966 cult classic novel, “Tarantula,” opens as a play August 14 at Santa Monica’s Powerhouse Theatre. Directed by Darrell Larson, the book has been adapted into a multi- media evening, featuring original music written by the play’s eight cast members. According to the show’s producer, Jeane Field, “Dylan is very interested in seeing a theatrical interpretation of Tarantula.” So are we. The play will be in previews August 6-9, and again on August 13. Tickets are $15 (plus service charge) and can be had in advance through Theatix (213) 466-1767, or at the box office on the night of the perfor- mance. Gregory Dobrin COVER STORY\ Richard Marx Steps Into The Limelight GregoryDobrin LOS ANGELES-“The irony of it aU is that most of the songs on this record were on the demo tapes that I sent to every record company in the world, and they all said, ‘You suck! ’” Richard Marx is on the phone from Cincinnati, one of the stops on his cur- rent club tour, discussing his self-titled debut Manhattan album, and address- ing the crap shoot that most singer/songwriters are engaged in if they’ve got any aspirations toward landing a recording deal. “I know a lot of struggling writers and singers read Cash Box," he con- tinues, explaining why he chose this particular forum for his observa- tions. “The idea that any one of those people should give up because they’ve been turned down - they should just remember that 90 percent of the people who make the decisions as to whether somebody gets signed could not hum a note of music if their lives depended on it.” Marx’ words might have been an ad- dendum to his current hit single, “Don’t Mean Nothing,” and its scath- ing view of Hollywood. Cynical stuff - harsh, even - especially for a 23-year- old. But his remarks, meant to en- courage, more than scold, are qualified by a surprising number of years in the recording business. Would you believe 17? Marx made his professional debut as a singer at age five, doing commercial jingles written by his father, Dick Marx, a Chicago jazz pianist-tumed- j ingle writer/producer (his mother, Ruth Marx, is also a singer). Singing spots for such products as Peter Pan Peanut Butter and Nestle’ s chocolate, he provided vocals for commercials until he was 17, when he began writing his own songs, and decided to get out of the jingle business. A year later, Marx’ demo tape caught the ear and interest of Lionel Richie. He then left his native Chicago and moved to L.A., where Richie signed him on as a back-up singer on his debut solo album (he can be heard on such Richie hits as “You Are, ’’“All Night Long” and “Run- ning With The Night”). Marx then co- wrote “Crazy” and “What About Me” with Keimy Rogers, ballads which both went #1. Chicago’s “Good For Nothing,” Philip Bailey’s “Love Is Alive” and Durell Coleman’s “Somebody Took My Love” fol- lowed, and Marx’ stature as a hit songwriter was established. Trouble was, he had his own ambi- tions as a recording artist, but feedback from the labels was hardly positive. What he wanted to record was rock'n’roll. “It just happened that the kind of music that I was involved with before doing this record, in order to eat, was mostly pop/MOR kind of stuff, and it was a great way to pay the rent, you know, but it was frustrating for me be- cause there’s writing that kind of music to survive, and there’s writing rock'n’roll for yourself. I was going home every night and writing my little rock'n’roll songs, hoping that someday I’d get a deal. Finally, after five years in L.A., it happened.” It was Bobby Colomby, founding member of Blood Sweat & Tears and a close friend of Marx, who introduced him to Manhattan Records president Bruce Lundvall, who signed him to the label last year. It was just the break Marx had been hoping for. “Bruce Lundvall didn’t want me to change anything, he just wanted me to do what I did,” he remembers. “There were no expecta- tions as far as hit singles or anything like that. He just gave me the room to do what I wanted to do.” Colomby was also instrumental in bringing Marx together with David Cole, with whom he wound up co- producing the album. “I was originally j f j® k ml dis tel p Bl I i!k iq m % fci (a k M Oil 1 E B, NEWFACES TO WATCH That Petrol Emotion That Petrol Emotion’s “Babble” is turbulent, tuneful, angry, crashing, brooding, abrasive, and intelligent - in short, a smashing U.S. debut by one of the U.K.’s best bands. ONJAZZ\ P ASSING ON-Trumpeter Howard McGhee died July 17 in New York after a long illness. McGhee was a fiery first generation bebopper whose vigorous, keening attack graced hundreds of bandstands and record sessions. Although McGhee was inactive for a number of years, I remember attending a record session in the late- ’70s in which he and Benny Bailey snarled through some fiery two-trumpet pieces. Howard McGhee, “Maggie” as he was fre- quently known, was 69. Photographer Bob Parent died in New York June 5. Parent photographed the jazz scene from the 1940s until shortly before his death, amassing over 100,000 photos, some of them the most famous images ever taken of jazz musicians. Bob Parent was 63. CALLING COLLECTORS-The International Association of Jazz Record Collectors will hold its 23rd convention August 12-15 at the Atlas Pacifica Hotel and Convention Center in Culver City, California. There will be concerts, speeches, films, records and books for sale, and a whole lot of talk about 78s, 10-inch LPs, maybe even CDs. For informa- tion about the event, contact the lAJRC at (213) 660-9061 or by mail to Box 1571, Glendale, CA 91209. KEY NOTES-What could be bet- ter than the 21 -record boxed set, “The Complete Keynote Collec- tion,” that PolyGram put out last year? That’s right, “The Complete Keynote Collection” on CD, and now, not surprisingly, PolyGram has begun releasing a good hunk of that collection on compact disc under the banner of “The Essential Keynote Collection.” The first five sets have just been issued, with five more due in August. They are ‘ ‘The Complete Lester Young On Keynote” (which immediately takes its place as one of the most essential jazz CDs yet released), “The Complete Lennie Tristano On Keynote,” “Early Be- bop” (Red Rodney, Dave Lambert etc.), “Roy Eldridge and the Swing Trumpets” (dates by Roy, Charlie Shavers, Jonah Jones, Buck Clayton, Joe Thomas and Emmett Berry, and the only double-CD of the first issue) and “The Fabulous El- lingtonians” (dates by Johnny Hodges, Rex Stewart and other El- lington alumni). Much of this music, as I explained here last year in a review of the boxed set, is brilliant. filled with a majesty and grace that is often breathtaking. The transfers (al- though, as always, when they crackled on record, hoo-boy, do they crackle on CD) are quite excellent. Other recent jazz CD reissues in- clude “For You For Me For Ever- more,” tracks by the Artie Shaw Or- chestra with strings and a 21 -year- old Mel Torme (Musicraft), and a pair of two-CD compilations from DRG’s Disques Swing line: “Ridin’ in Rhythm,” featuring some excep- tional early Coleman Hawkins and Benny Carter, and “Jazz in the Thir- ties,” featuring, among others, Joe Venuti, Benny Goodman and Gene Krupa NAJ NOTES-The Los Angeles- based National Academy of Jazz, which is “dedicated to the advance- ment and artistry of jazz and to estab- lishing chapters throughout the country so diat we can become a major force in helping make more Americans aware of the complete spectrum of music we call jazz,” has upped its two-year-old Board of Directors from 15 to 25 members. The NAJ brain trust now consists of Ray Avery, Frank Capp, Allyn Fer- guson, Bob Florence, Terry Gibbs, Red Holloway, Phil Hulsey, Ralph Jungheim, Sandra Kimberling, Mauri Lathower, Luis Conte, Ber- nie Lewak, Mundell Lowe, Marty Morgan, Chuck Niles, Kirk Pasich, Dave Pell, Sue Raney, George Rap- paport, Pancho Sanchez, Jim Shatz, Terri Tilton, Jim Washburn, LaRue Brown Watson and Jack Wheaton. The NAJ’s next member- ship meeting will take place on July 30 at the Hollywood Musician’s Union, 817 N. Vine St., and Bill Henderson, Jimmy Witherspoon and the Britt & Brown Sextet will perform. ROUND MIDI-In one of the great ironies of the day, Dexter Gordon, in Europe on his first jazz tour in four years, was prevented from entering Paris earlier this month when the computers at immigration control turned up a 20-year-old drug rap. Ironic because not only has Dexter Gordon been in France numerous times since then but that, of course, is where he filmed “Round Midnight” and, to boot, where he was last year made a chevalier in France’s Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, a highly- prized honor. In any case, after five hours of moping in the airport. Long Tall Dexter was loosed upon France. Dexter told the International Herald Tribune’s Mike Zwerin that next time he comes to France, he’s going to be wearing his chavliermeda.1. ALBUM RELEASES OUT OF THEBOX ROSANNE CASH - King’s Record Shop - Columbia FC 40777 - Producer: Rodney Crowell — List: $8.98 -Bar Coded Johnny’s oldest daughter returns in fine form with her fifth LP - again produced by husband Rodney Crowell. Her simple, heartfelt artistry is en- hanced by Crowell’s uncluttered production touches, best evidenced on the gorgeously aching “The Real Me,’’ and rockers like “Rosie Strike Back” and “Somewhere, Sometime.” Songwriting contributors include John Hiatt, Johnny Cash, Crowell, and Ben- mont Tench. OUT OF THE BOX LEVERT - The Big Throwdown - Atlantic 81773-1 - Producers: Various- List: $8.98 - Bar Coded This trio specializes in light soulful touches of Urban romance. Their style is perfectly epitomized by their current B/C smash “Casanova,” a sure pick to slide into the Cash Box top 10 Black singles this week. Look for Top 40 crossover soon. Side two picks up the tempo a bit, with four dance burners that to keep the charm alive. NEWAND DEVELOPING NEWAND DEVELOPING CARRIE MCDOWELL - Motown 6223ML- Producers: Various - List: $8.98- Bar Coded McDowell’s smooth chirp is sexy in its playfulness, and she puts it to good use in this collection of synth-powered crush grooves and loving ballads. There is a message behind her magic, attested to by the first single “Uh Uh, No No Casual Sex,” and the frisky “Just Dance.” TIFFANY - MCA MCA-5793 - Producer: George Tobin - List: $8.98 -Bar Coded Get past the novelty of her age - sure, she’s only 15, but this sparkling young redhead has the vocal tools and fiery spirit of Pat Benatar and the smoky, husky possibilities of Gloria Es- tefan. Hooky, toe-tapping pop vehicle - strong debut. The shopping mall tour is in full swing, and early sales accounts report good response from teens everywhere. FEATURE PICKS HEROES - Here We Are - RCA 5908-1-R - Producer: Richard James Bur- gess - List: $8.98 - Bar Coded Multilayered, glittering hard rock with a textured, melodic feel ala Mr. Mister. Horn inserts sweeten and keyboard fills glisten over the strong backbeat. Darren Costin’s vocals remind of Colin Hay on steroids. PETE WYLIE - Sinful - Virgin 90600-1 - Producers: Various - List: $8.98 - Bar Coded Wylie’s first for Virgin mixes guts and atmosphere with punchy production and insightful lyrics. Highlights from the former voice for Wah include the focused in- tensity of “If I Love You” and the wistful longing of “Fourelevenfortyfour.” BUCKWHEAT ZYDECO - On A Night Like This - Island 90622-1 - Producer: Ted Fox -List: $8.98- Bar Coded The foremost party animal on the zydeco scene today, Buckwheat has taken the form from the Creoles of New Orleans around the world. From the first note, this scorching set will lighten your heart and move your feet. Essential. JELLYBEAN - Just Visiting This Planet - Chrysalis BFV 41569 - Producer: Jellybean - List: $8.98 - Bar Coded The leading architect of the 80’s dance groove is spotlighted here on his first full-length solo LP as artist/producer. Thematic images of dreams, illusions, and personal intimacies are couched in an attractive package of glossy production values and lively vocal gymnastics. BLACK BRITAIN - Obvious - Virgin 90597-1 - Producers: Various - List: $8.98 -Bar Coded Serious funk - more ambitious than the majority of the genre. Social insight is evident in the lyrical outlook, engaging the brain while the constantly percolating, popping beat gets ‘cm out on the floor. AVA CHERRY - Picture Me - Capitol CLT-46918 - Producers: Various - List: $8.98 - Bar Coded Fat, sassy, sexy sounds from the former Bowie back-up singer. Guaranteed to bum up B/C playlists and club floors, with scintillating axe work from rocker pal Jon Butcher. BACK TO THE BEACH - Original Motion Picture Soundtrack - Columbia SC 40892 - Producers: Various - List: $8.98 - Bar Coded Fun-filled, sun drenched collection of light summertime fare. Featuring perfor- mances from Eddie Money, Dave Edmunds, Herbie Hancock, and Stevie Ray Vaughan. Added bonus is the inclusion of two of the most expressive vocalists of today, Marti Jones and Aimee Mann. THE WILD FLOWERS - Dust - Big Time 6044-1-B - Producers: Wild Flowers/Jones/Rivers - List: $8.98 - Bar Coded Raucous, driving guitar workout with rough edges recalling garage sounds of 60’s. RIPPINGTONS (Passport PJ 88019) 40 ROYAL GARDEN BLUESn 39 42 BRANFORD MARSALIS (Columbia FC 40363) RM250 JAZZFEATURE PICKS P ASSING ON - Dick Well- stood, one of the best ex- ponents of stride piano, died July 24 of heart failure in Palo Alto, California, where he had gone to play at a jazz party. Wellstood was one of a group of traditionalists who came up during the bebop era and, since then, his Fats Waller-influenced piano styl- ings have been a constant joy— whether heard solo in New York’s piano bars, or as part of such tradi- tional groups as the Classic Jazz Quartet. Dick Wellstood was 59. BIRELLI FOR THE WORLD - Bireli Lagrene (r) recently stopped by the Blue Note offices to showcase a few tunes from his forthcoming album for the label. With him here are (l - r): Blue Note's Michael Cus- cuna, jazz promotion manager Susan Levin, andpresident Bruce Lundvall. IT’S THAT TIMES AGAIN- “Jazz and the Media: Past, Present and Future” is the working title for this year’s JazzTimes Convention, set for October 14-17 at New York’s Roosevelt Hotel. Joe Williams will be this year’s Guest of Honor and Billy Taylor will deliver the Keynote Address, but that ain’t the half of it. For those who’d like a sampler, here are some of the things (and several of the people) in-store. October 14: Registration, general opening session, “I Paid My Dues” (Ira Gitler, Chubby Jackson), Blue Note party (Jack Walrath). October 15: Keynote, “Promoting Your Jazz Station: A Reality” (Rick Petrone), “Television: Past, Present & Future” (Leonard Feather, Steve Allen), “Jazz Radio Today: Syndi- cated Shows & Networks (Ben Sidran, Andy Denemark), David Chertok’s jazz films, CBS Records (Terence Blanchard & Donald Har- rison). October 16: “Increasing Media Coverage for Jazz with a Series” (Frank Malfitano, Brad Simon), “Jazz in Print Today” (Gary Gid- dins), “Ad Agencies Look at Jazz” (Hal Davis, Elliot Lawrence), “Joe Williams on Jazz,’ ’ RCA party. October 17: Record Fair, “The For- ces Behind the Continued Growth of Jazz” (George Wein, John Con- yers), “New Age and Fusion in the Media” (Roger Lifeset, Lee Abrams), “New Technologies” (Ken Furst, Larry Rosen), “Media Conclusion Session,’ ’ PolyGram party (Joe Williams). For information about all of this, get in touch with JazzTimes at 8055- 13th St., Silver Spring, MD 20910 or at (301) 588-4114. FESTIVALIA NEAR-The Green- wich Village Jazz Festival is set for August 28-September 7, the only jazz festival in the world that takes place where jazz is bom and bred: the jazz clubs of New York City. See, the Vil- lage Festival is, for the most part, real- ly not a jazz festival, since the clubs of Greenwich Village are a per- manent jazz festival. What the Fes- tival allows is the ability to save a bunch of money on club-hopping. A $15 Festival Pass (on sale now at the Village Gate) gets the bearer a 50% discount on the first and second sets at the participating clubs and free ad- mission to the third sets. All mini- mums, however, apply. Check the local listings, as they say, for exactly who is playing at the clubs in ques- tion (Arthur’s Tavern, the Blue Note, Bradley’s, Carlos 1, Fat Tuesday’s, Sweet Basil, the Village Comer, the Village Gate, the Village Vanguard, Visiones and the 55 Bar). Other ac- tivities involving the Festival are a free kick-off concert with Sun Ra and Jack Walrath at the Gate, a jazz film series at the Bleecker Street Cinema, Sweet Basil’s “Music is an Open Sky” series and a number of other free performances. FESTIVALIA LESS NEAR-The 10th Chicago Jazz Festival, which has earned the right to call itself the largest free jazz festival in the world, will fill Grant Park’s Petrillo Bandshell for five nights beginning September 2 with, among many others, Stephane Grappelli, Wynton Marsalis, Woody Herman, a tribute to Art Blakey, Dave Brubeck, and a tribute to JATP. Won’t cost you a far- thing. FESTIVALIA FAR-It will cost you a farthing to attend the McEwan’s Edinburgh International Jazz Festival, which will swing out in the beautiful Scottish city, August 15- 22. On tap (so to speak-the festival is sponsored by a brewery) are Jay McShann, Bob Wilber, Buddy Tate, Acker Bilk, Ken Colyer, “Sweets” Edison, Humphrey Lyt- telton and many others with a tradi- tional bent. LAND OF THE FAT-Fat City Productions has been formed to provide a weekly syndicated radio series recorded live at New York’s Fat Tuesday’s jazz club. “Fat City Jazz” is the name of the show, and it’s intended as a 52-week series, with the initial program airing the first week of October. Charles Brandt president of Fat City, says, “‘Fat City Jazz’ is not a disk jockey spinning records. Our program cap- tures the top artists in the field per- forming at a hot New York jazz club, so our audience can sense the adrenalin and experience the true es- sence of the artists’ work.” Fat City Productions is at 150 E. 74th St., New York, NY 10021 (212-517- 1640). TALENTONSTAGE FIRETOWNAND FRIENDS - Coinciding with the New Music Seminar, Atlantic Records recently hosted a party at the Marriot Marquis Hotel in New York City. Shown are (L-R): Fire Town's Doug Erikson; Roger Daltrey; Fire Town’s Tom Lavarada and Phil Davies; Twisted Sister's Eddie Ojeda; Fire Town s Butch Vig; JonAstley; and Astley' s manager, Ric Aliberte. T he Grateful Dead/Bob Dylan GIANTS STADIUM, N.J. - The Grateful Dead/Bob Dylan show here (7/12) broke all previous attendance records at Giants Stadium, attracting 71,598 fans, most of them teenagers in tie-dyed t-shirts. Sure, there were a few fortyish granola types, but for the most part it looked just like the Haight in ‘68, back when going to a Dead show was an act of rebellion. Today, however, going to a Deadfest is an act of conservatism by a new generation that listens to its parents’ music and wears its parents’ clothes. In fact, one can imagine fans rushing home after the concert to trade notes with mom and dad, and to hear them reminisce about Watkins Glen and Woodstock. Apparently, teenagers don’t have heroes particular to their own genera- tion anymore (even the Beastie Boys are modeled on the rebel stance of a previous era), and they seem content with hand-me-down icons. Still, the pairing of Bob Dylan with the Grateful Dead promised to be the big American folk music event of the year, and in a sense it was — though the ‘event’ aspect often drowned out the music. Stadium shows are always more like vast communal gatherings than rock concerts, and this one was no exception. People danced en masse in remote comers and corridors where one could barely hear the music, and many others partied, picnicked, and otherwise ignored the show. This is partly attributable to the fact that sound tends to get lost in stadiums; with a mass of amps stageside and two sets of speakers in the middle of the field, there was a lot of bounce, echo, and im- precision. When fans started clapping along to one song, there was even a time-lapse effect, with the clapping from one side of the stadium coming at you about a second or two after the clapping from the other side, destroy- ing the band’s rhythm. Nonetheless, the music was often im- mensely enjoyable. The Dead opened the concert, playing such old favorites as “Bertha,” “Playing In The Band,” and “Ramblin’ Rose,” along with several songs from their new top ten album, “In The Dark” (Arista). Dylan joined the Dead for the last part of the show, and his set included obscure gems from his golden days: “Chimes Of Freedom,” “The Wicked Mes- senger,” and “Queen Jane Ap- proximately.” But with the Dead as a backing band, most of his set sounded more like the Grateful Dead than Bob Dylan, which benefited some songs (“Wicked Messenger”) and ruined others (imagine two Deads and a Dylan howling “Joey”). In theory it was an inspired cou- pling, but in practice they need a smaller venue to make it work. Per- haps the Dead can be persuaded to play, say, seven nights at a small Man- hattan club, while Dylan goes solo for a two-week stand at New York’s Town Hall. Now that’s something worth tie- dyeing a t-shirt for. Paul Iorio T he North Sea Jazz Festival CONGRESGEBOUW, THE HAGUE HOLLAND - Look, there are zillions of jazz festivals at this point, but Holland’s North Sea Jazz Festival is, beyond a doubt, the Big Daddy of them all. No festival is big- ger, no festival presents a more impres- sive line-up of talent, no festival covers the wide scope of jazz that the North Sea Jazz Festival manages to choke into the Hague’s masssive Congres- gebouw convention center every year. And, the wonder of it all is that this is a weekend festival-three measly days. To try to convey a sense of the breadth of the festival, here’s a list of some of the trumpet players who were on hand this year: Dizzy Gillespie, Lester Bowie, Kenny Wheeler, Randy Brecker, Clark Terry, Woody Shaw, Freddie Hubbard, Don Cherry, Jon Fad- dis, Wynton Marsalis, Jimmy Owens, Doc Cheatham, Wild Bill Davison, James Morrison, Ornette Coleman, Ruby Braff, Arturo Sandoval, Palle Mikkelborg, Miles Davis, Benny Carter and Roy Hargrove. That’s a par- tial list-in one building, on one weekend! Of course, it’s impossible to see all of these people. In fact, it’s impossible to see almost everybody who is on the North Sea Jazz Festival, since 12 stages go full-tilt simultaneously for about 10 hours each of the three days. So, without going into details , about the enormous difficulties of just getting around this thing, here is a quick wrap- up of what I heard, in the order, more or less, that I heard it. Friday: I began with a set of Monty Alexander’s Jamaican Jazz Jamboree, a band that combines jazz and calypso quite effectively (thanks, in great part, to the excellent steel drum playing of Len “Boogsie” Sharp). I then scurried upstairs for a taste of Armando Cairo, a young Dutch tenor saxophonist whose playing was more impressive than his writing (which, on this set, was fea- tured). Stuck around in the same room for a set of Benny Carter-the inim- itable swing master-and guest James Morrison, an adroit young Australian multi-instrumentalist who was best, here, on trombone. Then, whoosh, across the building for the Dexter Gor- don “Round Midnight” Band (Dexter, Bobby Hutcherson, Pierre Michelot, Billy Higgins, Cedar Walton). Ole Dex’s chops, though not yet at their sharpest, were pretty damned good, and his sound-that phenomenal big sound—was intact. Then way upstairs for some Dutch boredom-Tam Tam Fanfare, saxophones and hand drums- and Courtney Pine. Now Courtney Pine is a big deal in England-he’s young, he’s talented, he’s English and he’s black—and he’s getting himself into the Wynton Marsalis conundrum. The jazz press helped make him a media star, and now that he’s a media star the jazz press is quick to point out how overrated he is. In any case, he showed, to me, an impressive ability to play the tenor saxophone-updated Coltrane, swinging and adven- turesome. His young band may not be much, but Mr. Pine is one to keep an eye on. To bed. Saturday: 1. The Lonnie Brooks Blues Band. Sharp, ringing Chicago blues. 2. Rockin’ Dopsie and the Cajun Twisters. Goodtime-rolling Louisiana zydeco. 3. Arturo Sandoval. Scorching modem day Cu-bop. 4. Adalberto Alvarez y Su Son. Scorch- ing modem day Cuban salsa (look, there were four Cuban bands on this festival, four Cuban bands who, at the moment, are no more likely to play in American than Fidel Castro is to pitch for the Pittsburgh Pirates). 5. Oliver Lake Quartet. Silken modem New York (yeah!) jazz. 6. Willem Breuker Kollektief. Yeah, the excellent mad- cap Dutch band in a not-quite-tongue- in-cheek set of George Gershwin’s con- cert music. Excellent. 7. Herbie Steward. Herbie Steward? Yep, the fourth Four Brother was rescued from , obscurity and, on alto only, he swung, swang, swinged. 8. Jeannie & Jimmy Cheatham and the Sweet Baby Blues & Jazz Band. Los Angeles-based blues and jazz, natch, and quite entertaining. Nice to hear trumpeter Clora Bryant and clarinetist Jimmy Noone in the flesh (got to go to Europe to hear bands from L.A.). To bed. Sunday: I listened to the Dizzy Gil- lespie Big Band, which was smoooooooking!!! I listened to Polish tenor saxophonist Tomasz Szukalski, which was booooooooooring! I lis- tened to Chuck Berry, who was per- functory (but who was to improve-see next week’s Nice Festival review). I listened to Alice Coltrane & the Coltrane Legacy which was, well, not good. Alice has taken her and John’s two sons, Ravi and Oran, stuck saxophones in their hands, and sent them up on stage in front of her, Reg- gie Workman and Rashied Ali. They are not ready-not ready at all-to be professional musicians. I listened to Ornette Coleman & Prime Time, with Don Cherry guesting, and it was a good blend of Ornette’s old and new dreams- and hearing Prime Time play “Lonely Woman” was a treat. I then listened to a rip-snorting 17-year-old trumpeter from Dallas named Roy Hargrove sit- ting in with Frank Morgan. The kid has got a nice, gruff sound and a wide- open approach. He’ll be graduating high school next summer. Then, as if all of this wasn’t enough, I stumbled back to my hotel and found Wynton Marsalis, Arturo Sandoval and young Hargrove jamming in the lobby-in the lobby!—with Wynton’s band. I listened for two hours before I went to bed. The sun was already up. Copyright under Univer sal Copyright Convention POSTMASTER Send address changes to Cash Box. 330 W 58th Street, New York. N Y 10019 Editorial Whatever Happened To The Eight Track Tape? T echnology is getting a little nuts. It is getting to the point where even Knowledgeable industry "experts" are hard pressed to keep up with the improvements, advances, improvements on advances and new tech- nological breakthroughs. We started with the video disc, then came CD's and now there are all forms of combined and interactive capability CD's. You've got your CD, CDV, CD ROM, CD I and, reports of an erasable, re-useable CD format that will be available in a few short years. In addition *o the CD format the general public is taking to in overwhelm, g numbers, there is already a floppy, re-useable CD available, very expensive at the mo- ment but, as we have seen, high prices have shown a great ability to decline as consumer demand grows. Lets not forget DAT, and, in the home video realm, 8 mm. Rumors are also spreading about an even newer generation of super fidelity audio format, software the size and shape of credit cards, capable of being encoded with up to ten stand- ard length Ip's. The fact that all of these developments require close study by every phase of the home entertainment in- dustry for self protection against copyright infringe pirate, bootleg and home tapeing and any and all other so ces of lost revenue is obvious and self evident. Safeguards are not the purpose of this editorial. Individual manufacturers and licensing organizations have been addressing these problems in conjuction with industry organizations for some time. We only wished to point out the obvious. The ever es calating technological advances (I call your DAT and raise you one CD ROM), the call for some sort of organizational sanity for making the hardware available to the public and giving software suppliers and manufacturers and the general public an opportunity to examine the available formats and make rational decisions based on individual need, and finally to wistfully wonder what ever did happen to the simple days of eight track tapes and quadrophonic sound? THE BEAT I S REAL RADIO DEAD?-As Americans once again eye the basics, conservative thought in action increases, babyboomers return to ballroom dancing and Fred Astaire Studios start booming, look for a new phenomenon: Black Adult Contemporary Radio. Ex- perienced program directors and music directors 35 years and older will be very much in demand. Look for Urban i Radio to reach for expanded demographics to include 25 plus, with the addition of Blues, Jazz and hard core Rhythm and Blues added to playlist in major markets. We will re- search, report and stay out front on this new happening. OVER 40 AND OUT??-Perhaps they are the viable talent from which new things can be learned!! They are out of the business, because nobody wants them, they are too old. I ask you the reader to think of as many black disc jockeys over 40 currently employed in a top ten market. The black disc jockey who came up in this country 10-20 years ago are gone or working in small market radio. After all of the years of working to perfect their craft they are virtually booted out of the business. What are the reasons: too old, too much of a threat or too much knowledge? Research is a great and necessary tool, but what ever hap- pened to gut instinct, simply being in tune with the listening habits of the market place, listening to music and determining whether or not the record has hit potential. Imagine the combina- tion of good sound research gut feel- ings. Some programmers are doing precisely that and arc winning big. Reflecting for a few moments, there are a number of incredibly talented professional black radio announcers who should be in major markets. Enoch Gregory,(he is reportedly happy doing what he does, but this man along with hundreds of other veteran professionals) E. Rodney Jones,(Mr. Chicago, who until monday August 3, 1987 was employed at KOKY in Little Rock. He reportedly was terminated for economic reasons) George "Boogaloo" Frazier,(met with the same fate as Rodney at KOKY) Mike Payne,(who once owned the Cleveland and Pittsburgh markets) Jesse Fax,(who put Washington radio lis- teners in a different sphere) and of course the list goes on and on. Com- pare if you would the number of black radio veterans in major markets over 40 with any other format and you will quickly realize the great numerical dif- ference. It seems that most businesses take full advantage of the wealth of knowledge and experience of their veterans. Most of you are aware and familiar with S.C.O.R.E.(Service Corp Of Retired Executives) Why not estab- lish a similiar organization, (wherein the vast knowledge of these veteran programmers could be utilized) with expansion into other areas of the enter- tainment business. A thought on being over 40 which has been said time and time again, most of these professionals have children therefore they could certainly relate to the younger listeners while capturing the older demographics. Per- haps they are the viable talent from which new things can be learned?? #1 FOR 8 YEARS-During a recent conversation with Joe Bullard, program director of WANM Tallahas- see, Florida, he told me of a remark- able feat. Joe’s 1000 Watt daytime AM’er has been #1 for eight straight years. When you hold a title that long you are king. Therefore Joe and his fine staff deserve all the praise in the world for a job well done. What is Joe’s secret for gamering a 25 share of the market/ He plays wi. he calls full circle music which encom passes Blucs,(as rare as the dino ,r on radio) Jazz, Currents and Oldies. Joe i apparently doing what we spoke about earlier, Black Adult Contemporary Radio. His numbers would certainly in- dicate he has dispelled the theories about there is no market for blues. Look at the number of blues oriented commercials. There is a market for blues! Joe went on to tell us about the mas- sive giveaways and the special per- sonality teams his 1000 Watt Daytime AM’er continues to defeat. When you see the evolution of Black Adult Contemporary charts, remember you read it in Cash Box. We will be checking and reporting on markets who program and are getting great ratings by playing the blues. I will keep an eye on the Chicago market where Sonny Joe White and Frankie Crocker are applying their special brand of radio, including Blues. ONJAZZ EL DOCTOR — Tito Puente was recently made a doctor of music by SUNY/Old Westbury. Here, draping the good doctor, are (l - r) Prof. Basileo Serrano, pres L. Eudora Pet- tigrew and trustee Dr. John L.S. Hol- loman. B luebirds of happi- NESS-Another nail has been driven into the coffins of the turntables of jazz col- lectors. RCA has 16 spank- ing-new Bluebird reissues on the market and, yes, they are available only on CD. As usual with the RCA jazz program, the reissues are an odd as- sortment and represent a number of different approaches to the concept of reissuing albums. Two of the reissues stand out: be- cause they have been unavailable for many years, because they are excel- lent and important albums, and be- cause they both include alternate takes. They are Duke Ellington’s “And His Mother Called Him Bill,” and The Sextet of Orchestra U.S.A.’s “Theatre Music of Kurt Weill.” The former is an Ellington masterpiece, pure and simple. Recorded in 1967 as a memorial to composer Billy Strayhorn, the album drips with brilliance, and this reissue includes an unreleased ver- sion of “Lotus Blossom” and alter- nate takes of “Smada” and “My Lit- tle Brown Book.” The latter is one of the hardest-to-find albums featur- ing Eric Dolphy. Arranged and con- ducted by Mike Zwerin, Dolphy is featured on three numbers- “Alabama Song,” “Havana Song,” and “As You Make Your Bed”-but the disc also includes fine work from Thad Jones, Jerome Richardson, John Lewis and others. There are three alternates here but, alas, none from the numbers with Dolphy. The other discs just released are Art Blakey’s “The Theory of Art” (the 1957 LP “A Night in Tunisia” plus two unusual previously-unissued septet numbers); “A Song After Sun- down,” Stan Getz and his excellent mid- ’60s group (Jim Hall, Gary Bur- ton, Steve Swallow, Roy Haynes) with Arthur Fiedler and the Boston Pops; “Just a Mood,” Red Norvo; “Say When,” JJ. Johnson; “Time Was,” Bud Powell; “Swingin’ Till the Girls Come Home,” Lambert Hendricks and Bavan (culled from three albums); “Artist’s Choice,” Gary Burton (a Burton-picked com- pilation disc); “Clap Hands Here Comes Charlie,” Charlie Barnet (compilation); “Begin the Beguinc,” Artie Shaw (compilation); “Major Glenn Miller & The Army Air Force Band 1943-44;” a sampler; and three Benny Goodman discs: “After You’ve Gone-The Original Benny Goodman Trio and Quartet Sessions Vol. 1,” “Sing, Sing, Sing” (an B.G. Orchestra compilation), and “Together Again!,” a 1963 reunion of the original quartet (Teddy Wil- son, Lionel Hampton, Gene Krupa, of course). The sound on the ones I’ve listened to is just fine, particular- ly on the post 78-Era sides. And the discs are, for the most part, generous, with at least half of them clocking in at over an hour. PolyGram, which has been one of the labels spearheading the CD-only trend, has just put out four jazz CD reissues from the Verve catalogue, three with extra tracks. They are Stan Getz’s “Big Band Bossa Nova” (the one without alternate takes), Lester Young’s “The Presi- dent Plays” (withfive extra tracks, in- cluding a Lester Young vocal-!-on “It Takes Two to Tango”), Wes Montgomery’s “Tequila” (four extra tracks), and Getz and Lionel Hampton’s aptly-titled “Hamp and Getz’ ’ (with two unreleased sides). CASH BOX ANYTHING ELSE ISA COMPROMISE AUDIO/VIDEO I M TV Europe Debuts ... - At midnight on August 1, 1987, MTV Europe made its debut, hitting the airwaves overseas. The network is filmed live via-satel- lite from Amsterdam to cable systems throughout Europe. Elton John had the honors of throwing the switch to turn on MTV Europe, the launch marked the latest and most ambitious of MTV Network’s international ven- tures, which include licensing agree- ments in Japan and Australia. Head- quartered in London, MTV Europe is said to reflect the musical tastes, life- styles and culture of the European Audience. The network will feature seven on-air VJ’s (video jockeys) from all over the world and a variety of programming that will differ slight- ly from MTV’s established stateside outlet, featuring what appears to be a meld of both the American MTV and its counterpart VH-1. Among the in- novative programming presented on MTV Europe will be: “New Visions,” a program devoted to New Age and contemporary jazz; “Reverb,” a half hour talk show, reviewing everything from films, records, books and videos; and “The MTV Gig Guide,” a regular feature that will focus on who’s currently on the road in Europe. MTV Network Entertainment President Tom Freston stated in a press release “This venture is key to MTV’s vision to be the world’s premiere outlet and driving force in youth oriented music and culture.” He continued “It is our hope that MTV’s expertise in communicating with the 12-34 year-old audience will help provide Europe with a rock music network that not only serves its audience, but provides the kind of benefits and opportunities for the music industry, the cable television industry, and the advertising com- munity that have occurred in the United States.” MTV Europe is a joint venture among the affiliated cor- porations of Mirror Group News- papers Limited, Viacom International Inc., and British Telecom pic. Explore China For Under $30.00- Paramount Home Video is association with Windham Hill are planning a September 16 release for “China.” “China” is Windham Hill’s latest video outing, showcasing spectacular footage from the country with a backdrop of music performed by many Windham Hill artists. Produced by Dan Moss, the film ex- plores regions of a land just opened to Western visitors and, thus offers a look at a China we’ve never seen before. Among those artists contribut- ing their musical talents arc William Ackerman, Phillip Aaberg, Sha- dowfax and Tim Story. The tape will hold a suggested $29.95 retail tag, available in both VHS and Beta HiFi. SCREEN SIREN SUSANNA Bangle Susanna Hoffs is featured in her motion picture debut in The Allnighter, a comedy about a young girl' s quest for true love on the last night before graduating college. Available October 8 from MCA Home Video. The Return of Kolchak ... - Com- ing in early October, MCA Home Video will release “The Night Stalker: Two Tales Of Terror.” Culled from the popular early 70’s television series “The Night Stalker,” which featured Darren McGavin as investigative reporter Carl Kolchak. As you may remem- ber, Kolchak seemed to have a knack for winding up in the midst of some of the scariest modem-day super- natural activities. Featured episodes on the forthcoming tape are “The Ripper” and “The Vampire.” Watch for this one to achieve cult status fast. Available in VHS and Beta. Aussie Breakthrough ... - Para- mount Pictures’ “Crocodile Dun- dee,” the highest grossing foreign film ever released in the United States ($174 million/box office), has just broken another world record. Ini- tial orders for "Crocodile Dundee” videocassettes represent almost S54 million at retail, Stated Tim Clott, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Paramount Home Video, * ‘This is a huge pre-order considering that our consumer media campaign has just begun, and will continue for three weeks.” HEY, YOU!!! - Remember, please address all future video cor- respondence to Tom De Savia c/o CASH BOX magazine (or call 1-213- 464-8241). M OORE’S SATELLITE- Former Miracle Pete Moore is realizing his dream of operating his own company, Satellite Records. Moore, who serves as presi- dent has never gotten the recognition he rightfully deserves as one of the in- dustry’s most brilliant songwriters. He has penned some legendary multi-mil- lion sellers, i.e. Ooh Baby Baby,(cur- rently enjoying tremendous success as a remake by a 19 year old artist called Romeo) Since I Lost My Baby-Tem- pations, Ain’t That Peculiar, I’ll Be Doggone-Marvin Gaye, Tracks Of My Tears, Love Machine-Miracles. His companys’ start somewhat paral- lels Motown Records beginning, in that all the artist are involved in every aspect of their record including market- ing and promoting at the radio and retail level. Satellite Records currently has three artists under contract, with other sign- ings forthcoming. Their first release features a group of four talented young men called The Main whose first single titled All Of Me just shipped to radio and retail outlets around the country. Scheduled for release in late August is Denise Stewart’s remake of Tracks Of My Tears, along with former Boardwalk recording artist Tierra and their remake of The Jack- sons’ 1969 smash I Want You Back. Albums have been readied for a fall release on all three artist. Pete has taken a hands on approach to running his family concept record company wherein everyone is involved and are striving to build a successful "company" as opposed to one record. In addition to Moore, other staff mem- bers include Mike Missile .(Motown alumni) serves as vice president and general manager, Darnell Johnson, na- tional promotion director and Ed Con- treras director of A&R and artist development. Pete Moore’s combination of street savvy, corporate business acumen and his fine staff of professionals will cer- tainly make Satellite Records a viable force in the music industry LAMAR’S SPOTLIGHT-Tom- bionca recording artist Lamar Barry Inc. will be featured in a gala fashion show and soiree hosted by Geno And Sylvia of Hollywood Hosiery on Satur- day August 15 in the grand ballroom of The Ramada Inn, 850 East Domin- guez, Carson, California. This youthful veteran and multi talented artist will also be featured in a special appearance at the world- reknown Carlos And Charlie’s on Sunset Blvd, 8:00pm, Monday, Septem- ber 28. Executive producer for the af- fair is William J. Brinkley. Hear Lamar performing selections from his latest album There’s Nothing Better Than Love on Tombionca Records. DOUBLE TAKE FORMED-The lovely idential twin entertainment lawyers Leona and Leonia Lloyd, who have played major roles in the career development of such artists as Ready For The World on MCA Records, Kiara recently signed to Arista Records and Davina formerly with Columbia Records have formed their own label. Appropriately called Double Take Records, these lovely and brilliant lawyers has everyone who sees them doing double takes to determine who is who. Their primordial release titled If You’re Single by Davina is an up tempo dance tune with some tremen- dous lyrics which should gamer major radio, club and sales activity around the country. Look for Lloyd and Lloyd to become a major musical force as operators of their own company, Double Take Records. SOUNDTOWN REBOUNDS- Memphis based Soundtown Records has returned to the music scene v. smash hit release entitled MS. X David Alexander. The new dance has hot lyrics and a funky dance groove. Reggie Jenkins, presidcnt/c.c. n. states, "we are expanding our market- ing approach which caters to the youth and young adult record buyers in the urban contemporary market." We have signed a roster of new artists with potential to excell in this industry. In- dustry veteran Rod Kenny serves as national independent consultant. David Alexander, the first artist to be released exemplifying Soundtown ’s new approach, is a gifted artist, writer and producer. He has worked with An- gela Bofill, Melba Moore, Pieces Of A Dream and Herbie Hancock. His album will be released near the end of summer and will contain a mixture of up-tempos and ballads that should propell David to superstardom. ONJAZZ W PATMETHENY P AT METHENY, ONE. THE SOVIET UNION. - “The place is a very high energy, intense place. And I mean, it’s a cliche, I think, to say this, but it’s really true: it’s much more like the States than anyplace else in Europe. The vibe is very similar to America. ’ ’ The place Pat Metheny refers to is the Soviet Union, where the Pat Metheny Group began its current world tour with 13 June dates. Pat says he went thinking, “Wow, what is this going to be?,” and came up with a few surprises. There was noth- ing John Le Carreish about the place, he says: you could go where you wanna go, do what you wanna do. He doesn’t think the phones were tapped, he doesn’t think he was fol- lowed anywhere, and he does think that all this glastnost business is for real. “The biggest surprise, though, may have been a few of the musicians that we met, most notably a young tenor player named Igor Budman. You know, we always like to go hang with musicians and play in clubs-we’ve always been known for that around Europe. Usually it’s fun, but it’s not usually all that exciting. Usually the players are not so good. When we played Poland the level of musicians was pretty low, so we ex- pected it to be something like that. We went into this club, and these guys were ripping, I mean tearing it upl But where are they getting it from? “The whole Voice of America thing is where they get their knowledge - Willis Conover. And everybody had tapes that are like 90% hiss - like sssssssssss- hhhhhhhhhhhhhh, and then, way in the background, you hear some music. Like 15th generation stuff. That was one of the other surprises- we went into these places and they would start playing our tunes. Guys that would know songs, changes and stuff, where the records are not avail- able there officially. ’ ’ One thing the Soviet audience is not, says Metheny, is very dis- criminating. When the posters went up with his name and “U.S.A.,” the concerts (some in arenas) sold out, bam. People knew it was an American pop-type group and that was good enough for them. Much of the audience, he says, didn’t know if they were going to be getting heavy metal or dixieland. But when the music started, he says, the 97% of the audience that didn’t walk out got right into it. “One thing that was nice was, after the concert, if there were 10,000 people there, 3,000 of them were waiting to get an autograph or just to take a picture or see you or some- thing. Which is really nice, because one thing in Europe which is true is that, especially in Northern Europe, you play a concert, and by the time it takes you to get off the stage, there’s not one person there — they’ve gone. But there everybody wanted to talk. And people would say, ‘I thought it was great, but what was the one thing you did - it was awful?’ I mean, they’re very frank. The bullshit level is very low - the tolerance for pretense. “And every night they’d bring us gifts. I have two flight cases, maybe a cubic yard, full of records, books, tapes, artwork, gifts, paintings that were done by hand. Every night after the gig, it was like people would just give us anything: they’d give us their children. ‘Here, you want my dog?’ It’s very embarrasing. Especially be- cause it’s a poor country and you feel it. People are always staring at your shoes and stuff.” But he says that, despite a couple of skeptics, he could sense that the people were, for the most part, ex- cited about glasnost, excited about the changes, and taking things like Pat Metheny’s appearance as further evidence that things are loosening up. “The sad part of it all is that, I made some great friends there, fantas- tic people. And, you know, when you meet somebody you say, ‘Hey, maybe I’m going to see you in the States some time,’ or, ~Maybe we’ll hook up in England or something.’ You start to say that and then you see the smile fade, ’cause they’re not going anywhere. That’s the one thing that totally pisses them off, and they hate their government for: that they’re prisoners, they can’t go. And they want to; not even to leave. I would say that 90% of the people that I put the question to, ‘If you could leave, would you leave?,’ would say, ‘No, this is my home, this is where I grew up, this is where I want to be. But I want to visit, I want to see things.’ And they can’t. And that is really heartbreaking. ’ ’ In Part Two (due in a week or so), Pat Metheny talks about his music.
