NATIONAL azz In Rio On, Rock In Rio Off, And Other Brazilian Matters By Christopher Pickard RIO DE JANEIRO-The Brazilian promoters Dueto have announced the line-up of 21 artists who will perform at the Third Free Jazz Festival, which is slated to take place September 2-7 in Rio de Janeiro and September 9-13 in Sao Paulo. In a very short time, the Free Jazz Festival has established itself as the most important in Latin America and mixes top international attractions with their Brazilian counterparts. The festival, which is a guaranteed sell-out, has helped introduce many of the international acts to a wider Brazilian audience thanks to the heavy media coverage the festival attracts. Last year’s festival helped establish David Sanborn, Larry Carlton, Stanley Jordan, Wynton Marsalis and Manhat- tan Transfer, with the resultant release and sales of their albums. The September festival will bring Sarah Vaughan, Philip Glass, Gil Evans, Chick Corea, Art Blakey, Lee Ritenour, King Sunny Ade, Spyro Gyra, Jim Hall and Michel Petrucciani to Brazil. They will share the bill with such Brazilian performers as Hermeto Pascoal, Doninguinhos, Laurindo Al- meida, Nivaldo Ornelas and Marcos Ariel. Glass, Corea, Evans, Blakey, Hall and Spyo’s Jay Beckenstein have also agreed to give a number of workshops for Brazilian music students. The record companies are now work- ing to suppport the festival, and a num- ber of releases will be scheduled before the event, which is also likely to stimu- late sales from the artists who per- formed in previous years. The event, even with Brazil’s cur- rent economic problems, continues to be viable thanks to the “Lei Samey,” a law which gives tax breaks to com- panies who support recognized cultural events. Among the main supporters of the festival are Free cigarettes and Pan Am... Despite the success of the giant Rock’n Rio festival in 1986, which had been planned as a yearly event, the promoters, Artplan, have had to moth- ball the second festival, slated for early 1988, because of the lack of a sponsor who is willing to invest the eight mil- lion dollars needed to realize the event. A number of major attractions have been rumored to be holding back from playing in Brazil—where, despite the crisis, record sales are holding firm-in the hope of playing Rock’n Rio. Most managers are now likely to turn to the Brazilian promoter Manuel Poladian, who has been quietly making a name for himself internationally with a series of well-organized Brazilian tours. 1986 saw visits from James Taylor and Miles Davis, and so far this year Poladian has toured the Cure and Echo and the Bunnymen, with Big Audio Dynamite due in August. Poladian also looks after most of the top Brazilian artists, and has just com- pleted a successful tour with Milton Nascimento, who was celebrating 20 years since the release of “Traves- sia”... Xuxa Meneghel, a model who fronts the top-rated children’s television series in Brazil, shipped one million units of her second album, “Xegundo Xou da Xuxa,” which her record com- pany, Som Livre, excepts to sell over 2.6 million units of by the end of the years. This would make her the big- gest-selling artist in Brazil for the second consecutive year. The album is now firmly planted at the top of the Brazilian charts and there is little chance it will be knocked off the top spot in the near future. The first CDs specifically aimed at the Brazilian market have started to ar- rive in the stores, having been imported for the occasion by PolyGram, EMI, WEA and RCA/Ariola. The releases are a mixture of top-selling Brazilian titles alongside sped ally -produced compilations. PolyGram, for example, is launching a package called “Per- sonalidade” which offers compilations of 18 Brazilian artists. The first six to hit the stores will feature Maria Bethania, Elis Regina, Gal Costa, Caetano Veloso, Chico Buarque and Gilberto Gil. The CD market in Brazil is es- timated to be worth around 400,000 units each year, but the figures are very basic as nobody knows, despite CDs being one of the few imports allowed by Brazil, just how many CDs are being illegally shipped to Brazil from Europe and the U.S.. The country’s first CD factory, to be run by Microservice, is expected to start operating in the next few months and should help lower prices in Brazil, where most CDs cost over US$30. ALL IN THE FAMILY - CBS record- ing artist Billy Joel recently completed a successful tour of Australia with a special presentation by CBS Australia of gold, platinum, and multi-platinum awards. Pictured at the presentation are the family of Denis Handlin, managing director CBS Records Australia and thefamily of Billy Joel. FULL HOUSE- In the eighth and final Countdown Music and Video Awards, EMI Records Australia/Capitol recording artists Crowded House picked up just awards for “Best Debut Act," “Best Debut Album," “Best Video," and “Best Songwriter" (Neil Finn). EMI Records Australia presented the group with an award representing triple platinum album sales of its debut album in Australia. Pictured (l-r) are: Rob Walker, head ofA&R and promotion for EMI Australia; Paul Hester, Finn and Nick Seymour of Crowded House; TV personality Ian ‘ ‘Molly’ ' Meldrum; and Brian Harris, general manager, EMI Australia. News From Japan TOKYO - According to a survey conducted by the Cash Box Tokyo of- fice, the total revenue reported by the 26 largest record and tape manufac- turers of Japan for the six months en- ding March 31, 1987 was 198,208,- 540,000 yen ($1,321,000,000). This is a 13% increase for the comparable months of last year and an increase of 10.7 over the past six months. Most manufacturers mentioned the growth came mainly from the new media such as CDs and Videos. CDs posted a 130.6% increase during the past six months, while analogue record sales dropped 67.8% compared to the same time last year. The Yamaha Music Foundtion will hold its 18th World Popular Song Fes- tival (WPSF) at the Budokanhall in Tokyo on Saturday, October 31, 1987. The foundation said this year’s festival should prove to be the most exciting ever as it marks the climax of the cont- memortive concerts for Yamaha’s cen- tennial year. Yamaha announced the finalists selected this year represent the finest “new talent” from around the world. WPSF gives many record com- panies an ideal forum to showcase and promote their new talent to the music world. Crown Records (president, Noboru , Saito) has signed with two U.S. jazz labels - Muse Records and Xanadu Records. First releases begin this j month. Joe Fields, president of Muse Records, was in Japan recently to meet with the executives of Crown records. He told Cash Box Muse offers tradi- 1 tional jazz and prides itself on its artis- tic excellence. Fields mentioned he was very pleased to be in partnership with Crown Records. He said,“We are very impressed with the sales and promotional capabilities of Crown Records. We believe our agreement will be benefit us both.” i Japan’s Top Ten Top Ten 45s 1. THE BEAT S OUND-ALIKE MUSIC As- sembly line productions, the automotive industry is losing by using this creative approach and the foreign imports and companies are showing significant gains in the U. S. auto industry. Think about this before reading further! Is it a case of Monkey see, Monkey do? During a recent conversation with record and radio industry movers and shakers, there seems to be an aware- ness, a slight awakening and/or con- cern for the direction music is and has been taking for years. Not unlike the big three in the auto industry, it is ap- parently because of disappointing sales and a lack of appeal to the emo- tional and psychological needs of the american consumer. The primary con- cern seems to be so much sameness of sound and the lack of real black music. More and more black artists have lost their identification as "black art- ist" by cutting crossover records, which have caused a great Identity Crisis for what was once black radio, artists, writers and producers. This creative approach is rapidly causing the demise of real African American Music,(Gospel, Blues, Jazz, R&B, ETC) the real crossover music. This music has made the most serious con- tribution to american music and the music of the world. A MIGHTY OAK TREE SEPARATED FROM ITS’ "ROOTS" WILL SOON DIE! Granted a few radio stations still program some of the aforementioned Art Forms, however, generally speak- ing, artist have been forced into a musical paradox whereby if they are to survive economically as artists and humans they must sacrifice their real music base in order to compete in the general marketplace. Unfortunately, because of the limited space on most radio station playlists, particularly the big gun powerhouse stations seeking crossover appeal, hundreds of pieces of top quality product never gets the opportunity for exposure to the american public or the industry. The obvious argument here is com- petition (Arbitron and Birch) and economic gains. This position is un- derstandable (as a former program- mer) and appreciated, however we humbly submit it lacks vision, sen- sitivity and awareness of the taste of the general american consumer. The point is, when high quality Root Music is intergrated with current Trend Music the listener-consumer base will be broadened. This argument suggest competing to establish an in- stitution. (21st Century WDIA’S, WVON’S, WDAS’S, etc) This phenomenon transcends the current Arbitron and Birch realities while yeilding a long term secure economic p>osition. Based on conversations and con- cerns of industry veterans, there seems to be a potent desire to get back to real music as opposed to the synthetic sounds heard on virtually every station on the AM or FM dial. As mentioned two weeks ago in The Beat, maybe more people are "really" beginning to realize the great musical void that has existed for many years. Hopefully the cychcal namre of the industry is caus- ing this change in attitudes and there will be a reaching out for some of the old professionals 35+ and a utilization of the bastion of knowledge possessed by these programmers, record execu- tives, writers, producers and artists, so as to get back to the real business- Profits of black music. Time has come, gone and is coming again for our industry to awaken to the realization of what is happening. The piblic is ready for some real music! The (proof) sales are not overwhelm- ing as records zoom up the charts and top ten records barely sell 150,000 copies on artists who are traditionally big sellers. A few questions, that may need answering are: Does anyone really care if records sell? Are chart posi- tions more important to keep a job, make excuses for the product and not make waves? Does anyone really work the stores anymore-physically visiting, setting up displays or doing in-store promotions? Does anyone promote and market using the basic fundamentals of record marketing ef- fectively? Will black artists ultimately crossover and out? Why are numerous records, as we say in the business, lost? JAZZ ON JAZZ AT METHENY, TWO. THE MUSIC. - Pat Metheny's new album, "Still Life (Talking)," is the first album in several years from the Pat Metheny Group (the core of which remains Lyle Mays, key- boards; Steve Rodby, bass; and Paul Wertico, drums). For his Gef- fen debut last year, Pat Metheny turned in "Song X," the spectacular collaboration with Ornette Cole- man that turned some heads; rarely does a label like Geffen release a jazz record as startlingly adven- turous and avant-garde as "Song X." 'The reason 1 went with Geffen," says Pat Metheny, "was a portion of a conversation I had with David Geffen, during what 1 think Cash Box called 'the bidding war period' - hahaha. He just said, 'Look, the reason we want you is we want you to do what you do. We don't want you to do something else, because what you're doing is working.' "When 1 did 'Song X,' 1 hadn't signed the bottom line. Everything was cool - it took months, with lawyers and all that stuff, and everything was ready for me to sign it; they had already signed it. So we did the record and 1 went to Califor- nia with the tape and the contract and said, 'Okay, you guys, this is my first record. Listen to this, and if you don't want me to sign this. I'm not going to sign it. But 1 want you to know that this is what it is.' And they listened to it. They played it and they said, 'Wow, that's really far out. It's great, it's great. This is going to be something special, we're going to really do this.' And then they said, 'Well, you know, maybe you can do a Group record next." "Still Life (Talking)" is that record and its a continuation of the Pat Metheny Group's unique sound - a jazz-rock fusion that leans much closer to jazz and, on this record, is beginning to sound more and more Brazilian. Brazilian percussionist Armando Marcal is there, as are two vocalists - David Blamires and Mark Ledford - whose wordless vocalizing is closely related to the work of Milton Nascimento. "I'm kind of becoming an honorary Brazilian," says Pat. "1 spend almost all my time there and I've had a Brazilian girlfriend for about a year or so. It's been real good for me, because 1 feel very at home there and I've kind of been adopted, almost, as a local cat. "A funny thing, though. If you go to Brazil now, you don't hear anybody playing like we play on this album - they're all trying to sound like they're from L.A.. You hear Gaetano Veloso's band or Ivan Lins and they're playing rock beats. Milton too. And I just don't under- stand it. I feel almost like we should deal with it because they're not. To me, the music that Milton in par- ticular came up with throughout the '70s is just infinitely expandable. 'The thing of having singers is directly related to that. Although it does have a practical side as well: as we're getting more and more into these synthesizer things, having natural elements in the music is be- coming more and more important." Pat Metheny and Milton Nas- cimento have been talking serious- ly about collaborating on an album - in fact the second Geffen release was almost that collaboration. But Milton has just signed to CBS in Brazil and both CBS/Brazil and Geffen were anxious for solo al- bums from their new artists (a Group album, in Metheny's case), so that project is temporarily on hold. However, it's likely that Metheny's next album will be another one of his side projects: he's sifting through hours of live tour tapes featuring his trio with Charlie Haden and Billy Higgins - one of those projects that Metheny turns to every few years which has numerous jazz critics pronouncing, "Gee, 1 didn't know he could play like that." "To tell you the truth," says Metheny, "whenever somebody says, 'Well, 1 didn't know you could play jazz,' 1 just assume they probably never really heard me play. The way 1 see it is, how could they miss it? Because if there's one thing about the way 1 play is that it's obviously rhythmically and har- monically a descendant of Wes Montgomery. And if somebody can't identify that instantly, then there's nothing to say." So Pat Metheny - Geffen or not - will bounce along his merry way. The current Group tour will go through the end of the year and then - who knows? - the tapes with Haden and Higgins are there (as is the possibility of a tour), the col- laboration with Milton Nascimento is still in the works, the collabora- tion with Ornette Coleman is some- thing both men want to pursue fur- ther, and film scores and other projects beckon. All of it - and here's the key - will sound like Pat Metheny. "I'm sensitive to this subject," says Pat, "because it bugs me when I see guys and they've got their syn- thesizer band and they play just electric stuff, and then they play only acoustic. To me, regardless of whether Tm playing with Ornette or whether I'm playing on a film score. I'm playing the same guitar, the same amps, etc., etc.. So it's a conceptual thing more than a physi- cal thing. Because none of it is like a shift in gears, it's just a different way of playing. And 1 like playing a lot of different ways." SOUNDS & VISIONS CD SPOTLIGHT The BEATLES THE BEATLES - The B eatles - Par- lophone/Capitol CDP 7 46443 2/7 46444 2 - Producer: George Martin The album that has been lauded as The Beatles most ambitious album ever has finally seen its com- pact disc incarnation. The self-titled recording (commonly known as 'The White Album") marvels in it's own haunting radiance and abstract imagery. Listening to such an album on compact disc is breath- taking, with all it's subtle brilliance emphasized with brimming clarity. The painstaking development of transferring the original recording to disc is apparent immediately, such classics as "Dear Prudence" and the infamous "Helter Skelter" gleam with sheer precision. If you must purchase only one of the Beat- les compact disc releases, this is it. THE BEATLES - Yellow Sub- marine - Parlophone/Capitol CDP 7 46445 - Producer: George Martin The second of the Beatles com- pact disc's released this time around is the soundtrack for their full length animated feature of 1969, "Yellow Submarine." The disc con- tains half Beatles' compositions and half musical score by the fab four's mentor/producer George Martin. Once again, we find painstaking perfection and care used in mixing the recording to disc, "All You Need Is Love," "All Together Now," "Hey Bulldog" and the classic title cut all glow (if you'll pardon the thesaurus) with divine virtue. The thoroughness in the original production is accented to near per- fection. In addition, NAB also will host semi- nars on AM directional antennas September 8-10, National Radio Systems Committee standards September 11 , and radio frequen- cy radiation regulation com- pliance September 12. All will be held at the Anaheim Convention Center, Anaheim ,CA. The convention is expected to attract more than 6,000 broad- casters and will showcase the latest management, programming , sales and technical innovations in the radio industry. The exhibit hall will contain the biggest, most com- prehensive variety of radio suppliers’ and manufacturers’ ex- hibits anywhere. Newly Discovered Stereo 78’s To Be Premiered On Na- tional Radio ... On September 6, music lovers and audio buffs will be treated to an almost unbeliev- able hour of 78 rpm recordings in stereo, featuring such great per- formers as Leopold Stokowski, Edgar Elgar, Serge Kous- sevitsky and Duke Ellington. The program will be heard on over 185 public radio and commercial classical stations. The recordings date from the years 1 929 through 1 932, primari- ly from the Victor label, and are not available commercially. They are featured on a special edition of the national radio program for for audio buffs. Audiophile Audition. Now in its third year, this program normally focuses on the latest classical and jazz CD’s, tapes and high-tech IP’s, plus interviews with recognized experts in the audio field. But host John Sunier felt this material from the past deserved a wider hearing. The stereo discoveries are the painstaking work of Los Angeles musician/ record collector Brad Kay. Although experiments were carried out in the early 1930’s in both the U.S.and Britain in record- ing stereo on phonograph records, these early efforts were not intended as stereo. They were not merely double sets of microphones, electronics and disc-cutting lathes for back-up purposes. However, the slightly different placement of the two microphones results in a startling stereo effect when the two record- ings are carefully synchronized - often resulting in hundreds of splices to preserve only the por- tions in perfect synch. Over 180 stations air Audiophile Audition at 2pm Eastern Standard time on Sun- days. Local stations who broad- cast should be contacted for times. The digital mastering of Audiophile Audition and live car- riage by most stations should en- sure the best possible sonics for the hour-long special broadcast of stereo 78’s. Making New “Connections" On WQXR ... If your looking for something different, its high time you discovered "Connections,” the only show of its kind in com- mercial classic radio. "Connections,” which airs every Saturday night from 10pm to midnight on WQXR in New York, looks at the worlds of classi- cal, jazz and New Age music. In fact, "Connections” is the first show on any commercial station in New York to delve deeply into the New Age phenomenon, featuring New Age music in all its manifestations and, more impor- tantly, relating these new sounds to other forms of music. "Connections” features the brightest musical personalities live in WQXR’s studios talking about their music and their world. People like Bobby McFerrin, Ravi Shanker, Joe Jackson, Joe Jackson, Betty Carter, Alex de Grass!, Phil Aaberg, Bobby Short and others. "Connections” creator, producer and host is Loren Tolagen, WQXR’s Qperations director. Tolagen has a diverse musical background as a classi- cally trained musician, jazz piano player and pop and New Age com- poser and brings a unique insight and versatility to joining musical ideas together.Experience what it’s all about. Tune into “Connec- tions,” Saturday nights at 10pm on 96.3FM, WQXR in New York. Michael Jackson Does Good: Provides 40 UNCF Scholarships NEW YORK-Michael Jackson has provided 40 scholarships for the 1987-88 academic year through the United Negro College Fund, making the total of such grants to 97 since Jackson formed the Michael Jackson Scholarship Fund in 1985. The 40 students are to be selected by a spe- cial Michael Jackson Scholarship Fund Committee. The MJSF provides financial assis- tance for a select number of "talented and gifted" students in the perform- ing arts (with an emphasis on music) and communications. To be eligible for assistance, students must be nominated by UNCF institutions. The Ramones And X Spur Return To No-Frills Rock By Paul lorio NEW YORK - If punk is old enough to be dead, isn't it also old enough to be revived? After all, disco happened at about the same time and it has recently re-emerged. On this eleventh anniversary of the short- lived movement, people have been throwing dirt on top of punk. But new albums by X and the Ramones capture the spirit of the genre with a brand of no-frills rock that once again presents a challenge to the mainstream. The Ramones single-bandedly in- vented punk in 1976, and X is largely responsible for popularizing a varia- tion of it on the west coast with their 1980 debut album, "Los Angeles" (Slash). Now, nine albums later, the Ramones have let loose "Halfway To Sanity" (Sire), and X has returned with a sixth album, "See How We Are" (Elektra). Neither album represents a real departure for either band, though both records sound surprisingly fresh in contrast to much of what is currently on the charts. Several new Ramones tracks, including "Bop Till You Drop" and "Death Of Me," rank with their best work of the eighties; and X's "See How We Are" presents a stripped-down rewed-up variety of west coast rock 'n' roll. EMI-Manhattan Makes It |g Official |tt NEW YORK - EMI-America Records and Manhattan Records have officially become EMI-Manhat- tan Records. EMI, under the leader- ship of ceo Sal Licata, will be head- quartered in New York, with fully staffed sales, promotion, A & R and publicity departments in the former EMI-America building in Los An- geles. Said Licata: 'The streamlined name and newly designed logo ("EMI" worked into the existing "Manhattan" logo} strengthen the identity of our newly merged label." itcoi idva ffasi liisli tanic pci System To Test In Stores In November Enigma Inks With Personics By Rob Yardumian LOS ANGELES - Enigma Records has signed an agreement vyith the Personics Corporation to distribute selected releases through the revolu- tionary Personics System, which al- lows retail customers to create per- sonalized, high-quality cassettes at various music retail locations. Four test machines will be unveiled in San Francisco area stores in November. Along with the Enigma Records agreement, Personics has already secured the support of major labels like Warner Brothers, Capitol, Atlan- tic, Manhattan, and Elektra/Asylum. Commenting on the agreement. Enigma president Wesley Hein told Cas/z Box "We're really glad to be the first independent involved. We're real strong believers in the system. To me, it makes a lot of intrinsic sense. We really want to be a major player in Personics." Enigma plans to initial- ly involve "about 25 to 50 titles" ac- cording to Hein, with emphasis on current product. He anticipates that the metal band Stryper will be Enigma's major drawing card for teens using the system. Personics president Charles Gar- vin is equally glad to have Enigma on board, stating "While Personics will shortly be announcing a number of other corporate partnerships, we have been working with Enigma longest, and are happy to announce their participation first among inde- pendent labels. We feel that Enigma as a company represents the kind of leadership that will set key directions for this industry over years to come, and we therefore see this as a com- pletely natural affiliation for Per- sonics." The major advantage of The Per- sonics System is that it is an affor- dable, high-quality alternative to home taping that will allow record labels and artists to recoup some of the millions of dollars in royalties lost each year in home taping. With the system, consumers will have the chance to preview and select music from a vast digital library located in the stores. Additionally, labels will have the opportunity to spotlight some of their lesser known artists through the in-store preview system. As Hein says, "If someone is cruising in to make a best of Madonna tape, and they look down and see one of our artists, say Agent Orange, maybe they'll click on an Agent Orange tape just to see if they like it. It's kind of a low-cost way for people to experi- ment with Enigma records. Our aim in this is not primarily 'let's combat home taping' as much as 'this is a great way for people to sample Enig- ma records.' Greg Ballard, Personics' vice presi- dent of business affairs, told Cash Box that the first four machines will be rolled out in the southern San Fran- I cisco area in November, providing the industry a valuable opportunity to observe the system in action before it goes nationwide. 'The basic idea is to run them for three to six months, principally to establish the technol- ogy. We know the technology works, it's just a question of what breaks first. Before we start manufacturing these things en masse, we want to make sure we have the design right." Two of the largest retail chains in the country. The Musicland Group and Wherehouse Entertainment, Inc., have signed up to participate in the program. Ballard said that more chains have expressed interest in par- ticipating, but with the program still in its infancy, the two initial chains are the only ones officially signed at present. THE BEAT B lack pope cam- PAIGN-In our continuing series focusing on black music, radio and 35+ an- nouncers we spoke with Gary Richardson station manager of WJLD B irmingham, Alabama. He spoke very excitedly about the Bring Back Black Pope Campaign. A week prior to the return of legendary radio personality Shelley Pope, WJLD ran the aformentioned promotion and gave away Pope T-Shirts during a live remote broadcast which attracted some 1200 listeners. During and after his first show the station was overwhelmed with non- stop phone calls. Listeners wanted to know if his return was temporary or permanent? Richardson and his staff assured the listeners it was permanent. Gary said, "Shelley has altered his style somewhat, he doesn’t use as many drop-ins as before." He further stated, "Pope is perfect for our station because we are strictly targeting adults 25+ and he captures that audience, as well as commands a tremendous teenage foOowing. I attribute this to his great personahty, because he can play a Blues song and the kids will call while he’s not playing their favorite rap song, but they continue to listen and follow him." Richardson went on to say, "black radio has and is being exploited in a sense." He spoke about an Urban and CHR station in Birmingham, "where the Urban stations’ numbers are declining because it appears that black people are caught up in the novelty of white djs’ or white stations playing black music. It isn’t the fact their programming is superior or the music is better, because they are playing the same music you hear on black sta- tions. Blacks have migrated to these stations in great numbers, particularly the 18-34 demos, who have not ex- perienced the hardships and trying times older black adults have gone through, therefore there is a lack of ap- preciation for black radio in general. If it were not for these stations in Birmin- gham, the effect of the civil rights movement would not have been what it is today. This listener movement is not only happening here, but in markets around the country-how quickly we forget!" Mr. Richardsons’ comments cer- tainly tie in with our previous topics dealing with 35+ aimouncers, the need for black radio to entertain, inform and educate their listeners and the real crossover music Gospel, Blues, Jazz and R&B. Remember, A MIGHTY OAK TREE SEPARATED FROM ITS’ ROOTS WILL SOON DIE. BLUES WEEKEND-During a recent conversation with Rick Stevens program director of WCKX Columbus, Ohio, he was bubbling over with excitement about his special live broadcast from The Ohio State Fair the past two weekends. The sig- nificant feature of the broadcast was the playing of Blues music by some of the all time great Blues makers. According to Rick and the reports I have gotten out of Columbus the lis- tener response was nothing short of sensational. Rick, along with many other top programmers around the country are winning big by incorp>orat- ing the blues into their formats. WIBB-AM #l-Congratulations to Big George Threaat, program direc- tor WIBB-AM Macon, Georgia and his fine staff on being the number one AM station in middle Georgia for the 6th consecutive year. George, a nine year veteran with WIBB attributes the stations’ success to loyal listenership and the continuing popularity, consistency and longevity of his announcers who are always in touch with the community. The station has maintained the same basic format for its listeners since 1956, by offering a Variety of programming for all seg- ments of the audience. BLUES RETURNS - Singer, songwriter and producer Leon Hayw(X>d and his staff at Evcjim Records are aglow over the initial response to their first blues album en- titled Dirty Work Going On by Lil Joe Blue. Sylvia Smith, a gifted vocalist, who serves as president of the label went on to say, "after a decade or more of blues being virtually forgot- ten, whereby radio had turned its’ knobs off to this art form. The Blues Is Back and we as industry people must not let it die." SUCCESSFUL RAPPER-In- dustry verteran Jack "The Rapper" Gibson’s Family Affair 87 was an overwhelming success. CRESCENT CITY SOUNDS- Jazztown is the name of a 13-part radio series on contemporary New Orleans jazz, set to air over public radio stations from October through December. A project of the Louisiana Jazz Federation, alor^ with stations WWNO and WWOz, Jazztown will be hosted by Ellis Marsalis and will feature inter- views, commentary and digitally- recorded live music. The worthwhile project will spotlight Alvin Batiste, the Improvisational Arts Quintet (led by Kidd Jordan), the New Orleans Saxophone Quartet, Earl Turbinton, Ellis Mar- salis, Fred Kemp/Smokey Johnson Quintet, the Young Tuxedo Brass Band/the Rebirth Jazz Band, Ger- maine Bazzle, Alvin "Red" Tyler and James Rivers, the Chester Zar- dis Band/the Pladde Adams Band, Tony Dagradi and Astral Project, Steve Masakowski and The Dirty Dozen Brass Band. GANELIN GONE-ALIN- Vyacheslav Ganelin, the leader of the Ganelin Trio (thanks to Leo Records, perhaps the best-known Soviet jazz group in the West), has applied for, ana received, permis- sion to emigrate from the Soviet Union to Israel. He will arrive in Is- rael early in September and will begin planning his new jazz career in the West. Leo Records still has some Ganelin Trio albums yet to release (including the band's first CD), and they have just put out "Con Amore,*^' Ganelin's first solo album. What this means for the fu- ture of the Trio, I do not know. EUROJAZZ-Stop the presses- the names of the six young European groups (all members under 30 years old) who have been nominated in the International Jazz Federation's Sixth European Jazz Competition have just been an- nounced. In no particular order they are Catalypso (Austria), Pageone (Denmark), the Toon Roos Quartet (Holland), Bad Circuits (Holland), the Jani Malmi Quartet (Finland) and Sprinx (West Ger- many). The alternates, in case of withdrawal, are the Legrand- Huber-Guettler Trio (West Ger- many), the Modem String Quartet (West Germany), and French Con- nection (Switzerland). The jurors are Pawel Brodowski, Lajos Dudas, Mitchell Feldman, Luca Cerchiari, Steve Lake and Bemd Hoffman. THE BEAT W AKE UP EVERYBODY - We are losing our iden- tity! Our unique identity set us apart from others, rendered our talents priceless and provided us, as an ethnic group, the opportunity to have a continual profound influence on music and entertainment. We are losing this! The adverse impact of this loss is limiting the growth and progress of black radio, music and record execu- tives and should be frightening. If for no other reason than job security. Let's examine some of the ramifications of this-DIS-EASE! Programmers are continually being told by non-ethnic owners and general managers to make the station sound like the CHR's. The stragety of 45 minutes of non-stop music or 10- 14 records in a row has taken the per- sonality out of black radio. It is deny- ing the listener the opportunity to know who performed the record they heard, not to mention the absence of entertainment. Designed to; Plug an announcer in, and pull another out. Anybody can do this job. It does not require any unique talent. URBAN CONTEMPORARY OR URBAN MAZAK? Record executives are getting lost in the corporate structure and are losing vital contact with The Streets and two-way communications (ex- changing meaningful ideas) with programmers. Further they are get- ting trapped into, keep the job and don't make waves, refuse to pioneer and discover - or even dare to venture and promote "the unique" syndrome. CORPORATE DIS-SERVICE? As one record executive put it, "we get so busy vp'ing, we wind up out of a job." Radio station KTWV (The Wave) in Los Angeles has clearly and suc- cessfully demonstrated what the "sameness of sound" can do. They have been playing music similiar to KUTE, "without any live an- nouncers" quite successfully whereby rumor has it that KUTE is considering changing their format. Fact is, their (KTWV) company has begun to syndicate this format. Will more jobs held by blacks be lost? Since black radio is seeking the crossover listeners, why not achieve this by breaking records and playing some jazz and blues. White listeners are not tuning to your stations to hear the same thing they hear on CHR radio. The challenge here is for programmers to educate non-ethnic owners and general managers to this uniquely profitable fact. Look at the attendees (18-34 whites) of blues concerts around the country, i. e., during a recent B. B. King show at Bogart's in Cincinnati, a record industry veteran told me, "I had to really search the crowd to find another black face." Does that tell you something about an available audience? When your account executives ap- proach advertising agencies, what is unique about your station, if you sound like the CHR's? Their (agen- cy) question is, why should I buy your station to reach the black lis- teners when 1 can buy the CHR and reach those listeners as well as whites? As we mentioned a couple of weeks ago in The Beat, the same-ness of sound is hastening the demise of black / irrban contemporary radio. A top programmer said, "most black or urban formatted stations are owned and operated by non-ethnic in- dividuals with little or no real back- ground and understanding of the broadcast business. One of their first steps is to hire a top named media visible programming consultant who sits in an ivory tower far away from the station and dictates the music that should be played, based on national chart information. We as programmers, must get back to the basics of listening to music - regard- less of the record label. A lot of hit music is lost because we rely so heavily on chart activity, instead of' combining our market knowledge, with gut instincts and using national activity as a barometer." As Lynn Tolliver, program direc- tor, WZAK in Cleveland stated in the column he writes for Impact: "Years back, radio made the charts, they do now, but radio dictated what the charts reflected." "NOW CHARTS DICTATE RADIO." URBAN MUZAK AND CORPORATE DIS- SERVICE! (L-r) Billy Higgins, Alan Broadbent, Ernie Watts, Charlie Haden.H ADEN-'There was a period in Los Angeles that's completely unique to L.A., like no other city. And that was around the '30s and '40s and came from the movie in- dustry-there was a real romantic flourish there. In architecture, in writing, in all the art forms. And the composers-Dimitri Tiomkin, Max Steiner, Franx Waxman, Vic- i tor Young-all these great com- posers that were writing romantic music for the films, the black and white films with John Garfield and Humphrey Bogart and Alan Ladd and Gregory Peck." Charlie Haden, an L.A. resident since 1979, is serenely eating a Caesar's salad on a trip to New York and talking about the motivation behind Quartet West, the band that ! he formed this year and which released an excellent self-titled album on Verve. "It's just a real special feeling, and there was a writer who was writing about that particular period, Raymond Chandler, and he's one of my favorite novelists. And so I wrote this piece and dedicated it to him and titled it 'Bay City,' which is how he referred to Santa Monica- which is where I live-in his novels. So part of the album is about that feeling, and part of it is my respect for beauty and reverence for listen- ' ing. There are some free lines that I wrote, there's a minor blues, there's a Charlie Parker tune, there's my favorite ballads, there's a hillbilly folk song that I wrote for my mom and dad, there's a Pat Metheny tune, an Ornette Coleman tune, a Duke Ellington tune. So there's a little bit of everything that I like to do, and I'm finding that it's attract- ing much more of a mass audience than I've ever had before as a leader." Quartet West is an interesting and unusual blend of players, one of those blends that just works. Tenor saxophonist Ernie Watts, pianist Alan Broadbent, drummer I Billy Higgins, and Haden don't necessarily look compatible on paper, but they make for a rich and harmonious quartet-a successful melding of its parts, tied together with Haden's own romantic vision of Los Angeles. "One of my loves in the music world is to get special people whose music I feel close to together and make music with them. I've done it so much, and so 1 did it again here. I called Ernie and Alan and Billy and said, 'Let's play a gig, man.' I found out when everybody was going to be in town, we played a gig at At My Place in Santa Monica, and it sold out and the music was tremen- dous. So I said, 'Let's make a record.'" Charlie Haden is himself a blend of unusual musical influences and experiences. He came into the world singing hillbilly music with the Haden Family Band (his parents were a popular radio attrac- tion in midwest country music circles), played bebop bass in L.A. until moving out into free jazz ter- ritory with Ornette Coleman in the late '50s, and has recorded and per- formed in diverse settings (with Pat Metheny, with Egberto Gismonti and Jan Garbarek, with Hampton Hawes, etc.) for some 30 years. This year, Charlie Haden hasn't been suffering from a lack of what to do. He's head of jazz studies at the California Institute of the Arts, he's part of the original Ornette Coleman Quartet (as is Billy Hig- gins) which reconvened this year for a marvelous album ("In All Lan- guages," Caravan of Dreams) and which is going to tour Europe in Oc- tober, and he's currently on the road with his Liberation Music Or- chestra (they'll be at New York's Cathedral of St. John the Divine on Sept. 12), now in it's 18th year of sporadic touring and recording. All of these things are important to him, he says, but Quartet West is, if he can help it, for real-not just a one- shot recording band. 'The working that we've done so far has been Los Angeles, San Fran- cisco, and the Vanguard in New York. We just played on my 50th birthday and the place was sold out-it was fantastic. We played the tunes from the record, everybody recognized the tunes, the next day we went to San Francisco to play the Great American Music Hall and the same thing happened. The guys want to keep the band together, and 1 want to play in Detroit and Chicago and Washington, D.C. and Boston and come back in the Van- guard. "And the more we play, the bet- ter the music gets and the more I'm finding out about the musical per- sonalities and the characters that are in the group, because they're really starting to play and to flourish, on free tunes even. We're even playing 'Lonely Woman' and we're stretching out." Charlie Haden is, in a word, thrilled at the positive response Quartet West has received in a short period of time. "It isn't like 1 sat down and said, '1 want to do this so more people will hear it,"' he says, "but that's what's happening." "Volume 1" is what it says. Produced by veteran Peter Asher and recorded using full digital technology, "In My Tribe" features some of the most breathtaking mo- ments ever recorded. Asher has brought a slick, but not overbear- ing, style to the Maniacs latest ef- fort - enabling them to fully utilize their talents. Lead vocalist and songwriter Natalie Merchant's haunting vocals stir with unbeliev- able power and conviction. The first single, an unlikely cover of Cat Stevens' 1971 classic "Peace Train," is exceptional. Merchant contributed 11 of the 12 songs in- cluded on the LP, some co-written with other members of the band - each breathtaking and wrung with genuine emotion. Guests on the LP include Michael Stipe of REM (on the stirring "A Campfire Song"), and the lushly-arranged "Verdi Cries" features work from musicians Don Grolnick and Den- nis Karmazyn. A must own... When veteran British producer Peter Sullivan (Tom Jones, Engelbert Humperdinck) first came across the term 'razorback' in a Newsweek fea- ture article, he thought it would be perfect for the as-yet unnamed group of Arkansas-based musicians whose fledgling career had recently been placed in his hands. Unaware of the predatory porker's longtime role as Arkansas state mascot, Sullivan's en- thusiasm for the porcine concept generated plenty of chuckles from the six piece band. But the Englishman eventually won the last laugh when all six group members dedided to adopt his idea, christening themsel- ves Razorback. For nearly three years, music fans in the Ft. Smith area have bragged that Razorback's polished blend of Motown-flavored pop and straight ahead country is "hotter 'n fish grease"., a claim due in part to the decade-long association among group members Bill White, Lacey Schaffer and Tom Ware. Breaking the regional mold. Razor- back was selected by Miller Genuine Draft Beer for a promotional sponsor- ship by way of their 1987 Miller Music Tour. That means concert appearan- ces nationwide for this Com- pleat/Polygram recording group. White, who contributes vocals and guitar, is the product of a musically in- CIVIA (continued from page 28) LOST IN THE HFTIES (1986, '87). He will perform a duet with Kenny Rogers on their #1 song MAKE NO MISTAKE, SHE'S MINE. Texan George Strait has become a virtual hit factory since signing with MCA Records in 1981 and one of Country's hottest properties. He has had at least one single on the charts each week since signing with MCA, and eight of his nine albums have achieved gold status. Strait has been named CMA's Male Vocalist Of The Year for two consecutive years, and in 1985, his LP titled DOES FORT WORTH EVER CROSS YOUR MIND, dined family. His siblings and other relatives have penned hits for Ray Price, Tommy Overstreet and Hank Thompson. White is no stranger to the charts, having scored three Top 100 tunes as a solo performer. Schaffer's spunky stage presence is complemented by the virtuosity of Tom Ware, whose prowess on lead guitar, fiddle and accordion serves as the band's instrumental cornerstone. From hillbilly heros to R&B smoothies and soul shouters, a litany of styles have figured prominently in crafting the career of keyboard whiz Larry Bedell. Bedell's uncle, a drum- mer for Billie Holiday and Peggy Lee, encouraged him to follow suit in the music business. It was while working a series of blues gigs, opening for B. B. King and Bobby "Blue" Bland, that Bedell got wind of Razorback's search for a stand-out keyboard man. Razorback's churning rhythm section showcases the combined energy of drummer Roland Stephens and bas- sist George Hughen. When you take these two talented musicians and add them to the above mentioned group, you've got one great band on their way to the pinnacle of show business. Their versatility makes them stand tall among the new groups on the music scene today. Keep your eyes on and your ears tuned in to Razorback... they have the "edge". was CMA's Album Of The Year. NEWS EXECUTIVES ON THE MOVE Jones Forms New Firm LOS ANGELES-Entertainment veteran Regina Jones has formed Regina Jones & Associates, a public relations /promotion /consulting firm in Los Angeles. Probably best known as the former owner and publisher of Soul magazine, a mainstay in the music in- dustry for more than 15 years, she also served as public relations chief for Dick Griffey's group of com- panies, including Solar Records. Jones has launched her company with three artists on Geffen Records. Vaneese Thomas and John White, both from the Hush Productions stable, and Jesse's Gang of Alive Enterprises. She plans an extensive publicity campaign for these artists and other clients as an initial thrust for her company. Her offices are located at 1230 South Van Ness Ave., Los Angeles, CA 90019. The telephone number is (213)734-6108. The original surgery had been related to a soccer injury, and although doctors termed the operation a success, additional work was required after the dis- covery of a tumor in Marley's right toe. The operation necessitated the removal of a portion of the right toe. Marley is now resting in Miami, and doctors hope that there will be no further complications. Pat Metheny, a rising young guitarist, opened the show with a surprisingly bright performance of contemporary jazz dynamics. Only 23, Metheny comes from the Gary Burton Quartet and if his first night in Los Angeles is any indication, he can only spiral upwards. While his accompanying musicians had fine credentials and the musical competence to match, it was Methcny's at- titude and reverence towards his music that carried the show. Methcny's fret work is accomplished and, with his eyes closed during every number, he paid tribute to concentration and musical priorities. There is no ques- tion that he can move from the melodic to the mainstream with equal dig- nity.. .Top five singles: 1. "Your Love Has Lifted Me (Higher and Higher)," Rita Coolidge. 2. THE BEAT B AD IS GREAT—Amid the massive media attention sur- rounding Michael Jackson's album Bad, we decided to quite simply say, "It would be a dis- service to the enormous talents of Michael Jackson, Quincy Jones and all of the gifted artists who par- ticipated in this great project to say anything other than, the album is really a great compilation of music that further distinguishes Michael's brilliance." The comments I have heard are: "It is not Thriller, he recorded too black, it's boring, he will be lucky to sell 10 million, ETC." The most important factors are: Michael the artist and the consumers being satisified! Most of the praise and/or criticism have come from individuals who received complimentary copies of the album. Opinions too, are like a certain portion of the body, everybody has one. Not that you asked, but, "my opinion is the man is talented beyond most (myself in- cluded) human comprehension. As Quincy once said, "When God touched Michael, he really touched him." Each of us should take a long hard look at the person in the mirror. KUTE CHANGES-As we indi- cated last week in The Beat, radio sta- tion KUTE will change their format. A press conference was called for late Wednesday afternoon (after my deadline) September 9, to make the official announcement. The current staff was given 30 days to seek other employment. Since KTWV'S (The Wave's announcer-less format) suc- cess reportedly had a direct effect on KUTE changing formats, and have begun syndication around the country, we will ask again, will more jobs held by blacks be lost around the country? Watch out, it could be any station, programmer, music director, announcer, anywhere U.S.A. CLUB NOUVEAU COOKED During their recent appearance in Los Angeles Warner Bros/King Jay recording artist Club Nouveau was nothing short of sensational, as they kept the capacity crowd on their feet throughout the hour-plus perfor- mance. This talented group consist- ing of Jay King, Denzil Foster, Thomas McElroy, Valerie Watson, Samuelle Prater and David Agent have been able to take a one album concept and build an entertainment filled show that leaves you wanting more. A very special highlight to this appearance was King inviting Bill Withers (writer of Lean On Me) on stage to sing the song that propelled the group to stardom. By the way. Bill still sounds good. PROTEGE SHOWCASE-I had the pleasure of seeing what could be- come one of the top hit making groups in the business. This talent laden 7 piece self contained group put on a tremendous showcase Sun- day September 6, at the infamous Carlos and Charlie's. Performing original material written by various members of the group, their stage presence, vocals, instrumentation and capative talent kept the audience on the edge of their seats throughout the performance. A&R vice presi- dents and directors don't let this talented group get away from your company. For more information con- tact Ray Miranda at 818-338-5337. YBPC MEETS-The Young Black Programmers Coalition, Incor- porated will hold their 10th annual national meeting November 20, 21 and 22 at the Hyatt Regency Hotel in Houston, Texas. Theme of the con- ference: The business of radio and records, the how too's. Sub-topics are: The operation of a radio station and The development and opera- tion of a record company. JAZZ ON JAZZ LUEBIRDS - Last month I reported on the release of 16 CD (and CD-only) reis- sues under the RCA Bluebird ban- nerhead, which, I announced rather boldly, were available on August 1. Hell, the press release said August 1, and I had most of the discs on August 1, but they just weren't available on August 1. Due to the usual problems, those 16 discs should just now be reaching the stores. COLLEGE GOES TO JAZZ - New York's New School for Social Research - always a hotbed of fas- cinating courses - is going heavy on the jazz this fall . The six courses, set to begin late this month or early next month, are "Jazz at 6" (in-class performances from Jay McShann, Ruby B raff/Dick Hyman and Jim Hall ); 'Jazz History: From Africa to Ellington," '(Jazz Repertoire of Es- sential Listening," "Jazz and the American Popular Song," "Jazz and the American Culture," and "New York Jazz: Five Live Perfor- mances." Complete descriptions and registration material are avail- able by calling (800) 422-3900. Not to be outdone, UCLA is offer- ing a jazz course of its own this fall, open, also, to all and sundry. "Live Jazz in Los Angeles: Known and Unknown" get under way October 1 and, before it's through, students will be taken to a heap of L.A. clubs and will have listened to more good music than they'll know what to do with. Call (213) 825-9064 for the lowdown on that. GG-CJB - Those in the know realize that those initials stand for the George Gruntz Concert Jazz Band one of the best big bands ex- tant. Now Gruntz, the exceptional composer and arranger, is Swiss, but calling his band Swiss is like calling the Toronto Blue Jays Canadian - the Swiss members of the band (at least the 1987 edition) can be counted on two fingers. In any case, it's always an extraordi- nary band, and this year's line-up looks particularly extraodinary. But what's most extraordinary of all is that the GG-CJB is about to tour the States. The locales are New York (Oct. 8 & 9), Atlanta (Oct. 10), Houston (Oct. 11), L.A. (Oct. 14), Fort Worth (Oct. 15-1 7), San Francis- co (Oct. 18) and Chicago (Oct. 20), and the band members are Sheila Jordan, Sharon Freeman, Marvin Stamm, Kenny Wheeler, Enrico Rava, Manfred Schoof, Franco Ambrosetti, Tom Varner, Ray Anderson, Art Baron, Dave Taylor, Howard Johnson, Lee Konitz, Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky, Joe Henderson, Larry Schneider, Mike Richmond, Bob Moses and, naturalmente, Gruntz. SMOKIN'- With Kool out of the jazz picture, the question has been asked: What cigarette company is going to take up the slack? Well, Benson & Hedges has jumped right into the jazz game (make that the jazz fusion game) by sponsor- ing "Benson & Hedges Command Performance," a 50-city tour, un- derway this week, by MCA's Larry Carlton and the Yellowjackets. Brings to mind the time at the Kool Jazz Festival/New York when Ira Sullivan dedicated a song to the sponsors: "You Leave Me Breath- less." WHYFRET? -Kevin Eubanks (r) smiles for the camera in the company of George Benson, co-producer (with Onaje Allan Gumbs) of Eubanks' upcoming GRP album "The Heat of Heat." WBGO NOTES - WBGO-FM, Newark's all-jazz station (read: New York's all-jazz station) has been awarded $312,000 by the New Jersey State Council on the Arts. Hear, hear!. ..To spread a little of that change around, the station is spon- soring an art competition to select artwork to use as the basis of a new promotional campaign, with a thousand bucks slated for the win- nner (and lots or prestige, of course). Entries must be submitted on 35mm slides and be accom- panied by the entry form and 20 bucks. To obtain a brochure and entry blank, call 'BGO at (201) 624- 8880. ..And the WBGO semi-annual Jazz Record Fair will stuff New York's Penta Hotel with all sorts of albums and whatnot (50 dealers are signed-up to participate) Septem- ber 20 from 10 am-6 pm. SWINGTIME - Jack Klein- singer's "Highlights In Jazz" series is a New York City stalwart: For 15 years it's been dishing up nice little swing and bebop jam sessions, and this year will be no exception. Tick- ets are a mere nine bucks a pop, all the concerts take place at NYU's Loeb Student Center, and the first four concerts of this season look something like this: "Rags, Stomps & Strides," with Sammy Price, Doc Cheatham, Judy Carmichael, the Harlem Blues & Jazz Band, Howard Johnson, Terry Waldo and Jan Rosemond (Oct. 1), "Birdland Revisited," with Billy Taylor, Roy Haynes, Jackie Paris and Candido (Nov. 5), "Jazz Singers/Song- writers," with Oscar Brown Jr. and Dave Frishberg (Dec. 10), and "Stars of Swing," with Panama Francis & the Savoy Sultans, Bucky Pizzarelli, Sol Yaged, Marty Napoleon and Jack Lesberg (Jan. 14). A call to (21 2) 998-4999 gets fur- ther details. NEWS Macola/Teldec Supports West German Pilot LOS ANGELES-The young West German flyer, Mathias Rust, who landed his small Cessna aircraft in Moscow's Red Square, and later put on trial and sentenced to four years in a Soviet labor camp, will receive special recognition on Tuesday and Wednesday, Sept. 15-16, at El Privado. All pilots in attendance those nights as a show of support for 19- year old Rust will receive a free copy of the newly-released Macola/Teldec Records single, "Fly To Moscow," which celebrates his historic penetra- tion of Soviet air space. The event was announced jointly by Don MacMillan, Macola presi- dent, and Bernice and George Altschul, managers of El Privado, who said they want to help keep world attention on the situation. 'The young man has now been in a KGB prison, Lefortovo, for over two months," MacMillan noted. "We are hoping our modest show of support will help inspire others and remind the Russian court that several years is a terribly long sentence for what was little more than a youthful prank." Rust's illegal penetration of Soviet air space earlier in the year led to the sudden retirement of the country's defense minister and the firing of the chief of air defenses by Soviet leader Mikhail S. Gorbachev. Rust sub- sequently was hailed back home as a folk hero. "Fly To Moscow" featuring the group Modern Trouble, memorial- izes the event. It is already a chart hit in Germany and other countries in Europe, where it was released by Tel- dec. The younger Zappa possesses excep- tional musical ability, and demonstrates such on this, his first effort. The adventurous Ryko label recently picked up the rights to release the compact disc version of last year's LP. Produced by dad Frank and Bob Stone and recorded utilizing full-digital technology, "Havin' A Bad Day" is a perfect high-tech showcase for Zappa's talent. Dweezil obtains lead vocal duties throughout most of the LP (best on "Blond Hair, Brown Nose," "I Feel Like I Wanna Cry" and the title cut), with sister Moon taking center on "You Can't Ruin Me" and the MTV video hit "Let's Talk About It." Comedian Bobcat Goldthwait cameo's on the hilarious "I Want A Yacht." Zappa delivers his best performances on powerhouse instrumentals "Electric Hoedown" and "The Pirate Song." Keep an open ear, big things are gonna come. REM Document - IRS (IRSD-42059) - Producers: Scott Litt-REM Fifth studio album from Athens, Georgia's REM is a pleasing fol- low-up to last year's breakthrough (and certified gold) "Lifes Rich Pageant." Meticulously co- produced by REM and Scott Litt, "Document" unveils a harder- edge, yet still somewhat commer- cial sound for the band. Released simultaneously with the LP - the compact disc delivers superb sound, very clean with brimming clarity and no apparent tape hiss. With the exception of "Strange," all songs included were penned by REM (Bill Berry, Peter Buck, Mike Mills and Michael Stipe). Best tracks include "It's The End Of The World As We Know It (And I Feel Fine)," "Welcome To The Occupation" and "Disturbance At The Heron House." The first single released, 'The One I Love," should obtain REM their first full taste of Top 40 success. Continued grow- ing attention and exposure should gamer this outfit a larger follow- ing, eventual arena-rock status (ala U2) is not implausible. POINTS V IVA, VIVA, VIVA... - Yes, readers. Points West has a story to tell this week. Last Friday night (September 11), Latin rocker/love God Em- manuel played the Circus Maximus at Caesar's Palace in Las Vegas. I know what you're saying - why, oh why are you telling us this? But wait. Points West was on the scene. Those terrific folks at Norman Winters Public Relations decided, for some warped reason they won't divulge, to fly your loyal correspon- dent to Vegas for the night to catch the show, so off I went. The airport scene was hectic and twisted, but we made the flight, and the limo ride on the Strip was a kick. Checking in at Caesar's was a nightmare, but the phrase "we're with Emmanuel" seemed to fool the desk clerk, so a room was made available. After dining with Emmanuel's family, we caught the gig, and let me tell ya, this guy is amazing... He's so big in Latin America that Julio takes his calls, and now I can see why. Decked head-to-toe in cop- per lame, he is a rivetingly charis- matic and physical performer with tremendous stage presence. There's no denying his sexuality onstage, but there are enough mo- ments of boyish charm stippled in amongst the ardor to please the male contingent as well. His first English LP will be recorded next year, and it is sure to establish him as a major American artist. His com- mand of our language is improving daily, and his English singing voice sounds strong and supple with enough of a quirky accent to work in his favor. EMMANUEL - He wants your sex... and he'll get it. After the exciting show, we cock- tailed upstairs in the man's suite, hobnobbing with the upper crust of Mexican TV, on hand to shoot a four-hour special on Emmanuel for Televisia. Bumped into Raul Velasco (the Mexican Johnny Carson, dontcha know?), who was hosting the special, and since my post-show babblings sounded like those of a trained mind, the Televisia people decided they wanted Velasco to in- terview yours truly the next morn- ing. So, unshaven and T-shirted, al- beit with sportcoat covering, the in- terview was conducted Saturday a.m.. Barring any cutting room floor mishaps, the special, with brain- dead critic's meanderings intact, will re - soon in 40 Latin American countries and on 520 U.S. stations. WEST Many thanks go to Parvene Michaels and Guy McCain of Nor- man Winters for extending the in- vitation, and to our intrepid guide/interpreter Luis Vega for running the show at Caesar's. Rob Yardumian COVER STORY Barry White By Murdoch McBride LOS ANGELES - "You can't kick Barry White's ass any harder that it's been kicked," explains the man who pioneered disco, rap, the 12-inch single, and almost started a major in- dependent label before his funding fell through. "You can't make me bit- ter. I didn't come to Hollywood to re- invent the wheel; the wheel's already been invented. But you can try and become a very valuable spoke in the wheel - if you've got positive power going for you." Coming off a four-year hiatus with a dynamic debut on A&M, White's The Right Night, signals a positive return for "the Maestro," a man who has earned substantial acclaim as a songwriter, producer, and arranger. By his own count, Barry White's 14 year recording career has produced 103 gold albums, 38 platinum al- bums, 20 gold singles, and 10 platinum singles, with total worldwide sales approaching 100 million units. Barry White's hits have always been distinctive, sensual statements on a singular, recurring theme — love. Thanks to the deep, biding resonance on his signature vocals, "I've Got So Much To Give," "Never, Never Gonna Give You Up," "Can't Get Enough Of Your Love," and "You're the First, the Last, My Everyth- ing/'have become some of the most memorable, popular dance releases from the seventies. "Even though a creator loves the work that he's doing," White says, "the consumer has the last word. Do they like it? Do they like it enough to buy it? Do they like it enough to just want to hear it? There are lots of levels of like, and to hear about people liking The Right Night is very nice." Assuming Barry White still has the magic touch, what is the secret be- hind this consumate ladies' man? "Everybody makes love," Barry BARRY WHITE explains, "I don't care what language you say it in, people know what going to bed means, what marriage means, all of it. So I have a common denominator that everybody relates to. 1 just put myself in the story, and I deal with it the way Barry White would do it, which is different than normal men." His artistic, emotional focus aside, Barry White admits that he has gone around the track more than once | since his last album. "I tried to go independent," Barry says, "1 tried to accumulate joint ven- ture capital and got very, very close, ; but the Texas oil business wiped our people out. So, it was back to produc- J tion - right where I started from. It's still about love, and that's the mes- sage I will constantly bring this world, as long as I feel there's a need for it. "You've gotta realize that this is not Barry White's first time around. This is my second go around. You look at the Rolling Stones' Mick Jagger. i Mick Jagger has been at the forefront for many years, even though there have been times when we didn't have j records from Mick. But when he comes back, he comes back banging. It's always been my philosohpy — since I was 16 — that it doesn't really matter when an artist comes back — if he's great — it's what he comes back with." TALENT ON STAGE |h’ rank Sinatra CARNEGIE HALL, N.Y.C. - Frank Sinatra, on the cusp of his 72nd birthday, is still one great singer. But there's only one way to really know this - you've got to go out and hear him. Not an easy thing to do (you've got to stand on line for hours, you've got to shell out 50 bucks a ticket, stuff like that). Forget the odd TV ap- pearance where the voice (formerly The Voice) cracks and groans. Forget the last album or two. You've got to go hear him. So, anyway, I went to hear Frank Sinatra on opening night of his eight- night engagement at Carnegie Hall and, no surprise to these ears, he sounded great most of the time. He didn't sound great all of the time - in fact, he came out sort of wheezy and uncertain, doing "My Heart Stood Still" rather than some punch-ya-in- the-gut Sinatra opener, sneaking peeks at a prompter set centerstage. Once he settled in, though, about midway through "Where or When" (the second number), he hit those notes, and tore at heartstrings and, oh, did his Frank Sinatra thing - that voice sounding like experience, like life. But, like at any Frank Sinatra con- cert, there were a bunch of songs I'd rather not have heard. He was in a Richard Rodgers mood, and 1 loved the Rodgers & Hart songs, and the Rodgers & Hammerstein songs. "I Have Dreamed" was gorgeous and dreamy, the "Soliloquy" from Carousel was a tour de force of dramatic singing, "Bewitched" was socked out with both fists flying. THE BEAT G old city formed- Chris Jasper of Isley Brothers and Isley-Jasper- Isley fame recently an- nounced the formation of his own label Gold City Records. Chris was born in Cincinnati, Ohio and has been a resident of the New York area since 1969. He attended Julliard School Of Music in New York City and received a bachelor of fine arts in music composition from C.W. Post while completing graduate work. He formed a trio in 1967 with the two younger members of the Isley family (Marvin and Ernie Isley) until the three joined the older Isley Brothers in 1969. He wrote ap- proximately 45 of the Isley Brothers songs during his career with them, including For The Love Of You (covered by Whitney Houston on her latest lp). The Pride, Live It Up, Don't Say Goodnight and Between The Sheets all of which were #1 singles. He was mainly responsible for the instrumentation and arrange- ment of all the Isley Brothers material, including all keyboard per- formances. In 1984, he split from the Isley Brothers and reformed his original trio (Isley-Jasper-Isley) with Marvin and Ernie. He has been responsible for writing most of the songs, in- strumentation, arrangement, keyboard performances and most lead vocals. He wrote and performed Caravan Of Love the group's (I-J-I's) first #1 single, which was covered by the British group The HouseMartins and hit #1 on the British charts, estab- lishing it as a worldwide hit. The group's latest album Different Drummer (was mostly written and performed by Chris) including the current hit single Givin' You Back The Love and the forthcoming single Brother To Brother, which is gaining a lot of attention for its powerful mes- sage of love and unity targeted towards the continuing travesty of apartheid in South Africa. Chris spoke very enthusiastically about his solo album on newly formed Gold City Records dis- tributed by CBS, entitled SuperBad, a project sure to establish him as a top producer, composer and artist in the recording industry. By the way Chris is looking for new talent for his label. Send tapes to Gold City Records, P.O Box 24, Armonk, New York, 10504. Congratulations and best wishes to a real gentleman and the consummate professional. MASSEY RETURNS-One of the founding members of the legendary O'Jay's is back. Bobby Massey presi- dent of Devaki Records who scored with 6 records that reached top 30 chart status or better between 1979- 1982 can be found in Las Vegas. Bobby is in town to record and produce a project on Lou Ragland, (one time manager of The O'Jay's) president of Casino Records. We will keep a close eye on this talented duo, because something major is about to happen. Will they merge their com- panies or will they colloborate on what is destined to be a winning situation? The greatest jazz composer of them all, by a very long shot, Ellington was also one of the most prolific artists of his time. One can compare him with Pablo Picasso in terms of the variety of his work, the originality of his work, and the sheer volume of his work. From the time he first started writing, as a teenager, until his death in 1974, Duke Ellington turned out a staggering amount of music. Much of this music has been heard, but a good deal of it - what Ellington referred to as his "stockpile" - hasn't. Ellington composed a lot, and he composed specifically for the players in his band (whose loyalty to their maestro is awe-inspiring). So when a piece was done - a piece, say, writ- ten with Johnny Hodges' alto specifically in mind - Ellington wanted to hear the piece. His band was on salary, so he spent a lot of time rehearsing them. He also spent a lot of time recording them - booking studio time here and there for no other reason than to get his material down. Was he thinking about the future - about the pos- sible value of this material in later years? Quite possibly he was. In any case, Mercer Ellington, Duke's son and the keeper of the flame, has tons of this stuff around (he's given lots of it to Danish radio) and now it's starting to come out. LMR Records (that's LeFrak, Fuhrman, Moelis) has just issued five Ellington compact discs of pre- viously-unissued material under the banner "The Private Collec- tion." Most of it, not surprisingly, is terrific -terrific! The discs are "Volume One. Studio Sessions, Chicago, 1956," "Volume Two. Dance Concerts, California, 1958," "Volume Three. Studio Sessions, New York, 1962," "Volume Four. Studio Sessions, New York, 1963," and "Volume Five. The Suites, New York, 1968 & 1970." The titles might be stuffy, but the music is wonder- ful. Excellent writing (imagine, all of this great writing, most of it never before heard) and magnificent play- ing by, amongst others, Hodges, Cootie Williams, Paul Gonsalves and Ray Nance. The sound quality is exemplary, the running times are generous (over 70 minutes on Volumes Two and Five) and the liner notes - by official Ellington an- notator Stanley Dance - are in- cisive and informed. Duke Ellington is listed as producer of all of this music, the ex- ecutive producers are Mercer El- lington, Mel Fuhrman and Stanley Dance, and Harry Hirsch produced the music for CD release. LMR Records is at 40 W. 57th St., New York, NY 10019 (212-586-3600). There is, they tell me, much more of this to come (with vinyl and cassette releases planned for the future). For Ellington lovers, for jazz lovers, for anybody interested in American music, this is an extraordinarily rich lode. KEYNOTE CDS, CONT. - Poly- Gram has just issued the second five sets in "The Essential Keynote Collection," the CD version of most of "The Complete Keynote Collection" boxed-set of LPs. They are "The Complete Coleman Hawkins" (a four-disc set collecting all the Keynote sessions featuring the great Hawkins and absolutely, positively an essential addition to any jazz CD collection), 'The Com- plete Benny Carter," "Red Norvo Improvisations," "The Keynoters with Nat King Cole," and "The Small Herd," the last two featuring different small-group sessions, the latter, of course, focused on Woody Herman bandmembers. It's funny how much of this brilliant stuff was out-of-print a couple of years ago and now, in two fell swoops, is available on vinyl and CD. And I remember somebody asking me recently - very recently - "you think they'll ever put any good Lester Young on CD?" Oh how digital we've all become. While we're talking about our friends at PolyGram, the next two months will see 20 new titles added to the mid-price Walkman Jazz/Compact Jazz series. October 19 will see ten of them released (Benny Goodman, Louis Armstrong, Mel Torme, others), with another ten (Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker, Ben Webster, others) due November 16. They're all compilations (a "Best of Bossa Nova" sounds particularly good to me) and they'll all chime in at about an hour each. SOUNDS & VISIONS CD SPOTLIGHT THE LONG RYDERS Two Fisted Tales - Island (90594- 2) - Producer: Ed Stasium Remember when rock and roll was fun? The Long Ryders do... and demonstrate such on their latest Island release 'Two Fisted Tales." 'Two Fisted Tales" has the distinction of being the Long Ryders' first compact disc release. The project is a exceptional analog recording complimented by digital mixing and mastering, providing an exceptional outing in technical- ly precise rock and roll with a punch. Best tracks include "I Want You Bad," "Man Of Misery," "Har- riet Tubman's Gonna Carry Me Home" and the recent AOR hit "Gunslinger Man." Guest spots on the disc include Los Lobos' David Hidalgo providing accordion ac- companiment on 'The Light Gets In The Way" and Bangles' Debbi and Vicki Peterson contribute backing vocals on the aforemen- tioned "I Want You Bad." Check this one out, you'll be pleasantly surprised! Hopefully Island will issue the Ryders' "State Of Our Union" on compact disc next... stay tuned! GEORGIA KELLY Seapeace - Global Pacific (WK 40724) - Producers: Georgia Kelly Georgia Kelly has just released her first recording for the Global Pacific label, a gorgeous excursion into musical bliss entitled "Seapeace." Four lengthy tracks make up the dreamlike "Seapeace," each radiates a chill- ing beauty all its own - painting a story for the mind. The song selec- tion is as follows: Clocking in at 11 minutes long is the opening "Nilapadma (Blue Lotus)"; the lilt- ing title cut follows, etching a precise landscape of musical tran- quility; next is the haunting "Aeolian Temple Music"; the final cut, the majestic "Chinese Sunrise" showcases the amazing compos- ing abilities of Georgia Kelly best - it's power and beauty shine super- bly. The analog recording was digi- tally mixed and mastered with careful and concentrated precision. "Seapeace" should introduce the talented Ms. Kelly to a wider audience... Rob Yardumian Donna Summer By Rob Yardumian LOS ANGELES - Donna Summer, the quintessential diva of the disco era, has returned to the world of vinyl with the scintillating grooves of All Systems Go (Geffen Records). But it's not what you think... Far from the cooing, moaning, grinding blitz of "Love To Love You, Baby" (num- ber 3 in early 1976) or the dramatic histrionics of "Mac Arthur Park" (number 1 in late 1978), this effort is more ma- ture, more emo- tionally secure than her earlier works. The initial single, "Dinner With Gershwin," penned and co- produced by Brenda Russell, is a picturesque, enthralling tale of longing that is not precisely sexual, evoking sophisti- cated images and emotions that mir- ror Summer's new-look reflection: I want to have dinner with Gershwinf I want to watch Rembrandt sketch/ I want to talk theory with Curie/ Impossible 1 guess/ I want to get next to you. her 'come on and try me, come on' so she's feeling all this stuff going on in- side her and she yet can't do it. So there are these voices crying out to her, and those lyrics I think are the best on the album. Musically, it's not a commercial song, but the message on the song is what it's about." These deeper, more reflective cuts seem to echo the well-publicized changes in her per- sonal life. "I've always regretted to some extent having started off the way I started off," Sum- mer admitted. "I don't regret it be- cause it was the in- roads to my career, but I regret it be- cause I've always had to try to erase it. I would have preferred to start off with a song like 'MacArthur Park' and have a hit record." Her rather public conversion to Christianity threw many of her fans, but her gospel roots have paid off well, with Grammy nominations for "I Believe In Jesus" (from I980's The Wanderer) and "Forgive Me" (from I984's Cats Without Claws, her last LP) coming in the Best Inspirational Song category. There are many other highlights on All Systems Go, especially the poig- nant intimacy of "Thinkin' Bout My Baby," Summer's favorite track, and the desolate inspiration of "Voices Cryin' Out." On the latter track. Sum- mer commented, " 'Voices Cryin' Out' is my socially critical song on the album. I started out writing it about people who are hungry, and then it ended up also being about kids my daughter's age. She's 14 now, and so she's almost as old as I am in her mind, and all these things that are yet to come in her life are screaming at "When you base yourself on your looks and on your sexuality, even- tually it wears thin. Thankfully, I changed my course after about the second or third album. If I shake my tailfeather, and five months later, someone else comes along with a big- ger, prettier tailfeather, you're going to be looking at them, and I just wanted people to know that there was more to me than that." With the release of All Systems Go, Donna Summer has proved that all over again.
