NEW FACES TO WATCH Julie Brown By Tom De Savia LOS ANGELES - Trying to describe the music of Julie Brown is like trying to explain (oh, let's see...) the mysteries of the Sphinx and the pyramids ...it just ain't easy! Many may be familiar with Julie Brown via her 1983 release "Homecoming Queen's Got A Gun" which instantly achieved impressive cult status. The success of that single led to an album recorded for the ad- venturous Rhino label. Goddess In Progress, (which, interestingly enough, became the label's biggest seller at that point). Most recently. Brown has signed with Sire records, who have just released her debut LP for the label Trapped In The Body OfA White Girl. Her current single and video of the same title are also creat- ing quite a stir around the nation. In addition to her recorded projects, filming has just been com- pleted on a major movie that Brown co-wrote and co-starred in "Earth Girls Are Easy" - based on a song of Brown's included on the Rhino LP. The film, directed by Julian Temple and starring Jeff Goldblum is due in theatres this spring. Brown is quick- ly rising to the public's attention in a frantic way. "I got a record deal on Sire and the movie deal at the same time." Brown stated during a recent interview with Cash Box. She continued, "It took me a while to get my album together, it took a long time to get the movie together, and I never intended for them both to be happening at the same time... it got real schizophrenic." She is quick to state that all the hard work is really paying off, and she feels nothing was in vein. On record, he vocal style ranges from a Betty Boop meets the Shangri- las stance on her more humorous cuts - to that of a genuine pop songstress on the LP's more straight ahead tunes. For the first time on vinyl, we are introduced to Julie Brown - the pop vocalist. With the Sire LP, Brown has dispelled the no- tion that she is solely a novelty act. In- Julie Brown eluded on the album are such top- notch pop gems as "Time Slips Away" and "Inside Every Girl." Brown explained "I really wanted to [record those songs], and I hope people accept it. People ask me 'why aren't you doing all funny stuff?' But I don't feel like that's the only thing I am, or the only thing that I'd like to do in life or put out there... To me, a lot of what I'm doing is like modem musical comedy. In that musical comedy has funny stuff, theatrical stuff and serious stuff. That's in a way how I perceive myself." "I get discouraged when people say 'oh, she's a novelty.' I don't think I'm a novelty... enough people like what I do that if you just sort of have faith in it eventually people will catch on to what you're doing - I feel it's very legitimate." Brown stated that although the rigors of working on the film proved trying at times, the results are ul- timately rewarding. She explained, 'The thing that's really fun to me is that with this movie I got to combine everything that I really love to do, and that is real exceptional. I got to sing and act and write and create original material. That, to me, is the most unbelievable high, it's in- credible." (continued on page 35) Top," the folksy gravel of "Jersey Girl," the gregarious growl of "In- nocent When You Dream." Tousled hair, a couple of concert changes, the band looking seedy but cute, fake seedy, Broadway seedy. The songs - especially the songs from those last three splendid albums, not "some of the old ones" (though that interlude seems to connect with a good portion of the audience, comfortable with Waits at the piano, rasping the songs they know) - are brilliant, a kaleido- scope of images and sounds that, 30 or 40 or 50 years ago, would have known no home but Broadway. The characters are real, the situations are real, the lyrics are poetic, and the music - here's the kicker - the music is sublime. Songs that you can go home humming. Not poems with music, none of this bogus beatnick bull, but songs. "Blind Love," "More Than Rain," "Walking Spanish," a magnificent version of "Rain Dogs," real songs. Songs woven into a well- detailed 100-minutes, songs turned into a Broadway show. But, of course, this was not a Broadway show. This was a Tom Waits concert which landed on Broadway for a week and then drizzled on to other spots. Still, the setting was becoming to the music. The music was becom- ing to the setting. I had a good time. I think Tom Waits - with his optigon and megaphone and baritone hornist and accordion player in a fez - is on to something. Lee Jeske SHng S TING - When Sting was about to begin his "Bring on the Night" tour a couple of years ago, he debuted his band during a three night stint at the Ritz. About to embark on his second 'round-the-world solo tour. Sting last week again introduced his new ensemble in a relatively small Manhattan venue. The spot was the Palladium and the occasion was the lOth anniversary of the founding of the New England Digital Corpora- tion (the m^ers of the Synclavier, which features so prominently in Sting's music). 2,500 invitees were on hand. The band, and the music, sounded great. I, for one, liked the sound that Sting's "Bring on the Night" band had -- sort of Weather Report meets the Police -- and I was a bit sorry when he indicated that it was a one- time thing, sort of, "Well, this jazz thing is good for now, but I can't see living with it." I think Sting is a talented songwriter in a classic idiom (he writes intelligent lyrics and stick-in-your-brain melodies, something that Stevie Wonder and very few others are able to do these days) and I think the band trans- lated those songs very nicely. So I was quite pleased when on to the stage of the Palladium came Bran- ford Marsalis and Kenny Kirkland. Sting, it seems, knew what a good thing he had. The band is a little different now - it's bigger and broader. There's a guitarist, a percussionist (Mino Cinelu), an extra keyboardist (Del- mar Brown), just about the best young jazz drummer going (Mar- vin "Smitty^' Smith), a new bassist, Branford, Kenny and, I guess, back- ground singers, though their presence on this night was strictly through the Synclavier. In fact, the Synclavier allows for a bigness and broadness all its own, something that is a bit scary to contemplate (Branford's first solo was per- formed without Branford, it had been programmed into the machine. "Why carry a band at all?" is a frightening question, but one that I think is going to be asked a lot in the near future). The 80-minute set presented most of the new album. "English- man In New York," "They Dance Alone," "Sister Moon," "Rock Steady," "The Lazarus Heart," "Be Still My Beating Heart," Jimi Hendrix's "Little Wing," etc., everything sounded fine. The band, although Sting kept pointing out that they were "only together for three days," was tight and loose, a combination that is attempted for in jazz, but rarely in rock. It's funny, but when Sting's last tour hit Radio City Music Hall, the group didn't sound as loose and relaxed as they had at the Ritz, something I men- tioned to Kenny Kirkland right after that concert, and something which he said, "Somebody else just said." I wonder if the freewheelingness will hold through this tour. In any case. Sting and his band cooked at the Palladium, and 1 think "...Noth- ing Like the Sun" is a fine piece ot work. Mercedes Sosa MERCEDES SOSA - 1 like a lo^ of different kinds of music from a lo of different places - Brazilian pof music, reggae, JuJu, Indian classica music, cajun music, tango - but ' had never in any of my travel: heard Mercedes Sosa. "You musi go hear Mercedes Sosa at Camegit Hall," said a friend whose musica taste I trust. —"But I like too man) kinds of music as it is," I said. "Gc see her," said my friend. I went to see her. Mercedes Sos£ is a hero in her native Argentina anc there was a palpable buzz in the hal - she represents the spirit of libera- tion in ^uth America and the spirii was on 57th Street on this evening. A short, square woman with In- dian features, though no Indiar blood, Sosa sang a selection of foil songs (from a variety of composers including Milton Nascimento and Cuba's Silvio Rodriquez). Seated center stage - she'd occasionally rise for a crowd-rousing dance - and accompanied by a three-piece band, she sang in a rich, affecting, folkish voice and, as can many greal singers (Edith Piaf, Joao Gilberto, Joseph Shabalala, Pandit Pran Nath), she conveyed passion and power without having a single word understood (by me that is - most of the audience understood everything). Earthy and authentic, singing completely unpretentious music in a direct, moving manner, Mercedes Sosa lifted Carnegie Hall, In the program notes, Mercedes Sosa says something that, very simply, explains why the forces ol freedom and liberation will always - whether it takes a month or a thousand years - win out. "My childhood was very poor," she says. 'The only thing that saved my family from misery was its togetherness." The togetherness at Carnegie Hall could be tasted. Lee Jeske

His particular talent conveys this love with a unique fi- nesse and flair. Born in South- hampton, Long Island, Pettus began teaching himself to play rbing piano and intensely absorbing gospel music. It wasn't until his teen years that he really listened to pop sounds with Marvin Gaye being a particular favorite. But gospel was his chief love, and he pursued it as a member of various groups. Developing a relatinoship with the New York office of Chappell Music, Pettus began to redirect his energies into pop sounds. First as a staff writer with Chappell, then as a writer/session player with H&L Records, he began to taste a measure of success. At H&L, he wrote tunes for the Soft Tones, played keyboards with the late Van McCi [cCoy and scored a dance club hit with Sandy Mercer's cover of You Are My Love. From there he moved on to performing live in the mid- west with the Satisfactions, front- ing the group in clubs for some three years. ^'All of these things were good learning experiences," Pettus recalls. "I developed my craft as a writer and singer in a serious ww." Relocating to Minneapolis in the early 80's, Pettus soon gained recognition on the local scene. He sang on local television programs and released a single. Working On My Strategy. One thing lead to another and armed with the right backing, he got a tape to MCA Records. It took time for all of the tracks included on his ip to come together, but the care ana attention to detail more than paid off. IS Giorge Pettus From the opening track (and first single) My Night For Love onward, Pettus is in command of his vocal gifts throughout. His approach h seductively romantic, often recall- ing the classic pop balladeers of the past. Can You Wait, You're Perfect and Make It Right all have this warmly intimate feel. He brings his assured touch to the Ip's upbeat tracks as well. Tm Good For You, One Track Mind and I Can Fix-U- Up have a natural verve and urgen- cy, while retaining the singer's sophistication. Helping Pettus make the most of his gitts are a number of top flight producers. La La, Kashif, David Z, Chuck Gentry and Louil Silas Jr. "Each producer gave me a different • •• tnr quality while stul locking into my style," says Pettus. "They all had something special to contribute. The idea was to have my vocals stay identifiable and tie it all together.' Giorge Pettus is an eclectic album, but the artist stays clearly in focus. Though this is his first album, Pettus brings considerable exper- tise and years of development to his 'abe' major label debut. A star on the rise, Minneapolis based vocalist Giorge Pettus is graced with a quality rare in contemporary music, a true sense of style combined with an easy elegance of passion in his ability to deliver a song. His polished way •R&E with modern pop/R&B is captured in his self titled album on MCA Records. JAZZ ON JAZZ CASH BOX JAZZ ALBUMS HERBIE'S (JOHN) HANCOCK -Herbie Mann (1) pens his new contract with the Moss Music Group's RBI label, as Moss Music Group president Ira L. Moss (c) and RBI general manager Rick Bleiweiss look on. B opping around Heard lots of talk at the JazzTimes Convention - most of it familiar talk. The turn-out was large and the mood seemed upbeat, though the Con- vention, in its sixth year, needs some new life, some new ap- proaches to the old problems. Maybe next year's planned move to L.A.'ll give the Convention some zest and bring out some new faces. ..Hackensack, New Jersey's The Special Music Company has signed an agreement with Milt Gabler, the legendary jazz producer, for LP, cassette and CD reissues of Gabler's historic, and very important. Commodore catalogue, featuring some of the best of Billie Holiday, Lester Young, Coleman Hawkins, and so many others. The first items are due in December, with CDs to carry an $11.98 list price and LPs and cas- settes to be tagged at $5.98. "We are delighted to be able to release this historic material in all configura- tions," says Special Music general manager Richard Greener, "and we intend to fully adhere to Milt Gabler's original quality stand- ards." "One of the finest jazz catalogues of the 40s has now been enhanced by the brilliant digital sound of the 80s," says Gabler...Henry Threadgill and Fred Hopkins, sometimes known collectively as Air, are angry as can be over the use of ThreadgilTs "Apricots On Their Wings" on Cas- sandra Wilson's excellent new JMT album, "Days Aweigh." See, Cas- sandra sang the song on Air's "Air Show #1" (Black Saint), but Threadgill says she stole his arran- gement for her own album. Taking Brian Llewyellen's advice, they're planning on taking the matter to coirrt.. .Delos is about to issue a CD by Cedar Walton and has signed up a project by Dwike Mitchell, WiUy Ruff and Dizzy Gillespie.. .Epic, so the rumor goes, is about to go heavy into the jazz thing, with David Murray, Ornette Coleman, and others rumored as signees...Tony Bennett's new album, "Ben- nett/Berlin," features guest shots by Dexter Gordon, George Benson and Gillespie. ..Anita Baker, a modern diva, fell by the Blue Note to catch Sarah Vaughan, a diva for the ages, and the two of them were said to have chatted about a col- laboration.. .Hey, what's going on here? New albums released on the same week by Joao Gilberto and Antonio Carlos Jobim? Sounds like 1962 all over again, and sounds like a good week for bossa nova fans like myself. In fact, Brazilian music in general seems to be in the air, what with Sarah Vaughan's "Brazilian Romance" on the charts, Caetano Veloso's excellent new Verve album in the stores, and Rykodisc, those people who happi- - ly scroimge aroimd looking for in- teresting and neglected items to put on CD, having just released Charlie Rouse's "Cinnamon Flower" album, a Brazilian project original- ly out on Douglas. I point everybody in the direction of Avery Fisher H^l, November 23, where Jobim, Gal Costa, Oscar Castro- Neves and Carlos Barbosa-Lima will be collaborating in what should be a seductive evening of music...Jazz West Coast is the name of a new tome by Robert Gordon ($19.95, Quartet). ..Roy Ayers has just launched a U.S. tour in support of his 'T'm The One (For Your Love Tonight" album (Columbia)...Tenor saxophonist Loren Schoenberg will perform a free concert at Cooper Union, October 30, and trumpeter Frank Gordon will do the same November 13. ..Heavenly Jazz, the jazz series at New York's Church of the Heavenly Rest, will offer Dave McKenna on November 8 and a tribute to Dick Wellstood with Dick Hyman, Kenny Davem and other friends and colleagues of the late stride pianist, December 6...Neioport Jazz '87, featuring per- formances by Branford Marsahs, Michael Brecker, Kenny G and Nancy Wilson, will air over PBS at the end of November.. .Vocal veteran Barbara Lea is making her long-overdue L.A. debut at Perino's Oak Room Bar, where she'll be through November 7...The two Ber- lin Jazz Festivals will take place the first weekend in November. The of- ficial one will have the Ornette Coleman Quartet and other big- gies. The other one, the Total Music Meeting, will have Curtis Clark, Butch Morris and other smal- lies...Joe Pass has re-signed a long- term exclusive agreement with Pablo Records, for whom he has al- ready recorded some - gulp -three dozen albums...Donald Byrd, who hasn't recorded in quite some time, has just signed a deal with Landmark...Red Rodney tells me that, although the original script for Clint Eastwood's The Charhe Parker Story -which started filming last week - was filled with factual errors, the new script is fine, a good representation of Bird. Red should know, but we shall see. They're using old recordings of Bird, rather than recreations, and that should help right there. NEWS BIRD BRAINS - After a recent LA. performance, the Fabulous Thunderbirds were greeted friends from all walks of life, including many EIP/A execs. Here, smiling a little smile, are r) Larry Douglas, E/PIA vp, marketing, west coast; Kim Wilson; Stephen Stills; Fran Chr tina; Jean Johnson, E/P/A local promotion manager; Jimmie Vaughan, Chuck Leavell, Dem Quaid, and Preston Hubbard. Long Ryders (From page 5) their most recent release (and second for Island), Two Fisted Tales. Prior to signing with Island, The Ryders released two independent projects: 10-5-60, their impressive debut EP was recorded for the PVC label; and Native Sons, released in the states on Frontier records, firmly established the band as songwriters and musicians to be reckoned with. Then- next project. State Of Our Union, the first recorded for Island, delivered near perfection for the band in both sound and style. With the release of the aforementioned Two Fisted Tales, The Long Ryders have affirmed to the public that they are here to stay. The band is currently putting together demos for an upcoming third Island LP. Although the band has yet to find acceptance by the masses. Island has showed tremendous support for The Long Ryders. Griffin explained "Is- land records is not the kind of label that breathes down your neck and says 'do this' and 'do that.' They have been real good to us, they will let you grow. They have a history of stand- ing by people..." Audiences overseas have wel- comed the fresh sound of the Ryders - both their albums and singles, as well as tours, have fared much better there than they have in the states. "Overseas we come real close to having hit records." Griffin ex- plained. He continued, "We've had several singles overseas that just graced the Top 40." Recently the band suffered the L of longtime member - bass player and vocalist Tom Stevens. Stevens amicably departed the ranks during the bands recent tour of the states to pursue a career fronting a new band. A frantic search for a replacement took place leaving the band in a bit of a lurch. Finally, bass player Larry Chatman, a friend of Griffin's, joined the Ryders. Griffin emphasized the importance of Chatman's hook-up with the band, "Larry learned [the songs] in no time flat and we went out and we were fine. He walked on stage with a band that he never walked on stage with, or rehearsed with - he never rehearsed with us. He went on the road with us and learned while driving across the country and in motel rooms at night. We never had a formal rehearsal. If it wasn't for Larry Chatman I think the band TOPS IN THE SOUTH - Miami based MCA salesman Joe Bucklew was recently presented with an award for “MCA Sales Rep of the YearISoutheast Region." Pictured left to right are: MCA's Barry Yarbrough, field sales manager; Bucklew and Carl Michelakos, regional branch manager/Southwest Region. would have had to cancel a very im- portant tour and it would have hurt us." The Long Ryders have constantly been recognized for their politically and socially conscious lyrics. Griffin insisted that the band does not sit around trying to come up with topi- cal material to incorporate into then- music. He explained, "...as you drive around the country you see in- credible things. And it seems evil to turn away from those things or drive around the world and not write about them. Especially when everyone else and his brother is more or less writing about romance. It seemed that some of these subjects were so colossal in scope that some- one should sing about them, and maybe getting people thinking about them and on the road to solving these problems." The Long Ryders have frequently been sight^ for their depictions of reality in their lyrics, as well as their political or socially conscious state- ments. The Long Ryders though, by any means, are not a poor-man's Bruce Springsteen or John Cougar Mellencamp - such songs as "State Of My Union," 'Trairie Fire" and "I Had A Dream" tell of life and bring awareness to overlooked issues without preaching or coming off as pretentious in any way. I know this has been said many times before, but for posterities sake I'll say it again: If the Long Ryders are ever accepted by the mainstream, just exposed a little bit to these audiences, watch out. Or as Griffin himself put it, "I believe that one day word of mouth will take over and then we'll start our own little brush fire that will then carry on into sales." He concluded "...I'm pleased with where the band is. The last tour we did was our best tour ever and we sounded the best." Brown (From page id Her interest in filmwork has car- ried over to her recorded projects. She has conceptualized the clips for "Homecoming Queen" and 'Trapped In The Body Of A White Girl," the later which she also co- directed. She explained the impor- tance of her involvement in her own music videos, "I always think theatri- cally... I wouldn't like turning over the whole project to some video director - because that's one of the things that I love to do." Brown's plans include a mini-tour in the near future with hopes of put- ting a regular touring band together and hitting the road. Also in the wings are ideas for other film scripts - and hopes to direct feature films lie in her aspirations. For the time being, however. Brown is quite happy and satisfied with her career thus far. "[Where I am now] is exactly where I wanted to be from the beginning. I'm achieving exactly the things that I wanted to do. I want to do more of this and get better and better at it." Competing on Friday is the first part of the Metal Marathon. "Metal has always been rock's most aggres- sive and rebellious music," say CMJ president Robert Haber and vice president Joanne Abbot Green. "It's the music parents hate and kids love, and it's the music that sells records, and sells out arenas regardless of radio's fickle love-hate relationship with it. Like it or not, heavy metal and hard rock are here to stay, and CMJ seeks to appreciate the serious artistic, cultural and financial forces they are." Set for the Metal Marathon are panels addressing such issues as "Metal & Radio: Hell in Your Home," "Image vs. Substance: Is It the Look or the Lick?," "Hard Rock Artist Development & Marketing: Forging Scrap Metal Into Platinum," "Sheet Metal: The Role of Media in Breaking Hard Rock Artists," "Metal Cros- sover: New Breed or Hip Hype," and a Hard Rock Artist Panel. NEWS tXtCUTlVtS ON THE MOVE Ramone, Bachrach Spotlight L.A.S.S. Songwriters Expo LOS ANGELES - A thousand songwriters attended the 11th An- nual Songwriters Expo in Pasadena October 24 and 25. The Expo, produced by the BMI-sponsored Los Angeles Songwriters Showcase, fea- tured a line-up of industry speakers including Phil Ramone, Burt Bachrach, Robbie Nevil, Cynthia Weil and Barry Mann. Ramone, who has produced projects for Billy Joel, Paul Mc- Cartney, and Kenny Loggins among others, kicked off the affair with a keynote speech, and then headed a well-attended afternoon master ses- sion on record producing. Bachrach, composer of such famous songs as "Do You Know The Way To San Jose?" and "Raindrops Keep Falling On My Head" taught a master class on melody writing. Other well-received classes in- cluded Nevil's "How I Thought It Would Be And How It Really Is," detailing his rise from songwriter to recording star; a master songwriting class by veterans Weil and Mann; and for producers. Jay Graydon and Michael Omartian headed the Hit Producers Panel, Jerry Knight and Aaron Zigman discussed turning demos into songs, and Jeff "Skunk" Baxter taught a class on unconven- tional recording techniques. For television and film scorers, Steve Dorff taught TV theme melody writing, and Doreen Ringer led a panel on film music. A bonus for the attending songwriters was the "US Sprint THEY WRITE THE SONGS - Songwriters and industry folk gathered recently in Pasadena for Songwriters Expo '87. T hat Petrol Emotion THE ROXY, HOLLYWOOD = That Petrol Emotion already has a strong local following judging from the sar- dine-packed to capacity crowd at the Roxy on Wednesday, C)ctober 21 . The band had been highly touted by the local media for days preceeding the show, helping to generate further ex- citement. This was not, however, a stock audience all in the same age or cultural bracket. The band would have their work cut out for them trying to appease every listener. During the first three numbers, "Split," "Belly Bugs" and "It's a Good Thing" the flavor of the now British quintet was being estab- lished. They were a strange blend of the spirit of the 60's communal feel- ing, the energy of the punk/new wave movement of the late 70' s, the politically purposeful music of the 80's, and even implied a multi-meld o' styles for the 90's. "Chester Burnette"was a moving ballad that further showed that this is not just a groove oriented band, but one with real heart. It was the first of several sensitive yet gritty tunes during the set. Guitarist Sean and brother Demian O'Neil (on bass), Reamann O'Gorman (guitar), and drummer Ciaran Mclaughlin are all originally from Northern Ireland. Lead Vocalist Steve Mack is actually from Seattle and they all currently make their residence in London. After their cur- rent tour, which culminates at The Ritz in New York, the band heads directly back to England to begin working on an upcoming LP for Vir- gin Records. That Petrol Emotion has previously released two albums,- Manic Pop Thrill on Demon Records and the Polydor release of Babble. As the show continued to unfold, a couple of noteable highlights were "Big Decision," their most commer- cially successful dance club single, "Genius Move," their newest 12" single, and a powerful version of Neil Young's "Cinnamon Girl." It was sometimes hard to pin down all of Petrol's influences as they men- tioned artists from Howling Wolf to Kurt Vonnegut during the set, and even dedicated a tune to our own Nancy Reagan (with a healthy shovel of sarcasm). Although That Petrol Emotion has some rough edges, perhaps most re- lated to maintaining sound quality in their more up-tempo numbers, their act makes you think, feel, and wanna' dance. Not too many bands on the contemporary circuit could boast all three. With another hit single and a strong response from the upcoming album on Virgin, That Petrol Emotion might have all the fuel they need to become a resound- ing commercial success. M uhal Richard Abrams CARLOS 1, N.Y.C. - Muhal Richard Abrams, highly influential as the guiding force behind Chicago's important Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians, is somewhat underrecog- nized as a pianist, composer and bandleader. Part of this is due to the uncategorizability of his music = it doesn't have a strong identity of its own but is a kaleidoscopic synthesis of numerous styles. During a late set mid-week in a six- night stint at New York's petite Car- los 1, Abrams and his quintet shifted gears tune by tune. From a misty bal- lad, to a knotty avant-garde piece, to a couple of Monk tunes, to a deep- fried Chicago blues, Abrams and company offered intelligent, pas- sionate music. Despite a small turn-out (the com- bination of cold weather and the World Series has been known to keep jazz clubs barren), the quintet played with force and spirit. Heard to par- ticularly good advantage were saxophonist John Purcell and trum- peter Stanton Davis. With Muhal laying out during most of the horn solos, Purcell and Davis took different paths. Davis played pretty, using a mute to good advantage, playing feathery, touch- ing solos on the flugelhorn. Purcell played hard, slashing with air with his tenor saxophone, boiling over with gruff, roof-raising. Sonny Rol- linsish forays. Abrams' solos, like his writing, took on different colors for each tune - distilling bits of such seemingly strange pianistic bedfellows as Otis Spann, Cecil Taylor, Thelonious Monk and Willie "The Lion" Smith. Drummer Reggie Nicholson and bassist Lindsey Horner, comfortably riding the flow of Abrams' pieces and supporting each soloist differently according to their needs, contributed to a well-rounded and deeply-satis- fying set of music. Rob Yardumian She was on the road for 30 days prior to the Country Music Associa- tion Awards Show, where she won the coveted Horizon Award. She ar- rived in Nashville at 5:30 a.m. the day before the awards. She had to spend time in rehearsals for the show and being fitted for her wardrobe. She had to perform for the show, and when it was all over. Holly Dimn was very happy and completely ex- hausted. Holly Dunn is in the vanguard of the new coimtry music female acts. And, much like Randy Travis, her career has sky-rocketed to amazing heights in the past two years. How does it happen? How does Holly react to all the glitter, glamour, hard work, and expectations? It happened because Holly Dunn is a sincere, intellegent, dedicated young lady. She is totally involved in the direction of her career. She has an insight into the music business, which very few artists can equal, be- cause she has gained an educational background through her involve- ment. She arrived in Nash'V'ille in 1982, and progressed through self- confident and wise decisions. She was the second member of the family to relocate from San Antonio, Texas to Nashville. Her brother, Chris, was already writing some hit songs for noteable acts when Holly graduated from Abilene Christian University. Holly had visited Chris, in Nashville, while she was still in college. Two weeks after her gradua- tion, she packed the car and headed for Music City. Chris gave Holly good advice and led her through some of the lessons the music industry teaches. Holly Dunn did it the way it should be done. She began writing with Chris and other talented songwriters. She signed as a writer/receptionist with April Blackwood Music. About that. Holly says, "At first, I resented the receptionist position. But, now, I realize that I learned a lot about the inner-workings of the business from that job." Holly started getting a lot of work as a demo and backgroimd singer. LOS ANGELES - North Carolina native Don Dixon has a problem that would turn many of his peers green with envy. See, he's too busy. As a successful producer, he is constantly besieged with offers from friends, as- sociates, and strangers to 'help us with our record.' And as a singer /guitarist/ songwriter, he is currently riding the wave of his And, all this time, she was meeting a lot of important and influential people, not the least of whom was Tommy West, her current MTM Records producer. When Tommy secured that position, he signed Holly to the MTM label. Holly says, "It was a big break for me. The label was new, and I had to prove myself to them. Now, however, I have the chance to be involved in all areas of my career because I was able to gain their confidence. Being totally in- volved in my career is very impor- tant to me." So, Holly Dunn did learn from the route she followed through the music industry maze. Obviously, there is something more which helped make Holly Dunn a star... her exceptional talents! I say talents be- cause Holly is not only a fine record- ing artist, she is a super songwriter, a producer, and a business agent, as well. That's a synopsis ofhow it hap- pened for Holly. Now, how does she react to her success? I'll let her tell you... 'Tommy West saw a lot of good in me, and he told me to follow my heart when it came to my music. He told me to dig down deep and dis- cover who Holly Dunn really is. Then, to write songs that were, and are, true to myself. I'm just a singer and a writer. I go out there and do what I do. It has been my goal to es- tablish myself as both. I feel like I'm much the same as I've always been. I kind of take it as it comes. If I see progress, then, that's okay. I guess I'm just that way. If it happens for me, it happens. And, if it should not happen, I really haven't lost a thing." It has happened in a big way for Holly. She shares her success with those who love her: her family, her friends and fans, and those who work behind the scenes for her at MTM Music. Holly Dunn sings and writes from the heart, and she is sing- ing and writing her way into the hearts of millions of coimtry fans, in- cluding me. "That title has a few different meanings," explains Steve, whose career as a successful recording artist began in 1978 with his sHnt as a member of the popular R&B band. Slave. "This album is full of powerful music, real aggresive jams. Like every- thing Tve ever done, it reflects my com- mitment for my music to be honest and real" V\^th Jampacked, Steve continues a musical odyssey he says began with his 1984 album Dancin' In The Key Of Life which combined his deeply felt sriritual beliefs with a strong desire to make potent (xtntemporary music. The new album also represents Steve's reunion with Slave's producer Jimmy Douglas, with whom he co-produced the project. "We've both matured musically and in our production skills. It has been great working with Jimmy again and what we've created is definitely new music which deals with the issues of the day." Steve Arrington's musical journey started in Dayton, Ohio when he showed an obvious preference for play- ing drums; by age eight, he was sitting in with his brother's group. The Soul Agents, playing bongos. Arrington's musical tastes began to expand during his adolescent years. He listened to every type of music from Jimi Hendrix to Theolonius Monk. A career in music seemed inevitable and Steve worked with a number of bands in Ohio and California, honing his skills by playing everything from Pop to Broadway, Latin music to Polkas and Jazz to R&B. STEVE ARRINGTON After a brief period in Berkeley, California playing with the duo of Pete and Sheila Escovedo (later known as Sheila E) in the late 70's, Steve was look- ing at what was next in his career when he received a call from one of the bands he'd known in Dayton. The results was his link with Atlantic recording artists Slave. After three albums with the group Steve was ready for the next step in his career. In 1982 he formed Steve Arrington's Haill Of Fame, joined by three other former members of Slave. Following two highly successful al- bums, Steve set out on his own, record- ing two highly acclaimed albums Dancin' In The Key Of Life and The Jammin' National Anthem. Steve signed with Manhattan Records in 1986 and began working on Jampacked immediately. The album represents a new phase in his musical evolution. Heavy funk tracks like Let It Loose or the strongly rock-oriented I Just Wanna Be With You typify the powerhouse music Arrington has put together to launch this stage of his il- lustrious career. The rock and rap Kelly 16-33 is all about the streets. Jampacked is a high-powered collec- tion of rock and soul funk with a mes- sage, representing the talents of Steve Arrington at his musical best. "Whether iti s Stone Love, (current single) a state- ment about keeping a love relationship together in spite of any outside pres- sures, or the imconditional love I speak of in What I Do For You, there is an im- derlying theme throughout the record; that love, be it personal, universal or romantic, perserveres. My music's aU about telling the truth, being straight ahead with what's happening in the world today." This writer would like to thank Steve for a most refreshing inter- view and commend him on the lyrically powerful Jampacked album. I will close by (juoting an awesome line from one of his songs, think about this, "WHAT I DO FOR YOU, DOES NOT DEPEND ON WHAT YOU DO FOR ME! SOUNDS & VISIONS CD SPOTLIGHT ROBBIE ROBERTSON Robbie Robertson - Geffen (9 24160-2) - Producers: Daniel Lanois-Robbie Robertson Geffen has just released the solo debut outing from Robbie Robertson - and it's a stunner! Robertson left the ranks of The Band a few years back, the group 3f which he was a key member for years. On the self-titled outing, Robertson is joined by an array of top-quality musicians; U2 (Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen, Jr.), The BoDeans, Peter Gabriel, Maria McKee (of Lone Justice), Tony Levin and Ivan Neville among them. Each track is exceptional, offering standout per- formances by Robertson & Co., ex- ceptionally noteworthy are "American Roulette," "Sweet Fire Of Love," "Showdown At Big Sky," "Testimony" and "Broken Arrow." The analog recording transfers brilliantly to this compact disc formation. Painstakingly produced by Daniel Lanois and Robertson, Robbie Robertson should instantly attract both critical ac- claim and commercial success. Recorded live at the Copacabaoa. New York City. SAM COOKE Sam Cooke At The Copa - Abkeo (CD 2970) - Producer: Al Schmitt Abkeo, the adventurous label responsible for reissuing many of the Rolling Stones early works on compact disc, have just issued the classic Sam Cooke At The Copa. Recorded live in 1964 at New York's fabled Copacabana, Sam Cooke At The Copa features the legendary soul singer at his best. The transfer of the original analog recording to state-of-the-art digit^ sound is amazing, delivering a crystal clear product. Included on the disc are an array of timeless classics performed with the inten- sity that only Sam Cooke could deliver. Among the highlights: 'The Best Things In Life Are Free," 'Twistin' The Night Away," the beautiful "When I Fall In Love," and a blistering medley featuring readings of 'Try A Little Tender- ness," "(I Love You) For Sentimen- tal Reasons," and Cooke's #1 hit of 1957, "You Send Me." Sam Cooke At The Copa is deserving of any music lover's immediate attention. Listen for yourself... NEW FACES TO WATCH The Royal Court of China "Basically, when the band got together we had four very strong- willed, ambitious guys who just wanted to get out there and play music and do it their way. As far as goals, that was it. Of course - as I would imagine most bands do - we want to be as enormously wealthy and fabulously popular as we can be. But we want to do it on our terms. That's how I would sum up our game plan - we just want to get as far as we can as quickly as we can, our way." The Royal Court of China, accord- ing to bassist/mandolinist/spokes- man Robert Logue, wants to have it all. How can this be? A yuppie rock band from Nashville with the name The Royal Court of China (the same name, not coincidentally, as their new A & M album)? Can they really have it all? "So far, we've been able to do it our way," says Logue. "We produced the album, we did the album cover, we did the video, and all the music is ours. So far, so good." Let's backtrack a second. How did this come to be? 'The band will be two years old in December," says Logue. "Oscar Rice (guitarist) and I have been best friends since high school. After high school, I went off to college for about a year-and-a-half. Then I came back. C^car and I ran into Chris Mekow (drummer, vocalist) playing drums with a band in an arcade outside of Nashville. It was like a top 40 band, and he was just walking all over them. So we hooked up with him - we played with him for several months - and then after that he started playing in a band that Joe Blanton (lead vocalist, guitarist) was in. And that band ran its course for about a year, and then they sort of disintegrated. Then the four of us THE ROYAL COURT OF CHINA - (L-R) Robert Logue, Oscar Rice, Joe Blanton, and Chris Mekow. got together." Simple as that. They put an inde- pendent EP out in the summer of '86, five or six months later they were signed, and now - a year after that - 'The Royal Court of China" is on the streets. Now make no mistake about it - though there are coimtryish elements running throughout the album, this is a guitar-bas^ rock band. A guitar- based rock band from Nashville. "Nashville is known for country music, because that's been the dominant thing there for years," says Logue, "but, I can say honestly, that, as far as good rock bands goes, Nash- ville is one of the top unrrecognized places in the country. There are just some really good bands down there that are waiting to be discovered." And where, then, does the Royal Court of China fit in? "We're really eclectic," says Robert Logue. "Probably, of the bands in Nashville, we're the most eclectic that I've seen. Uh, I don't really know where we fit. We listen to a whole lot of different kinds of music, and it all sort of seeps into what we do." Lee Jeske Having become known for his un- mistakeable electric guitar sound, Carlton's new LP is entirely acoustic. Why the transition? 'The story is really very simple. Jimmy Bowen had an idea for a label (MCA Nash- ville) where certain artists would I make an album with complete liber- ty to do what ever they wanted to. In fact, he was encoraging me to do something completely different. He said 'Make an album of all mandolin music!' So I wanted to do something I had never done before. I had never I done an all acoustic album, so I decided to give it a shot." I Carlton's pla5nng is very spare, j eluant, and well stated throughout 1 Discovery, an approach he may have 1 gleaned from one of his mentors, ; John Coltrane. "On Coltrane's Ballads album, all he does is play the melody, , and it's beautiful. It was a great les- I son for me in how to phrase a melody and make real music out of it." "Minute by Minute," "Hello Tomor- row," and "My Home Away From Home" are memorable examples of this talent on the Discovery album. Having developed a long list of devoted fans from his electric days, and having attracted many new fans with his acoustic material, it seemed as though satisfying every fan during his live performance might be a problem. Following the Yellow Jack- ets on stage during their recent tour, Carlton found a very creative and captivating solution. The show opened with three of his well known electric numbers, "Don't Give it Up," "Strikes Twice," and "10 P.M." to grab the attention of the audience. Then an acoustic segment followed, featuring "Smiles and Smiles to Go," "Minute by Minute," "Hello Tomor- row," and a stirring ballad, "Song for Katie/The Lord's Prayer," dedicated to his Mom at The Universal Am- (continued on page 10) I EAST COASTINGS T wentieth street FREEZE OUT - How nice for EMI-Manhattan Records that a big-wig like Russell Simmons wanted to see their Friday, October 30 showcase at New York's nightspot Limelight. The Red Hot Chili Peppers were headlining a rap-rocking CM] Music Marathon bill that included Cabaret Voltaire and Big Mouth. Two bad for the bands that tne Run-DMC manager/producer couldn't get a foot in the door. Neither could a passel of fans and CMJ participants whose CMJ ID badges - $95 student rate, $175 regular humans - were supposed to gain them automatic entry into all CMJ Music Marathon shows across town. "No jeans. No sneakers," they were told by the doorman. Never mind that a dress code wasn't mentioned in the CMJ list- ing, or on the invites EMI-Manhattan had included in CMJ regstration pack- ets, or on the invites EMI-Manhattan had sent out to rock critics (like me). "Qub policy." Not that club policy kept a bunch of middle class schmoes wearing jeans (gray, black, and blue) and sneakers (black, red, and white) from entering, no problem. For folks in the civilized world where clubs don't pull this kind of crap, limelight has a tradi- tional N.Y.C. 'selective door policy,' which pretty much means if they don't Like the way you look, you don't get in, and no amount of cash will pay your ad- mission. A chic nightspot doesn't want a bimch a single men, especially those who affect the low-life scum look of your average rock fanatic, standing aroimd the bar because thaFd give the place the look of a low-life sctam pick-up pint. When the doorman was con- fronted with his obvious and obnoxious double standard (which was especially weird since it wasn't like the folks he was letting in would give the place that cer- tain moneyed look of boho elegance or anything) he explained, "May^ some people have more priority. Maybe they're with the band." Which, of course, is the sort of thing he knows just at a glance. It's not class warfare that's the issue here (not many of the low-life scum rock fans seemed to be actually lower dass); iFs not even something like record company mismanagement (EMI- Manhattan says it wasn't their decision to have the gig at Limelight, CMJ scheduled it); breech of contract jumps to mind, but the blame can't be pinned on CMJ itself. David Marguliez, who was responsible for bringmg a wide range or excellent bands into town for the Music Marathon, says "EMI-Man- hattan wanted to throw a party and Limelight was very willing and able to accomodate someming that large." He was surprised to hear, Monday after- noon, that invited guests were barred admission. "We might be more carefiil in selecting clubs to work with in the fu- ture. That's disgusting, and I don't want to work with a dub like that anymore." What's realN digusting are the racist overtones of the whole thing. A white guy wearing a festive Halloween down outfit (orange baggy pants, matching orange blouse, face painted orange, sneakers) strolled in, and believe me, ne looked like a hippy leftover, not real hip, not well groomed; Russell Simmons, a black guy dressed to the standards of B- Boy elegance (blue baggy sweats, sharpy- styled athletic jacket, sneakers I couldn't begin to afford), couldn't get near the door, even when his companion told the doorman he was a record-biz hotshot, and believe me, he looked well off. It may just be that Limelight doormen have a hard time overcoming their cul- tural boimdaries, and they can't recog- nize the standards of black street elegance. But the refusal to acknow- ledge the standards of another culhore as Intimate is equal to refusing to recog- nize the legitimacy of the culture itself. You draw your own conclusion, but I've already jumped to mine: if, say, a white guy showed up dressed to the standards of B-Boy elegance (tike the Pet Shop Boys were once wont to), he'd get in, no problem. Accusing a club like limelight of having a racist door policy is easy. Catching them is the hard part. Limelight was unavailable for comment. (SLIGHTLY) HAPPIER STUFF - It's not like any or all of the CMJ convention was as ugly as Limelight's door policy. Heck no, most of it was fun or funny. Fun was a Chris Stamey show at the Lone Star and a Russ Toleman show at CBGB. Stamey injected some of the soul his Southern upbringing should have provided into tunes from his recent It's Alright (A&M). The guy got off some an- gtolarly emotional guitar solos I would have sworn you couldn't have recreated out of the studio. Passionate stuff, in a bare, minimal pop context, and it sent me running back to the album. Russ Toleman charged through a set of guitar rock that soimded like Television at 45 rpm, which is an awful good thing to soimd like. Former member of True West, Toleman works the same drone- rock territory as Green On Red and Dream Syndicate, but live he added definition to those drones, packing them with all the hook-happy fervor of garage-band r&b thrashing. On record the reckless passion gets drowned in the drone, but there are standouts on Totem Poles and Glory Holes (Restless), that cap>- ture a crazed imdercurrent in American mythos, sort of On The Road as gothic horror. HEART OF GOLD - On his RCA debut album Buster Poindexter covers everything from soca (Arrow's "Hot Hot HoF') to soul (Chuck Jackson's "Are You Lonely For Me Baby") and still has room for yovrr basic assortment of screwy music: iazzbo, jump band, maudlin p>op ballads. Poindexter is a tuxedo clad lounge singer with a big voice and a lot of soul. He's been seen coast to coast on Saturday Night Live and as the picture of sartorial splendor in a bunch of Amaretto ads, but the ™y rarely leaves New York, probably be- cause he's really David Johansen's alter ego, and David lives on Staten Island. Johansen's had the Poindexter shtick going for three years now, acting the part of 'a real show person' with such obvious delight it overcomes the in- herent irony and camp. His Hve shows are the hottest regular gigs in New York, real entertainment: lots of tall tales told over a smoke and a drink; a crack band running down show times, r&b gems, cajim songs, soca, and soul; relentess mugging and stage business; and the thriB of that big voice expertly navigat- ing a hipster's/schlockster's repertoire. The Buster Poindexter album sounds great, so great it overcomes its obvious drawbacks (albums of oldies, like roots rock records, are basically a collection of redeved ideas, and this one carries the unholy ghost of Joe Jackson's Jumpin' Jive). The Banshees of Blue charge the songs head on, and there's crystal dear production, tasty horn parts, and the thrill of one the great rock 'n' roll voices. Johansen/Poindexter has a voice that can invest any song with a sense of com- plete charader, providing a depth of emotional experience that exceeds what's sketched out in lyrics and melody. He's also funny as hell. Joe Levy Cash Box November 14, 1987

Add a lot of versatility and a wide vocal range, and there's no toppir^ the rich sounds emanating from Glenn Jones, his new album on Jive Records. Glenn has co-written six of the nine songs (including the hit We've Only Just Begun on his new album, a fact he finds incredibly rewarding. "Each recording I've made I love as part of me and my artistiy," he said. *'Each song serves as its own in- spiration, affording me even more insight and depth into my music." A native of Jacksonville, Rorida, who now resides in Queens, New York, Glenn was four years old when heJoined the Bivens Special, a gospel family from his hometown, with whom he toured extensively. By 16, Glenn had joined Savoy Records, where he worked witn Savoy's resident gospel master, James Cleveland, taking to the na- tional gospel circuit, Glenn refined his robust baritone/tenor voice while sharing the st^e with some of the music greats: Tne Reverend Cleveland, Shirley Caesar, and The Mighty Clouds of Joy. Glenn admits that some of his friends thought he had sold out by turning to the pop mainstream but as he explains, H knew that the gospel stage wasn't enough for me, and getting positive messages across to a wider audience meant singing in the popular market. The truth is that I've never stopped sing- ing gospel. I sing in the chur(m often. What I've done by seeking a solo career as a popular singer is to extend myself." Chad YOUTHFUL TALENT-Singer / songwriter / producer Chad makes his solo recording debut on the RCA Records label with the very funky album. Fast Music, Love and Promises. Co-produced with songwriter / drummer Howard King, the LP is a sizzling collection of impassioned love songs punctuated by Chad's riveting gos^l-tinged vocal gymnastics. y music IS hardcore R&B," he admitted. "I grew up listening to Sly Stone, Jimi Hendrix, James Brown, Little Richard and Otis Redding. They were my earliest in- spirations ana that's the particular genre and direction I'm coming from with the times on Fast Music, Love And Promises." "There are no flamboyant gimmicks when I per- form," he confessed, 'T just get on st^e and sweat." Bom and raised in new York City, Chad has lived all over the country and has been performing since he was a teen ager, due to his father's musical influences and solo career at CBS Records. Chad studied at New York's Music and Art High School but explained, "the real deal was hanging out with my father and Sly Stone at the studio. That ex- perience brought me even closer to what it was I eventually wanted to do." Chad later attended Morehouse College, returned to the Big Apple and worked for Equi- table Life Insurance. It wasn't long before he realized that he was not cut out for the regimented cor- porate life of a computer program- mer. Currently riding high on the charts with the hit Luvs Passion and You, Chad also has a very clear understanding of the "business" side of the music industry and will not be left high and dry when he does not have a hit! MIAMI'S SUNTOWN-The city of Miami comes to the forefront with another in the long line of hit making record companies. This time the creative genius is Ed Meriweather who serves as presi- dent of I Spy/Suntown Records. In- dustry veteran Lany Maxwell is a special consultant. The company is currently enjoy- ing a tremendous amoimt of suc- cess with a great remake of the Stevie Wonder hit Signed, Sealed, Delivered performed by Louise Freeman and Terry Blount. The song features some super produc- tion ala the Club Nouveau sound, and some marvelous vocals by Freeman & Blount. Other artist signed to the label are B.V.S.M.P. with their single I Need You and Prime Time with their single He's Def/So Damn Tuff, both are con- tinuing a strong upward sales pat- tern. Again, we say the musical direc- tion of the record business is and has been set by determined, strong independent labels like Suntownl! ON JAZZ ANTONIO CARLOS JOBIM Antonio Carlos Jobim J OBIM - did music because I love music. I love music. And when I started to be a musician, when I started to travel as a musician, people said, Ton'ro going to die of hunger, in the gutter, drunk. In the gutter.' Claus Ogerman and I thought we were going to finish on the ^wery, you Imow - I will play the guitar and he will play the accordion. At the end, when the world is off bossa nova." Antonio Carlos Jobim punctuates this with a laugh, a hearty belly laugh. In fact, Antonio Carlos Jobim - a man with a definite air of contentment - punctuates everything with a belly laugh. The world, of course, has never gotten off bossa nova. In fact - with Jobim's first album in years, 'Tassarim" (Verve), getting to the record stores at about the same time as Joao Gilberto's first album in years, "Live at Montreux" (Elektra- Musician) - it seems that bossa nova is experiencing something of a resurgence. "I have 600 songs," says Jobim. "And always, you write ^0 songs and you are known for one or two. Like if the traffic policeman is going to give me a ticket, I say, 'Listen, I wrote 'The Girl From Ipanema.'"" That, of course, is an under- statement. "Wave," "Corcovado," "No More Blues," "One Note Samba," "Dindi," "Desafinado," and on and on. Jobim has perhaps written more enduring standards than any songwriter of his genera- tion, something he acknowledges with a shrug and a hearty laugh. On 'Tassarim" there are several Jobim songs that stand up with the rest of his ouevre - notably the tricky and melodic "Chansong" and the lovely "Gabriela." There are also, surprisingly, several songs written by other composers, including his son Paolo's "Samba do Soho," and "Izabella," and an interesting bossa nova version of Gershwin's 'Tascinatin' Rhythm." 'T had to perform," he says, "but I'm singing better now. I'm singing better than I used to sing. I us^ to sing like a composer - Uke Johnny Mercer. Now Tm getting better - like the old wine, it gets better." When Antonio Carlos Jobim came to America, in the early '60s, he came, he says, with "delusions." "When I came to America, I thought the Americans were all blonde with blue eyes - all im- perialists and racists. Which was not true at all. And I had all sorts of problems. My English was very poor. And I had no say on the songs that were already published by Brazilian publishers, I couldn't have an opinion. They had all these crazy lyrics and what could I do? The Italians have a wonderful ex- pression; 'translators/traitors. 'Tf had the money, I would buy the works of Antonio Carlos Jobim. I would buy my own catalogue - the complete works of Jobim - from the publishers, I would like to own my own stuff. Not for money reasons, for artistic reasons - for the integrity of the songs. Look, I don't need any money. But I'd like to own my songs. See, popular music is something that's less serious - more ephemeral, more transient, more short-lived. So people take licenses. They take a leg here, they take an eye there, and then it loses its strength." An anecdote from the early days of bossa nova: Jobim is in his New York hotel room and Gerry Mul- ligan phones up from the lobby. "'Antonio, come with me.' I said, 'It's too cold, come up and we'll have some coffee together.' 'No, come down and put your overcoat on.' I put my overcoat on, we hopped in a cab, and 1 asked him, 'Where are we going?' He said, 'We're going to Mount Sinai Hospi- tal.' To do what?' To see some- body you worship. Cole Porter.' Cole Porter was an amputee and was dying. 'T said, 'Stop the car at the next block, 1 want to get drunk im- mediately' Gerry fcrew that I ad- mired him so much - 1 knew all his songs, I had two biographies - but 1 didn't want to see him dying. I would approach him and I would say, 'I love you, I love your songs.' It would have been pathetic. 'I love your songs.' And he would say. Thank you.' "So I never went - I got drunk. Because a myth should remain a myth. Many poets talked about that, you know: A myth should remain a myth. You don't have to touch it." Ce Ce WInans (Capitol ST 12573) 75 GIVE ME THE REASON 73 58 Luther Vandross (Epic FE 40415) THE BEAT T he BEST-Concert promoter John Ray, president of Turning Point Productions, Inc,, and his recently formed Magic City Records is a first class human being and businessman. Ray, for the past 12 years had promoted concerts basically in the southeast region of the coimtry. Turning Point (Ray) broke onto the national scene last year as the national promoter for Anita Baker's highly suc- cessful debut tour. John attributes the tour's success to the incredible talents of Anita as well as a loyal committment from she and her manager Sherwin Bash of BNB Associates. Anita broke through in 1986 with her multi- platinum selUng album Rapture. Of course, John had a tremendous amoimt of belief in Ms. Baker's talents prior to the success of her album. Needless to say, many of his peers thought he was crazy to make an investment committ- ment in an unknown and unproven art- ist. Looking at the overwhelming suc- cess this combination has enjoyed, this reporter would say, "Theman has a mar- velous sense for talent." During his days as a regional promoter, John would constantly en- counter situations in various cities where he was Icxjked upon with great disdain, because some other promoters had made trips through those cdties without paying their biUs. That stigma wiU "never" be associated with John Ray of Turning Point Productions, "he pays his biUs." In fact, John has built such a great reputation around the country, he can secure facilities or artists with a mere phone call and the venue operators and artists know they will be paid regardless of the show's success. It seems that 1986 was a tum-around year for Ray with most of his promo- tions. He promoted Stevie Wonder in Lafayette, La., New Orleans, Albany, Ga, Mobile and Birmingham, AL. John says, "I probably had the most successful run of dates on Stevie in 1986. I also co- promoted Luther Vandross with Stage Right Productions in New Orleans, Montgomery and Birmingham, AL. He sold out in advance the 15 year old Bir- mingham Jefferson Civic Center Cohseum and became only one of five artists to ever do that. He attracted 18,629 people." Ray also played Lionel Richie in Biloxi, Birmingham, Atlanta and Baton Rouge. "1986 was my banner year," he proclaims. "It was my biggest year. I also picked up the Off-Broadway Musical, Mama, I Want To Sing, whicii has been very, very succesful." John is the nation- al promoter, Vi Higgersen and Klen Wydro are the producers. The per- manent company is at The Hecksher Theatre in New York, and John has promoted the road company since November with one or two week runs starting in Memphis. Then New Or- leans, Dallas, Washington, D.C., Cincin- nati, Houston, Qeveland, Miami, Bos- ton, Indianapolis and Los Angeles. Doris Troy, who used to record for the Beatles', Apple Records and earlier had a big hit with Just One Look in 1963, is the star of the show as well as Higgersen's sister. John has built such a credible reputa- tion aroimd the country as a first class concert promoter (who happens to be black) until he is now being offered ex- clusive rights to serve as national promoter for many of the top acts in the business. According to Sidney A. Seidenberg, manager of B.B. King and Gladys Knight & The Pips, "John Ray is a reliable promoter, who we have worked with in the past 10 years. I can recommend him to any artist with con- fidence." Bill Washington, president. Dimensions Unlimited, says "there should be more concert promoters Hke John Ray. He's honest, straight and very professional. He lends credibility to con- cert promotions in this country." John, who recently turned 42 has formed his own record label. Magic City Records and his own management com- pany, John Ray Associates. The initial signing to both label and management company is the Atlanta based Brick with all original members. Brick, the cornerstone of R&B and Funk with such hits as Dazz, Dusic, Ain't Gonna Hurt Nobody and We Don't Wanna Sit Down, We Wanna Get Down, (certified platinum) are back or( the music scene. The group composed of drummer Eddie Irons, guitarist Reggie Hargis, bassist/vocalist Ray Ransom and brass/reeds/vocalist Jimmy Brown is funkier than ever after a five year hiatus. Although Brick disppeared from the music scene, their platinum hit Dazz has been getting a lot of air play all over the coimtry, and of late. New York's rapster Dana Dane used the bass and drum lines from Dazz to hurl him into nation- al prominence. All of the recent energy around Dazz has prompted the group to re-release this devasting hit with more of a 1987 flavor, hitting home to the teen and dance crowd. During the recent debut of the record at Uptown Atlanta, the crowd response was nothing short of sensational. Brick is back and they will be bigger than ever! Other artists signed to the label are David Sea who not only has that "strong" black male image, but an absolutely sensational vocal style that win sky rocket him to the top. Other sig- nees are Ikie, Eric Von Isaac and Stan Granger. Ray said, "One of the reasons I wanted to start my own record com- pany, was to seek out and find good talent in the vast reservior of unsigned talent." To further enhance the success, (des- tined for Magic City Records) John has named J.C. Futrell as vice president. Futrell is a graduate of Shaw University with a degree in Radio-TV-Fihn. Prior to joining Turning Point Productions Inc., /Magic City Records, Futrell was president of Rockwell Futrell Produc- tions, Inc. of Atlanta, Georgia. (A multi- facet entertainment, marketing, promo- tions firm) J.C. has worked with numerous recording artist, most notable. The Fat Boys. In adition he has taught at colleges and managed several public radio sta- tions. He also found time to serve as audio engineer for such acts as Whodini, Joeski Love, UTFO, LA Dream Team, Fat Boys and The Latin Rascals. This vibrant young man's ad- ministrative, managerial, technical, sales and marketing skills are indeed part of the charisma behind Turning Point Productions and Magic City Records. This reporter wHl go on record and say, you can expect some marvelous things from Magic Qty Records under the direction of a first class human being and businessman John Ray, who gives all credit to God! Bob Long

ON JAZZ P SI LOVE YOU - PoIyGram Special Imports, the division that has been bring- ing in such important and innovative European labels as Black Saint/Soul Note, Owl, Sound Aspects, Minor Music and Red Records is more or less on its way to kaputville, due to manager Paul Del Campo's promotion to another part of the company. However, Poly- Gram Jazz, under the guidance of Richard Seidel, is going to pick up some of this product - specifically, they're going to be releasing items from the PSI labels on a selected basis, in addition to picking up some of PSPs other international ac- tivity. PSI, under Del Campo, has done a fantastic job of, as their saying goes, "Bringing America's Music Back Home." PASSING ON - Two talented jazz musicians died within a few days of each other recently and at- tention should be paid. Willis "Gatortail" Jackson, a rough-and- tumble, blues-based tenor saxophonist, died in New York after heart surgery at the age of 59. Jorge Dalto, a rollicking Argentinian pianist with a fiery latin-jazz style, died of cancer in New York at the age of 39. They were both lively presences on the New York scene, and they will both be sorely missed. A RARE BATCH OF SATCH » Queens College has recently estab- lished a Louis Armstrong Archive, as part of the school's Aaron Copland School of Music. Donated by the estate of Louis and Lucille Armstrong, the collection includes five trumpets, hundreds of personal tapes and discs, dozens of photograph albums, scrapbooks, correspondence, musical score, etc., etc. - in other words, a treasure trove material about the greatest jazz musician of them all. In addi- tion to all of this, the College has made an agreement with the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs to run the longtime Armstrong home in Corona, Queens as a museum. This is, as you don't need to be told, wonder- ful news. WORLD PACIFIC REDUX Beginning in January, Blue Note (ur, Manhattan), will turn its attentions to yet another historical jazz label with a hefty catalogue ~ World Pacific. Under the banner, "EMI- Manhattan Jazz Classics," the CD- only midline series will debut in January with reissues of material by, amongst others, Gil Evans, Gerry Mulligan, Lambert, Hendricks & Ross and Clifford Brown, and will continue in April with items from Evans, Mulligan, Jim Hall, Hoagy Carmichael and others. Yeah! BENEFICIALLY YOURS = Two big jazz benefits are coming up in New York in the next couple of weeks: "A Party for Zoot" - is a memorial bash (the second) to raise money for the Zoot Sims Scholar- ship Fund of the Jazz and Contem- porary Music Program at the New School. Urbie Green, Tommy Flanagan, Jim Hall and Scolt Hamilton are among the per- formers, November 22nd is the date, the New School (66 W. 12th St.) is the place, and (212) 741-8950 is the number to call for details. Then comes a concert at the Beacon Theatre, December 7th, to raise money for WBGO-FM's Capital Campaign. The concert, the kick- off of a Philip Morris Superband tour (annual events that go to the Far East and South Pacific), will fea- ture Ahmad Jamal, Kenny Burrell and The Superband All-Stars (James Moody, Clark Teny, Dee Dee Bridgewater, Jimmy McGriff, Grady Tate and George Mraz). GOOD TIME -Marian McPartland (cen- ter) celebrated the release of her book All In Good lime at a New York party in her honor attended by, among others, Sylvia Syms (left) and Margaret Whiting. SOUNDS & VISIONS CD SPOTLIGHT PAUL CARRACK One Good Reason - Chiysalis (VK 41578) - Producer. Chris- topher Neal Chrysalis records has just released the latest solo effort by the incredible (yes, incredible) Paul Carrack - and it is outstanding. Car- rack has long been one of the most talented, yet imfortunately over- looked, pop musicians aroimd. He has provided lead vocal duties on hit songs for such bands as Ace, Squeeze and Mike & The Mechanics. Each track is an im- deniable gem - with Carrack giving a soulful, passionate perfor- mance on each cut. The presumed full-digital recording gleams with sheer clarity. Best tracks include ''Button Off My Shirt," "Fire With Fire," "Collrane," "Give Me A Chance" and "Don't Shed A Tear." Don't miss the brilliant reworking of Jackie DeShannon's 1964 classic "When You Walk In The Room" and the Carrack/Nick Lowe com- position "Double It Up." One Good Reason has all the makings of a modem-classic album - listen, and enpy. The firm is Bon AMI Records, Inc. Robinson has helmed two previous record labels: All Platinum and Sugar Hill Records. Those companies were both, to quote The New York limes, among “the hot- test independent recording companies in the country." Sugar Hill, for example, landed half a dozen gold 12" singles, was responsible for the eight million selling Rapper's Delight (still the big- gest seUing 12" in industry history), and literally launched the genre of rap with The Sugar Hill Gang, Grandmaster Flash and The Furious Five. As a singer, Robinson has top ten pop chart hits to her credit including the early 70's hit Pillow Talk. As a songwriter, she penned classics like Shirley and Company's, Shame, Shame, Shame and Love Is Strange, the late 50's R&B smash which she sang as part of the duo Mickey And Sylvia. Love Is Strange has since been recorded by Paul McCartney and over a dozen other artists. The song appears in the original Mickey And Sylvia version of the soirndtrack album to Dirty Dancing. SYLVIA ROBINSON As a producer, Robinson has put together hits for artists ranging from Ike and Tina Turner, The Moments, Grandmaster Flash, The Furious Five and Grandmaster Melle Mel. In addi- tion, Sylvia Robinson has been a suc- cessful music publisher. Bon Ami Records officers include: Joey Robinson, Jr. (Sylvia's son and producer or co-producer of gold 12" hits for Grandmaster Flash, The Sugar Hill Gang and his own group. The West Street Mob) as chairman and ceo; Syl- via, vice chairman; Robert Jeffery Karpe president, comptroller and head of the pop division; Norman Gorden ex- ecutive vice president of the R&B division; David Gunthrope head of A&R; Darryl Greene, head of manage- ment; Leonard "Red" Forbes, vice presi- dent, sales marketing and promotion, Bernard "Spider" Harrison vice presi- dent, west coast operations Donna Jones, head of R&B promotion; Leland Robinson head of A&R for rap produc- tions; Dina Andrews manager interna- tional A&R and Miangelo Moore manager computer services. The first two releases, on the inde- pendently distributed Bon Ami Records, are Rock Me Baby by Sylvia Robinson and The Rhythm by The Great Peso. Welcome back to this lovely and most gifted lady. GENE'S DREAM-Music industry veteran Gene Burleson has realized his dream! This personable music industry professional wanted to take the many years of knowledge and practical ex- perience he had gained, and put things to work in developing a major inde- pendent record company. This dream is now a sensational reality as Points East Records introduces its roster of exciting artists to the american record buying public. Burleson in building this unique com- pany, brought in some of the best ad- minstrative talent available. Music in- dustry veteran Barbara Thomas serves as adminstrative assistant at Points East. Atlanta business woman Carolyn Bill- ingsly is secretary-treasurer. Willie Hunter handles press and publicity. The company is currently enjoying some great radio activity with Nate Evans' (former lead singer with The Im- pressions) debut single entitled Get In Touch With Me. This heart felt soulful ballad showcases the versatile and smooth vocal style and ability of Evans. Points East Records also distributes other independent labels. On Midtown Records is a bluesy rendition of the I960's soul hit Steal Away performed by Earnest Farmer. While these releases are busy heating up the airwaves aroimd the country. Points East is finishing preparations on more exciting music. Another soulful ballad is on the way through the vocal talents of Harvey | Scales entitled Are You Still In Love. In a very short time Points East is al- ready attracting attention from all ares of the music industry Company presi- dent Burleson is noving the company in the direction of becoming the next great success story in the music industry DAVIS AT K-98-Radio veteran Lee King ceo of Phoenix Broadcasting and general manager of K-98/KYEA-FM recently appointed Julian Davis to the position of operations manager. Davis, from Chicago, co-owner with King, is a veteran broadcaster and formerly King's music director of WOKJ in Jack- son, Mississippi. Davis is King's partner and stage manager for the concert promotion com- pany, Lee King Productions. King en- thusiastically added, "Julian has been my partner and best friend for over ten years, he is a team player and one of the hardest workers I've ever met." Julian brings a variety of talent to the New K-98, he worked for the Jackson, Mississippi based WJMI not long after it signed on the air. He has worked for various top forty stations, served as art- ist manager, advertising agent and has been a screen actor. King said, "this is a dream that we both shared and worked together to make reality." Davis indicated the sta- tion will target the 18-34 audience. Best wishes for much success to King, Davis and the staff of the New K-98. Bob Long 12 Cash Box November 28, 1987

ON JAZZ IRD IS THE WORD - This week Sony Video will release Celebrating Bird: The Triumph of Charlie Parker ($29.95), a one-hour documentary about the life and times of one ofthe most important jazz musicians of them all. The video is part of an un- usual three-way tie-in - last year. Beech Tree Books published a book by the same name, by Gary Gid- dins (co-director of the video), and there's a Columbia Records album due as well. Like the book, the video is a plain, straight-forward account of Parker's life, with the sensational aspects kept to a reasonable mini- mum. It isn't overly cluttered - due, in great part, to the fact that there are only a few minutes of film footage of Parker. The video, of course, makes use of these - a couple of minutes of silent film and the famous clip of Bird and Dizzy Gillespie playing "Hot House" on an early television program. The rest of it is, like most conven- tional documentaries of this sort, taken up by a spoken chronological narrative and by talking head inter- views with a reasonable selection of commentators; one of Parker's first bosses (Jay McShann), his partner in bebop (Gillespie), a Bird protege (Frank Morgan), a critic (Leonard Feather), and a pair of Parker's wives; his first (Rebecca Parker Davis), and his last (Chan Parker). There is nothing surprising here, and nothing, really, that hasn't been seen, heard or said before. And one thing that the video doesn't really do = and, frankly, something that no one-hour video can really be ex- pected to do - is give a full measure of Parker's genius, of the changes that he wrought in music. What it does “ and does quite well - is lay out the basic facts in a pleasing and attractive manner. Clint Eastwood, of course, is cur- rently working on a film biography of Charlie Parker. One senses that Celebrating Bird will stand as a wel- come slice - if only just a slice - of the real thing. BIG BATCHES - I've been trying to keep up with the influx of jazz product but, forget it, I can't. This, I assume, is a healthy sign. Anyway, here's a snatch of it: Sound Aspects (via PSI) has just issued four welcome avant-garde items: "Outerbridge Crossing," by the Gerry Hemingway Quintet (in- cluding Ray Anderson and Mark Helias); "Another Kind of Groove" by Kahil El'Zabar's The Ritual (Zabar, Billy Bang, Malachi Favors), "Deadline," by the prolific Steve Lacy and pianist Ulrich Giunpert; and "Nine Below Zero," by Wayne Horvitz, Butch Morris and Bobby Previte. Red Records (via PSI) has just is- sued four welcome post-bop items: "Sphere Live at Umbria Jazz," "Chet Baker at Capolinea," Steve Grossman's "Way Out East Vol. 2," and Cedar Walton's breezy, solo "Blues for Myself." Doctor Jazz has, typically, put out a mix of new albums, reissues from Bob Ihlele's many past labels, and Teresa Brewer records. "The Big Three," reissues wonderful sides from Ben Webster, Coleman Haw- kins and Lester Young; "Whatever Happened to Johnny Bothwell?," reissues tracks from a neglected Swing Era alto saxophonist; and Brewer with Svend Asmussen ("On the Good Ship Lollipop") and The World's Greatest Jazz Band ("Good News") offers what it ad- vertises. NEWPORT NEWS - Michael Breaker blows up a storm on Newport Jazz '87, airing Nov. 25 over most PBS stations. Branford Marsalis, Nancy Wilson and Kenny G are also featured. Leo Records, that important English label that, for the most part, documents the avant-garde sounds of Eastern Europe, serves up four unusual items: "A Night in East Berlin," by Sun Ra; "Don't As- sume," by Maggie Nichols and Pete Nu; "Better and Better," by Kenny Millions (an alter-ego of saxophonist Keshavan Maslak), and "Snapshot from the Island," new electronic music by Hungarian composer Hbor Szemzo. Atlantic has, quietly, uncorked a new set of CD reissues. They are "Backlash," Freddie Hubbard; "Joe Turner: Rhythm and Blues Years" (minus four tracks from the double-LP), "Gentle Giant," Yusef Lateef, "Zawinul," "Woody Her- man Live at Monterey," "European Encounter," Svend Asmus- sen/John Lewis; 'Thil Woods and the European Rhythm Machine at the Frankfurt Jazz Festival," "Blue Tattoo," Passport; "AU the Things We Are," Dave Brubeck (with An- thony Braxton and Lee Konitz); and "Songs of the Beatles," Sarah Vaughan. And the Fantasy people have come up with two welcome, pre- viously-unissued items: "The Ser- mon," a delightful 1958 album of spirituals from pianist Hampton Hawes, and "Jazzhouse," a 1969 live session by the Bill Evans Trio.
